- Seed deposition: sparse Zn-Car_MOF monolayer on ITO via electrophoretic deposition or electrostatic LbL. Quantify areal density by QCM (if available) or AFM counting/TEM plan-view; target: 5–20% surface coverage (explicitly sub-percolating).
- Sol–gel infiltration: Sn(IV) alkoxide route (preferred for lower chloride residue) with controlled hydrolysis (H2O:Sn = 2–4) and chelation (acetylacetone) to slow condensation; Bi precursor at 0/1/3 at% relative to Sn. Spin-coat to achieve 20–40 nm total ETL.
- Conversion: use the Phase 1 accepted chemistry window temperature/atmosphere (not pre-fixed at 150–200 °C).
2.2 Zn–O–Sn bonding quantification:
- XPS: look for systematic shifts/shoulders in Zn 2p and O 1s consistent with Zn–O–Sn environments vs Zn–O–Zn or Zn–carboxylate alone; acceptance: a reproducible bonded-component area fraction ≥15% of total Zn-associated oxygen signal (pre-registered threshold) in the infiltrated/converted composite.
- EXAFS (Zn K-edge; Sn K-edge if feasible) or total scattering/PDF:
  * Acceptance: Zn first-shell coordination consistent with Zn–O at distances compatible with mixed Zn–O–Sn environments; and evidence of Zn next-nearest neighbors consistent with Sn proximity (vs only Zn–Zn as in ZnO). Minimum: statistically significant increase in Zn–Sn scattering path amplitude vs MOF-only converted control.
2.3 Dipole/energetics correlation:
- UPS and/or KPFM mapping: quantify work-function shift (ΔWF) vs Bi–SnO2 control. Acceptance: ΔWF magnitude ≥80 meV (directionally consistent with improved electron extraction) and spatially uniform (KPFM RMS variation not increased by >20%).
Go/no-go #2 (Bonding + dipole): proceed to full device optimization only if Zn–O–Sn bonding fraction threshold is met and ΔWF ≥80 meV without worsening ETL conductivity gate.

Phase 3 — Hysteresis mechanism deconvolution (ionic vs electronic) (Weeks 18–34)
Goal: separate reduced ionic polarization from reduced recombination/trap filling using decisive protocols.
3.1 IMPS/IMVS (mandatory):
- Perform IMPS/IMVS under 1 sun equivalent at multiple biases near Voc and near MPP.
- Extract transport time constants (electron extraction) and recombination lifetimes; acceptance for “ionic polarization reduction” claim requires: (i) reduction in low-frequency phase features associated with slow processes, and (ii) improved IMPS transport without solely mirroring IMVS changes.
3.2 Temperature-dependent ionic activation energies:
- EIS from 0.1 Hz–1 MHz under illumination at several temperatures (e.g., 280–330 K). Fit low-frequency capacitance/ionic resistance to Arrhenius behavior.
- Acceptance: increased apparent ionic activation energy by ≥0.05–0.10 eV or reduced ionic capacitance by ≥30% at matched bias compared to Bi–SnO2 control, while recombination resistance trends are independently tracked.
3.3 Drift–diffusion modeling constrained by measured EIS + TPV/TPC:
- Pre-register two competing models: (A) reduced interfacial trap density only, (B) reduced ionic mobility/accumulation + trap reduction.
- Acceptance: only claim “ionic polarization reduction” if model (B) is required to reproduce simultaneous hysteresis index + low-frequency capacitance + IMPS/IMVS features.
Go/no-go #3 (Hysteresis causality): if hysteresis decreases without any reduction in ionic capacitance/activation-energy signatures and can be fully explained by recombination-only model (A), then re-scope claims to “electronic trap management” and adjust success criteria accordingly.

Phase 4 — Interfacial recombination pathway identification and SRV/trap metrics (Weeks 24–42)
Goal: make the recombination claim falsifiable (bulk vs interfacial SRH vs surface recombination velocity).
4.1 Trap distributions and interfacial states:
- Thermal admittance spectroscopy (TAS) on full devices (frequency/temperature) to extract energetic trap distribution; acceptance: reduction of ETL/perovskite-associated shallow/deep features by ≥30% integrated trap density vs Bi–SnO2.
- Complement with DLTS-like transient capacitance (where applicable) focusing on interfacial signatures.
4.2 Absolute PLQY vs injection + PL lifetime mapping:
- Measure absolute PLQY of perovskite on ETL stacks (no HTL) under calibrated carrier densities; fit non-radiative recombination components.
- Acceptance to support “Voc increase via reduced interfacial non-radiative loss”: ΔVoc,non-rad improvement ≥20 mV and consistent with PLQY increase at the same injection.
4.3 Interfacial SRV extraction (pre-registered):
- Use time-resolved PL with optical modeling (thickness, absorption) to extract effective SRV at ETL/perovskite interface.
- Acceptance: SRV reduced by ≥2× vs Bi–SnO2 control.
Go/no-go #4 (Recombination mechanism): if Voc improves without SRV/trap-density reduction signatures, do not attribute gains to interfacial passivation; instead reassess band alignment or bulk perovskite quality effects.

Phase 5 — Device build, controls, and optimization (Weeks 30–60)
5.1 Full device matrix (DoE maintained from original, but bounded by go/no-go windows):
- Variables: MOF coverage (5/10/20%), Bi (0/1/3 at%), conversion condition (selected 1–2 from Phase 1), thickness (20/30/40 nm).
- Responses: PCE, stabilized MPP, hysteresis index, Rs/Rsh, Voc, Jsc, FF, ΔVoc,non-rad, ionic capacitance, SRV.
5.2 Controls (mechanism isolation; unchanged but enforced with new metrics):
- Control A: Bi–SnO2 heterophase without MOF.
- Control B: SnO2 + MOF seeds without infiltration/conversion (explicit “insulating interlayer” test; must fail transport gate to validate risk awareness).
- Control C: SnO2 infiltrated/converted without Bi.
- Control D: inert nanoparticle seeds (SiO2) at matched coverage.
5.3 Stability qualification:
- MPP tracking 45–65 °C, 1 sun, 500–1000 h encapsulated; damp-heat screening (50% RH) for interface-driven degradation sensitivity.
- TOF-SIMS depth profiles after stress for iodide ingress; acceptance: ≥50% reduction in iodide signal within ETL vs Bi–SnO2.

Updated success criteria (now tied to decisive mechanistic gates)
S1 (chemistry): at least one conversion condition meets Go/no-go #1 and does not degrade ETL transport gate.
S2 (bonding/energetics): Zn–O–Sn bonded-component ≥15% + ΔWF ≥80 meV (Go/no-go #2).
S3 (hysteresis): hysteresis index <0.02 across scan rates/pre-bias AND ≥30% reduction in low-frequency ionic capacitance or ≥0.05–0.10 eV increase in ionic activation energy (Go/no-go #3).
S4 (recombination): SRV reduced ≥2× and/or TAS trap density reduced ≥30% with ΔVoc,non-rad improvement ≥20 mV (Go/no-go #4).
S5 (performance): Jsc +0.5 to 1.0 mA/cm2 and Voc +20–50 mV without FF loss >1% absolute; stabilized MPP improvement.
S6 (stability): T80 at MPP ≥2× vs Bi–SnO2 control and reduced iodide penetration into ETL by ≥50%.
Feasibility: 1) Chemistry feasibility is treated as an experimentally bounded question, not an assumption. The reviewer’s concern (150–200 °C may yield ill-defined organics/carbonates/ZnO-like phases) is directly addressed by a conversion matrix plus TGA–MS/FTIR, Raman, ssNMR (if available), and NAP/synchrotron XPS with quantitative acceptance thresholds (carbonate fraction, retained coordination signatures, –OH reduction). This creates a narrow, validated “acceptable conversion window” rather than relying on generic partial carbonization.

2) Zn–O–Sn bonding is elevated from a narrative step to a required structural descriptor with minimum fraction criteria. The plan combines surface-sensitive XPS component analysis with structure-sensitive EXAFS/total scattering to confirm Zn–Sn proximity (distinguishing Zn–O–Sn from ZnO-like segregation). The bonding requirement is further coupled to a measurable energetic consequence (UPS/KPFM ΔWF), ensuring the interfacial dipole/energetic alignment claim is physically anchored.

3) Hysteresis causality is deconvoluted using decisive, orthogonal observables rather than conflating mechanisms. IMPS/IMVS separates transport and recombination dynamics; temperature-dependent EIS yields ionic activation energies/ionic capacitance trends; and drift–diffusion modeling is constrained by EIS + TPV/TPC to discriminate “recombination-only” from “ionic polarization reduction” scenarios. The proposal explicitly commits to downgrading or revising the hysteresis mechanism claim if ionic signatures do not change.

4) The risk that porous carbonaceous residue introduces midgap states/energetic disorder is handled by an explicit electronic benignity gate: ETL conductivity (four-point probe), electron-only SCLC mobility, leakage behavior, and work-function uniformity (KPFM RMS) must not degrade beyond pre-registered limits. Only chemistries that pass these gates are permitted to proceed to device optimization.

5) The recombination claim is made falsifiable by specifying which recombination pathway must change. Instead of loosely invoking “lower interfacial carrier density → reduced bimolecular recombination,” the plan targets and quantifies (i) interfacial SRV (TRPL + optical modeling), (ii) trap distributions (TAS/DLTS-like), and (iii) non-radiative Voc loss (absolute PLQY/EL). This directly links the ETL modification to Voc/Jsc changes via established photovoltaic loss channels.

6) Empirical anchoring to literature assets remains coherent with the original concept chain. Asset 3 supports heterophase Bi–SnO2 as a hysteresis-free, low-recombination ETL baseline; this proposal adds a second lever—chemically bonded coordination/dipole sites—while preventing the MOF-as-insulator failure mode via sparse seeding and bonding/transport gates. Asset 2 supports the general principle that interfacial coordination chemistry and reduced hydroxyl reactivity improve Voc/Jsc and stability; here, coordination is made concrete through Zn–O–Sn and Zn/ligand-derived passivation metrics. Asset 4 (FRET) is explicitly excluded mechanistically; any optical changes must be consistent with trap/SRV reductions rather than energy-transfer claims.

Overall, feasibility is ensured by staged escalation with go/no-go milestones: chemistry validation → bonding/energetics proof → hysteresis causality separation → recombination-pathway quantification → device optimization and stability.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-structured proposal that elevates a speculative MOF-derived interfacial concept into a falsifiable, gate-driven research program. Engineering resolution is very high: the conversion chemistry matrix, bonding quantification thresholds, transport gates, and multi-modal hysteresis deconvolution (IMPS/IMVS, temperature-dependent EIS, constrained drift–diffusion modeling) exceed typical state-of-the-art proposals in perovskite ETL engineering. Logical consistency is strong, particularly in rejecting generic 'partial carbonization' narratives and explicitly decoupling recombination effects from ionic polarization. Minor deductions arise from the cumulative experimental burden: reliance on NAP-XPS/EXAFS/ssNMR may strain feasibility in non-synchrotron-access environments, and the ≥15% Zn–O–Sn bonded-component threshold, while commendably pre-registered, is somewhat arbitrary without prior sensitivity analysis linking fraction to ΔWF or ionic metrics. Evidence grounding is excellent: the concept chain is respected, and no extraneous phenomena (e.g., FRET) are inappropriately invoked. Rationale quality is high, as the work targets a genuine bottleneck—ETL-induced hysteresis and ionic interfacial polarization—using a structurally novel but carefully constrained coordination-chemistry lever rather than incremental dopant or surface treatment tweaks.
hypothesis_summary: A MOF-seeded SnO₂ electron transport layer eliminates hysteresis in perovskite solar cells by forming Zn–O–Sn bonds that passivate defects, reduce ionic polarization, and improve energy alignment.

original_chain: Hydroxyl radical (OH) -> Short-circuit current (Isc) -> Zn-Car_MOF -> Tribo-piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) -> Cu-HHTP -> Selectivity -> Reverse osmosis (RO) -> Membrane permeability
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a membrane-inspired, *precursor-selective crystallization and interfacial charge-regulation strategy*—rather than a post-deposition interlayer—can simultaneously enhance short-circuit current (Isc) and long-term stability in perovskite solar cells. Specifically, reverse-osmosis (RO)-purified perovskite precursor solutions will be crystallized through a transient Zn-Car_MOF sacrificial scaffold that enforces ionic selectivity during film formation, suppressing halide inhomogeneity and defect clustering. Subsequently, an ultrathin Cu-HHTP conductive MOF will be integrated as a redox-buffered hole-extraction layer whose Fermi level and selectivity are dynamically tuned by a remotely coupled tribo-piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG). Mechanical activation of the TPHG induces a low-amplitude alternating interfacial field that modulates Cu-HHTP redox states, selectively scavenges interfacial OH-mediated defect states without penetrating the perovskite bulk, and improves carrier extraction kinetics—thereby increasing Isc without introducing additional permeation barriers or encapsulation layers.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Purify mixed-cation/mixed-halide perovskite precursor solutions (FA-Cs-Pb-I/Br) using solvent-compatible reverse osmosis membranes to remove trace metal ions, colloidal aggregates, and oxidized iodide species; quantify impurity reduction via ICP-MS and UV–vis.
1.2 Synthesize Zn-Car_MOF nanoplates (20–50 nm lateral size) designed to be weakly coordinated to perovskite precursors via reversible carboxylate–lead interactions.
1.3 Prepare defect-engineered Cu-HHTP ultrathin films (≤15 nm) with controlled HHTP/HITP ratios to tune conductivity and redox activity near the perovskite valence band.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Selective crystallization via sacrificial MOF templating: Disperse Zn-Car_MOF nanoplates into the RO-purified perovskite precursor at low volume fraction (<1 wt%). During spin-coating and antisolvent quenching, the Zn-Car_MOF acts as a transient ion-selective scaffold that locally regulates Pb–halide coordination and suppresses halide-rich secondary phases.
2.2 Scaffold removal without film damage: Apply a mild, orthogonal chelating rinse (e.g., dilute amino-alcohol vapor) post-crystallization to selectively dissolve Zn-Car_MOF, leaving behind enlarged grains, reduced halide segregation, and lower ion permeability pathways within the perovskite film.
2.3 Redox-buffered hole extraction: Deposit Cu-HHTP directly atop the perovskite as a hole-extraction layer, replacing conventional doped spiro-OMeTAD. Align its Fermi level through ligand-ratio control to maximize hole selectivity and minimize interfacial recombination.
2.4 Remote tribo-piezoelectric modulation: Couple an external TPHG to the Cu-HHTP layer via capacitive (non-contact) coupling through the top electrode. Mechanical excitation (ambient vibration) induces a weak oscillatory potential that periodically shifts the Cu-HHTP redox state, promoting selective OH-mediated passivation of interfacial Pb0/iodide defect states while avoiding bulk perovskite oxidation.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Photovoltaic performance: Measure J–V curves, stabilized MPP, EQE, and Isc under static and mechanically stimulated conditions; deconvolute optical vs extraction-driven Isc gains.
3.2 Crystallization and defect analysis: Use GIWAXS, SEM, and ToF-SIMS to verify improved grain orientation, reduced halide segregation, and lower ion permeability after Zn-Car_MOF templating/removal.
3.3 Interfacial energetics and dynamics: Conduct UPS/XPS and transient photocurrent/photovoltage to assess band alignment and extraction kinetics at the perovskite/Cu-HHTP interface.
3.4 OH selectivity verification: Employ in-situ EPR spin trapping and operando XPS to confirm confined OH generation at the Cu-HHTP interface during TPHG activation, correlating with reductions in non-radiative recombination (PLQY, ideality factor).
3.5 Stability testing: Perform ISOS-L and ISOS-D protocols and bias-stress tests to link reduced ion migration and membrane-like selectivity during crystallization to enhanced operational stability.
3.6 Controls: (i) no RO purification, (ii) no Zn-Car_MOF templating, (iii) Cu-HHTP without TPHG coupling, and (iv) conventional HTL benchmarks.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: RO purification is known to improve precursor homogeneity, while MOFs can impose ionic selectivity at the nanoscale. Cu-HHTP provides high conductivity and tunable redox behavior, and prior studies show TPHGs can generate sufficient potential for interfacial modulation without direct electrical contact.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Instead of adding passive barriers, this strategy embeds membrane selectivity into the *formation pathway* of the perovskite and uses optoelectronically active MOFs as transport layers—directly addressing defect density, ion migration, and extraction losses central to PSC performance.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with interfacial caps or encapsulation layers, this approach avoids additional series resistance and permeability trade-offs. It uniquely links RO-derived chemical purity, MOF-guided crystallization selectivity, and mechanically tunable interfacial energetics to boost Isc and stability in a scalable, fabrication-compatible manner.
final_critique: This is an ambitious, technically sophisticated proposal with strong integration of materials chemistry, interfacial physics, and device engineering. The RO purification of precursor solutions and sacrificial Zn-Car_MOF–guided crystallization are conceptually sound and plausibly impactful for halide homogeneity and defect suppression. However, several elements remain weakly bounded experimentally: (i) solvent-compatible RO membranes for typical perovskite solvent systems (DMF/DMSO mixtures) are not well established and may introduce throughput or selectivity ambiguities; (ii) complete Zn-Car_MOF removal without residual Zn or carboxylate-induced defect formation is asserted but not quantitatively risk-assessed; and (iii) the TPHG-induced OH-mediated passivation mechanism, while creative, risks crossing from controlled redox buffering into stochastic interfacial chemistry, with potential for accelerated degradation if field amplitudes or frequencies drift. The logic linking oscillatory redox modulation to a net Isc increase is plausible but would benefit from a clearer quantitative kinetic model distinguishing beneficial defect scavenging from parasitic recombination or oxidation pathways.
hypothesis_summary: A membrane-inspired crystallization and interfacial charge-regulation strategy simultaneously boosts perovskite solar cell current and stability by suppressing defects during film growth and dynamically tuning hole extraction.

original_chain: Release profile -> Piezoelectric response -> Tribo-piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) -> Zn-Car_MOF -> Open-circuit voltage (Voc) -> Charge separation
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding an *oriented*, piezoelectrically addressable Zn–carnosine MOF (Zn-Car_MOF) population as a perovskite grain-boundary (GB) infill additive can increase PSC Voc **only if** it produces a *persistent, stress-free bound charge* at GBs that measurably bends bands and lowers SRH recombination beyond what chemical passivation alone achieves. We therefore refine the mechanism to be falsifiable and quantitatively bounded: (i) **Field mechanism (testable bound):** during crystallization, a low-amplitude AC field aligns anisotropic Zn-Car_MOF nanocrystals, and a post-crystallization residual strain (thermal-mismatch clamp) plus interfacial anchoring to Pb–I framework maintains a *metastable polarization state* (piezoelectret-like retention / strain-biased piezoelectric polarization rather than requiring continuous dynamic stress). This creates GB-local fixed bound charge density |σb| on the order of 1×10⁻⁴–1×10⁻³ C·m⁻², which drift–diffusion predicts is sufficient to generate ~10–50 meV GB band bending over a 5–20 nm electrostatic screening length, reducing GB carrier accumulation and raising QFLS and device Voc by ~20–60 mV. (ii) **Chemical reservoir mechanism (quantified kinetics):** Zn-Car_MOF pores deliver a humidity/thermal-triggered, self-limited release of carnosine-derived ligands (±SCN⁻ or FAI micro-loading) directly into GB volumes, reducing GB trap density Nt,GB by ≥3–10× within 10–100 h under 45–65 °C / 30–60% RH, which a kinetics-to-QFLS model links to a measurable PLQY/QFLS recovery and Voc stabilization during aging. Critically, we separate these effects by (a) bounding the necessary σb and ΔVGB to explain Voc gains, (b) directly measuring persistent GB fixed charge/field with two orthogonal probes under stress-free conditions, and (c) using a decisive ‘piezo-suppressed but chemistry-matched’ MOF control so that any additional Voc gain attributable to the field is isolated from passivation/nucleation effects.
Plan: Step 0 — Quantitative targets, falsification criteria, and device baseline
0.1 Define the performance target and required electrostatics: target ΔVoc = +30–70 mV in FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I0.6Br0.4)3 (Eg ~1.75–1.80 eV) inverted p–i–n (ITO/2PACz/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag). Baseline Voc deficit is established via absolute PL (QFLS) and Voc under identical illumination. Falsification rule: if stress-free persistent |σb| extracted from two independent methods is <1×10⁻⁴ C·m⁻² and KPFM/SPV shows <5 meV GB photovoltage contrast (after removing chemical-passivation-only controls), the field mechanism is considered non-contributory and the proposal reverts to purely chemical GB passivation.
0.2 Drift–diffusion + GB electrostatics pre-model: implement a 2D/3D drift–diffusion model with explicit GB regions (width 2–10 nm) containing (a) trap-assisted SRH with Nt,GB and capture cross-sections, and (b) a sheet bound charge ±σb at GB interfaces. Sweep σb = 1×10⁻⁵–5×10⁻³ C·m⁻²; compute (i) ΔVGB band bending (meV), (ii) QFLS change, (iii) ideality factor trend, (iv) expected KPFM/SPV contrast at GBs. Output: a quantitative mapping linking σb and Nt,GB reductions to ΔVoc.

Step 1 — MOF design: (A) piezo-active and (B) piezo-suppressed chemistry-matched control, plus solvent/halide stability gates
1.1 Synthesize anisotropic Zn-Car_MOF nanocrystals (target: rods/platelets; 20–80 nm diameter/thickness, 100–300 nm length/major axis). Characterize PXRD, BET, TEM, zeta potential, and PFM (d33 distribution) on drop-cast films.
1.2 Create a decisive ‘piezo vs non-piezo’ control with matched chemistry: prepare a *centrosymmetric / piezo-suppressed analog* while keeping Zn–carnosine coordination chemistry as constant as possible. Two routes are run in parallel:
  - Route B1 (symmetry engineering): tune synthesis (modulator concentration, pH, solvent ratio) to obtain a polymorph/phase verified by single-crystal/PXRD to be centrosymmetric (no piezoresponse by PFM within noise). Same Zn:carnosine stoichiometry and similar surface chemistry are required.
  - Route B2 (domain suppression): introduce controlled linker/metal-site disorder (e.g., partial substitution with achiral histidine/carnosine ratio or deliberate defect incorporation) designed to cancel net piezoresponse while maintaining porosity and functional groups; confirm by PFM and second-harmonic generation (SHG) absence.
Decision gate: proceed only if piezo-suppressed MOF retains (i) comparable surface functional groups (XPS), (ii) comparable pore volume (BET within ±20%), and (iii) similar colloidal behavior.
1.3 Surface functionalization that anchors to GBs but limits ionic leakage: graft a low-density anchoring shell (≤0.5–1.0 ligand·nm⁻²) using phosphonic-acid or carboxylate-terminated alkylammonium iodide that (i) transiently coordinates Pb2+ during nucleation and (ii) promotes expulsion from growing grains into GBs. Verify ligand density by XPS/TGA, and ensure no strong halide exchange that decomposes MOF.
1.4 Chemical stability and diffusion risk screening (mandatory): expose MOF and functionalized MOF to perovskite precursor solvents (DMF/DMSO/GBL; iodide/bromide salts; FA/Cs) at processing temperatures (25–100 °C) and time (0.5–4 h). Assays:
  - PXRD + FTIR for framework integrity;
  - ICP-MS for Zn leaching into solution and into perovskite films;
  - ToF-SIMS depth profiling for Zn migration after anneal.
Go/no-go criterion: Zn leaching must be <0.5% of MOF Zn content under processing exposure; no new Zn–I signatures indicative of ZnI2 formation above background.

Step 2 — Film formation with bounded electrochemical side effects of AC alignment
2.1 Additive loading and deposition: incorporate functionalized MOF at 0.01–0.20 wt% relative to perovskite solids. Use a delayed antisolvent quench (or gas-knife in blade/slot-die) to force late-stage solute enrichment at GBs. Primary architecture: inverted p–i–n to avoid TiO2 oxygen-vacancy confounds; secondary test: n–i–p (FTO/SnO2/perovskite/Spiro/Au) to assess generality.
2.2 AC alignment protocol with electrochemistry bounds (mandatory): apply AC electric field *during wet-film window* using a parallel-plate jig (top transparent electrode separated by inert dielectric spacer; avoids direct contact). Parameters start at: 1–10 kHz, 0.1–1.0 V·µm⁻¹ effective field, duration 5–30 s. Implement in-operando current monitoring through the jig; integrate charge passed (Qpassed) and enforce Qpassed < 10 µC·cm⁻² to limit ionic redistribution/redox.
2.3 Quantify and bound ionic redistribution caused by alignment (mandatory):
  - Immediately after alignment and after anneal, perform ToF-SIMS (I−/Br−/FA+/Cs+/Zn fragments) lateral and depth mapping to detect any field-induced segregation.
  - Compare aligned vs non-aligned films at identical MOF loading; if halide segregation or Zn redistribution exceeds pre-set thresholds (e.g., >10% change in I/Br ratio at GB vicinity or detectable Zn drift toward contacts), alignment amplitude/time is reduced or replaced by shear-assisted alignment (blade-coating shear) to preserve the orientation concept without electrochemistry.
2.4 Residual-strain ‘lock-in’ without dynamic stress: apply post-anneal under controlled mechanical constraint to impose mild uniform residual strain (ε ~ 10⁻⁴–10⁻³) using a clamp/curvature fixture matched to substrate CTE (validated by wafer curvature). This aims to stabilize a metastable polarization state (strain-biased piezoelectric polarization / piezoelectret retention). No cyclic mechanical actuation is used in operation.

Step 3 — Direct verification of persistent polarization/field under stress-free conditions (two orthogonal probes + extraction of σb)
3.1 Probe 1: temperature-dependent KPFM/SPV mapping at GBs (stress-free): map local surface potential and illumination-induced SPV contrast across GBs (resolution <50 nm) from 25–85 °C. Persistence criterion: GB potential contrast attributable to MOF must remain after removing external stress and must show a temperature dependence consistent with fixed charge screening (not transient ion migration). Control subtraction: (i) piezo-suppressed MOF, (ii) same chemistry but pores blocked (no release), (iii) no-AC alignment.
3.2 Probe 2: electrical extraction of fixed charge via C–V/impedance with GB-capacitance elements: fabricate lateral/vertical test structures (metal/perovskite:MOF/metal and full devices). Fit impedance spectra with an equivalent circuit including GB chemical capacitance + an added fixed-charge element (modeled as a parallel capacitance with bias-offset) to extract an effective σb or fixed charge density. Cross-validate σb with drift–diffusion predictions for the measured ΔVoc.
3.3 Auxiliary bound-charge metric (optional but planned): SHG microscopy (or PFM in a non-invasive configuration) on perovskite:MOF composites to confirm non-centrosymmetric ordering is present only in piezo-active aligned samples, absent in piezo-suppressed controls.

Step 4 — Embedded-GB release: in-film retention/release metrology and a kinetics-to-Voc model
4.1 Define the required dose and kinetics: using the SRH formalism in the drift–diffusion model, specify the Nt,GB reduction rate dNt/dt needed to recover QFLS by 10–30 meV over 10–100 h under 45–65 °C / 30–60% RH. Translate this into a target local areal concentration of passivating species at GBs (mol·m⁻² GB area) using GB volume fraction estimates (from grain size statistics).
4.2 Measure guest retention/release inside real perovskite films (mandatory):
  - Label carnosine/guest with isotopic markers (e.g., 15N-carnosine or 34S-SCN−) to enable unambiguous detection.
  - Track retention/release in perovskite:MOF films during controlled aging via ToF-SIMS (isotope fragments) and depth-resolved profiles.
  - Map local coordination changes at GBs using AFM-IR/nano-FTIR (amide bands for carnosine) and/or STEM-EELS for N and S signatures (for SCN−) specifically at GBs vs grain interiors.
4.3 Link kinetics to optoelectronic recovery: monitor time-evolution of (i) absolute PLQY/QFLS, (ii) thermal admittance spectroscopy-derived trap signatures, and (iii) device Voc at MPP tracking during aging. Fit with the pre-defined kinetics-to-QFLS model; require that extracted kinetic parameters agree (order-of-magnitude) with in-film retention/release observations.

Step 5 — Mechanistic separation and decisive control matrix
5.1 Control matrix (each at matched loading, same film protocol):
  - C0: no additive.
  - C1: piezo-active Zn-Car_MOF, no alignment.
  - C2: piezo-active Zn-Car_MOF + alignment + strain lock-in.
  - C3: piezo-suppressed (centrosymmetric/disordered) MOF + alignment + strain lock-in (chemistry-matched decisive control).
  - C4: piezo-active MOF with pores pre-blocked by inert bulky guests (chemistry and field present, release suppressed).
  - C5: non-porous Zn–carnosine-derived nanoparticles (chemistry present, no porosity; isolates release/porosity).
Interpretation rules:
  - Field contribution is supported only if C2 outperforms C3 and C4 in σb/SPV metrics and shows additional ΔVoc beyond chemical passivation signatures.
  - Release contribution is supported if C2 and C1 show time-dependent stabilization/recovery absent in C4.
5.2 Verify that electronic selectivity is preserved: confirm no conductive percolation (lateral conductivity), mobility change <15%, and no enhanced ionic conductivity via temperature-dependent impedance.

Step 6 — Scale relevance and stability
6.1 Demonstrate blade/slot-die films (5×5 cm) with same GB localization: PL imaging/hyperspectral maps for uniformity; ToF-SIMS for additive distribution.
6.2 Stability protocols: ISOS-L-2 (MPP, 65 °C) and encapsulated damp-heat screening. Track Voc drift, hysteresis, and ion-migration activation energies. Confirm that improvements correlate with measured σb persistence and/or release-driven Nt suppression rather than uncontrolled compositional changes.

Feasibility: 1) Resolving the ‘static polarization’ uncertainty with a bounded, falsifiable claim: Rather than assuming continuous piezoelectric actuation, the proposal explicitly targets a *persistent fixed bound charge* at GBs (σb) sustained by crystallization-time orientation + interfacial anchoring + mild residual strain (piezoelectret/strain-biased retention). The required σb (10⁻⁴–10⁻³ C·m⁻²) and resulting ΔVGB (10–50 meV) are pre-calculated by drift–diffusion, making the field mechanism quantitatively testable. If extracted σb and GB SPV contrast fall below threshold, the field claim is rejected and the remaining value is attributed to chemical/passivation pathways.

2) Orthogonal verification of stress-free field/polarization: The workplan adds two independent, stress-free probes demanded by reviewers—(i) temperature-dependent KPFM/SPV mapping of GB photovoltage contrast and (ii) extraction of fixed charge via C–V/impedance models with explicit GB-capacitance elements—so that a persistent electrostatic effect is not inferred indirectly from Voc alone.

3) Decisive piezo vs non-piezo control while keeping chemistry constant: Beyond randomized orientation, the plan introduces a *chemistry-matched piezo-suppressed MOF* (centrosymmetric/disordered analog) validated by PXRD/SHG/PFM, enabling direct attribution of any additional σb/SPV/Voc effect to piezoelectricity rather than carnosine chemistry, nucleation control, or porosity.

4) Bounding electrochemical artifacts from AC alignment: The alignment step is redesigned with a non-contact parallel-plate jig, strict charge-passed limits (Qpassed < 10 µC·cm⁻²), in-operando current monitoring, and mandatory post-process compositional mapping (ToF-SIMS) to quantify ionic redistribution and exclude redox/halide migration as hidden drivers of Voc changes.

5) Translating ‘release profile’ to embedded GB reality: The release mechanism is upgraded from model-film QCM-D alone to in-film, GB-resolved measurements using isotopic labeling plus nano-FTIR/AFM-IR and/or STEM-EELS for N/S signatures at GBs, and is coupled to a kinetics-to-QFLS/Voc model that specifies the required dose and timescales for meaningful SRH suppression.

6) Chemical stability and diffusion risk are treated as go/no-go gates: Framework integrity in halide-rich polar solvents and at annealing conditions is screened upfront, and Zn diffusion/leaching is quantitatively bounded (ICP-MS/ToF-SIMS). This prevents the additive from becoming an uncontrolled dopant/ionic pathway at GBs.

Together, these refinements preserve the original concept chain (Zn-Car_MOF piezoelectricity + porosity-enabled release targeted to GB recombination) while making the polarization-field component testable, quantitatively constrained, and separable from confounding chemical and processing effects.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-structured proposal that directly addresses a known weak point in piezoelectric-PSC claims: the lack of falsifiable, stress-free evidence for persistent polarization effects distinct from chemical passivation. Engineering resolution is very high, with clearly bounded parameters (σb, Qpassed, Nt,GB kinetics), decisive go/no-go gates, and orthogonal measurements that would convince a skeptical reviewer. Logical consistency is strong: the electrostatic field mechanism is quantitatively pre-modeled, explicitly separable from chemistry, and rejected by design if thresholds are not met. Minor deductions arise from residual physical uncertainty around long-term stability of strain-biased piezoelectret-like states in a soft, ionically active perovskite matrix, and from the practical complexity of reliably extracting σb from impedance models with GB-specific elements, which may introduce model degeneracy. Evidence grounding is solid and stays within the perovskite/MOF/optoelectronic domain, though the tribo-piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator framing in the target concept chain is only weakly operative in the final, stress-free device physics and reads more as legacy framing than an active mechanism. Rationale quality is high: the proposal does not merely apply passivation, but redefines the piezoelectric claim into a quantitatively bounded electrostatics problem with decisive controls.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding oriented piezoelectric Zn-carnosine MOF at perovskite grain boundaries creates a persistent bound charge that bends bands and reduces recombination, boosting voltage beyond chemical passivation alone.

original_chain: Nanocomposites -> Hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) -> H2O2 -> Near-infrared light (NIR) -> Glucose oxidase (GOx) -> Hypoxic tumors -> Fenton reaction -> Metal-containing linker strategy
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A NIR-activated, HOF-derived “oxygen-buffer + peroxide-sink” interphase built from metal-containing linkers will extend perovskite solar cell operational stability by preventing ROS-driven surface chemistry without invoking Fenton radical pathways. Mechanism: (i) a hydrogen-bonded organic framework (HOF) that is grown in situ from perovskite-compatible tectons forms a 3–8 nm supramolecular interphase that passivates under-coordinated Pb2+/halide-vacancy defects via directional H-bonding and Lewis-base coordination, thereby increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting and Voc; (ii) the HOF hosts redox-isolated Fe(III)/Cu(II) complexes introduced through a metal-containing linker strategy that catalytically disproportionate interfacial H2O2 to H2O/O2 (catalase-like, non-·OH pathway) by outer-sphere electron/proton transfer coupled to HOF proton relays, thus removing H2O2 formed during oxygen/light exposure before it oxidizes iodide or organic cations; (iii) an embedded NIR-absorbing molecular heater (non-plasmonic, e.g., aza-BODIPY or croconaine dye covalently tethered to HOF tectons) provides mild, spatially confined photothermal activation (ΔT 3–8 °C at <50 mW cm−2) that accelerates H2O2 disproportionation kinetics and desorbs weakly bound O2/H2O at the interface without perturbing visible absorption. Methodological adaptation: instead of inserting a pre-synthesized nanocomposite membrane (rejected approach), we adapt a metal-containing linker strategy used in coordination polymers into an interfacial, on-device supramolecular polymerization—‘interphase-from-tectons’—where the HOF forms directly on the perovskite surface from orthogonal, nonpolar vapor/solid-state precursors, locking redox complexes and NIR heaters into a defect-sealing, diffusion-selective skin that remains electronically thin and non-radical-generating.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1) Baseline device platforms (two architectures for generality):
   a) p–i–n: glass/ITO/MeO-2PACz/FA0.83Cs0.17Pb(I0.8Br0.2)3/C60/BCP/Cu.
   b) n–i–p: glass/FTO/SnO2/(optional KCl interfacial rinse)/same perovskite/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au.
2) Define ROS-relevant accelerated aging that specifically produces interfacial peroxide without introducing liquid water:
   a) Dry O2 (1 bar) + 1 sun + 45–65 °C.
   b) Controlled O2 partial pressure (0–21%) at fixed RH (0–20%) to decouple oxygen vs moisture.
   c) Light-soaking with periodic NIR pulses (808 or 980 nm) to test activation logic.
3) Build quantitative ROS diagnostics on model stacks (perovskite on quartz or transport layer):
   a) Surface H2O2 quantification by chemiluminescent probe on extracted films (luminol/HRP) and complementary electrochemical microprobe on interfacial layers (Prussian blue-modified microelectrode placed on model interface).
   b) Validate that hydroxyl radical generation is below detection: EPR spin trapping (DMPO) under illumination in O2.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
1) Interphase-from-tectons HOF growth (structurally novel vs pre-made composites):
   a) Tecton design: choose a neutral, planar aromatic core (e.g., pyrene/terphenyl) functionalized with (i) urea/amide arrays for strong H-bonded HOF assembly, (ii) a single Lewis base anchor (pyridine/thiophene-oxide/phosphine oxide) to bind surface Pb2+ without excessive energetic disorder, and (iii) a chelating pocket (e.g., salen-like or terpyridine-like) that pre-coordinates Fe(III) or Cu(II) in a redox-inert geometry that disfavors Fenton cycling (Fe(III) stabilized; Cu(II) ligand field stabilized).
   b) Deposition route (orthogonal and solvent-safe): sequential vapor/solid-state infusion.
      i) Sublime/evaporate the organic tecton (no polar solvent contact) onto the perovskite at room temperature to form a sub-monolayer to few-nm film.
      ii) Expose to a controlled vapor of a benign acid/base trigger (e.g., low-pressure acetic acid or ammonia) to promote supramolecular rearrangement and HOF crystallization via hydrogen-bond network locking.
      iii) Introduce metal ions by low-temperature atomic layer infiltration (ALI)-like exposure to volatile metal precursors (e.g., FeCl3 or Cu(acac)2 vapor at low dose) that coordinate only to the chelating pockets; follow with mild anneal (50–70 °C) to remove weakly bound residues.
   c) Thickness control: target 3–8 nm (verified by ellipsometry/XRR) to keep tunneling/extraction intact.
2) Integrate NIR molecular heater without plasmonic nanoparticles:
   a) Covalently attach a NIR dye (aza-BODIPY/croconaine) as a pendant group on a minority fraction (5–15%) of tectons so the HOF remains electronically wide-gap but absorbs 800–1000 nm.
   b) Ensure the dye is electronically decoupled from perovskite bands by inserting an insulating linker (alkyl/ether spacer) to avoid new midgap states.
3) Engineer the peroxide-sink pathway (avoid Fenton):
   a) Select Fe(III) complexes that catalyze 2 H2O2 → 2 H2O + O2 via outer-sphere pathways; tune local proton relays by placing imidazole/urea motifs adjacent to the metal pocket to accelerate proton-coupled electron transfer.
   b) Add a built-in radical quencher motif inside the HOF pores (hindered phenol or TEMPO-like tether) positioned away from the perovskite contact plane to neutralize any trace radicals formed inside the framework.
4) Device integration points:
   a) Apply the HOF interphase either on top of the perovskite before ETL/HTL deposition (primary route) or on transport layer before perovskite deposition (secondary route for buried interface).
   b) Confirm energy alignment is preserved: adjust tecton dipole moment (fluorination or methoxy substitution) to tune interfacial vacuum level shift by <0.2 eV.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
1) Optoelectronic performance and defect physics:
   a) Absolute PL/PLQY on complete stacks to extract quasi-Fermi level splitting; compare Voc deficit.
   b) TRPL and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to separate surface recombination vs transport limitations.
   c) Impedance spectroscopy (light-intensity dependent) to quantify recombination resistance and interfacial capacitance; extract ideality factors pre/post aging.
2) Chemical mechanism proof (peroxide sink, non-Fenton):
   a) Operando H2O2 tracking on model interfaces under O2 + light, with and without NIR pulses; report formation/decay kinetics and activation energy with/without NIR.
   b) EPR spin trapping under illumination: demonstrate suppressed/undetectable ·OH compared to intentionally Fenton-active controls.
   c) XPS/ToF-SIMS depth profiling after aging: quantify suppression of Pb–O/I–O species, reduced iodate/iodine signals, and stable metal localization in the interphase.
3) Stability benchmarking and controls:
   a) MPP tracking at 45–65 °C under 1 sun in controlled O2/RH; report T80 and retained Voc/FF.
   b) Controls to isolate each function: (i) HOF without metal pocket, (ii) HOF with metal pocket but no NIR dye, (iii) NIR dye only (no HOF), (iv) metal pocket in non-HOF amorphous film, (v) intentionally Fenton-active Fe(II) pocket to show failure mode.
   c) Scaling: demonstrate uniform interphase formation on 1 cm2 and 5×5 cm substrates via vapor deposition mapping; correlate thickness uniformity with Voc distribution.

Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Perovskite photo-oxidation in O2 proceeds via superoxide/peroxide intermediates that generate H2O2 and oxidized iodide species, accelerating defect creation and ion migration; removing H2O2 at the interface is a direct lever to suppress this degradation channel. HOFs can form dense hydrogen-bonded networks that simultaneously passivate ionic defects and act as diffusion-selective barriers. Metal complexes can catalyze H2O2 disproportionation without generating ·OH when the redox cycle is constrained (Fe(III)-stabilized, outer-sphere pathways), and mild heating increases catalytic turnover while enabling desorption of physisorbed O2/H2O.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The metal-containing linker strategy is translated from porous framework chemistry into an on-device interphase synthesis that is perovskite-compatible (no polar solvents, low temperature) and explicitly targeted to PSC bottlenecks: interfacial non-radiative recombination (defect passivation) and oxygen/light instability (peroxide removal). NIR is leveraged as an optoelectronic control knob that does not compete with the perovskite’s visible absorption, enabling ‘maintenance-mode’ activation during operation.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike passive hydrophobic coatings that only slow ingress, this interphase actively consumes H2O2 while avoiding Fenton radical risks by design (redox-isolated metal pockets + radical quenchers). Unlike nanoparticle-based photothermal layers, the molecular NIR heater avoids plasmonic hot-carrier injection and minimizes band-edge perturbation. The interphase-from-tectons approach provides conformal, thickness-controlled coverage and eliminates the reproducibility and energetic-disorder issues associated with depositing pre-formed nanocomposites onto soft perovskite surfaces.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and unusually detailed proposal with strong command of perovskite interfacial degradation chemistry and modern framework concepts. The engineering resolution is high: vapor-phase tecton deposition, ALI-like metal incorporation, thickness control, and a comprehensive ROS diagnostic suite are all well specified and largely perovskite-compatible. Logical consistency is generally strong, particularly the rationale for targeting interfacial H2O2 rather than bulk oxygen ingress, and the explicit effort to avoid Fenton-active metal states. However, there are nontrivial speculative gaps. Chief among them is the assumption that Fe(III)/Cu(II) complexes embedded in a thin HOF can achieve catalase-like H2O2 disproportionation at relevant rates under dry or near-dry PSC operating conditions without cycling into transient reduced states that could still seed radical chemistry. The proposal also underestimates the kinetic competition between peroxide diffusion to the metal pocket and peroxide attack on iodide at the perovskite surface. Evidence grounding is solid within the PSC/ROS/HOF domain, but the target concept chain is only partially honored: GOx and hypoxic-tumor analogies are conceptually inspirational rather than mechanistically mapped, which slightly weakens strict chain integration. The rationale quality is high and creative, yet the proposal verges on over-integration: defect passivation, diffusion selectivity, catalysis, photothermal control, and radical quenching are all loaded into a 3–8 nm layer, raising realistic concerns about synthetic yield, reproducibility, and mechanistic deconvolution even with the proposed controls.
hypothesis_summary: A NIR-activated, HOF-derived interphase with oxygen-buffer and peroxide-sink functions extends perovskite solar cell stability by removing H₂O₂ without generating harmful radicals.

original_chain: Utilization ratio -> Bicontinuous structure -> Schwarz P surface -> bmFeSAC -> Bicontinuous structure -> Half-wave potential -> Synergistic effect -> Heteroatom doping
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a Schwarz P–type bicontinuous interfacial layer (20–50 nm curvature length scale) between the perovskite and SnO2 can generate a measurable, geometry-driven modulation of interfacial electrostatics (surface potential/work-function landscape) that improves electron-selective contact behavior only when (a) the curvature length is comparable to the interfacial screening length (Debye length) of the perovskite/ETL contact region, and (b) the interlayer chemistry is tuned to avoid midgap states and parasitic redox. Mechanistically, negative Gaussian curvature increases the interfacial area-normal electric-field components and redistributes charge accumulation at the perovskite/ETL boundary, producing a spatially averaged contact dipole and reduced local barrier for electron transfer into SnO2, thereby lowering interfacial recombination velocity (S) and increasing QFLS-derived Voc. In parallel, atomically dispersed Fe–N4 sites with secondary heteroatom coordination (Fe–N–S or Fe–N–O) are hypothesized to provide chemically specific passivation of undercoordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy-associated deep traps (VPb/I, VI, Pb–I antisites, and SnO2 oxygen-vacancy surface states) via Lewis acid–base and coordination interactions, but only if Fe sites are electronically insulated from the perovskite to prevent catalytic halide redox and to suppress shunting. Therefore, the central, falsifiable claim is: (i) curvature alone produces a UPS/KPFM-detectable surface potential shift (ΔWF/ΔCPD) and band-bending change at the perovskite/SnO2 boundary; (ii) Fe–N–X chemistry primarily reduces trap-assisted interfacial recombination (lower S, higher PLQY/QFLS) without introducing new midgap states; and (iii) combining curvature + Fe–N–X yields a super-additive reduction in recombination (synergistic effect) while meeting strict optical/shunt/stability gates.
Plan: Step 0 — Device-physics targets (pre-registered, pass/fail):
0.1 Band alignment target: shift the effective electron-contact selectivity such that the perovskite surface work function decreases by ΔWF = 0.10–0.25 eV (electron-favoring) relative to the control SnO2 contact, measured by UPS (secondary cutoff) and KPFM (ΔCPD mapping). Sign requirement: reduced perovskite-side WF (or increased SnO2-side WF) consistent with reduced electron-extraction barrier and suppressed hole leakage.
0.2 Interfacial recombination target: reduce interfacial recombination velocity by ≥3× vs control, extracted from absolute PLQY (QFLS) + transient PL/TPV fits on full stacks; and show Voc increase ≥30 mV at matched Jsc.
0.3 Shunt/optical gate: added parasitic absorption/scatter must reduce Jsc by <0.3 mA cm−2 (integrated EQE) and device shunt resistance must not decrease by >20% relative to baseline SnO2.
0.4 Stability go/no-go: Fe-containing variants must not accelerate perovskite decomposition under bias/light; criterion: ≤10% increase (relative) in PbI2 fraction by GIWAXS and no increased I− accumulation at the interface by ToF-SIMS after 100 h MPP at 1 sun, 60 °C.

Step 1 — Interlayer architecture synthesis with curvature control (decouple geometry from chemistry):
1.1 Prepare three curvature states using polymer cubosome templating to obtain Schwarz P bicontinuous carbon frameworks with controlled periodicity L = 20, 35, 50 nm (verified by SAXS/TEM; quantify mean curvature distribution and pore connectivity). Prepare a ‘flat/zero-curvature’ mesoporous carbon analog with matched composition and thickness but without long-range Schwarz P negative Gaussian curvature (e.g., disordered mesoporous carbon with similar pore size distribution).
1.2 Thickness control: deposit interlayers at 5, 10, 15, 20 nm (ellipsometry/XRR), targeting percolating pathways only within the layer while minimizing optical loss.
1.3 Chemical states at identical geometry:
  (A) Carbon-only (C-SchwarzP; C-flat)
  (B) N-doped carbon (N-C-SchwarzP; N-C-flat)
  (C) Fe-free heteroatom controls: N,S-C and N,O-C (no Fe)
  (D) Fe–N4 single-atom sites: Fe–N4@N-C (Fe loading kept low, e.g., 0.05–0.2 wt% for PV safety; AC-STEM/XAS confirm single atoms)
  (E) Secondary coordination: Fe–N–S and Fe–N–O variants at matched Fe density.
This matrix enforces the mandatory control logic: curvature (Schwarz P vs flat) and chemistry (Fe-free vs Fe–N4 vs Fe–N–X) are orthogonally varied.

Step 2 — Barrier strategy to eliminate shunting while keeping extraction fast (mandatory):
2.1 Introduce an ultrathin conformal insulating/semiconducting barrier on the carbon scaffold before perovskite contact:
  Option 1: ALD Al2O3 (0.5–1.5 nm; 5–15 cycles) or ALD TiO2 (0.5–1.0 nm) to electronically suppress direct carbon/perovskite contact while allowing tunneling.
  Option 2: Self-limiting molecular passivation (phosphonic acid or ammonium halide-anchored monolayer) grafted onto the carbon/Fe sites to tune dipole and block redox.
2.2 Gate criterion: interlayer stacks must show leakage current <10−6 A cm−2 at −0.1 V in dark on electron-only test structures (ITO/SnO2/interlayer/perovskite/PCBM/Ag) compared to baseline.

Step 3 — Interface integration in PSCs with PV-grounded metrology (replace half-wave potential):
3.1 Baseline device: ITO/SnO2/(interlayer)/perovskite (FA/Cs; I/Br)/HTL (e.g., Spiro-OMeTAD or PTAA)/Au. Keep perovskite thickness and composition fixed.
3.2 Measure interfacial energetics:
  - UPS: WF and valence onset of perovskite surface with/without interlayer; extract ΔWF and infer band alignment changes.
  - KPFM: nanoscale CPD maps across grains to see if Schwarz P curvature reduces potential heterogeneity (std. dev. of CPD) and introduces systematic potential offset.
  - Cross-sectional Kelvin probe (where feasible) or surface photovoltage spectroscopy to support band-bending interpretation.
3.3 Measure recombination/kinetics directly linked to Voc:
  - Absolute PLQY on full stacks (glass/ITO/SnO2/interlayer/perovskite) under 1-sun equivalent excitation to extract QFLS; compare QFLS–qVoc deficit.
  - TRPL (early-time extraction vs long-time recombination) and TPV/TPC to extract carrier lifetime and recombination order; derive effective interfacial recombination velocity S by thickness-dependent PL decay or established interfacial quenching models.
  - Temperature-dependent J–V (200–320 K) to extract activation energy of recombination; target shift toward band-to-band limit (Ea → Eg) if interfacial SRH is suppressed.

Step 4 — Trap identification and defect-specific passivation claims (mandatory specificity):
4.1 Quantify trap density and energetic distribution:
  - Thermal admittance spectroscopy or DLTS on dedicated stacks (ITO/SnO2/interlayer/perovskite/metal) to obtain Nt and activation energies.
  - SCLC in electron-only and hole-only configurations to separate bulk vs interfacial contributions.
4.2 Identify targeted defects and chemical bonding:
  - XPS/UPS core levels (Pb 4f, I 3d, Br 3d, N 1s, S 2p, O 1s, Fe 2p) before/after perovskite deposition to detect coordination shifts consistent with passivation (e.g., reduced metallic Pb0 signal; shifts indicating Pb–X interactions).
  - FTIR/Raman (if molecular functionalization used) to confirm surface groups.
4.3 Midgap-state avoidance gate: if sub-bandgap EQE (sEQE) or photothermal deflection spectroscopy shows increased midgap absorption compared to control, Fe–N–X chemistry is revised (lower Fe loading, stronger barrier, or Fe-free heteroatom doping path).

Step 5 — Curvature–electrostatics model tied to measurable length scales (reviewer-required quantitative framing):
5.1 Estimate screening: extract effective Debye length (LD) proxy from capacitance–frequency/temperature data of perovskite/contact stacks and from carrier density estimates; treat curvature periodicity L as the tunable geometric parameter.
5.2 Testable prediction: maximum ΔCPD and recombination suppression occurs when L ~ (1–3)× LD; if L ≫ LD, curvature-induced electrostatic modulation should average out; if L ≪ LD, potential becomes spatially oscillatory but may not translate into net band bending.
5.3 Fit KPFM CPD spatial spectra to quantify whether curvature introduces a systematic offset (dipole-like) versus only roughness-induced heterogeneity.

Step 6 — Chemical stability and ion-migration compatibility (mandatory go/no-go):
6.1 Aging protocols: MPP tracking under 1 sun at 60 °C (ISOS-L2-like) and thermal aging at 85 °C in N2; include bias-stress at Voc and MPP.
6.2 Operando/after-aging diagnostics:
  - GIWAXS to track PbI2 formation and phase segregation (I/Br).
  - ToF-SIMS depth profiling to map I−/Br− accumulation at the interface and Fe migration.
  - XPS depth profiling to detect Fe–halide formation (Fe–I/Fe–Br) and changes in Fe oxidation state.
6.3 Go/no-go: if Fe-containing layers show increased halide accumulation or Fe–halide signatures together with accelerated PbI2 growth, pivot to Fe-free N,S or N,O doping while retaining Schwarz P curvature (salvage curvature mechanism independent of Fe chemistry).

Deliverables (Milestones):
M1 (Month 1–3): Library of curvature/chemistry interlayers + barrier layer; confirm single-atom dispersion (where applicable) and optical/shunt gate.
M2 (Month 4–6): UPS/KPFM + PLQY/QFLS establish whether curvature yields measurable ΔWF/ΔCPD and whether chemistry reduces QFLS deficit.
M3 (Month 7–9): Device matrix with orthogonal controls; extract S, Ea(recomb), and demonstrate Voc/FF improvements without Jsc penalty.
M4 (Month 10–12): Stability validation + interfacial ion profiling; finalize go/no-go on Fe path.
Feasibility: 1) PV-grounded endpoints replace electrocatalysis half-wave potential: The proposal now uses UPS/KPFM (ΔWF/ΔCPD) for interfacial energetics, absolute PLQY-derived QFLS to directly bound achievable Voc, and temperature-dependent J–V to identify whether recombination is interfacial SRH-limited. These metrics are standard, falsifiable, and not dominated by ionic CV artefacts.

2) Quantitative curvature rationale linked to screening length: Rather than asserting band bending, the plan tests a specific geometry–screening condition (L relative to LD) and predicts a non-monotonic dependence of ΔCPD and recombination suppression on curvature periodicity. This makes the curvature claim mechanistically constrained and experimentally checkable.

3) Risk controls for carbon/Fe in PSCs are built in: (i) a mandatory ultrathin ALD oxide or self-limiting functional barrier suppresses shunts and blocks direct catalytic contact; (ii) strict optical and leakage gates prevent Jsc loss and shunting; (iii) Fe loading is intentionally kept far below typical electrocatalyst levels, and Fe-free heteroatom controls are included to preserve the curvature thesis if Fe proves incompatible.

4) Defect specificity and midgap-state avoidance: The proposal specifies targeted defect families (undercoordinated Pb, halide vacancies, SnO2 oxygen-vacancy surface states) and couples passivation claims to DLTS/thermal admittance/SCLC plus XPS chemical-shift evidence and sEQE/PDS midgap checks. This prevents unsubstantiated ‘trap passivation’ assertions.

5) Stability compatibility is treated as a first-class deliverable with go/no-go criteria: Operando/after-aging GIWAXS and ToF-SIMS/XPS depth profiling directly address Fe–halide reactivity and ion accumulation under realistic bias/light, enabling an early decision to pivot toward Fe-free designs if degradation is catalyzed.

6) Coherence with the original concept chain and literature assets: The bmFeSAC-inspired Schwarz P bicontinuity is retained as the geometric engine to raise utilization ratio of interfacial charge-transfer area (now quantified via reduced CPD heterogeneity and improved extraction/recombination parameters). The synergistic effect concept is translated from dual-factor performance (geometry + coordination chemistry) into PV-relevant super-additivity on QFLS/Voc and recombination velocity, while heteroatom doping is treated as chemically specific passivation rather than a generic benefit.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-controlled proposal that demonstrates high engineering maturity and strong logical discipline. The central claim—geometry-driven modulation of interfacial electrostatics when curvature length matches screening length—is clearly falsifiable and experimentally constrained, avoiding vague 'band bending' assertions. Orthogonal control of curvature and chemistry, mandatory shunt/optical gates, and explicit go/no-go stability criteria significantly reduce interpretive ambiguity. The use of QFLS, UPS/KPFM, temperature-dependent J–V, and defect-resolved spectroscopy firmly grounds the work in photovoltaic device physics rather than borrowed electrocatalysis heuristics. Score deductions are minor and stem from residual risk: (i) the assumed magnitude of curvature-induced ΔWF (0.10–0.25 eV) may be optimistic given ionic screening and disorder at realistic perovskite interfaces; (ii) extraction of an effective Debye length in mixed ionic–electronic perovskites remains model-dependent and may complicate quantitative fitting in Step 5; and (iii) the synthetic and integration complexity of polymer-templated Schwarz P carbons plus ALD barriers may limit throughput and statistical power within a 12‑month window. These are executional risks rather than conceptual flaws.
hypothesis_summary: A bicontinuous Schwarz P interlayer with nanoscale curvature modulates perovskite/SnO2 interfacial electrostatics to reduce electron-extraction barriers, while atomically dispersed Fe–N–X sites chemically passivate deep traps, together synergistically lowering recombination and boosting voltage.

original_chain: bmFeSAC -> Utilization ratio -> Schwarz P surface -> Specific surface area -> Core-shell structure
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Introducing a curvature-engineered Schwarz P (triply periodic minimal surface, TPMS) interfacial access layer between the perovskite absorber and the electron-selective contact will *quantitatively suppress interfacial ionic hot spots and non-radiative recombination* by redistributing electrostatic fields and enforcing bicontinuous electronic connectivity, while avoiding the recombination penalties of conventional mesoporous ETLs. Mechanistically, this occurs because (i) **negative Gaussian curvature spreads electric field lines over a continuous minimal surface**, reducing peak field intensity that otherwise drives iodide accumulation at sharp corners typical of positive/zero-curvature pores; (ii) **bicontinuous TPMS connectivity ensures a near-unity electronic utilization ratio**, such that every chemically passivating site is electronically active, unlike dead-end mesopores; and (iii) a **transport–chemistry–energetics–decoupled core–shell nanolaminate** (SnO₂ core for electron transport; sub-nm Al₂O₃/MgO tunneling shell for defect/ion blocking; dipolar fullerene-SAM for band alignment) maintains low contact resistivity while stabilizing interfacial energetics under bias and heat. This hypothesis is falsifiable via coupled Poisson–Nernst–Planck (PNP) + drift–diffusion (DD) modeling and pre-registered quantitative targets: ≥30–50% reduction in peak iodide concentration at the electron contact under operating bias, ≥25 mV increase in implied Voc at fixed Jsc, and no increase in contact resistivity beyond 10 mΩ·cm² compared to planar SnO₂ controls.
Plan: ### Step 1: Predictive modeling and quantitative design rules (mandatory pre-experiment)
1.1 **Geometry-resolved electrostatic/ionic modeling**: Reconstruct representative TPMS (Schwarz P) and benchmark mesoporous geometries (positive/zero curvature) from synthetic CAD and early FIB-SEM data. Solve coupled Poisson–Nernst–Planck (iodide and vacancy species) + drift–diffusion (electrons/holes) equations under steady-state illumination and forward bias (0.8–1.1 V). Explicitly include curvature-dependent boundary conditions for surface charge density at SnO₂/perovskite interfaces.
1.2 **Dimensionless groups and curvature window**: Define and sweep key ratios: (i) Debye length (λ_D ≈ 1–5 nm) / local radius of curvature (R_c), (ii) lattice constant a (80–200 nm) / perovskite grain size, and (iii) ion mobility × electric field / diffusion coefficient (Pe_ion). Identify regimes where negative Gaussian curvature yields ≥30% reduction in peak |E| and ≥30% reduction in peak iodide density relative to planar and mesoporous controls.
1.3 **Pre-registered quantitative targets**: From modeling, lock target ranges: TPMS lattice constant a = 100–150 nm; TPMS height = 40–60 nm; predicted peak iodide concentration reduction ≥40%; predicted implied Voc gain ≥25–40 mV. These become go/no-go criteria for fabrication.

### Step 2: Fabrication with infiltration/shunt-avoidance criteria
2.1 **Removable Schwarz P template**: Deposit block-copolymer cubosome or lyotropic TPMS-forming phase on ITO/SnO₂; photopolymerize/crosslink. Measure intrinsic template pore size and curvature by GISAXS.
2.2 **Conformal SnO₂ core (electronic backbone)**: Spatial ALD at 120–150 °C, thickness 6–10 nm, ensuring sheet resistance <10⁵ Ω/□ and full bicontinuous percolation.
2.3 **Core–shell nanolaminate**:
- Shell A: 0.3–0.7 nm Al₂O₃ or MgO (3–7 ALD cycles). Pre-registered limit: contact resistivity increase ≤10 mΩ·cm² vs bare SnO₂.
- Shell B: Fullerene-phosphonic-acid SAM (C₆₀-PA or PCBM-PA), target dipole 0.2–0.4 eV. Pre-registered stability criterion: work-function shift change ≤50 meV after 100 h at 85 °C under bias.
2.4 **Template removal and ‘necking’ step with capillarity control**: Remove polymer via solvent + mild O₂ plasma. Apply ultrathin SnO₂ sol–gel necking layer (<5 nm equivalent). Quantify capillary infiltration risk using Young–Laplace pressure (ΔP = 2γcosθ/r): require ΔP < critical crystallization pressure. Measure contact angle and solvent surface tension; define go/no-go window where perovskite infiltration depth <10 nm (verified by cross-sectional TEM/SEM).
2.5 **Perovskite deposition**: Use viscosity-controlled precursor and gas-assisted quench to enforce overlayer crystallization. Criterion: void fraction at interface <5% and no continuous shunt pathways (verified by conductive-AFM and dark JV leakage).

### Step 3: Operationalizing utilization ratio (U)
3.1 **Interface recombination velocity (S)**: Extract absolute S from time-resolved PL on perovskite/ETL stacks (no HTL), calibrated with optical modeling. Define S_planar as baseline.
3.2 **Spatial collection probability (P_c)**: Obtain EBIC maps across TPMS curvature; normalize to planar control to yield ⟨P_c⟩.
3.3 **Utilization ratio definition**: U = (S_planar / S_TPMS) × ⟨P_c⟩, reported with confidence intervals from ≥10 devices. Pre-register expected U ≥1.5–2× relative to planar SnO₂.
3.4 **Device correlation**: Correlate U with Voc deficit (ΔVoc from SQ limit) and hysteresis index; require monotonic correlation for mechanistic validation.

### Step 4: Transport and stability decision layer
4.1 **Contact resistivity and FF risk**: Extract contact resistivity via TLM and electron-only devices. Go/no-go: FF loss ≤1% absolute at matched Jsc.
4.2 **Energetic stability**: UPS/Kelvin probe before/after ISOS-L-2 stress (65–85 °C, bias). Criterion: work-function drift ≤50 meV.
4.3 **Ionic suppression validation**: ToF-SIMS after ±1 V bias stress; require ≥40% reduction in peak iodide accumulation vs planar and mesoporous controls.

### Step 5: Device KPIs and scaling
Demonstrate ≥25 mV Voc and ≥2–3% absolute FF gain vs planar SnO₂; T80 ≥2× at 65–85 °C MPP. Validate blade-coated 1–10 cm² devices with LBIC uniformity <10% variation.
Feasibility: The revised proposal directly addresses reviewer-identified weaknesses by embedding a **predictive, falsifiable modeling layer** prior to fabrication, ensuring that curvature length scales (80–200 nm) and TPMS height are not arbitrary but derived from PNP+DD simulations. This mirrors the logic used in bicontinuous single-atom catalysts (Asset 1), where negative Gaussian curvature and bicontinuity maximize utilization ratio; here, the same geometry is translated into a PSC-relevant electrostatic/ionic framework. The **capillarity-based infiltration criterion** transforms the qualitative ‘necking’ concept into a quantified processing window, reducing shunt risk. The **operational definition of utilization ratio** replaces indirect chemical proxies with device-physics-grounded metrics (recombination velocity and collection probability) and enforces correlation with Voc and hysteresis. Finally, explicit **contact-resistivity and energetic-stability bounds** mitigate the risk of sub-nm oxide + SAM layers degrading FF or stability. Together, these measures convert an ambitious architectural concept into a controlled, decision-driven research program with clear success/failure criteria, high reproducibility, and strong relevance to scalable perovskite photovoltaics.
final_critique: This is unusually strong in execution planning (model-first, quantified targets, explicit failure criteria) and in anticipating manufacturability risks (template removal, shunt avoidance, contact resistivity bounds). The main scientific vulnerability is that the central mechanism—negative Gaussian curvature *quantitatively* suppressing ionic accumulation by redistributing fields—remains under-justified in the specific electrochemical environment of perovskites. In PNP-type systems, peak ionic density is often dominated by local boundary conditions (surface charge, defect chemistry, interfacial reaction terms), mixed ionic–electronic coupling, and microstructural heterogeneity (grain boundaries, local stoichiometry), not curvature alone; your plan mentions curvature-dependent surface charge but does not specify a physically validated constitutive relation for SnO2/perovskite surface charge vs bias, illumination, and chemistry, nor how it will be parameterized and independently measured. In addition, the fabrication pathway has multiple compounding uncertainties: (i) ensuring continuous bicontinuous SnO2 conduction at 6–10 nm within a removed-template TPMS without breaks/necking bottlenecks and without raising series resistance, (ii) achieving a *truly* sub-nm conformal Al2O3/MgO tunnel barrier that blocks ions/defects yet preserves low ρc across a high-area interface (area scaling could make 10 mΩ·cm² difficult), and (iii) the infiltration-control criterion (ΔP < critical crystallization pressure; <10 nm infiltration) is directionally good but currently underspecified because crystallization pressure, solvent exchange kinetics, and antisolvent quench dynamics are not captured by a static Young–Laplace bound. Finally, the utilization ratio U is a helpful metric, but EBIC in perovskites can be field- and damage-sensitive and may not cleanly map to operational carrier collection without careful beam-condition controls and complementary optoelectronic extraction (e.g., absolute quasi-Fermi level splitting under 1 sun, transient photocurrent/photovoltage).
hypothesis_summary: A curvature-engineered Schwarz P interface layer suppresses ionic hotspots and recombination in perovskite solar cells by redistributing electric fields and ensuring bicontinuous electronic connectivity without typical recombination losses.

original_chain: Nonlinear optical (NLO) properties -> Charge transfer -> Interfacial synthesis -> Hierarchical micromesoporosity -> Ni-HITP -> Electrochemical energy storage
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A buried, hierarchically micro/mesoporous, partially converted Ni-HITP@NiOx core–shell nanomesh (“charge-transfer metasurface”) grown *on the hole-selective contact prior to perovskite deposition* will improve p–i–n perovskite solar-cell performance and operational stability through three explicitly testable mechanisms: (1) **Energetics/transport homogenization without barrier formation**: an ultrathin, laterally percolating Ni-HITP shell (target 2–10 nm) increases the interfacial electronic coupling and effective hole collection area while maintaining a continuous oxide backbone, yielding a reduced effective contact resistivity and a narrower interfacial energetic-disorder distribution (σE) provided that the shell work function is matched to the perovskite valence band and that the core–shell does not create a hole-injection barrier. This will be verified by a priori band-diagram hypotheses and UPS/KPFM under dark/illumination plus temperature-dependent transport and CT-rate extraction (drift–diffusion / Marcus-type). (2) **Chemically specified, capacity-bounded ion buffering with selectivity and reversibility**: the nanomesh provides dual-mode ion interaction sites—Ni–N chelation/π pores in Ni-HITP (micropores) and Lewis-acid/base sites on residual NiOx/Ni(OH)x—whose binding energies and adsorption isotherms for PSC-relevant ions (I−, Br−, FA+, Cs+) determine whether the interface acts as a benign buffer (low-activity reservoir) or a deleterious trap/catalyst. The hypothesis is *not* that “more uptake is better,” but that there exists a bounded interfacial uptake window (Qmax,allow) below which ion accumulation at the perovskite/HTL junction is reduced and above which electronic degradation or redox chemistry emerges; thus the design is tuned to operate below Qmax,allow with reversible uptake/release under bias. (3) **Mechanistically identifiable NLO diagnostic**: because π-delocalized Ni-HITP exhibits strong third-order nonlinearity that is sensitive to carrier delocalization and interfacial charge transfer (Asset 1), a calibrated χ(3) observable—extracted via multilayer optical modeling and simplified reference stacks—can be made *identifiable* to an interfacial electronic parameter (surface recombination velocity S or interfacial transfer rate kCT) rather than generic absorption/doping artifacts. The specific claim is that, across intentionally perturbed samples with controlled energetics and ion loading, the modeled χ(3) amplitude/relaxation component attributed to Ni-HITP interfacial coupling will predict extracted kCT or S within predefined error bounds, enabling non-destructive monitoring of interfacial “health” during aging.

Design constraints to address reviewer risks are embedded: (i) chemical selectivity and saturation are quantified and bounded (go/no-go) to avoid catalytic decomposition; (ii) band alignment and percolation are explicitly modeled and measured to prevent barriers/Fermi-level pinning; (iii) χ(3) is made uniquely attributable to interfacial coupling using decoupling controls and optical transfer-matrix modeling; (iv) micro/mesoporosity is engineered to avoid shunts/pinholes by limiting accessible pore depth and enforcing an ultrathin, conformal top seal while maintaining lateral percolation.
Plan: A. Device context, baselines, and success metrics
A1. Platform: p–i–n PSCs: ITO / NiOx (baseline HTL) / perovskite / C60 / BCP / Ag. Keep electron-contact stack constant across all experiments.
A2. Reference perovskite: FA/Cs-based mixed-cation, low-Br (or Br-free) wide-process-window composition chosen for high Voc and reduced phase segregation; use a single baseline recipe for all packages.
A3. Baseline HTL: compact NiOx (sol–gel or sputtered), UV–ozone tuned work function. Record baseline contact resistivity (TLM), QFLS (PLQY), Voc/Jsc/FF, hysteresis index, and stability T80.
A4. Target device-level metrics (tracked at matched absorber thickness and optics): ΔVoc ≥ +40 mV with |ΔJsc| ≤ 0.3 mA cm−2; contact resistivity reduction ≥ 3×; hysteresis index decrease ≥ 50%; MPP T80 ≥ 2× under ISOS-L-2 (60–85 °C).

B. Fabrication of the core–shell porous nanomesh (RT-IMC) with explicit architectural parameters
B1. Mesoporous Ni(OH)x/NiOx nanoseed mesh on NiOx (pre-perovskite):
- Solution: nickel acetate (or nitrate) + block copolymer template PS-b-PEO (or equivalent micelle former) in alcohol solvent.
- Template-set mesopores: target 5–30 nm diameter; thickness of seed mesh: 10–25 nm (thin enough to avoid optical/electrical penalties, thick enough for percolation control).
- Anneal: ≤200 °C to form an anchored Ni(OH)x/NiOx network without damaging ITO/NiOx.
- Template removal: UV–ozone or solvent extraction. Verify open porosity and continuity by GISAXS/ellipsometric porosimetry and AFM.
B2. Selective, partial conversion to Ni-HITP shell (RT-IMC):
- Delivery of HITP via vapor-phase infiltration (VPI) or scCO2 carrier to avoid liquid solvent exposure and to confine reaction to accessible surfaces.
- Conversion depth control: vary exposure time/temperature to achieve shell thickness tShell = 2, 5, 10 nm (three discrete design points). Maintain an unconverted NiOx/Ni(OH)x core for mechanical anchoring and to prevent full porosity penetration.
- Lateral percolation target: continuous conducting path across device area at minimal areal coverage. Use 4-point probe sheet resistance mapping and conductive-AFM to verify percolation.
B3. Anti-shunt design rule (process integration): enforce a “top-seal” criterion—after conversion, the nanomesh must present a continuous, pinhole-free top surface at the nm-scale even if subsurface is porous. Achieve via (i) limiting pore necks/openings through conversion conditions and/or (ii) an ultrathin conformal NiOx (≤2 nm) or molecular dipole layer as a shunt-suppression cap (control variable) that does not block hole extraction.

C. Mandatory Subpackage (1): Ion-chemistry/selectivity—quantitative, capacity-bounded, reversible
C1. Define the ion-interaction landscape (computation + experiment on three materials):
Materials: (a) Ni-HITP (dense reference film), (b) NiOx, (c) partially converted Ni-HITP@NiOx core–shell nanomesh.
Ions: I−, Br−, FA+, Cs+ (and optionally additives like BF4− if used).
C2. DFT binding-energy matrix (screening-level):
- Compute adsorption/binding energies (ΔEbind) for each ion on representative Ni-HITP motifs (Ni–N sites, pore walls) and NiOx surfaces (Ni2+/O2− terminations), including possible coordination/complexation geometries.
- Output: predicted selectivity ordering and identification of “dangerous” strong-binding/redox-prone motifs.
C3. Adsorption isotherms and capacities (experimental):
- Prepare films on inert substrates (glass/ITO) and expose to controlled ion sources:
  (i) halide exposure via volatile halide salts or controlled halide-containing vapor/aerosol;
  (ii) cation exposure via FA/Cs salts in non-reactive carriers; and
  (iii) electrochemical gating/ionic-liquid contact as a controlled way to dose ions without dissolving films.
- Measure uptake isotherms: Q(μion) or Q(C) for each ion type using quartz crystal microbalance (QCM), XPS quantification, and ToF-SIMS depth profiling.
- Determine saturation capacity Qsat and the Langmuir/Freundlich parameters for each ion/material.
C4. Bias-driven uptake/release and reversibility (operando):
- Build metal/HTL/(nanomesh)/blocking layer test structures (no perovskite) and perovskite/HTL stacks.
- Apply bias (and light) to drive ion motion; quantify uptake and release kinetics (kads/kdes) by time-resolved ToF-SIMS (before/after), operando Kelvin probe shifts, and transient ionic current.
- Reversibility metric: fraction released after bias removal/thermal anneal; define acceptable hysteresis in uptake ≤ 20% after 3 cycles.
C5. Predefine “maximum allowable ion uptake” criterion Qmax,allow (go/no-go):
- Couple ion uptake to electronic degradation: measure conductivity/work function shift, trap density (SCLC), and QFLS reduction as a function of ion loading.
- Define Qmax,allow as the uptake at which any of the following occurs: ΔWF > 100 meV irreversible shift, ΔQFLS drop > 20 meV, or interfacial recombination increase > 2× (from TPV/impedance). Designs must operate at Qoper ≤ 0.3·Qmax,allow under stress conditions.

D. Mandatory Subpackage (2): Energetics/transport—band diagram, percolation, CT-rate extraction
D1. Band-diagram hypothesis (before experiments):
- Construct expected energy levels: NiOx VB/EF, Ni-HITP EF/work function, perovskite VB/QFLS.
- Hypothesis: the nanomesh reduces interfacial energetic disorder (σE) and contact resistivity provided ΔEv (perovskite VB to effective HTL EF) is not increased and no interfacial dipole creates a blocking barrier.
D2. UPS/KPFM (dark + illuminated) and disorder quantification:
- UPS: measure work function and valence onset for NiOx, Ni-HITP, and core–shell nanomesh.
- KPFM mapping: spatial distribution of surface potential/work function to extract σWF as a proxy for energetic heterogeneity. Goal: σWF reduction vs baseline NiOx.
- Under 1-sun equivalent illumination: track photovoltage-induced surface potential changes to diagnose Fermi-level pinning.
D3. Temperature-dependent transport and percolation threshold:
