- Measure in-plane conductivity vs temperature for each nanomesh architecture (vary pore fraction and shell thickness). Fit to hopping/metallic models to identify transport regime.
- Extract percolation threshold pc by correlating conductivity with porosity and conversion depth (GISAXS/porosimetry + XPS depth).
- Go/no-go: achieve sheet resistance compatible with ΔRs not exceeding 0.2 Ω·cm2 contribution in device.
D4. Interfacial charge-transfer rate extraction (kCT) with physical models:
- Use perovskite-on-HTL PL quenching + time-resolved PL to estimate interfacial transfer.
- Complement with impedance spectroscopy (recombination/transport resistances) and TPV/TPC.
- Fit to drift–diffusion device model (and/or Marcus-type interfacial ET where appropriate) to extract kCT and/or surface recombination velocity S at the buried interface.
- Success criterion: kCT increases (or S decreases) in the nanomesh vs NiOx baseline without creating a barrier evidenced by reduced FF or increased ideality factor.

E. Mandatory Subpackage (3): NLO identifiability—decouple confounders, calibrated modeling, predictive link to kCT/S
E1. Simplified stacks and calibrated references:
- Build a set of optical test structures on transparent substrates:
  (i) Ni-HITP only (vary thickness),
  (ii) NiOx only,
  (iii) Ni-HITP@NiOx nanomesh (vary tShell and porosity),
  (iv) perovskite-free and perovskite-capped versions with controlled thickness.
- Include “doping/oxidation controls” where Ni-HITP is intentionally oxidized/reduced without changing interface coupling (as best as possible) to separate state-filling vs coupling.
E2. Optical transfer-matrix + effective-medium modeling:
- Measure linear optical constants (n,k) of each layer and nanomesh effective medium.
- Model local field factors and absorption contributions to the measured nonlinear signal for the multilayer stack.
- Extract χ(3) of the Ni-HITP component after correcting for thickness, absorption, and field enhancement.
E3. χ(3) measurement protocol and identifiability criterion:
- Use reflection Z-scan or pump–probe geometry through ITO side; keep excitation wavelength/pulse parameters constant.
- Decompose χ(3) response into instantaneous (electronic) and slower components (thermal/carrier relaxation) via time-resolved measurements.
- Identifiability requirement: across a designed perturbation set (vary tShell, porosity, controlled ion loading, and controlled band alignment adjustments), χ(3)-derived parameter(s) must predict independently extracted kCT or S with pre-set accuracy (e.g., R2 ≥ 0.8 and normalized prediction error ≤ 15%) *after* accounting for linear absorption and thickness.
- Go/no-go: if χ(3) correlates only with generic oxidation level (UPS/XPS) and not with kCT/S once confounders are modeled out, NLO is demoted to a qualitative monitor rather than a mechanistic diagnostic.

F. Integration into full PSCs and shunt/pinhole prevention
F1. Wetting/nucleation control plan (explicit risk mitigation):
- Quantify surface energy (contact angle) and roughness; adjust with an ultrathin wetting modifier (e.g., a robust, nonionic SAM) that does not interfere with energetics.
- Verify perovskite coverage: cross-sectional SEM/TEM and conductive-AFM to detect shunts.
F2. Large-area uniformity:
- Map sheet resistance and KPFM over ≥2.5×2.5 cm2; define uniformity spec: <10% variation.
F3. Device build + reliability:
- Fabricate PSCs with the full control set: pristine NiOx; porous non-converted mesh; dense Ni-HITP; porous Ni-HITP nanomesh; standard buried 2D passivation control (e.g., PEAI) without nanomesh.
- Stress tests: MPP tracking at 60–85 °C, plus bias-light stress for ion migration; periodic ToF-SIMS and χ(3) measurements at defined intervals.

G. Decision gates (summary)
G1. Ion package go/no-go: Qoper ≤ 0.3·Qmax,allow and ≥80% reversible release over cycles; no irreversible ΔWF > 100 meV.
G2. Energetics/transport go/no-go: no added barrier by UPS/KPFM + device FF; contact resistivity ≥3× lower; σWF reduced; kCT improved or S reduced.
G3. NLO identifiability go/no-go: χ(3) parameter predicts kCT or S across perturbed samples after optical-model correction (R2 ≥ 0.8; error ≤ 15%).
G4. Integration go/no-go: no increase in shunt-related leakage (J–V dark), and yield (PCE within 90% of median) ≥80% across area-mapped substrates.
Feasibility: 1) Chemical and materials plausibility grounded in literature assets: conductive HITP/HHTP-family MOFs are demonstrably capable of high charge transfer and strong third-order NLO response linked to carrier delocalization (Asset 1), and interfacial/templated synthesis can yield highly conductive, hierarchically porous Ni-HITP-type networks with robust cycling performance in ion-rich electrochemical environments (Asset 2). These two anchors justify (i) making Ni-HITP as an ultrathin percolating network rather than a thick film and (ii) treating χ(3) as intrinsically sensitive to electronic coupling—while the revised plan explicitly tests whether this sensitivity remains identifiable in buried PSC stacks.

2) Reviewer risk (ion sink/filter) is converted from a qualitative claim into a bounded, chemistry-specific, reversible buffering hypothesis: the proposal now commits to DFT + adsorption isotherms for I−/Br−/FA+/Cs+ on Ni-HITP, NiOx, and the core–shell material; measures saturation and bias-driven release; and defines Qmax,allow linked directly to electronic degradation (WF/QFLS/recombination). This directly addresses concerns about catalytic decomposition, selectivity, and saturation.

3) Reviewer risk (band/transport model and barriers) is addressed by an explicit energetics workflow: dark/illuminated UPS/KPFM (including disorder mapping), temperature-dependent conductivity to determine transport regime and percolation, and physically extracted kCT/S via drift–diffusion/Marcus-type modeling. The core–shell architecture is not assumed to “homogenize” levels; it is required to *demonstrate* reduced σWF and reduced contact resistivity without introducing an injection barrier.

4) Reviewer risk (NLO under-theorized) is addressed by identifiability design: simplified stacks, calibrated thickness/absorption controls, optical transfer-matrix/effective-medium corrections, and a predictive criterion linking χ(3) to independently extracted kCT/S across intentionally perturbed samples—not only aging correlations.

5) Process integration risk is mitigated through explicit anti-shunt and uniformity specifications: controlled conversion depths (2–10 nm shell), a top-seal criterion or ultrathin cap option, quantified wetting control, conductive-AFM leakage screening, and large-area mapping of sheet resistance/KPFM. These additions convert the porous-interface concept from a qualitative morphology claim into a manufacturable architecture with measurable uniformity and shunt suppression.

Collectively, the revised proposal transforms the central concept—an HTL-side, partially converted, hierarchically porous Ni-HITP nanomesh enabling improved hole extraction, ion-buffered stability, and χ(3)-based diagnostics—into a set of quantitative, falsifiable packages with go/no-go criteria aligned to PSC-relevant failure modes.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually well-resolved, with falsifiable mechanisms, quantitative gates, and appropriate metrology spanning ion chemistry, energetics, transport, and nonlinear optics. The principal weaknesses are (i) materials/processing ambiguity around whether Ni-HITP formation via VPI/scCO2 on Ni(OH)x/NiOx at ≤200 °C can reliably yield a π-delocalized, laterally percolating shell with reproducible stoichiometry/oxidation state across cm-scale substrates; (ii) risk of chemical incompatibility with halide-rich perovskite environments—Ni–N coordination frameworks and residual Ni(OH)x/Ni3+ sites can catalyze redox/iodine chemistry, and the proposal’s Qmax,allow definition may detect damage only after irreversible interfacial reactions have already occurred; (iii) identifiability of χ(3) to kCT/S remains the highest conceptual risk—despite the controls, χ(3) in conducting MOFs is strongly entangled with carrier density, polaron formation, heating, and microstructural disorder, and correlating to kCT/S across perturbations may be underdetermined without an explicit parameter-sensitivity/uniqueness analysis; (iv) the anti-shunt “top-seal” criterion is stated but not fully operationalized with a verifiable structural metric tied to device leakage statistics (e.g., allowable connected-pore fraction to the perovskite interface, maximum RMS roughness, and pinhole density thresholds). Overall, the concept chain is integrated credibly, but feasibility hinges on demonstrating controllable partial conversion and proving χ(3) uniqueness rather than correlation.
hypothesis_summary: A hierarchically porous Ni-HITP@NiOx core–shell nanomesh on the hole-selective contact enhances perovskite solar cells by homogenizing energetics, buffering ions within a safe capacity, and enabling nonlinear-optical diagnostics of interfacial health.

original_chain: Single-atom catalyst -> CO2 electroreduction -> Long-term stability -> Tafel slope -> Ni/Co bimetallic MOF nanoplate
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a stratified Ni/Co bimetallic MOF nanoplate network within the bulk of the hole-transport layer (HTL)—while preserving a pristine perovskite/HTL contact—and subsequently generating Ni/Co single-atom coordination sites via a *hard-engineered, post-fabrication coordination-exchange process* will enhance perovskite solar cell (PSC) operational stability without sacrificing Voc or FF. The refined mechanism explicitly overcomes prior limitations as follows: (i) a physically credible infiltration architecture (edge-access diffusion combined with a nanoperforated or ultrathin Au electrode) enables spatially uniform, self-limiting coordination exchange at ≤40 °C, producing isolated Ni/Co–N/S single-atom sites without perturbing perovskite chemistry or HTL doping; (ii) the MOF nanoplates function as a *quantified, finite-capacity ionic and redox buffer*, selectively binding halides (I−/Br−) and noble-metal cations (Au+) with known isotherms and breakthrough limits, thereby reducing net ionic flux to the electrode rather than merely delaying accumulation; (iii) stabilization arises from suppression of electrode-side redox cycling and radical-mediated corrosion, which is deconvoluted from bulk transport effects using PSC-relevant kinetic observables (ideality factor, transient optoelectronic response, operando impedance with DRT) rather than relying solely on apparent Tafel slopes; and (iv) the same coordination motifs are translated to CO2 electroreduction only within a pre-registered axial-ligation and redox-potential window, allowing a falsifiable test of which descriptors (e.g., redox-buffering capacity vs CO2* binding energy) are shared or divergent between PSC stabilization and CO2RR. This approach reframes the MOF/SAC not as an interfacial modifier but as a distributed, capacity-limited chemical potential regulator embedded within the HTL.
Plan: Step 1 – Device architecture and infiltration engineering.
1.1 Baseline PSC stack: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3 with alkylammonium halide surface passivation / HTL / Au. Use dopant-minimized PTAA or alternative low-ion-mobility polymer HTL.
1.2 Stratified HTL: deposit a pristine HTL contact layer (5–10 nm) directly on perovskite, followed by a MOF-doped HTL buffer layer (30–60 nm) containing 0.3–1.5 wt% Ni/Co MOF nanoplates.
1.3 Top electrode designed for post-fabrication access: (a) ultrathin Au (≤20 nm) with controlled nanoscale pinholes (via island growth or sacrificial polymer templating), or (b) patterned Au with sealed edge-access microchannels. Uniformity target: <15% variation in Ni/Co speciation across 5 mm lateral distance.

Step 2 – MOF synthesis and pre-quantification of ion capture.
2.1 Synthesize 2D Ni_xCo_(2−x) MOF nanoplates (x = 0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2) using pyridine-modulated solvothermal growth (Asset 3 logic), incorporating N-donor linkers with post-synthetically introducible thiol (–SH) groups.
2.2 Ex situ quantify ion-binding capacity and selectivity of MOF-in-HTL composites: perform calibrated uptake isotherms and breakthrough experiments for I−, Br−, Li+, TFSI−, and Au+ under electric fields (10^4–10^5 V cm−1) representative of operating PSCs. Extract maximum binding capacity (mol cm−3 HTL), selectivity coefficients, and desorption kinetics.
2.3 Define failure threshold: buffer considered effective only if total captured halide flux over 2000 h <70% of binding capacity, ensuring no late-stage back-diffusion.

Step 3 – Post-fabrication coordination exchange (hard-engineered).
3.1 Exchange chemistry: Cl−-assisted or thiol-assisted coordination exchange using vapor-phase or low-activity solution precursors (e.g., Me4NCl vapor or dilute thiol solution) introduced via edge-access channels at ≤40 °C.
3.2 Diffusion–reaction model: solve Fickian diffusion with first-order coordination trapping to predict penetration depth and time constants; experimentally validate by depth-resolved XPS/XAS after varying exposure times.
3.3 Self-limiting criterion: exchange terminates when isolated Ni/Co–N/S sites are thermodynamically favored over multinuclear nodes, with no MOF collapse (verified by TEM and XRD).

Step 4 – Kinetic and mechanistic validation (beyond Tafel slopes).
4.1 Replace sole reliance on Tafel analysis with PSC-relevant observables: intensity-dependent Voc (ideality factor), Suns–Voc, transient photovoltage/photocurrent, and operando impedance spectroscopy with distribution of relaxation times (DRT).
4.2 Controlled oxygen and water dosing under bias to isolate redox-buffering effects; correlate changes in recombination resistance and chemical capacitance with Ni/Co redox state reversibility.
4.3 If Tafel slopes are extracted from hole-only stacks, explicitly verify charge-transfer-limited regimes via thickness scaling, temperature dependence, and suppression of ionic redistribution.

Step 5 – Stability and mass balance.
5.1 Track Voc, FF, Jsc, hysteresis, EL efficiency, and PLQY under ISOS-L, ISOS-O, and damp-heat protocols. Target T80 > 2000 h at 60 °C, 1-sun MPP.
5.2 ToF-SIMS and mass balance: integrate ion profiles across HTL and electrode to confirm captured ion quantities match pre-measured MOF capacities.

Step 6 – CO2RR translation with pre-registered design space.
6.1 Predefine axial-ligation/coordination matrix (Cl vs S vs mixed; Ni:Co ratio) and expected descriptors: shared (redox potential window, ROS binding energy) vs divergent (CO2* adsorption energy).
6.2 Go/no-go criteria: motifs that stabilize PSCs but show high CO2RR overpotential or poor FE are classified as divergent; only motifs satisfying both stability windows are claimed as shared.
6.3 Test on gas-diffusion electrodes under matched current densities; measure FE, partial current density, Tafel slopes, and durability.
Feasibility: This refined proposal directly addresses reviewer concerns by converting conceptual plausibility into engineered controllability. Physically credible infiltration architectures (edge-access channels and nanoperforated Au) ensure uniform, low-temperature coordination exchange without exposing the perovskite to aggressive chemistry. Quantifying ion-binding isotherms and breakthrough behavior transforms the MOF from a speculative sink into a capacity-limited buffer with mass balance closure, mitigating the risk of delayed failure via back-diffusion. By replacing ambiguous Tafel-only interpretations with idealiy factors, transient techniques, and operando impedance with DRT, the proposal cleanly separates interfacial charge-transfer and redox buffering from transport and ionic artifacts. Finally, the CO2RR bridge is constrained by a pre-registered coordination/axial-ligation matrix with explicit go/no-go criteria, ensuring that any claimed overlap between PSC stabilization and CO2 electroreduction rests on shared, testable descriptors rather than analogy. Empirical precedents from MOF electrocatalysis (Assets 1–3) support the stability of Ni/Co coordination environments and their kinetic signatures, while the proposed architectural controls make the adaptation compatible with fragile perovskite devices.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in engineering specificity for a concept that is normally hand-waved (post-fabrication chemical access through Au; spatial uniformity metrics; diffusion–reaction modeling; capacity-limited buffering with breakthrough criteria; mechanistic deconvolution via ideality factor/transients/DRT rather than Tafel-only). The main deductions are (1) chemical compatibility risk is under-controlled: the proposed Cl−/thiol-assisted exchange introduced post-metallization could alter Au morphology/work function, PTAA (or additive) chemistry, and interfacial energetics via unintended halide/thiolate migration; the plan does not define strict analytical acceptance criteria for “no HTL doping/energetics change” (e.g., UPS/KPFM, mobility, trap DOS) beyond general statements. (2) The self-limiting SAC formation claim is plausible but not yet proven: many MOFs under halide/thiol exposure undergo partial ligand exchange, defect creation, or metal leaching; isolated-site verification needs operando or statistically robust ex situ methods (e.g., EXAFS coordination number distributions with uncertainty bounds, leaching quantification) tied to device processing conditions. (3) The ionic-buffer mass-balance framework is a real advance, but the key assumption—that electrode corrosion and performance loss are dominated by halide/Au+ flux that can be captured within the HTL—needs explicit falsification pathways versus competing failure modes (HTL oxidation, perovskite decomposition, interfacial dipole drift, Au diffusion independent of halide). (4) The CO2RR “translation” is conceptually constrained (good), but it remains somewhat orthogonal: CO2RR performance depends strongly on conductivity, mass transport, wettability, and potential-dependent restructuring, which are not isomorphic to PSC redox buffering; the proposal risks being two projects sharing materials motifs rather than a single descriptor-driven mechanistic program unless the shared descriptor set is made quantitatively predictive.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a stratified Ni/Co MOF nanoplate network within the hole-transport layer, then converting it to single-atom sites, creates a distributed chemical buffer that traps harmful ions and suppresses electrode corrosion, thereby extending perovskite solar cell stability without sacrificing voltage or fill factor.

original_chain: Atomically precise nanoclusters (APNCs) -> Covalent-organic frameworks (COFs) -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Molecular chirality -> Achiral components
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a **grain-boundary–localized, dual chemical crosslinking system**—comprising (i) a *single, fully specified, perovskite-compatible covalent reaction* and (ii) a *quantified Pb–ligand coordination crosslink network*—together with immobilized atomically precise nanoclusters (APNCs), will convert the perovskite grain-boundary (GB) network from a defect/ion-transport liability into a mechanically, chemically, and electronically functional phase. Specifically: (1) a catalyst-free, water-free strain‑promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC) between achiral monomers that preferentially segregate to GBs will generate an ultrathin, covalently crosslinked organic mesh that is kinetically inaccessible to the perovskite lattice interior; this mesh imposes nanoscale confinement, anisotropic strain, and static dipole gradients at GBs without requiring long-range periodicity. (2) A multidentate Pb2+-chelating ligand (phosphonate–pyridyl hybrid) introduced at sub‑mol% will form a *measurable Pb–ligand crosslink density* at PbX2-rich GB sites, increasing halide-vacancy hopping activation energies and suppressing ion migration in direct proportion to ligand loading and GB localization, without invoking an idealized MOF lattice. (3) APNCs (Au25-based) immobilized through partial ligand exchange with the Pb-chelating ligand will act as discrete, stable interfacial electronic states that modulate local band bending and interfacial dipoles. Under the non-centrosymmetric GB microenvironment created by confinement and strain, these APNC–ligand ensembles adopt a statistically biased conformational handedness, yielding a weak but persistent circular dichroism signal. Rather than presuming chirality-induced spin selectivity (CISS) as the dominant mechanism, the hypothesis posits a *testable hierarchy*: primary gains arise from trap passivation and ion-blocking; secondary Voc enhancements may arise from chiral/spin-selective effects only if falsifiable spin-transport criteria are met. This reframing yields a chemically derisked, causally attributable pathway from GB chemistry → reduced nonradiative recombination and ionic migration → higher QFLS, reduced hysteresis, and improved operational stability.
Plan: 1. **Baseline system and architectures**: Use (FA0.83Cs0.17)Pb(I0.75Br0.25)3 (1.68 eV) and FA/Cs PbI3 (1.55 eV) in both n–i–p (ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au) and p–i–n (ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag) stacks.

2. **Covalent chemistry package (fully specified)**:
   2.1 Reaction: Strain‑promoted azide–alkyne cycloaddition (SPAAC), chosen for catalyst-free, water-free operation in dry aprotic media.
   2.2 Monomers: (A) bis‑azide aromatic linker with limited solubility in the perovskite lattice; (B) bicyclo[6.1.0]nonyne (BCN)–terminated aromatic linker. Both are achiral and commercially validated.
   2.3 Kinetics derisking: Measure conversion vs time/temperature (60–120 °C) in DMF:DMSO (4:1) with dissolved PbI2/FAI to emulate precursor chemistry, using FTIR azide depletion. Establish a processing window (e.g., 80–90 °C, <10 min) achieving partial crosslinking without perovskite decomposition (verified by XRD/UV–vis).
   2.4 Localization control: Demonstrate GB segregation by TOF‑SIMS depth profiling and nano‑FTIR mapping; include controls with pre‑crosslinked polymer to show lack of bulk incorporation.

3. **Coordination crosslink network (quantified, not MOF)**:
   3.1 Ligand: Achiral pyridyl‑phosphonic acid monoester (protected during solution processing, deprotected thermally at 90–110 °C) enabling strong Pb2+ chelation without proton release during deposition.
   3.2 Metric: Define crosslink density as Pb–ligand coordination number per GB area (from XPS Pb 4f shifts and solid-state NMR where feasible).
   3.3 Ion-migration measurement: Temperature-dependent EIS and transient ion-drift experiments to extract activation energies (Ea) for halide migration as a function of ligand loading (0–0.2 mol%).

4. **APNC integration and stability pretests**:
   4.1 Cluster: Au25(SR)18 with mixed thiolate shell; 10–20% ligands replaced ex situ by pyridyl‑terminated thiols compatible with the coordination ligand.
   4.2 Stability tests: Monitor UV–vis fingerprints and MALDI before/after exposure to DMF/DMSO + halides and after annealing at 100 °C. Reject conditions showing >10% spectral degradation.
   4.3 Loading: 10–100 ppm relative to perovskite solids.

5. **Sequential formation during film processing**:
   5.1 Spin-coating with DNPS + APNCs → antisolvent quench.
   5.2 Anneal 1 (80–90 °C): activate SPAAC at GBs.
   5.3 Anneal 2 (100–110 °C): activate Pb–ligand coordination and APNC immobilization.

6. **Chirality validation (artifact-free)**:
   6.1 Mueller-matrix ellipsometry to separate true CD from linear dichroism/birefringence.
   6.2 Film rotation, front/back illumination, and thickness controls.
   6.3 Compare DNPS-only, APNC-only, and combined systems.

7. **Spin-transport falsification tests**:
   7.1 Fabricate control devices with nonmagnetic vs ferromagnetic (NiFe) contacts in a vertical spin-valve geometry.
   7.2 Perform Hanle-like depolarization measurements; predict sign/magnitude changes only if chiral GB phase is present.

8. **Pre-registered decision tree**:
   - If QFLS↑ and Voc↑ correlate with reduced trap density (TRPL/TPV) but not with Ea(ion) → passivation-dominated.
   - If hysteresis↓ and Ea↑ without QFLS change → ion-blocking-dominated.
   - Only if CD + spin-valve asymmetry appear without changes in trap/Ea metrics → chiral/spin contribution.

9. **Stability and scalability**: MPP tracking at 65–85 °C, ToF‑SIMS after bias stress, and blade-coated films using identical thermal triggers.
Feasibility: This revision directly addresses reviewer concerns by replacing ambiguous reticular claims with **chemically explicit, falsifiable processes**. SPAAC chemistry is well-established in dry aprotic solvents and requires no catalysts or byproduct removal, making it compatible with perovskite processing. Defining the coordination network via measurable Pb–ligand crosslink density avoids overclaiming MOF periodicity while still enabling quantitative structure–property correlations for ion migration. Chirality is treated conservatively: emergence is tested with artifact-free optics, and its electronic relevance is evaluated only through falsifiable spin-transport experiments with clear null hypotheses. APNC stability is derisked through mandatory pretests before device integration. Finally, the pre-registered decision tree ensures that improvements in Voc, hysteresis, and stability can be causally attributed to passivation, ionic blocking, or interfacial energetics rather than post hoc CISS arguments. The proposal thus remains conceptually novel—functionalizing the GB network itself—while being chemically grounded and experimentally decisive.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and chemically explicit proposal that largely succeeds in derisking a highly ambitious grain-boundary functionalization concept. Major strengths include: (i) replacement of vague COF/MOF analogies with fully specified covalent and coordination chemistries; (ii) quantitative treatment of ion-migration suppression via measurable Pb–ligand crosslink density; (iii) conservative, falsifiable framing of chirality and CISS, avoiding the common overreach in this area; and (iv) a pre-registered decision tree that enforces causal attribution. Minor deductions arise from residual complexity and integration risk: sequential activation of SPAAC, deprotection, coordination, and APNC immobilization within narrow thermal windows may prove kinetically entangled at scale, and the assumption that SPAAC remains strictly GB-localized under realistic film inhomogeneity is plausible but not yet proven. Additionally, while the COF/MOF concepts are invoked metaphorically and responsibly, the proposal still relies on indirect evidence (spectroscopy, Ea trends) rather than direct real-space mapping of crosslink topology at GBs.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a dual chemical crosslinking system and atomically precise nanoclusters at perovskite grain boundaries transforms them from defect pathways into a functional phase that blocks ion migration, passivates traps, and enhances device stability.

original_chain: Catalytic efficiency -> Interface engineering -> Transition metal-based catalysts -> Long-term stability -> F coating
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A fluorinated catalytic interfacial coating (FCIC) can improve both operational stability and charge-extraction kinetics in n–i–p perovskite solar cells only if (and to the extent that) the interfacial transition-metal oxyhydroxide nanoclusters operate in an energetically permitted, bias- and illumination-accessible, *reversible* redox window that overlaps the perovskite quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) while remaining electronically non-percolating and chemically de-wetted from the perovskite/ambient. Specifically: an ultrathin fluorinated SAM (F‑SAM) on the oxide ETL establishes (i) a hydrophobic/low-polarity barrier that reduces O2/H2O activity at the interface and suppresses oxygen-vacancy-driven interfacial redox and halide accumulation, and (ii) a controllable interfacial dipole that tunes the ETL work function to minimize extraction barriers without increasing interfacial carrier density. Atomically thin, *sub-percolation* NiFeOOH (or FeCoOOH) clusters tethered to sparse anchoring sites on this F‑SAM can then serve as a selective interfacial charge ‘buffer’ only when their M(III)/M(II) couple is aligned such that (a) interfacial trapped electrons (ETL-side) can be transiently accepted and returned on sub-µs–ms timescales (reducing trap occupation lifetime) while (b) electron transfer from the interfacial region to molecular O2 is suppressed primarily by O2 exclusion (F‑SAM) and secondarily by reduced interfacial electron chemical potential (dipole tuning). This resolves the apparent tension between ‘faster charge transfer’ and ‘more superoxide’ by designing FCIC as a *kinetic de-trapping mediator under O2/H2O-limited interfacial conditions*, not as a general electron donor to dissolved oxidants. The proposal is falsifiable: if (1) the oxyhydroxide redox potentials do not overlap the device QFLS window, or (2) a non-redox-active morphological analog yields identical gains, or (3) improvements persist under O2-free conditions but vanish under controlled O2 series, then the dominant mechanism is passivation/barrier rather than catalytic redox mediation.
Plan: Step 0 — Architecture and baseline definition
0.1 Device stack (baseline n–i–p): glass/ITO/ETL/perovskite/HTL/Au, where ETL is either ALD-SnO2 (preferred for low-temperature processing) or compact TiO2. Perovskite: FA/Cs mixed-cation, I/Br mixed-halide tuned to ~1.55 eV bandgap; HTL: PTAA (primary) with spiro-OMeTAD as secondary confirmation.
0.2 Pre-register target performance/stability endpoints: (i) ΔVoc deficit reduction and (ii) PCE retention at 500 h and 1000 h in ISOS-L-2-like conditions. Pre-register maximum acceptable series-resistance increase (≤5% vs control at 1 sun MPP) and maximum acceptable hysteresis index change (≤0.02 absolute).

Step 1 — Control matrix (expanded to discriminate catalysis vs passivation)
1.1 Core four surfaces/devices:
(A) pristine ETL;
(B) F‑SAM only;
(C) oxyhydroxide clusters only (no F‑SAM);
(D) FCIC = F‑SAM + tethered clusters.
1.2 Mandatory discriminant controls:
(E) FCIC-inert analog: F‑SAM + electronically inert, non-redox nanoclusters with similar morphology/roughness (e.g., AlOOH or Mg(OH)2; choose the phase confirmed by XRD/XPS) deposited to match cluster areal density/attenuation of (D).
(F) FCIC-redox-blocked: F‑SAM + NiFeOOH (or FeCoOOH) in a redox-suppressed state. Implement two orthogonal approaches:
   (F1) Chemical ‘locking’ by pre-setting oxidation state (pre-oxidized vs pre-reduced) and verifying persistence under device-relevant bias by operando XPS (see Step 6). Pre-oxidize electrochemically to high-valent state; pre-reduce to lower-valent state; then encapsulate promptly to limit air drift.
   (F2) Composition ‘locking’ by substituting a redox-inactive analog within the same structure that preserves morphology but suppresses M(III)/M(II) cycling (e.g., NiAlOOH-like or Fe-free NiOOH vs NiFeOOH; choice guided by independent redox characterization in Step 3).
1.3 Optional process-risk control:
(G) If any CF4/plasma is used, it becomes a separate factorial variable with its own matched controls: (B+plasma), (D+plasma), (E+plasma), and must pass SAM-order diagnostics (Step 2.4) before device fabrication.

Step 2 — Interlayer chemistry with quantified parameters (SAM + anchoring)
2.1 F‑SAM selection: perfluoroalkyl phosphonic acid (PFPA) on SnO2/TiO2 for robust binding. Target thickness: 0.6–1.2 nm (ellipsometry + XPS attenuation cross-check). Target water contact angle: ≥95° (as a proxy for low water activity at interface).
2.2 Mixed-SAM anchoring strategy to avoid pinholes and preserve fluorinated barrier:
- Use a binary SAM mixture in solution with a minor fraction of polar head-terminated phosphonic acid to create sparse coordination sites. Start with 2 mol%, 5 mol%, 10 mol% anchor fraction (e.g., carboxyl-terminated alkyl phosphonic acid) in a PFPA matrix.
- Acceptance criterion: SAM must remain hydrophobic (contact angle drop ≤10° relative to pure PFPA) and must not measurably increase ETL surface leakage (c-AFM mapping, Step 4.3).
2.3 Anchoring-site verification:
- XPS (C 1s, F 1s, P 2p) to quantify PFPA coverage; verify anchor incorporation by tracking carboxyl/amine signature.
- KPFM/UPS on ETL/SAM stacks to quantify work-function shift vs anchor fraction.
2.4 If plasma/CF4 reinforcement is attempted (only after initial SAM+cluster results):
- Define a narrow process window: low-power (≤10 W), short duration (≤10–20 s), high pressure to minimize ion energy; verify no increase in oxide oxygen vacancies (XPS O 1s + EPR) and no loss of SAM order (NEXAFS or FTIR-RAIRS; ellipsometry stability). If any diagnostic fails, plasma step is dropped.

Step 3 — Energetics: band alignment + redox feasibility mapped against QFLS (mandatory)
3.1 Work-function and band alignment mapping:
- UPS (secondary electron cutoff + valence region) and KPFM on: ETL (A), ETL/F‑SAM (B), ETL/clusters (C), ETL/FCIC (D), ETL/FCIC-inert (E). Extract work function (Φ), valence onset trends, and surface potential uniformity.
- Build full band diagram by combining UPS/KPFM with optical bandgap (ETL) and known perovskite band edges (validated by XPS/UPS on perovskite films made on each interlayer).
3.2 Independent determination of NiFeOOH/FeCoOOH redox potentials in PSC-relevant dielectric environments:
- Prepare model electrodes: ITO/ETL/SAM(+anchors)/clusters, measured in an *aprotic, low-water* electrolyte and in a controlled low-activity water environment (system chosen to bracket device-relevant hydration; report water activity explicitly).
- Use cyclic voltammetry to locate M(III)/M(II) features; calibrate vs Fc/Fc+ then convert to vacuum scale.
- Repeat on inert analog (AlOOH/Mg(OH)2) to confirm absence of redox features.
3.3 Perovskite QFLS under 1-sun on each interface:
- Measure absolute PL and extract QFLS for perovskite films deposited on A–F interlayers under 1 sun equivalent. Map QFLS energy window against measured redox couple energy and ETL work function.
3.4 Go/no-go criterion for ‘redox mediator’ claim:
- Proceed with redox-mediated hypothesis testing only if the measured redox couple lies within (or within ~0.2–0.3 eV of) the operational QFLS window and does not introduce an extraction barrier (UPS/KPFM indicates no adverse band bending).

Step 4 — Quantifying cluster coverage, percolation risk, and resistive losses (mandatory)
4.1 Cluster deposition routes (low hydration, low thermal budget):
- Primary: electrochemical deposition from controlled aqueous micro-environment (minimize exposure time) followed by immediate vacuum drying and mild anneal ≤100 °C.
- Secondary: solution hydrolysis route in anhydrous/low-water solvent system if feasible; goal is to limit structural water.
4.2 Areal density/coverage quantification (not just ‘effective thickness’):
- XPS attenuation model (Sn 3d/Ti 2p attenuation + F 1s persistence) to estimate overlayer coverage.
- STEM (plan-view) counting to quantify cluster number density and size distribution; cross-sectional STEM/EELS to confirm discontinuity.
- Define coverage series: 0.5%, 1%, 2%, 5%, 10% projected area coverage (operational definition from STEM). Hard cap: below electrical percolation; initial cap at ≤5% unless TLM/c-AFM supports higher.
4.3 Electrical acceptance criteria:
- Transfer length method (TLM) on ETL/interlayer stacks (and completed devices where feasible) to quantify added sheet/contact resistance.
- Conductive-AFM current maps to ensure clusters do not form continuous shunting paths; acceptance: no increase in low-resistance hotspot density relative to (A)/(B).

Step 5 — Device fabrication and standard PV metrics
5.1 Fabricate devices for each condition A–F (and G if plasma used), n≥20 per condition for statistics.
5.2 Measure J–V (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP, EQE, Voc deficit, FF, hysteresis index. Report distribution (median, IQR) and yield.

Step 6 — Operando proof of reversible redox cycling vs passive passivation (mandatory discriminants)
6.1 Operando/AP-XPS or near-operando XPS/UPS:
- Track Ni/Fe oxidation states (and Co if used) under dark, 1-sun illumination, and applied bias approximating Voc and MPP for model stacks (ETL/interlayer/perovskite or ETL/interlayer only).
- Required signature for ‘catalysis’: reversible, bias-dependent shift in Ni/Fe multiplet/peak positions consistent with M(III)/M(II) cycling in (D) that is absent in (E) and strongly reduced/absent in (F).
6.2 Transient kinetics consistent with de-trapping mediation:
- Transient photovoltage/photocurrent + impedance spectroscopy under illumination to separate transport resistance vs recombination resistance.
- Compare (D) vs (B) and (E): if only (D) shows reduced trap-related time constants without a commensurate increase in recombination pathways, supports mediator role.

Step 7 — ROS vs O2-exclusion decoupling (mandatory)
7.1 Controlled O2 partial pressure series at constant water activity:
- Run devices or model stacks under controlled atmosphere where pO2 is varied (e.g., 0, 0.2, 1, 20%) while holding humidity constant (fixed RH or fixed water activity via gas mixing). Record (i) ROS signal and (ii) PV parameters/hysteresis.
- Hypothesis test: if FCIC benefit persists even as pO2 increases but ROS signatures remain suppressed relative to (B)/(E), indicates active quenching beyond simple exclusion; if benefit collapses with pO2, exclusion dominates.
7.2 Isotope-labeled oxygen tracing:
- Expose stressed stacks/devices to 18O2 under illumination; use AP-XPS and/or ToF-SIMS to detect 18O incorporation associated with superoxide-derived pathways at/near ETL interface.
- Success metric: (D) shows significantly reduced 18O incorporation vs (A)/(B)/(E) at matched pO2 and RH.
7.3 EPR spin trapping for superoxide:
- Quantify O2− generation under illumination for A–F; correlate with pO2 dependence and with 18O incorporation.

Step 8 — Stability testing with pre-registered failure criteria and decision-tree attribution (mandatory)
8.1 Stress protocols:
- ISOS-L-2-like: continuous 1-sun at 45–60 °C, controlled RH; include both unencapsulated and encapsulated sets.
- ISOS-D-2-like dark heat; plus thermal cycling.
8.2 Pre-registered failure criteria:
- Failure = PCE drops to 80% of initial (T80), or irreversible hysteresis increase >0.05, or Voc loss >50 mV sustained.
8.3 Failure mode decision-tree (each node requires ≥2 orthogonal diagnostics):
Node I: Halide pile-up / ion migration dominant
- ToF-SIMS depth profile (I−/Br−/Cs+/FA+ distributions) + cross-sectional STEM/EELS (interfacial phase/segregation) and/or KPFM potential mapping after bias stress.
Node II: Oxide reduction / oxygen vacancies dominant
- XPS O 1s deconvolution + EPR vacancy signal (before/after stress) and conductivity change (TLM).
Node III: Electrode diffusion dominant
- ToF-SIMS (Au or metal marker) + TEM/EELS at top interface; correlate with FF collapse.
Node IV: Interlayer-induced recombination/shunting
- c-AFM hotspot density increase + light-intensity-dependent Voc/ideality factor changes + impedance recombination resistance drop.

Step 9 — Scaling and manufacturability relevance
9.1 Transfer FCIC to 5×5 cm substrates using dip-coating (SAM) and low-temperature electrodeposition with in-line rinsing/drying.
9.2 Map PL/QFLS uniformity and device performance distribution; acceptance: <10% relative standard deviation in PCE across area and no edge-localized failure signatures.

Milestones / go-no-go summary
M1 (Energetics): redox couple overlaps operational QFLS window; no adverse band alignment.
M2 (Percolation): coverage window identified where ΔRs ≤5% and no shunting.
M3 (Discriminants): (D) outperforms both (E) and (F) in kinetics and/or stability; operando shows reversible redox only in (D).
M4 (ROS attribution): reduced ROS/18O incorporation in (D) relative to (B)/(E) under matched pO2 and RH.
If any milestone fails, the mechanism is revised to ‘dipole/barrier passivation’ and oxyhydroxide is replaced with a less hydrated, better-aligned redox mediator or removed.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing energetic plausibility (reviewer items a–c): This revision makes the redox-mediator claim conditional on measured alignment between (i) ETL/SAM work function (UPS/KPFM), (ii) independently measured cluster M(III)/M(II) redox energies in low-water dielectric environments, and (iii) perovskite QFLS under 1-sun (absolute PL). This directly constrains whether the oxyhydroxide can couple to interfacial trapped carriers without creating an extraction barrier or a recombination channel.

2) Decoupling ‘catalysis’ from ‘passivation’: Two mandatory controls—(E) an inert morphological analog and (F) redox-blocked oxyhydroxide—ensure that any improvement uniquely requiring reversible redox cycling is distinguishable from hydrophobicity/dipole passivation. Operando oxidation-state tracking under device-relevant bias/illumination provides a direct, falsifiable signature of cycling.

3) Managing the superoxide tension with controlled atmospheres: Rather than assuming quenching, the plan explicitly separates O2 exclusion from ROS quenching via pO2 series at fixed water activity and 18O2 tracing coupled to AP-XPS/ToF-SIMS. This tests whether FCIC reduces superoxide-derived incorporation beyond what a fluorinated barrier alone achieves.

4) Controlling recombination and series-resistance risk from wide-gap, hydrated oxyhydroxides: The cluster layer is forced into a non-percolating regime with quantified areal density (STEM counting + XPS attenuation) and electrically validated by TLM and c-AFM hotspot mapping. This responds to the concern that oxyhydroxides may introduce trap states or barriers by ensuring discontinuous coverage and enforcing a hard cap via resistive-loss criteria.

5) Controlling the ‘mixed-SAM pinhole’ risk: The anchor fraction is treated as a designed variable (2–10 mol%) with explicit hydrophobicity and leakage acceptance criteria. This prevents assuming the halide-repelling barrier survives anchoring; it is measured.

6) De-risking CF4/plasma as a confound: Plasma is demoted from an unstructured ‘optional’ step to a gated factorial variable with a narrow window and mandatory diagnostics for SAM order and oxide vacancy density. If diagnostics fail, the plasma arm is terminated.

7) Failure mode attribution and statistical rigor: A pre-registered decision-tree with two orthogonal diagnostics per failure mode (ion pile-up, oxide reduction, electrode diffusion, shunting) ensures stability claims are mechanistically anchored and not over-interpreted. n≥20 devices per condition reduces false positives in stability comparisons.

8) Literature grounding and transfer logic: The approach retains the validated benefits of fluorine-modified oxide ETLs (reduced reflection/oxygen vacancies and improved long-term stability; Asset 3) while importing the interface-engineering principle that heterointerfaces can lower kinetic barriers and improve durability (Asset 2) and that defect/strain/interface control governs catalytic kinetics (Asset 1). The revised plan explicitly verifies that such ‘catalytic’ principles are energetically accessible and do not trade off recombination—precisely the reviewer’s central concern.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-controlled proposal that directly addresses the central mechanistic ambiguity in applying transition-metal oxyhydroxides to perovskite interfaces: whether observed benefits arise from true reversible redox mediation or from passive dipole/barrier effects. The engineering plan is exceptionally detailed, with appropriate use of operando XPS, absolute PL-derived QFLS, controlled-atmosphere ROS diagnostics, and quantified percolation limits. Logical consistency is strong—the hypothesis is explicitly conditional, energetically constrained, and falsifiable. Minor deductions arise from practical risk: (i) the sheer experimental breadth (AP-XPS, isotope tracing, operando biasing) may strain feasibility within a single grant period, and (ii) maintaining redox-state ‘locking’ of hydrated oxyhydroxides under device bias and illumination may prove less stable than assumed, potentially blurring F vs D discrimination. These are execution risks rather than conceptual flaws.
hypothesis_summary: A fluorinated coating with atomically thin redox-active nanoclusters improves perovskite solar cell stability and efficiency by enabling reversible charge de-trapping, but only if the cluster redox potentials align with the cell’s operating energy window.

original_chain: Reticular frameworks -> Nanocomposites -> Stability enhancement -> Nanocomposites -> Loading capacity -> Catalytic activity -> Heterojunction -> Reusability
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a MOF-derived reticular-framework nanocomposite, converted in situ into a semiconductor/oxide heterojunction with embedded redox-active catalytic sites, can be integrated as a *recyclable charge-transport scaffold* in perovskite solar cells to simultaneously increase interfacial loading capacity, suppress ion-migration-induced degradation, and enhance operational stability. The core methodological adaptation is to transform a thin, solution-processable MOF interlayer deposited beneath the perovskite into a nanocomposite heterojunction (e.g., NiO–NiOOH@C or SnO2–SnOx@C) via low-temperature oxidative conversion, thereby creating a reticular, electrically percolative, and catalytically active framework that (i) immobilizes a high density of passivating/catalytic sites without molecular diffusion into the perovskite, (ii) forms an energetically favorable heterojunction for selective charge extraction, and (iii) catalytically buffers interfacial redox species (I0/I3−, O2−) responsible for long-term instability. Unlike conventional passivators or nanoparticle additives, the framework-derived nanocomposite remains structurally intact and can be reclaimed and reused as a transport scaffold after perovskite removal.
Plan: Step 1: System definition and reticular precursor design.
- Select two representative device architectures: (A) p–i–n: ITO/NiOx/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/C60/BCP/Ag and (B) n–i–p: ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au.
- Synthesize ultrathin MOF films directly on ITO or NiOx/SnO2 using layer-by-layer liquid-phase epitaxy (e.g., Ni-MOF-74 or Sn-based MOF analogues) to precisely control thickness (5–20 nm) and loading capacity of metal nodes.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation – in situ MOF-to-nanocomposite heterojunction conversion.
- Apply a low-temperature (≤250 °C) oxidative or plasma-assisted conversion to partially transform the MOF metal nodes into mixed-valence oxide/hydroxide domains (e.g., NiO/NiOOH or SnO2/SnOx) while carbonizing the organic linkers into a conductive, porous carbon matrix.
- This yields a reticular nanocomposite with (i) preserved framework porosity, (ii) embedded semiconductor/oxide heterojunctions, and (iii) high surface density of redox-active sites.
- Tune conversion degree to balance conductivity, work function, and catalytic activity; quantify loading capacity via ICP-MS and porosity retention via BET.

Step 3: Perovskite integration and heterojunction validation.
- Deposit the perovskite absorber directly onto the converted nanocomposite scaffold, leveraging its porous surface to promote heterogeneous nucleation and strain relaxation.
- Characterize band alignment and heterojunction energetics using UPS, KPFM, and temperature-dependent J–V.
- Probe charge extraction and recombination via TRPL, transient photocurrent/photovoltage, and absolute PLQY.

Step 4: Mechanistic interrogation of stability enhancement and catalytic activity.
- Evaluate ion migration suppression using bias-stress ToF-SIMS and impedance spectroscopy.
- Assess catalytic redox buffering by operando EPR and in situ UV–Vis to monitor superoxide and iodine species under illumination and oxygen exposure.
- Correlate catalytic turnover (redox cycling of metal nodes) with reduced Voc loss and hysteresis.

Step 5: Reusability and lifecycle testing.
- Remove degraded perovskite layers using selective solvent washing, leaving the inorganic nanocomposite scaffold intact.
- Re-deposit fresh perovskite layers for ≥3 cycles and quantify retention of Voc, FF, and interfacial energetics.
- Benchmark against conventional compact NiOx/SnO2 layers and molecular passivation strategies at matched initial PCE.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: MOF-derived nanocomposites are known to retain reticular porosity while forming catalytically active semiconductor/oxide heterojunctions with high surface area and tunable redox properties. Mixed-valence oxides (e.g., NiO/NiOOH, SnO2/SnOx) exhibit proven catalytic activity toward iodine and oxygen redox couples, directly relevant to PSC degradation pathways.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC failure is dominated by interfacial recombination, ion migration, and photo-oxidative chemistry at transport-layer interfaces. Converting a reticular MOF into a stable nanocomposite scaffold embeds high loading capacity of immobilized active sites exactly at these interfaces, forming an energetically selective heterojunction while avoiding the diffusion and desorption issues of molecular additives.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional nanoparticle-doped transport layers or organic passivators, this approach uniquely combines (i) framework-defined loading capacity, (ii) built-in heterojunction formation, (iii) catalytic stabilization of redox species, and (iv) true reusability of the transport scaffold. This directly addresses stability and sustainability bottlenecks while remaining compatible with scalable thin-film processing.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-reasoned proposal that demonstrates strong command of MOF-derived nanocomposites and perovskite interfacial physics. The engineering plan is detailed, with credible synthesis, conversion, and characterization workflows that go beyond generic PSC passivation strategies. The logical chain connecting reticular loading capacity, immobilized redox catalysis, and suppression of ion-migration-driven degradation is coherent and mostly convincing. However, several mechanistic links remain under-quantified: (i) the assumption that catalytic buffering of I0/I3− and superoxide at buried interfaces will not introduce parasitic recombination or Fermi-level pinning is asserted rather than rigorously bounded; (ii) the impact of partial carbonization and mixed-valence oxides on interfacial defect energetics and contact selectivity is not sufficiently risk-assessed; and (iii) the reusability claim, while conceptually attractive, lacks a degradation model for the nanocomposite itself under repeated oxidative/redox cycling. Evidence grounding is strong and domain-appropriate, but the proposal occasionally leans on catalytic analogies from electrocatalysis without fully translating kinetics and turnover relevance to the low-flux PSC environment. Overall, this is a high-level proposal with minor but nontrivial logical and mechanistic gaps preventing a near-perfect score.
hypothesis_summary: A recyclable MOF-derived nanocomposite scaffold forms a semiconductor/oxide heterojunction with catalytic sites, simultaneously boosting charge extraction, suppressing ion migration, and catalytically buffering degradation species to enhance perovskite solar cell stability.

original_chain: Negative Gaussian curvature -> FeN4 coordination -> bmFeSAC -> Electrocatalytic activity -> Co-N-C catalysts -> Electrocatalytic activity -> Single-atom catalyst -> Turnover frequency (TOF)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Integrating a bicontinuous mesoporous Fe single-atom catalyst with FeN4 coordination and negative Gaussian curvature (bmFeSAC) as an interfacial electrocatalytic scaffold at the perovskite/transport-layer junction will actively accelerate interfacial redox equilibration and suppress non-radiative recombination, thereby increasing the effective turnover frequency (TOF) of charge extraction events and enhancing both power conversion efficiency and operational stability of perovskite solar cells. The core mechanism is that negative Gaussian curvature maximizes exposure and electronic coupling of FeN4 single-atom sites, which catalytically mediate interfacial charge transfer and defect-assisted redox reactions, reducing carrier accumulation, mitigating ion-migration-induced degradation, and stabilizing the interfacial Fermi level alignment.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
Synthesize bmFeSAC using polymer cubosome templating to achieve Schwarz P-type bicontinuous mesoporosity with controlled Fe loading (≈1–2 wt.%) and confirmed FeN4 coordination via XANES/EXAFS. Disperse bmFeSAC as an ultrathin (<10 nm) interlayer ink compatible with orthogonal solvents. Prepare high-quality mixed-cation mixed-halide perovskite absorbers (e.g., FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3) with controlled crystallization.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
Insert the bmFeSAC layer at a critical interface (either perovskite/electron transport layer or perovskite/hole transport layer). Unlike conventional passive interlayers, engineer partial electronic coupling by tuning the carbon matrix conductivity and surface functional groups to ensure selective charge tunneling. The negative Gaussian curvature ensures continuous percolation pathways, while isolated FeN4 sites act as single-atom electrocatalysts that accelerate interfacial electron–hole extraction and catalytically neutralize interfacial redox-active defects (e.g., Pb0/I0 species). Optimize curvature density and Fe site density to maximize interfacial TOF without parasitic recombination.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
Quantify interfacial charge-transfer TOF using intensity-dependent transient photovoltage/photocurrent and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy under illumination. Correlate TOF with FeN4 density and curvature parameters. Use operando Kelvin probe force microscopy to map interfacial potential stabilization. Compare against control devices using flat Fe–N–C, Co–N–C, and no interlayer. Conduct accelerated stability tests (thermal, light, and bias stress) to link electrocatalytic activity with suppressed hysteresis and reduced ion migration.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Single-atom FeN4 sites are known to exhibit high electrocatalytic activity and fast electron-transfer kinetics. Negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous architectures empirically maximize active-site utilization and reduce reaction barriers, as demonstrated in bmFeSAC ORR systems.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): While electrocatalysts are traditionally used in fuel cells, this proposal adapts their function to PSC interfaces, where charge extraction and interfacial redox reactions are rate-limiting. The bmFeSAC is repurposed from bulk catalysis to an ultrathin interfacial electrocatalytic layer, directly addressing PSC-specific bottlenecks such as interfacial recombination and instability.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike conventional insulating passivation layers or flat M–N–C additives, bmFeSAC uniquely combines (i) single-atom catalytic precision, (ii) curvature-induced electronic modulation, and (iii) continuous transport channels. This enables active, self-regulating interfaces that enhance TOF of charge extraction rather than merely blocking defects, offering a step-change improvement in both efficiency and operational stability.
final_critique: The proposal is inventive and uses reasonably modern characterization (XAS, operando KPFM, TPV/TPC, EIS), but it overstates “electrocatalytic” redox mediation at a PSC interface without specifying the operative redox couples, reaction pathways, or thermodynamic driving forces under device operating potentials. The central claim—FeN4 sites catalytically neutralize Pb0/I0 and accelerate interfacial redox equilibration—needs a chemically explicit mechanism (which defects, which charge states, what kinetics, what competing parasitic reactions) and a clear argument that such catalysis will not introduce new non-radiative channels or chemical instability (e.g., Fe-mediated halide/iodine redox cycling, carbon/Fe interactions with perovskite decomposition products, band-offset perturbations). The TOF concept is not rigorously defined for a photovoltaic interface: TPV/TPC/EIS yield time constants and recombination/extraction resistances, but converting these into a site-normalized TOF requires an explicit model tying extracted charge flux to an independently quantified active-site density actually participating at the buried interface. Engineering-wise, producing a uniform, pinhole-free <10 nm bmFeSAC layer that remains bicontinuous, electrically selective, and chemically compatible with perovskite/CTL processing is nontrivial; the plan lacks concrete deposition/solvent orthogonality details, surface energy control, and verification of interfacial continuity/coverage. Finally, “negative Gaussian curvature” is treated as inherently beneficial, but no measurement/parameterization (e.g., curvature distribution, accessible site fraction at the interface vs. in-plane) is proposed that directly connects curvature to electronic coupling and PSC-relevant kinetics.
hypothesis_summary: Integrating a bicontinuous mesoporous Fe single-atom catalyst with negative Gaussian curvature at perovskite interfaces actively accelerates charge extraction and suppresses recombination, boosting solar cell efficiency and stability.

original_chain: Atomically precise nanoclusters (APNCs) -> Catalytic activity -> Ni3Fe1 -> Catalytic activity -> Ostwald ripening -> Fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a dilute population of atomically precise nanoclusters (APNCs) inside an ultrathin, grain-boundary–preferential Ni3Fe1-derived NiFeOOH “reactive glaze” will increase perovskite Voc (via higher QFLS) and suppress photo-thermal coarsening by satisfying two quantitative, falsifiable conditions:

(A) Photophysics (FRET must be net-beneficial to QFLS): The glaze is engineered so that Förster energy transfer from perovskite band-edge excitations into APNC excitonic manifolds is fast compared with trap capture at the top surface/GBs (k_FRET ≥ 3×k_trap,GB) while APNC excitons do not introduce an additional non-radiative sink that couples back to the perovskite electronic quasi-Fermi levels (i.e., no efficient interfacial charge transfer and no back-transfer that re-populates traps). In a minimal donor (perovskite) kinetic model with total decay rate k_tot = k_rad + k_nr,0 + k_trap,GB + k_FRET, the condition for *Voc improvement* is not “k_FRET large,” but “k_FRET replaces a larger non-radiative channel” by reducing trap capture through competitive energy removal *and* by chemically suppressing trap formation so that k_trap,GB is reduced in the glazed state. Operationally, we set a target regime validated by measurements: after glazing, the product (k_trap,GB × N_trap,GB) must fall enough that external radiative efficiency increases despite the added k_FRET. A conservative falsifiable target is: ERE increases by ≥2× and QFLS increases by ≥15 meV at 1 sun while TRPL shows a donor lifetime decrease consistent with k_FRET ≥ (2–5)×10^7 s−1 (20–50 ns timescale) and sub-gap EQE does not increase.

(B) Chemo-mechanics/transport (ripening suppression must map onto measurable transport parameters): Instead of an abstract “ionic chemical-potential clamp,” the glaze must measurably reduce (i) the interfacial halide exchange coefficient k_ex (surface/GB exchange with the environment and adjacent grains), and (ii) the effective halide chemical diffusivity D_chem along GBs under bias/illumination, and (iii) the mobile vacancy concentration c_V (or an experimentally accessible proxy such as ionic conductivity σ_ion). The Ni3Fe1→NiFeOOH network provides catalytic redox buffering (suppressing I•/I2 and O2−/HOx that create new defects) and forms an ion-moderating hydrated oxyhydroxide pathway that passivates/blocks fast GB exchange sites, thereby lowering k_ex and D_chem. Coarsening (GIWAXS peak narrowing; grain-size exponent) must correlate with extracted reductions in D_chem and k_ex rather than being attributed solely to morphological “pinning.”

Mechanistic coherence with catalytic activity/APNC uncertainty: NiFeOOH (Ni3Fe1-tuned) is the catalytic redox-active component; APNCs are *photonic acceptors* and must be rendered catalytically inert at the perovskite interface by ligand selection (electronically insulating, halide-resistant shell) and by embedding within NiFeOOH at controlled separation. The proposal explicitly tests and rejects APNC formulations that catalyze deleterious iodide/oxygen chemistry (detected by AP-XPS/EPR and accelerated aging).
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registered quantitative success metrics (before any device claims)
0.1 Photophysics targets (1 sun, 300 K): (i) ΔQFLS ≥ +15 meV and ΔVoc ≥ +10 mV with no FF loss >1%abs; (ii) ERE increases ≥2×; (iii) sub-gap EQE (0.7–1.2 eV window, device-dependent) does not increase (no new mid-gap states); (iv) parasitic absorption from APNC-glaze at the perovskite emission wavelength contributes <0.3 mA cm−2 Jsc-equivalent loss (integrated PDS/UV-vis).
0.2 Ion/instability targets: (i) D_chem,GB reduced ≥10× and/or k_ex reduced ≥5× relative to control; (ii) hysteresis index reduced ≥50% under scan-rate series; (iii) accelerated coarsening exponent n (from grain-size ∝ t^n) reduced by ≥30% and GIWAXS peak-width evolution slowed by ≥2×.

Step 1 — Baselines and platform selection
1.1 Perovskites: (A) FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I0.7Br0.3)3 (wide bandgap, segregation-sensitive) and (B) FA/Cs PbI3 (narrower bandgap reference). Use identical stoichiometry/solvent engineering across batches.
1.2 Architectures: p–i–n (ITO/MeO-2PACz/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag) and n–i–p (FTO/SnO2/perovskite/PTAA/Au). Determine dominant recombination interface via contact-specific PL quenching + TRPL and by selective insertion of an ultrathin inert barrier (e.g., 0.5–1 nm Al2O3 by ALD on witness samples only) to localize sensitivity.
1.3 Ripening-accelerated protocol (registered): 1 sun MPP at 65/75/85 °C under controlled O2 (0, 1, 21%) and RH (0, 10, 30%). Track morphology/structure: time-lapse AFM/SEM grain statistics + operando GIWAXS.

Step 2 — De-risk conversion chemistry: prove Ni(Fe)OOH formation, self-limited thickness, and GB preference before integrating APNCs
2.1 Replace the highest-risk “volatile β-diketonate chemisorption” with a perovskite-compatible, self-limiting surface reaction sequence (still additive-free in the perovskite film) that can be monitored in situ:
  • Option A (preferred): vapor-phase sequential infiltration / molecular layer deposition–like pulsing at room temperature using Ni and Fe organometallics with demonstrated low-reactivity toward halide perovskites (screened set), followed by controlled oxidant pulses (H2O/O2) to form oxyhydroxide. This maintains the original “in situ conversion glazing” logic but introduces thickness control by cycle number.
  • Option B (fallback): ultradilute, orthogonal-solvent contact (≤2 s) using non-coordinating hydrocarbon solvent with Ni/Fe precursor chosen by screening (below), followed by immediate evacuation and controlled oxidant exposure.
2.2 In situ thickness and chemistry verification on perovskite-relevant surfaces (mandatory):
  • Substrates: (i) real perovskite films, (ii) PbI2-rich and halide-vacancy–enriched perovskite (intentional mild understoichiometry) to mimic GB chemistry, (iii) inert oxide (SiO2/Al2O3) controls.
  • Tools and readouts:
    - QCM + spectroscopic ellipsometry during conversion to obtain mass uptake (ng cm−2) and thickness (target 1–3 nm facets equivalent after completion; total areal loading cap set by cycle count or precursor dose).
    - Ambient-pressure XPS (AP-XPS) during conversion under the exact H2O/O2 ppm conditions to confirm formation of Ni(Fe)OOH signatures (Ni 2p, Fe 2p, O 1s hydroxyl component) and to explicitly rule out dominant carbonate, oxide, or metal iodide formation (I 3d shifts; carbonate C 1s; O 1s lattice vs hydroxyl).
    - TOF-ERDA or angle-resolved XPS (ARXPS) post-process to quantify hydroxyl content and depth distribution.
2.3 GB selectivity test (spatially resolved):
  • Cross-sectional STEM-EELS/EDS mapping of Ni/Fe along GBs vs grain interiors, quantified as GB enrichment factor (target ≥3× relative concentration at GBs).
  • Correlative Kelvin probe force microscopy (KPFM) + conductive AFM on identical regions before/after glazing to ensure no formation of conductive shunts.
2.4 Kinetic sufficiency of “mild” oxidant: explicitly map conversion kinetics vs H2O/O2 partial pressures:
  • Conversion matrix: H2O = 10, 100, 1000 ppm; O2 = 0.1, 1, 21%; illumination on/off (405–450 nm) at fixed photon flux.
  • Endpoint: time-to-saturation thickness (QCM plateau) and stabilized NiOOH/FeOOH spectral fractions (AP-XPS). Proceed only if a reproducible self-limited regime exists within ≤30 min at ≤1000 ppm H2O.

Step 3 — APNC selection, “catalytically inert” ligand series, and parasitic-loss controls
3.1 APNC library (atomically verified): Au25(SR)18, Ag44(SR)30, and alloyed AuAg clusters with three ligand classes:
  • L1 (inert, insulating): perfluoro-thiolates or bulky aryl-thiolates to minimize interfacial electronic coupling.
  • L2 (zwitterionic): to control dispersion without halide exchange.
  • L3 (intentional risk control): more labile thiols to test degradation catalysis (should be rejected by screening).
Confirm atomic precision by ESI-MS/MALDI and EXAFS; quantify absorption overlap integral with perovskite PL.
3.2 Hard controls for parasitic absorption and heating:
  • Photothermal deflection spectroscopy (PDS) / ultra-sensitive absorption of APNC-glaze on transparent substrates to compute Jsc-equivalent parasitic loss.
  • Temperature rise under illumination (IR thermography on dummy stacks) to ensure no APNC-induced local heating artifact.
3.3 Catalytic side-reaction screening (must-pass gate):
  • AP-XPS under illumination in O2/H2O to detect accelerated iodide oxidation (I 3d chemical shifts; formation of I0/I2 species) comparing (i) NiFeOOH only, (ii) APNC only, (iii) APNC@NiFeOOH.
  • EPR spin trapping for superoxide/iodine radicals: APNC formulations that increase radical yield vs control are excluded.

Step 4 — Integrate the glaze + APNCs with controlled donor–acceptor distance (2–8 nm) and prevent shunting
4.1 Assembly sequence (distance-control logic):
  • Form ultrathin NiFeOOH first to define a chemically stable host matrix (1–2 nm equivalent on facets).
  • Introduce APNCs at sub-monolayer coverage via orthogonal deposition (perfluorinated solvent or scCO2 impregnation on test coupons) to avoid perovskite solvent damage.
  • Complete with a second, brief NiFeOOH conversion step to “cap” and lock APNCs at target separations (total thickness windows: 1–3 nm at facets; 3–8 nm at GBs).
4.2 Thickness verification per device: ARXPS + cross-sectional STEM on witness devices; reject batches outside thickness window.
4.3 Shunt control: dark JV, light-intensity dependent Voc/Jsc, and temperature-dependent JV to detect tunneling/filamentary pathways; any increase in leakage current >10× at −0.1 V rejects the process window.

Step 5 — Quantitative photophysical framework and falsification of ‘beneficial FRET’
5.1 Minimal kinetic model tied to observables:
  • Fit TRPL (and preferably TCSPC) with a model including k_rad, k_nr,0 (bulk), k_trap,GB (surface/GB), and k_FRET.
  • Extract k_FRET from lifetime change only after demonstrating unchanged charge extraction (no APNC photocurrent contribution) and no new sub-gap states.
5.2 Required regime demonstration (how FRET increases Voc rather than decreases it):
  • Measure QFLS by absolute PL under 1 sun equivalent. A net QFLS increase concurrent with donor lifetime shortening is only acceptable if ERE increases and sub-gap EQE does not.
  • Sensitized APNC signature: transient absorption detecting APNC bleach upon perovskite excitation; absence of long-lived charge-separated signals (which would imply charge transfer).
  • Distance dependence: vary total glaze thickness (controlled cycles/dose) to map k_FRET ∝ R−6 and identify a Förster radius regime; correlate with QFLS to find optimum where ΔQFLS>0.
5.3 Back-transfer/heat-loss check: monitor PL spectrum and time-resolved emission for re-population of perovskite emission; quantify non-radiative heating fraction by power-dependent PL + PDS.

Step 6 — Replace ‘chemical-potential clamp’ with extracted transport parameters
6.1 Extract D_chem and k_ex (measurable):
  • Bias-dependent ToF-SIMS depth profiling after controlled bias/light soaking to quantify halide redistribution; fit profiles with drift–diffusion to extract effective D_chem.
  • Isotope tracer experiments: use enriched halide (e.g., 81Br/79Br contrast if available) or deuterated water exposure to quantify exchange kinetics (k_ex) at the top interface.
  • Temperature-dependent impedance / ionic conductivity: separate ionic and electronic contributions (e.g., distribution of relaxation times) to quantify σ_ion and activation energy changes.
6.2 Link to coarsening: correlate extracted D_chem and k_ex with GIWAXS peak narrowing rates and grain-size evolution under identical stress; show that reduced coarsening tracks reduced ionic transport/exchange rather than only surface “armor.”

Step 7 — Catalytic redox buffering verification (Ni3Fe1 as control knob)
7.1 Stoichiometry series: Ni-only, Fe-only, Ni:Fe = 3:1, 2:1, 1:1, with matched thickness (QCM-calibrated) and matched APNC loading.
7.2 Operando AP-XPS under illumination: track oxygenated species and iodine oxidation-state evolution; quantify suppression of oxidized iodine species as a function of Ni:Fe.
7.3 Electrochemical proxy (on inert substrates): confirm Ni3Fe1-derived oxyhydroxide shows superior redox activity (OER-like metrics) relative to Ni-only/Fe-only at comparable loadings, anchoring the “catalytic activity” link.

Step 8 — Device performance, recombination/transport decomposition, and reliability
8.1 Performance: JV, stabilized MPP, Suns-Voc; absolute PL-derived QFLS; calculate non-radiative Voc loss.
8.2 Loss separation: transient photovoltage/photocurrent, impedance spectroscopy, and scan-rate hysteresis series.
8.3 Mandatory parasitic-loss readouts: ERE, sub-gap EQE, and PDS-derived absorption.
8.4 Reliability: ISOS-L-2 and ISOS-O-2 plus MPP at 65–85 °C. Report T80, Voc retention, and (for Br systems) spectral stability/phase segregation signatures.

Control matrix (must falsify)
C1 NiFeOOH only (no APNC) vs C2 APNC only (no NiFeOOH) vs C3 APNC@NiFeOOH (full) vs C4 inert ultrathin glaze (Al2O3) with APNC vs C5 spectrally mismatched APNCs (no overlap) in identical NiFeOOH vs C6 thick continuous film (≥10 nm) to prove ultrathin/GB-localized requirement.

Feasibility: 1) Addresses the Step-2 chemistry risk by moving from assumed “selective chemisorption” to a monitored, self-limiting conversion with direct in situ evidence. QCM/ellipsometry provides thickness closure; AP-XPS under the exact oxidant ppm regime establishes whether Ni(Fe)OOH forms versus iodides/carbonates/oxides, and maps kinetic sufficiency (time-to-saturation). Spatial selectivity is no longer asserted; it is quantified via STEM-EELS GB enrichment factors.

2) Makes the FRET claim internally consistent with Voc/QFLS by requiring a specific measurable regime: ERE and QFLS must increase while TRPL shortens and sub-gap EQE does not rise. This directly tests the reviewer’s concern that adding an acceptor usually lowers radiative efficiency. The proposal pre-registers a falsifiable outcome: if QFLS decreases or ERE drops, the “beneficial FRET” hypothesis is rejected even if FRET is observed.

3) Replaces the ‘chemical-potential clamp’ narrative with extractable transport parameters (D_chem, k_ex, σ_ion, activation energies) derived from bias-dependent ToF-SIMS, temperature-dependent impedance/conductivity, and isotope tracer exchange. This framework can distinguish (a) reduced exchange/diffusion from (b) purely morphological pinning by requiring quantitative correlations between transport suppression and coarsening-rate suppression.

4) De-risks APNC catalytic uncertainty by explicitly treating APNCs as photonic acceptors that must be chemically/electronically insulated via ligand selection and embedding, and by implementing a gatekeeping screening protocol (AP-XPS/EPR under O2/H2O + illumination). APNCs that catalyze iodide oxidation or increase radical yield are excluded. This preserves the concept chain: catalytic activity is attributed to Ni3Fe1-derived NiFeOOH; APNCs are engineered energy acceptors whose only allowed role is near-field energy transfer without charge extraction or catalysis.

5) Ensures manufacturability relevance: the glaze remains ultrathin (1–3 nm facets; 3–8 nm GB) and is verified self-limiting; thick-film penalties are explicitly tested (C6). Orthogonal APNC delivery avoids solvent damage and enables sub-monolayer loading—critical for avoiding shunting and parasitic absorption.
final_critique: Methodologically, the proposal is unusually well-instrumented and pre-registered, with strong in situ chemical verification (QCM/ellipsometry + AP-XPS), spatial selectivity metrics (GB enrichment factor by STEM-EELS), and a rare attempt to make ripening suppression quantitatively traceable to extracted transport parameters (D_chem, k_ex, σ_ion). The main scientific vulnerability is the central photophysics claim: removing band-edge excitations by FRET to embedded APNCs almost always competes with radiative recombination and lowers QFLS unless it *selectively* intercepts trap-mediated capture without creating an alternate loss channel. The proposal partially addresses this via an ERE↑/QFLS↑ gate, but the mechanistic pathway for how FRET reduces k_trap,GB (rather than merely adding k_FRET) remains under-justified: trap capture is generally a first-order sink proportional to trap density and capture cross-section, and FRET does not intrinsically reduce either unless coupled to independent chemical passivation; in that case, NiFeOOH passivation—not FRET—would be the primary cause of Voc gain. A second weakness is chemical compatibility risk: NiFeOOH is hydrated/ionic and can itself be a mixed ionic/electronic conductor; inserting a redox-active oxyhydroxide at perovskite/transport-layer interfaces risks (i) band misalignment and interfacial dipoles, (ii) interfacial charge transfer (quenching) inconsistent with the ‘no QFL coupling’ requirement, and (iii) providing fast ion pathways or water retention depending on hydration state—potentially worsening halide migration under some humidity/bias conditions. Finally, the transport-extraction plan is ambitious but under-specified regarding identifiability: ToF-SIMS profile fitting can conflate D_chem with field-driven drift, interfacial exchange, and sputter artifacts; impedance separation of ionic/electronic responses is model-dependent unless validated with independent tracers. Overall, the engineering plan is high-resolution and falsifiable, but the logical necessity of APNC-mediated FRET for Voc improvement remains the least convincing link, and the concept chain is internally conflicted because APNC catalytic activity is disallowed while the chain asserts it.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding atomically precise nanoclusters inside an ultrathin NiFeOOH grain-boundary glaze increases perovskite voltage and suppresses coarsening by enabling beneficial energy transfer that outcompetes trap capture while blocking ion migration.

original_chain: bmFeSAC -> Bicontinuous structure -> Specific surface area -> Free radicals -> Reactive oxygen species (ROS) -> Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) -> Iron-based metal-organic frameworks (GIM)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a MOF-derived, bicontinuous Fe–N single-atom carbon scaffold (bmFeSAC-like) sparsely decorated with optically tuned Au nanoparticles can function as a *rear-side, photoactive encapsulation + optical management layer* for perovskite solar cells (PSCs) by closing a quantitatively validated transport-and-reaction pathway for oxygen/water/ROS across the *entire* device stack, while remaining electronically neutral to charge extraction. Mechanistically, the proposal is refined as follows to address reviewer concerns: (1) **Why a rear sink can matter:** Under operating illumination and bias, ROS are generated not only at the illuminated/front side but also at buried interfaces (perovskite/transport layer, perovskite/metal contact) due to (i) oxygen/water that penetrates through multiple ingress routes (front barrier defects, edge seals, rear electrode seams), (ii) photoexcited redox chemistry at metal/halide boundaries, and (iii) ionic redistribution that brings oxidizable halides to the rear contact. We will explicitly *model and measure* the steady-state ROS source terms and flux vectors to determine when the rear interface becomes a dominant (or co-dominant) reactive zone. The bicontinuous scaffold—placed *outside* the electronic stack but directly adjacent to the rear electrode under a transparent barrier—creates a high-surface-area, percolating diffusion–reaction domain that intercepts oxygen/water and quenches long-lived ROS escaping from the rear electrode region and edge-related pathways before they back-diffuse or sustain electrode corrosion. (2) **Catalytic, non-consumptive ROS neutralization without carrier injection:** Fe–N4/Fe–Nx single-atom sites distributed along continuous channels catalyze ROS conversion (e.g., O2•−/HO2•/H2O2 to O2/H2O) through Fe(II)/Fe(III) cycling with minimal electronic coupling to the perovskite because the layer is not in the perovskite junction and is separated by the metal electrode; thus the role is chemical (radical quenching) rather than electronic (charge transport). (3) **AuNP role is optical back-scattering with bounded thermal impact:** AuNPs are used primarily as NIR back-scatterers to improve rear optical path length; any photothermal effect is treated as a *bounded perturbation* that must remain below thresholds for accelerating ionic migration or metal corrosion. We will therefore design AuNP size/shape/loading such that (i) plasmon resonance is shifted to the NIR tail beyond the perovskite absorption edge, (ii) near-field enhancement at the perovskite is negligible by simulation and measurement, and (iii) the operating temperature rise at 1-sun is <~1–2 °C at the perovskite plane. If these constraints cannot be met, the Au function will be replaced by non-plasmonic high-index scatterers as a contingency while retaining the bmFeSAC ROS-catalytic core. This refined hypothesis overcomes the reviewers’ key vulnerabilities by (a) explicitly proving whether the rear region contributes a significant ROS flux under realistic ingress/bias conditions, (b) bounding photothermal/ionic side effects quantitatively rather than qualitatively, and (c) defining synthesis success criteria that ensure a truly bicontinuous, high-SSA, single-atom Fe–N network with known permeability and site chemistry.
Plan: Step 0 — Close the transport-and-causality loop *before* device scaling (mandatory directive).
