- Use electron-only devices and contact resistance extraction to ensure the capping does not dominate series resistance.

Deliverables and decision gates
- DG1: Demonstrate reproducible gate charging/retention in MOS test vehicles: ΔVox ≥ 0.1 V equivalent, τret ≥ 10^3–10^4 s at 60 °C, breakdown yield >90%.
- DG2: Show electrostatics-correlated Voc gain in PSCs with external charge programming (no TPHG), ΔVoc ≥ 30–80 mV with stable MPP gain and reduced ΔVnr.
- DG3: Validate ionic-suppression window: reduced potential drift and reduced ToF-SIMS interfacial ion pile-up under designed actuation frequencies without accelerating degradation.

Feasibility: 1) Charge-injection feasibility into a buried PC71BM gate is made practical by a dedicated edge bus/via layout outside the active area and an explicit high-impedance coupling circuit that never references PV electrodes. The gate is a contacted internal node (like a MOS floating-gate test structure), not an inaccessible buried island; leakage/shunt risks are managed via perimeter passivation, guard-ring geometry, and explicit resistance targets (>10^10–10^11 Ω).

2) Effect-size realism is bounded by capacitance-based charge rules. With 2–5 nm Al2O3/SiOx, Cox lies in ~0.7–4 µF/cm², so Q/A in ~0.07–1.2 µC/cm² yields ΔVox ~0.1–0.3 V. These charge densities are within the reach of high-Voc, high-impedance mechanical generators (TPHGs) when delivered through rectified pulses into a capacitive load (Asset 1 supports large Voc and usable charge pulses), and they correspond to plausible ΔVoc bounds (tens of mV up to ~0.1 V) via reduction of interfacial SRH recombination currents.

3) The ionic-transport claim is converted into a predictive actuation window using a PNP-based relaxation-time comparison. By choosing oscillation frequencies (≈1–50 Hz) faster than ionic relaxation in the near-interface region (order 0.01–1 s depending on D and L) and keeping field amplitudes in a modest range (ΔVint ~0.05–0.15 V across ~10–50 nm), the design aims to reduce net ionic pile-up rather than drive it. Operando potential-drift mapping and ToF-SIMS are explicitly used as pass/fail readouts.

4) Materials risks are front-loaded into manufacturable test vehicles (MOS-cap arrays) that provide breakdown/leakage statistics, retention, and endurance before committing to full PSC stacks. This addresses pinhole risk (dielectric continuity), PC71BM percolation uncertainty (LbL vs thickness thresholds), and TiO2 capping trap/series-resistance risks (method/thickness matrix).

5) Chemistry vs electrostatics is discriminated by (i) external calibrated gate programming (no TPHG), (ii) temperature-dependent retention correlations, and (iii) inert floating-gate replacements (nanocarbon/Au nanomesh) that preserve electrostatics while removing PC71BM chemical passivation. This suite ensures that any measured mobility/energetic-disorder changes can be attributed to field effects rather than solely morphological or chemical interfacial changes.

6) Alignment to literature assets: the approach leverages (a) high-voltage, charge-pulse capability of TPHG-class devices (Asset 1) as an isolated gate programmer; (b) the known sensitivity of Voc and performance to fullerene morphology/phase continuity (Asset 2) motivating LbL PC71BM formation; (c) the centrality of phase separation to performance stability (Asset 3) motivating ionic/field control; and (d) the relationship between contact engineering and electron mobility/extraction in oxide-based ETLs (Assets 4–5) motivating controlled TiO2 interfaces and band bending; plus LbL fabrication logic for precise nanostrata (Asset 6).
final_critique: This is unusually well-resolved for a speculative electromechanical–photovoltaic coupling concept: the electrostatics (Cox, Q/A→ΔV) and the fabrication-risk plan (ultrathin dielectric continuity, leakage statistics, retention/endurance, edge-passivation strategy) are concrete and manufacturable. The major logical vulnerability is the claimed “ionic suppression by AC shake” while simultaneously maintaining net stored DC gate charge: the proposal does not provide a quantitatively consistent waveform/circuit model showing that the perovskite interface experiences the intended zero-mean (or controlled-mean) field while the floating gate retains a DC bias, nor does it bound parasitic capacitive coupling from the gate pad/bus into the PV electrodes during mechanical actuation (which could inadvertently bias the device or drive ions). Additionally, mapping ΔVox to a 5×–50× reduction in n_int is asserted but not derived from a coupled semiconductor electrostatics/transport model for TiO2/perovskite (band bending, accumulation/depletion in TiO2, interfacial state occupancy), so the ΔVoc expectation is plausible but not yet rigorously predictive. Finally, PC71BM is both (i) a potential chemical passivant/energetic modifier and (ii) the charge-storage node; while controls are proposed, the baseline mechanism still risks conflating electrostatic field-effect with chemical/interface dipole effects unless energy-level shifts and recombination pathways are independently quantified (e.g., UPS/KPFM under programmed charge states, interfacial trap spectroscopy).
hypothesis_summary: A mechanically driven nanogenerator injects charge into a buried floating gate inside a perovskite solar cell, electrostatically tuning the interface to suppress recombination and reduce ion pile-up.

original_chain: Zn-Car_MOF -> Release profile -> Electrocatalytic activity -> Electrochemical performance -> Nickel hydroxide (Ni(OH)2) -> High specific capacitance -> Oxygen evolution reaction (OER) -> Nickel(II) acetate tetrahydrate
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding an electrochemically addressable Ni(OH)2/NiOOH-in-Zn-Car_MOF nanolayer as a wired, redox-buffering interfacial contact on the electron-selective side of perovskite solar cells will suppress oxygen-induced interfacial degradation and reduce non-radiative recombination by quantitatively lowering steady-state electron accumulation at the ETL interface rather than by invoking true oxygen evolution. Under 1-sun operation, the dominant oxygen chemistry at PSC electron contacts is oxygen reduction (O2 + e− → O2•−, E° ≈ −0.33 V vs NHE in aprotic media) and subsequent superoxide/peroxide interconversion. The Ni(II)/Ni(III) redox couple (Ni(OH)2/NiOOH, formal potential ≈ +0.45–0.50 V vs NHE in mildly hydrated environments, shifted cathodically in confined/solid-state conditions) does not drive OER under PSC conditions but instead acts as a fast, reversible electron reservoir with high areal pseudocapacitance. By providing a local redox density that can accept excess photogenerated electrons on sub-ms timescales, the Ni redox layer clamps the electron quasi-Fermi level at the ETL interface to values insufficient to sustain O2 → O2•− reduction, thereby shortening superoxide lifetime and suppressing downstream peroxide- and radical-driven perovskite oxidation. Any residual reduced oxygen species are further mitigated by rapid, catalytic electron back-transfer and disproportionation pathways occurring at the Ni sites within the MOF nanoreactor environment, spatially displaced from the perovskite by a molecular buffer. The Zn-Car_MOF is repurposed from a release medium into a programmable redox-access scaffold that controls the temporal accessibility and density of Ni active sites without ionic leaching. Quantitatively, the hypothesis predicts that achieving an interfacial pseudocapacitance ≥5–10 mF·cm−2 with a charge-transfer resistance ≤5 Ω·cm2 at ≥1 kHz will reduce the steady-state interfacial electron density by ≥3× under illumination, yielding a ≥20–40 mV increase in implied Voc and ≥2× improvement in oxygen-limited T80 lifetime, without introducing additional recombination or series resistance.
Plan: Step 1 – Architecture and energetic baselining. (1.1) Fabricate inverted p–i–n (Glass/ITO/NiOx or MeO-2PACz/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag) and reference n–i–p stacks to isolate polarity effects. (1.2) Establish baseline band alignment and electron quasi-Fermi level position at the C60 interface using UPS and KPFM under dark and 1-sun conditions; target EFn(C60) ≈ −3.9 to −4.0 eV vs vacuum under operation. (1.3) Synthesize 20–50 nm Zn-Car_MOF nanocrystals with 1–5 mol% π-conjugated carboxylate co-linker to enhance electronic coupling; verify porosity (BET), crystallinity (PXRD), and defect density (FTIR/XPS).

Step 2 – Wired MOF interlayer with non-alkaline Ni conversion. (2.1) Form a 3–10 nm ultrathin Zn-Car_MOF film co-deposited with 0.1–0.3 wt% carboxylated graphene quantum dots to achieve in-plane conductivity ≥10−6 S·cm−1 while keeping vertical leakage <10−7 A·cm−2 at ±1 V. (2.2) Deposit the wired MOF between C60 and BCP, or between perovskite and C60 separated by a ≤1 nm fullerene-SAM, confirmed by cross-sectional TEM. (2.3) Introduce Ni via nickel(II) acetate tetrahydrate infiltration from anhydrous ethanol with excess acetate ligand; convert to Ni(OH)2/NiOOH using a fully non-alkaline solid-state route: brief electrochemical oxidation/reduction pulses (charge density 1–10 mC·cm−2) through ITO using a solid polymer electrolyte containing bound hydroxide donors (e.g., quaternary ammonium hydroxide immobilized in PEO), followed by vacuum annealing to remove residual species. Verify absence of free OH− ingress by ToF-SIMS depth profiling.

Step 3 – Quantitative redox and capacitance tuning. (3.1) Measure Ni redox potential and kinetics in symmetric test stacks (ITO/C60/wired MOF:Ni/C60/ITO) via CV and EIS; tune Ni loading to achieve areal pseudocapacitance ≥5–10 mF·cm−2 at 1 kHz and redox time constants <1 ms. (3.2) Ensure added series/contact resistance ≤1 Ω·cm2 and DC leakage ≤10−7 A·cm−2 at operating bias. (3.3) Encode time-dependent active-site accessibility via reversible MOF pore-gating (Zn2+ back-coordination or linker protonation), monitored as gradual increases in redox charge over 10–100 h without Ni migration.

Step 4 – Oxygen-redox mechanism validation (ORR-focused). (4.1) Operando oxygen analysis in sealed micro-chambers under controlled O2 (200 ppm–air): quantify O2 consumption, H2O2 formation/decay (colorimetric or electrochemical probes), and compare superoxide lifetime using in situ EPR spin trapping on witness stacks. The discriminating signature is reduced O2•− signal amplitude and lifetime without net O2 evolution. (4.2) Correlate Ni redox state (operando Ni K-edge XAS or Raman) with transient photovoltage/photocurrent and EIS-derived recombination resistance under MPP.

Step 5 – Optoelectronic and degradation diagnostics. (5.1) Measure absolute PLQY and implied Voc of perovskite/C60/contact stacks; target ΔVoc,implied ≥20–40 mV. (5.2) Perform dark J–V (ideality factor), SCLC trap DOS, and temperature-dependent recombination analysis to verify no new trap-assisted pathways. (5.3) Conduct MPP stability at 45–65 °C under controlled oxygen; success criteria: ≥95% PCE retention after 500 h at 1% O2 and ≥2× T80 in air. (5.4) Post-mortem ToF-SIMS, XPS, and STEM-EDS to confirm suppressed iodide oxidation, Pb0 formation, and metal halide migration.

Step 6 – Controls and falsification. Compare against (i) wired MOF without Ni, (ii) Ni(OH)2 without MOF, (iii) Ni acetate without electrochemical conversion, (iv) MOF without nanocarbon wiring, and (v) oxygen-free encapsulation. The mechanism is falsified if superoxide lifetime, implied Voc, or stability gains are observed without achieving the targeted pseudocapacitance or if added redox density increases recombination or leakage.
Feasibility: The revised framework aligns the oxygen chemistry with thermodynamically accessible pathways at PSC electron contacts, replacing the unrealistic OER claim with an ORR/superoxide-suppression model grounded in known redox potentials and kinetics. MOF@Ni(OH)2 composites are empirically demonstrated to provide high pseudocapacitance and fast Ni(II)/Ni(III) redox, supporting the quantitative capacitance targets defined here. Nickel(II) acetate tetrahydrate is a validated precursor for ultrathin hydroxide phases, and the proposed solid-state, non-alkaline electrochemical conversion eliminates hydroxide ingress risks. Band-alignment (UPS/KPFM), leakage, and recombination diagnostics directly address materials-compatibility concerns, while explicit numerical thresholds for capacitance, resistance, and leakage create clear go/no-go criteria. By spatially separating the redox buffer from the perovskite and proving function through falsifiable oxygen-species signatures rather than assumed OER activity, the approach de-risks integration and tightly links electrochemical design parameters to measurable device-level gains in Voc and operational stability.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in mechanistic specificity and falsifiability for an interfacial-stability concept in PSCs: it correctly reframes the oxygen chemistry away from unrealistic OER toward ORR/superoxide-driven degradation, and it translates the redox-buffer idea into measurable interface-electrochemistry metrics (areal pseudocapacitance, Rct, time constants) tied to Voc and lifetime predictions. However, several high-risk elements remain under-resolved. (i) The central quantitative claim—clamping the interfacial electron quasi-Fermi level sufficiently to suppress O2→O2•−—is not rigorously linked to a device-relevant electrochemical model (e.g., coupling pseudocapacitance/kinetics to interfacial electron density and local potential under MPP), so the ≥3× reduction in electron accumulation and 20–40 mV implied-Voc gain reads aspirational without a derived relationship. (ii) Achieving ≥5–10 mF·cm−2 at ≥1 kHz in a 3–10 nm solid-state interlayer is aggressive; many Ni(OH)2/NiOOH pseudocapacitive responses are far slower (diffusion/PCET-limited) and shift to much lower effective capacitance at kHz. The proposal acknowledges confinement shifts but does not provide a clear plan to prove sub-ms PCET in the intended dry/weakly hydrated stack. (iii) The non-alkaline ‘bound hydroxide donor’ polymer-electrolyte conversion step risks introducing mobile ionic species, residual water, or quaternary ammonium fragments that can themselves accelerate perovskite/C60 interface degradation; ToF-SIMS alone may not be sufficient to exclude electrically active ionic contamination. (iv) The added nanocarbon wiring and redox sites could introduce new surface states and increase interfacial recombination; while controls are listed, there is no explicit strategy for chemical passivation of Ni/MOF surfaces toward the perovskite/ETL or for maintaining a benign density of states. (v) Some operando oxygen analytics (EPR spin trapping, H2O2 quantification) are technically challenging in thin-film device-like stacks and can generate ambiguous signals without careful calibration and oxygen mass-balance; the plan would benefit from more explicit artifacts/blank protocols and detection limits. Overall, the concept is coherent and methodologically detailed, but the key performance-enabling electrochemical kinetics and the contamination/recombination risks need tighter quantitative mitigation plans.
hypothesis_summary: A redox-buffering nickel hydroxide layer embedded in a conductive MOF scaffold suppresses oxygen-induced degradation in perovskite solar cells by accepting excess electrons and preventing harmful superoxide formation.

original_chain: Half-wave potential -> Zinc-air batteries -> Quasi-solid-state (QSS) -> Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) -> Electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) -> Ni/Co bimetallic MOF nanoplate
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Integrating an ultrathin Ni/Co bimetallic MOF nanoplate interlayer at the perovskite/electron-transport-layer (ETL) interface will suppress oxygen-induced interfacial recombination by catalytically regulating the oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) under operational bias, thereby enhancing quasi-solid-state (QSS) device stability and open-circuit voltage. The key mechanism is that the high electrochemical active surface area (ECSA) and tunable half-wave potential of the Ni/Co MOF selectively shift interfacial ORR pathways away from superoxide (O2−) formation toward benign four-electron reduction, mitigating oxygen-driven perovskite degradation while simultaneously improving electron extraction.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
Fabricate inverted (p–i–n) perovskite solar cells using a mixed-cation/mixed-halide FA/Cs-based perovskite absorber and a QSS electron-transport architecture (SnO2 nanoparticle matrix infiltrated with an ion-gel electrolyte). Synthesize 2D Ni/Co bimetallic MOF nanoplates via pyridine-modulated solvothermal growth, targeting lateral dimensions of 200–500 nm and thickness <10 nm.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
Deposit a conformal sub-5 nm Ni/Co MOF nanoplate interlayer between the perovskite and SnO2 ETL using a ligand-exchange-assisted self-assembly process to ensure electronic coupling. Fine-tune the Ni:Co ratio to modulate the MOF’s ORR half-wave potential (measured ex situ by rotating disk electrode), aligning it slightly positive to the perovskite conduction band to kinetically suppress superoxide formation while preserving electron extraction. The MOF is not used as a conventional transport layer but as a redox-active interfacial regulator that converts interfacial oxygen species under QSS conditions.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
Quantify interfacial recombination via time-resolved photoluminescence and transient photovoltage measurements under controlled oxygen partial pressures. Correlate device Voc, non-radiative recombination losses, and operational stability with MOF ECSA and half-wave potential. Use operando EPR and in situ XPS to directly probe suppression of O2− species at the interface. Benchmark against control devices lacking the MOF or using monometallic Ni- or Co-MOFs.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Prior ORR and Zn-air battery studies show that Ni/Co bimetallic MOFs exhibit high ECSA and tunable half-wave potentials due to synergistic metal sites, enabling control over oxygen adsorption and reduction pathways.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Oxygen-induced degradation and interfacial recombination are critical bottlenecks in perovskite solar cells, especially under quasi-solid-state architectures where oxygen diffusion is limited but persistent. Repurposing ORR-active MOFs as interfacial redox regulators directly addresses this degradation mechanism rather than passivating defects empirically.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike inert passivation layers or simple 2D perovskites, the Ni/Co MOF interlayer provides an active, self-regulating electrochemical function. Its high ECSA and engineered half-wave potential offer a mechanistically controllable route to stabilize PSCs under realistic operating conditions without sacrificing power conversion efficiency.
final_critique: The proposal demonstrates high technical sophistication and a rare level of mechanistic intentionality for perovskite interfacial engineering. The engineering plan is largely credible, with realistic materials synthesis, deposition, and operando diagnostics. However, there are nontrivial unresolved risks: (i) the assumption that a sub-5 nm MOF layer can sustain continuous ORR catalysis under low oxygen flux and photovoltaic bias is not quantitatively justified; (ii) electronic coupling across an organic-linker-based MOF/perovskite interface may introduce resistive losses or trap states that are not addressed beyond ligand exchange claims; and (iii) the alignment argument based on half-wave potential versus perovskite conduction band is conceptually appealing but oversimplifies interfacial electrochemical kinetics under non-equilibrium solar cell operation. These issues slightly weaken the logical closure between ORR electrochemistry and steady-state PSC Voc improvements.
hypothesis_summary: Integrating an ultrathin Ni/Co bimetallic MOF nanoplate interlayer at the perovskite/ETL interface catalytically shifts oxygen reduction pathways to suppress superoxide formation, enhancing quasi-solid-state solar cell stability and voltage.

original_chain: Cu-HHTP -> HITP -> Spray layer-by-layer assembly method -> Electronically conductive metal–organic frameworks (EC-MOFs) -> Response–recovery curve -> Selectivity improvement -> Cu-HHTP
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a percolative, charge-selective electronically conductive MOF (EC‑MOF) network inside a porous NiOx hole-transport contact—rather than forming a continuous MOF interlayer on the perovskite—will reduce interfacial non‑radiative recombination and improve Voc/FF/stability by decoupling (A) lateral current homogenization from (B) interfacial energetics tuning under perovskite-safe chemistry. Mechanistically: (1) **Lateral percolation/hotspot suppression**: a Cu‑HHTP/HITP nanonetwork formed primarily in NiOx pore volume and along NiOx grain boundaries provides a low-resistance lateral extraction mesh that reduces local current crowding at NiOx/perovskite microcontact points. This lowers local hole accumulation and electric-field inhomogeneity that otherwise accelerates interfacial SRH recombination and drives ionic pile-up; the measurable signature is a reduction in TPV-derived recombination rate (longer τ_TPV at fixed Voc) and lower ideality factor without requiring a large work-function shift. (2) **Defect/coordination-mediated dipole tuning without direct perovskite exposure**: controlled HITP incorporation into Cu‑HHTP adjusts EC‑MOF Fermi level and defect landscape (as in dual-ligand EC‑MOFs that increased conductivity from ~0.02 to ~0.2 S·cm−1 and altered selectivity/response–recovery behavior), enabling a modest but targeted interfacial dipole at the *effective* HTL surface while preserving electron-blocking. Because the MOF is embedded, the perovskite is not repeatedly wetted by Cu precursors/ligands, and any dipole effect is mediated through the composite’s surface potential rather than direct MOF/perovskite chemical contact—minimizing Cu-induced recombination centers. **Testable separation of mechanisms** is central: performance improvements should correlate strongly with measured percolation thresholds (sheet resistance/contact resistivity) when percolation is achieved, while sub-threshold loadings may yield similar work-function shifts (dipole) but smaller gains in TPV/TPC kinetics and FF.
Plan: A. Chemistry set definition (perovskite-qualified, bounded windows)
1) **Device baseline (kept constant):** glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs,MA)Pb(I,Br)3 perovskite (single fixed composition + fixed surface passivation)/NiOx(:EC‑MOF)/Au. All groups use identical perovskite processing and encapsulation.
2) **NiOx scaffold HTL (porous, perovskite-safe deposition):**
   - Target thickness: 50 ± 15 nm; porosity tuned by nanoparticle (NP) solids loading.
   - Route: NiOx NP ink in 2‑methoxyethanol:terpineol (7:3 v/v) with ≤0.5 vol% ethanolamine (optional) for wetting; spin or blade coat on perovskite with immediate N2 knife drying.
   - Thermal budget: ≤100 °C, 10 min (hotplate) to avoid perovskite degradation.
   - Porosity control: NP diameter 10–20 nm; solids 2, 5, 8 wt% to create “low/med/high porosity” scaffolds.

B. Perovskite-compatible spray-infiltration / ligand-conversion LbL process (fully specified)
3) **Half-cycle solutions (selected to minimize redox/etching of perovskite and avoid halides):**
   - **Cu(II) node precursor:** copper(II) acetate monohydrate, Cu(OAc)2·H2O (acetate is weakly coordinating, halide-free, relatively mild).
     • Solvent: anhydrous acetonitrile (MeCN) with 2 vol% tert‑butanol (tBuOH) to moderate drying and improve pore wetting.
     • Concentration window: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 mM.
     • Additive: 0.05 mM acetic acid (HOAc) to buffer hydrolysis and improve reproducibility (kept minimal to avoid perovskite acid attack).
   - **Mixed-ligand solution:** HHTP + HITP (total ligand 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 mM).
     • Solvent: anhydrous MeCN:IPA = 9:1 (v/v). (Avoid DMF/DMSO; avoid water; minimize protic content.)
     • HITP mol% in ligand feed: 0, 5, 10, 15, 20 mol% relative to total ligand.
   - **Rationale:** MeCN provides fast evaporation and low perovskite solubility; acetate avoids halide-induced perovskite conversion; the ligand solvent is kept low polarity relative to perovskite solvents and low protic content.
4) **Spray parameters (bounded):**
   - Substrate temperature: 25–35 °C (no hot spray).
   - Nozzle: ultrasonic spray head (or airbrush with verified droplet size), target droplet size <50 µm.
   - Spray flux: 0.20 ± 0.05 mL·min−1; N2 carrier 1.0 bar.
   - Pass strategy: 2 passes per half-cycle to limit wet time.
   - **Dwell time after each half-cycle:** 15 s (allows infiltration into pores).
   - **Purge/dry:** N2 knife, 60 s after each half-cycle.
   - **Mild conversion pulse:** 80 °C for 120 s after completing a full Cu+ligand cycle (not after each spray) to drive coordination while limiting perovskite stress.
5) **LbL cycle counts / MOF loading:**
   - Cycle numbers: 2, 5, 10, 15 cycles (maps sub-threshold → percolating → overloading).
   - Total loading is defined by cycle count × concentration; primary variable for percolation studies.
6) **Witness films for electrical metrology:** In parallel, deposit identical NiOx scaffolds on glass/ITO (no perovskite) and run identical infiltration to enable aggressive characterization (TLM/cTLM, UPS where appropriate) without perovskite constraints.

C. Mandatory compatibility pre-screening with explicit go/no-go thresholds (before device fabrication)
7) **Half-cycle compatibility assay (perovskite exposed to each step separately):** Prepare perovskite/SnO2 stacks; subject to:
   - (i) Cu-spray only; (ii) ligand-spray only; (iii) full Cu+ligand cycle; (iv) repeated cycles at max planned exposure (15 cycles) but on perovskite without NiOx (worst-case).
   Measure *before vs after* each condition:
   - GIWAXS: no new PbI2 peak area increase >5% relative; no peak broadening >10%.
   - XPS (surface-sensitive): Pb 4f/I 3d ratio change <10%; emergence of metallic Pb0 below detection (Pb0 fraction <1% of Pb signal).
   - Steady-state PL and PLQY: PLQY retention ≥90% (or PL intensity retention ≥85% under fixed excitation) after full exposure; TRPL slow-component lifetime retention ≥85%.
   **Go/no-go:** if any threshold fails, reduce concentration by 2× and/or reduce dwell to 5–10 s and repeat; if still failing, switch Cu salt to Cu(OTf)2 at 0.2–0.5 mM in MeCN (non-nucleophilic counterion) and requalify.

D. Hard structural criterion: “embedded, not interlayer” (quantitative, multi-modal)
8) **Definition of success (must satisfy all):**
   - (S1) Cross-sectional STEM-EDS/EELS: Cu signal spatially confined within NiOx thickness with <10% of integrated Cu signal in the first 5 nm adjacent to the perovskite interface.
   - (S2) Angle-resolved ToF-SIMS: ligand fragments (HHTP/HITP markers) peak within NiOx, with interface intensity (normalized to NiOx bulk) <0.2.
   - (S3) Surface topography/ellipsometry: no continuous MOF top film; AFM RMS roughness change ≤1.5 nm and ellipsometric thickness increase at NiOx top surface ≤5 nm relative to pristine NiOx.
   - (S4) Cross-sectional tomography (FIB-SEM or STEM tilt series): percolative features inside pores; absence of a laterally continuous layer at perovskite boundary over >80% of field of view.
9) **Explicit negative benchmark:** fabricate a deliberate thin MOF interlayer (continuous) by depositing Cu‑HHTP/HITP directly on perovskite (2–3 cycles with extended wet time to force surface film), confirm continuity by AFM/ellipsometry and ToF‑SIMS surface enrichment; compare performance and degradation versus embedded architecture.

E. Chemical-state verification to rule out Cu diffusion/reduction and unintended doping
10) **Chemical-state mapping (mandatory):**
   - Cross-sectional XPS (angle-resolved or sputter-assisted with calibration) and/or STEM-EELS for Cu L-edge: quantify Cu(I)/Cu(II) ratio across thickness.
   - Criterion: no Cu accumulation in perovskite; Cu below XPS detection at perovskite surface after removing NiOx (or <0.1 at%).
   - Monitor Ni 2p and O 1s to determine if NiOx is unintentionally doped/reduced by the process.

F. Quantitative percolation targets linked to device metrics (TLM/cTLM + TPV/TPC)
11) **Electrical design targets (set before optimization):**
   - Composite HTL sheet resistance (Rs,HTL) on ITO/NiOx(:MOF) witness: achieve Rs ≤ 200 Ω/sq at percolating loading; sub-threshold region expected Rs ≥ 2 kΩ/sq.
   - Contact resistivity (ρc) extracted by cTLM on ITO/NiOx(:MOF)/Au and on perovskite/NiOx(:MOF)/Au analog stacks: target ρc ≤ 1×10−3 Ω·cm2 (percolating) and demonstrate monotonic reduction vs cycle count.
   - Device series resistance impact: require ΔRs(device) reduction ≥10% relative to pristine NiOx for percolating samples; FF increase should track ρc reduction.
12) **Mechanism-linked transient metrics:**
   - TPV at matched Voc: percolating samples must show ≥1.5× longer τ_TPV (or ≥30% lower recombination rate constant) than pristine NiOx.
   - TPC: faster extraction (shorter charge collection time constant) with reduced dispersive tail (stretched-exponent β increases toward 1).
   - Chopped-light response–recovery: define recovery half-time t1/2; percolating samples should reduce t1/2 by ≥30% vs pristine NiOx at identical illumination and bias.

G. Decisive mechanistic discriminators (separating dipole vs percolation vs chemistry)
13) **Percolation vs dipole separation experiment:**
   - Choose two loadings: (Lsub) just below percolation (Rs ≈ 2–5 kΩ/sq) and (Lperc) percolating (Rs ≤200 Ω/sq).
   - Adjust HITP fraction (e.g., 10–15%) to match work-function shift between Lsub and Lperc (measured on witness stacks by Kelvin probe/UPS on ITO/NiOx(:MOF) surfaces).
   - Prediction: if percolation governs recombination suppression/hotspot mitigation, Lperc outperforms Lsub in TPV/TPC and FF even when work-function shift is similar.
14) **Chemistry vs conductivity control:**
   - Controls: (i) spray solvent exposure only; (ii) Cu-only infiltration; (iii) ligands-only infiltration; (iv) NiOx chemically doped to match conductivity (e.g., mild Li doping) without MOF; compare to isolate the role of structural percolation.
15) **Interface-risk control:** introduce a thin inert barrier at perovskite/NiOx (e.g., 1–2 nm ALD Al2O3 or molecular passivant) in a subset to test whether any residual Cu proximity contributes; if embedded architecture is truly non-contacting, barrier should not be required for gains.

H. Device fabrication, statistics, and stability
16) **Device matrix:** Porosity (3 levels) × HITP fraction (0–20%) × cycle count (2–15) with focus on identifying percolation threshold per porosity; ≥30 devices per key condition.
17) **Performance readout:** stabilized MPP PCE, Voc/FF/Jsc; hysteresis index.
18) **Operational stability:** MPP tracking 1 sun at 25 °C and 65 °C; humidity-controlled (e.g., 50% RH) with encapsulation constant; post-aging ToF‑SIMS for halide/cation accumulation near HTL and correlate with percolation/contact resistivity.

I. Data analysis/model linkage (mass transport + percolation)
19) **Infiltration bounding model:** use a simple infiltration metric based on (a) NiOx porosity (from ellipsometric porosimetry or gas adsorption on analog films) and (b) delivered precursor dose per cycle (spray flux × time × concentration). Fit Cu areal density (ICP-MS on dissolved witness films) vs cycle count to identify saturation; require saturation without surface film formation (validated by AFM/ellipsometry).
20) **Percolation analysis:** fit Rs vs loading to percolation law Rs ∝ (p − pc)−t for p>pc; extract pc and compare across porosity. Correlate TPV/TPC improvements with (p − pc) rather than with work-function shift to test the central claim.
Feasibility: 1) **Perovskite compatibility is bounded, not assumed:** the chemistry set is halide-free (Cu acetate), low-water, and DMF/DMSO-free; spray flux/dwell/purge are specified to minimize wet residence time. Compatibility is pre-qualified at the *half-cycle* level with GIWAXS + XPS + PLQY/TRPL retention thresholds and an explicit fallback (lower concentration/dwell; alternative Cu(OTf)2) before any full device matrix.
2) **Quantitative link from percolation to device metrics:** the proposal sets measurable electrical targets (Rs ≤200 Ω/sq; ρc ≤10−3 Ω·cm2) and explicitly ties expected FF/Voc changes to TLM/cTLM and TPV/TPC parameters. This addresses the reviewer concern that lateral conduction might not be the bottleneck by requiring (i) demonstrable reductions in ρc/Rs and (ii) correlated improvements in TPV-derived recombination at matched Voc, not merely J–V changes.
3) **Mechanistic discrimination is built-in:** sub-threshold vs percolating loadings with matched work-function shifts directly test whether gains originate from dipole alignment alone or from lateral percolation/hotspot suppression. Additional controls (Cu-only, ligand-only, solvent-only, conductivity-matched NiOx doping) separate chemical passivation/unintended doping from the structural percolation effect.
4) **Hard ‘embedded-not-interlayer’ criteria + deliberate interlayer benchmark:** multi-modal structural criteria (quantitative Cu distribution near interface, ToF‑SIMS angle profiles, AFM/ellipsometry limits, tomography) prevent ambiguous localization claims. A deliberately formed continuous MOF interlayer provides a negative benchmark to prove that embedding is uniquely beneficial (e.g., better stability and lower recombination risk) rather than MOF presence per se.
5) **Cu-related recombination risks are directly addressed:** cross-sectional chemical-state mapping (XPS/EELS) and strict thresholds on Cu proximity to the perovskite limit the possibility that Cu acts as a recombination center. Post-aging depth profiling tests whether the architecture suppresses ion accumulation, consistent with the homogenized extraction hypothesis.
6) **Transfer logic from EC‑MOF literature is coherent and targeted:** the dual-ligand (HITP/HHTP) approach is used not only to raise conductivity (enabling percolation at lower loading) but also to tune defect/coordination environments that can adjust the composite contact potential—analogous to selectivity tuning in EC‑MOF chemiresistors—while the response–recovery concept is translated into optoelectronic transient extraction/recovery metrics (TPC/TPV/chopped-light kinetics) as a mechanistic readout.
final_critique:
The proposal is unusually well-engineered for a perovskite interface study: it defines chemistry windows, spray parameters, compatibility gates (GIWAXS/XPS/PLQY/TRPL), and rigorous localization criteria (STEM-EDS/EELS, AR-ToF-SIMS, ellipsometry/AFM, tomography), and it pre-specifies percolation/electrical targets (Rs, ρc) tied to mechanistic transient metrics (TPV/TPC). The central logic—decoupling lateral current homogenization from interfacial energetics by embedding an EC‑MOF within NiOx—is coherent and testable via the proposed percolation-vs-dipole discriminator.

Key scientific risks and logical soft spots remain. (i) The hotspot/percolation → reduced SRH recombination link is plausible but not yet quantitatively justified: it assumes lateral current crowding at NiOx/perovskite microcontacts is a dominant recombination/ion-migration driver in the given baseline; without direct field/current mapping, TPV changes could also arise from altered interfacial capacitance, mobility, or inadvertent chemical passivation/doping. (ii) The “dipole tuning without direct perovskite exposure” claim is partially undermined by the fact that the effective HTL surface still contacts perovskite; even if Cu is confined, ligand fragments/solvent exposure and NiOx surface chemistry changes can still modify interfacial energetics and trap density. (iii) Cu-EC‑MOF formation inside a 50 nm porous NP scaffold at ≤100 °C with very short dwell times may yield discontinuous/poorly crystalline coordination networks or primarily adsorbed complexes rather than an electronically coherent MOF; conductivity values cited from the EC‑MOF literature may not transfer to this confined, low-T, spray-LbL context. (iv) Several characterization criteria (e.g., “<10% Cu within first 5 nm”) push the spatial-resolution/quantification limits of EDS/EELS/ToF‑SIMS deconvolution in such thin, rough, porous stacks, risking ambiguous pass/fail outcomes unless carefully calibrated.

Overall, the concept chain is used appropriately and the methodological adaptation is genuinely novel, but the causal attribution of Voc/FF/stability gains to lateral percolation (vs interfacial chemical passivation or NiOx modification) needs stronger, more direct discriminators.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a percolative conductive MOF network inside porous NiOx, rather than as a continuous interlayer, reduces interfacial recombination and improves device performance by decoupling lateral current homogenization from energetic tuning.

original_chain: Half-wave potential -> FeN -> COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900 -> Electrochemical accessible surface area (EASA) -> Half-wave potential -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A redox-gated, Fe-porphyrin–functionalized porous oxide contact (RG-FeN@MOF-derived contact) enhances perovskite solar cell Voc, FF, and operational stability through two *chemically and electrochemically distinct but testable mechanisms*: (1) **Specific axial coordination and dipole-mediated passivation at the buried interface**, where under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy complexes interact preferentially with the *axial Fe center or anchoring-group oxygen atoms* of surface-grafted Fe-porphyrins (rather than porphyrin ring nitrogens), reducing interfacial trap density and non-radiative recombination; and (2) **Solid-state redox gating of interfacial ionic charge**, where reversibly addressable Fe(III)/Fe(II) centers embedded in an electrochemically accessible internal surface act as a distributed charge reservoir that buffers ionic space-charge accumulation under operation without engaging in parasitic halide redox. The hypothesis explicitly rejects nonspecific “Pb–N ring coordination” and instead posits a falsifiable binding hierarchy (Fe axial site > anchoring group > dipole-only interaction) and a requirement that Fe redox activity remains reversible, spatially confined to the contact, and electronically coupled to the oxide backbone under device-relevant quasi-Fermi levels.
Plan: Pre-registered discriminator phase (mandatory before scaling):

**A. Chemical binding locus discriminator (go/no-go #1)**
A1. Model buried-interface system: fabricate PbI2-terminated perovskite thin films and PbI2 single-crystal surfaces contacted with RG-FeN@MOF-derived porous SnOx or NiOx films grafted with (i) Fe-porphyrin, (ii) metal-free porphyrin, and (iii) Fe-porphyrin with blocked axial site (e.g., CO- or pyridine-ligated Fe).
A2. Spectroscopic probes:
- N K-edge XAS/XANES: detect shifts indicative of axial ligation at Fe vs unchanged porphyrin ring N.
- Fe K-edge XANES/EXAFS: identify changes in Fe coordination number/bond length consistent with axial Pb–I/Pb–O interaction.
- 15N-labeled porphyrin ssNMR (where feasible) to rule out ring-N involvement.
- DFT-calibrated Pb 4f / I 3d core-level shifts to assign binding energetics (target ΔEbind ≥ 0.2–0.3 eV for specific interaction).
A3. Go/no-go criterion: proceed only if axial-Fe or anchor-mediated interaction is detected with metal-free and axial-blocked controls showing ≤20% of the effect.

**B. Solid-state redox-gating discriminator (go/no-go #2)**
B1. Solid-state operando spectroelectrochemistry: integrate the RG-FeN@MOF contact into a solid stack (ITO/contact/Al2O3(1–2 nm)/inert semiconductor) and bias across ±0.2–0.6 V vs perovskite-relevant quasi-Fermi levels.
B2. Probes: UV–Vis–NIR (Fe-porphyrin redox fingerprints), Fe Mössbauer/EPR (Fe(III)/Fe(II) ratio), or Fe K-edge XAS under bias and illumination.
B3. Correlation: simultaneously measure low-frequency capacitance (10–1–10–2 Hz) to confirm suppression of ionic accumulation concurrent with reversible Fe redox.
B4. Go/no-go thresholds: ≥90% reversibility of Fe redox signal after 100 h bias at 85 °C; no emergence of I3−/I2 spectral signatures; leakage current increase <10%.

**C. Quantified porous-contact architecture (risk mitigation)**
C1. Morphology targets: porosity 30–45 vol%, pore diameter 15–40 nm, contact thickness 30–60 nm, oxide volume fraction above vertical percolation threshold.
C2. Transport targets: sheet resistance ≤2× compact oxide; vertical conductivity ≥10−3 S cm−1; contact resistivity ≤10−2 Ω·cm2.
C3. Fabrication window: MOF-900 nanocrystals 40–60 nm; oxide:MOF volume ratio tuned 55:45–65:35; MOF removal via UV–ozone + ≤150 °C anneal.
C4. Surface functionalization density: Fe-porphyrin coverage 0.3–0.8 nm−2 (sub-monolayer) verified by QCM/XPS.

**D. Solvent and processing orthogonality**
D1. Anchoring chemistry: phosphonate/catechol binding tested for stability against DMF/DMSO/GBL exposure (<10% loss by XPS after soak).
D2. Perovskite deposition: viscosity-tuned precursor (η ≥ 10 mPa·s), brief antisolvent (<3 s) to avoid pore infiltration; confirm continuity by cross-sectional SEM/TEM.

**E. Descriptor translation and device validation (post go)**
E1. Measure EASA (Cdl) and solid-state E1/2 analogue/k0 on the same films; confirm trends persist without liquid electrolyte by solid-state charge-modulation spectroscopy.
E2. Correlate with Voc, FF, hysteresis index, ideality factor, and T80 lifetime; apply falsification logic (EASA-only vs kinetics-only regimes).
Feasibility: The revised plan directly addresses reviewer concerns by narrowing the mechanistic claims to *testable, orthogonal interactions* and embedding explicit failure criteria. Chemical passivation is no longer assumed to arise from porphyrin ring nitrogens; instead, the proposal specifies axial Fe coordination or anchor-mediated Pb interaction as the dominant pathway, supported by orthogonal spectroscopy and DFT-calibrated signatures. This sharply reduces interpretational ambiguity inherent in buried-interface HAXPES alone. Redox gating is explicitly validated in the solid state—without electrolyte—using operando spectroelectrochemistry tied to ionic-capacitance suppression, ensuring relevance to device physics and ruling out parasitic halide redox. Quantitative morphology, transport, and solvent-orthogonality windows convert porous-contact integration from a qualitative risk to a bounded engineering problem. By enforcing pre-registered go/no-go discriminators, the proposal ensures that only if specific binding and reversible solid-state redox accessibility are demonstrated will the EASA/E1/2 descriptor program be scaled to full devices, thereby aligning ambition with credible mechanistic validation.
final_critique: The proposal is methodologically strong and unusually falsifiable for an interfacial-mechanism claim in perovskites: axial-site blocking controls, metal-free porphyrin controls, and multiple orthogonal spectroscopies are appropriate to reject the common but ambiguous “Pb–N ring” narrative. The redox-gating test usefully insists on solid-state operation and couples redox-state readout to low-frequency capacitance—this is a coherent device-physics discriminator. Key deductions: (i) the half-wave potential/E1/2 concept is imported from electrochemistry but the translation to a solid-state, electrolyte-free stack remains underdefined (reference scale, band-alignment dependence, and how an ‘E1/2 analogue’ is extracted reproducibly across morphologies); (ii) the ionic-buffering claim risks non-uniqueness—changes in low-frequency capacitance/hysteresis can also arise from altered interfacial recombination, dielectric response, contact selectivity, or ion-blocking by Al2O3/porosity, so the current correlation plan may not isolate ‘redox reservoir’ causality; (iii) the buried-interface binding assignment remains challenging because Pb 4f/I 3d shifts and N K-edge signatures can conflate chemical interaction with electrostatic dipoles and band bending—DFT-calibrated shifts help, but the proposal does not specify how it will deconvolute electrostatic vs chemical contributions experimentally (e.g., via thickness dependence, hard/soft XPS depth profiling, or Kelvin probe). Overall, strong engineering and logic, with the main weakness being the incomplete, quantitative closure of the half-wave-potential descriptor chain under device-relevant solid-state conditions.
hypothesis_summary: A redox-gated Fe-porphyrin porous contact boosts perovskite solar cell performance by chemically passivating defects through specific axial binding and electrochemically buffering ionic charge via reversible solid-state redox.

original_chain: Utilization ratio -> Electrocatalytic activity -> Nickel hydroxide (Ni(OH)2) -> Metal organic framework (MOF) -> Electric conductivity -> Superexchange mechanism -> Reorganization energy -> HOMO-LUMO gap
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A 2D RP surface cap can be converted from an electronically passivating barrier into a conductive, virtual-state–mediated charge relay if (and only if) (i) the π-acceptor spacer introduces energetically *off-resonant* (virtual) states that enhance interlayer electronic coupling without forming a real charge-transfer complex (CTC) and (ii) transport shows a decisive *distance (thickness) dependence* consistent with superexchange/tunneling rather than barrier-limited hopping. In this design, a TCNQ-like π-acceptor spacer is incorporated as the organic layer of an n=1–3 RP cap on a 3D perovskite. The spacer’s acceptor level is tuned to sit near—but not within—the perovskite band edges such that carriers traverse the RP cap via virtual-state participation (superexchange), yielding: (a) a steeper-than-activated increase in through-plane conductance with decreasing RP thickness and a weaker temperature dependence of the interfacial transfer rate, and (b) maintained or improved Voc via reduced interfacial recombination velocity from defect passivation and ionic blocking.

A sparse, chelation-anchored Ni(OH)2·x decoration is introduced *only if Ni remains in an acceptable hydroxide/oxyhydroxide speciation window* under halide exposure and bias. The Ni decoration is not intended to provide percolative conductivity; instead it functions as a localized, high-accessibility redox/ion buffer at the 2D/HTL contact where halide/radical activity initiates. By enforcing a sub-percolation, site-pinned distribution (high “utilization ratio” of accessible Ni sites analogous to high active-site utilization in bicontinuous catalysts), the interfacial redox buffering mitigates iodide/bromide oxidation products and suppresses bias-stress hysteresis and degradation without introducing shunts or creating new recombination centers.

This refined hypothesis directly addresses prior ambiguities: superexchange is claimed only if (1) conductance scales exponentially with RP thickness with a decay constant distinct from simple thermionic barrier modulation and (2) ultrafast interfacial hole-transfer kinetics are weakly temperature dependent while recombination decreases; spacer-induced electronic states are acceptable only if sensitive sub-gap and CTC probes remain below strict thresholds; Ni chemistry is accepted only if operando/ex situ speciation confirms hydroxide/oxyhydroxide dominance and negligible Ni–X formation.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registered go/no-go criteria (applies throughout)
0.1 Superexchange/virtual-state “go” criteria:
- Through-plane conductance G vs RP thickness d must fit G(d)=G0·exp(−βd) over ≥3 distinct d values (quantified by n and nm), with β in the tunneling/superexchange regime (operationally: β ≥ 0.8 nm−1 and stable within ±20% across bias window where band-bending changes are minimal).
- Interfacial hole-transfer time constant (fs–ps TA) changes by <2× between 200–320 K while recombination indicators improve (ΔQFLS ≥ +20 meV at matched carrier density).
0.2 Spacer electronic “no-harm” criteria:
- Sub-gap absorption (PDS and sensitive sub-gap EQE) attributable to spacer/CTC must be below 10−4 relative EQE (or equivalent absorption coefficient threshold pre-defined per instrument) and show no new broad CTC band.
- Absolute PLQY-derived nonradiative loss must not worsen by >10 meV in implied Voc (vs alkyl-spacer RP control) at equal excitation density.
0.3 Ni chemistry “go” criteria:
- Ni speciation: ≥80% Ni(OH)2/NiOOH-like components by operando XAS linear-combination fitting (LCF) under relevant bias/illumination; Ni–X fragments in ToF-SIMS must remain below a pre-set detection ratio (e.g., NiI+/Ni+ and NiBr+/Ni+ below 0.05) after stress.
- No measurable RP/3D decomposition: GIWAXS signatures preserved; ex situ FTIR/NMR of extracted films shows no increase in common decomposition markers beyond control.

Step 1 — System definition and thickness-quantifiable RP cap formation
1.1 Device stack (isolated top interface): glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)(Pb,I,Br)3 (high-Voc composition)/2D RP cap/HTL/Au in n–i–p; all variants share identical 3D perovskite recipe and HTL to isolate interface effects.
1.2 RP cap thickness control with explicit n/distribution:
- Form RP cap by post-treatment using π-spacer salts in orthogonal solvent (IPA/EtOAc), controlling water content <0.5 vol%.
- Target discrete RP phases: n=1, n=2, n=3 by controlling spacer concentration (e.g., 0.5–5 mM), contact time (5–60 s), and anneal (70–100 °C, 1–5 min) to avoid bulk conversion.
- Quantify d and n distribution via GIWAXS (out-of-plane RP peaks), spectroscopic ellipsometry (nm-scale thickness), and cross-sectional STEM for calibration (limited set). Only samples with narrow n distribution (pre-defined GIWAXS peak ratio window) proceed to transport tests.

Step 2 — Spacer library with bounded energetics and explicit CTC avoidance
2.1 Spacer design rules (chemically explicit):
- Use pyridinium/ammonium-anchored π-acceptors derived from TCNQ/F4-TCNQ-like motifs, but incorporate insulating “linker spacing” (e.g., short alkyl/ether spacer of 2–4 atoms) between the cationic anchor and the acceptor core to reduce direct orbital overlap that promotes real CTC formation while still enabling virtual-state coupling.
- Systematically tune electron affinity (EA) via fluorination/cyano density to scan from near-resonant to more off-resonant coupling.
2.2 Screening workflow (must pass all):
- DFT (periodic slab + dielectric embedding) to estimate level alignment and interfacial dipole; reject spacers predicted to yield real integer charge transfer at equilibrium.
- UPS/IPES in dark and under controlled illumination (to reveal photoinduced pinning) on 2D-capped perovskite surfaces to confirm no Fermi-level pinning consistent with deep acceptors.
- Sub-gap state exclusion: PDS + sensitive sub-gap EQE on complete stacks and on simplified perovskite/2D films; reject any spacer producing new broad sub-gap bands consistent with CTC.
- Quantify interface recombination velocity surrogate: absolute PLQY and QFLS vs carrier density on perovskite/2D and perovskite/2D/HTL coupons; only spacers that improve or maintain QFLS at matched density proceed.

Step 3 — Decisive transport falsification: thickness scaling + field/bias dependence
3.1 Conductance vs thickness (primary superexchange test):
- Fabricate vertical test structures: ITO/SnO2/3D perovskite/RP(π-spacer; n=1–3, quantified d)/thin inert top contact (e.g., MoOx/Au for hole collection or C60/BCP/Ag for electron collection depending on polarity) to isolate one-carrier injection.
- Measure J–V and small-signal admittance over frequency; extract G at low-field regime to minimize band-bending artifacts.
- Fit ln(G) vs d to obtain β; compare to alkyl-spacer RP controls. A genuine virtual-state pathway must show (i) robust exponential distance dependence and (ii) reduced apparent activation of transfer kinetics without relying solely on SCLC-derived Ea.
3.2 Bias-dependent admittance spectroscopy (secondary discriminator):
- Map capacitance and conductance vs frequency and bias to separate barrier-height modulation from bulk-like hopping; identify interfacial state response times. Consistency requirement: changes in β with bias must be small in the regime where superexchange dominates; strong bias sensitivity suggests barrier-limited conduction.
3.3 Ultrafast kinetics cross-check:
- fs–ps transient absorption (selective excitation) on perovskite/RP/HTL coupons to measure hole transfer and back-transfer; confirm weak temperature dependence of forward transfer for accepted spacers while recombination slows (TPV/TPC).

Step 4 — Ni(OH)2·x incorporation with non-destructive chemistry and speciation control
4.1 Replace humidity/base vapor with orthogonal, low-water alkoxide hydrolysis:
- Pre-complex Ni(II) to a chelating motif on the spacer (catechol or hydroxamate) in anhydrous alcohol (e.g., iPrOH) using Ni(OR)2 or Ni(acac)2 with controlled ligand exchange.
- After RP formation, introduce Ni via the same orthogonal solvent, then trigger *mild* hydrolysis using a precisely metered alkoxide-to-hydroxide conversion (trace water delivered via Karl–Fischer-verified micro-addition, total water <0.2 vol%) at room temperature, short exposure (<30 s), followed by immediate drying.
- Aim for sub-percolation loading: target areal Ni density defined by XPS atomic % window (pre-registered, e.g., 0.05–0.3 at% relative to Pb at surface). Verify no continuous Ni-rich phase by c-AFM (no low-resistance shorts).
4.2 Acceptable speciation window and verification:
- Ex situ Ni 2p XPS with shake-up analysis to distinguish Ni(OH)2/NiOOH from NiX2; operando XAS (Ni K-edge) under bias/illumination with LCF against Ni(OH)2, NiOOH, NiI2/NiBr2 references.
- ToF-SIMS to detect Ni–X fragments after stress; reject conditions showing significant NiX2 formation.
- GIWAXS before/after Ni incorporation to confirm RP/3D integrity.

Step 5 — Make “utilization ratio” measurable using dedicated symmetric/blank test cells
5.1 Build faradaic-isolation structures (mandatory):
- Metal/RP(π-spacer:Ni)/Metal vertical capacitors (e.g., Au/RP:Ni/Au) on inert substrates to measure Ni redox without perovskite ionic currents.
- Symmetric HTL/RP:Ni/HTL stacks and (separately) HTL/3D perovskite/RP:Ni/HTL to bound contributions.
5.2 Operational utilization ratio definition (measurable):
- Define utilization ratio U = Qredox,rev / (nNi·F), where Qredox,rev is reversible faradaic charge from CV/chronoamperometry in an inert, non-halide electrolyte or solid-state ion-gel that does not attack the RP; nNi is Ni moles (from calibrated XPS/ICP on replicate films).
- Confirm that redox peaks persist with cycling and correlate U with stability improvements in full PSCs.

Step 6 — Control matrix (expanded per reviewer directive)
Mandatory controls (in addition to original):
- Chelating spacer without Ni (isolates chelation/dipole effects).
- Ni-complexed spacer without hydrolysis trigger (isolates Ni coordination vs hydroxide cluster formation).
- Inert hydroxide/oxide analog with same chelation motif (e.g., Mg(OH)2 or Al2O3-like via alkoxide route) at matched loading (decouples redox buffering from physical ion scavenging).
- π-spacer RP with intentionally “too-strong” acceptor (expected to show CTC/sub-gap features) as a negative mechanistic control.

Step 7 — Device-level endpoints and stress protocols
7.1 Performance:
- Report Voc, FF, stabilized PCE; quantify hysteresis with forward/reverse scans and stabilized MPP.
- Correlate FF gains with thickness-scaling β and with extracted interfacial transfer rates.
7.2 Stability:
- MPP tracking under 1 sun at 60–85 °C (pre-defined), controlled RH (e.g., 20–40%), with periodic QFLS/PL checks.
- Degradation forensics: ToF-SIMS depth profiles for halide redistribution and Ni–X; GIWAXS for phase changes.

Step 8 — Decision logic to prevent post hoc fitting
- If spacer passes transport falsification but fails sub-gap/CTC thresholds → revise spacer EA downward (more off-resonant) or increase anchor–acceptor separation.
- If Ni speciation fails (Ni–X rises) → stop Ni pathway and proceed with spacer-only superexchange cap as primary deliverable; Ni branch only continues under validated speciation window.
- If neither transport falsification nor QFLS improvement is met → abandon superexchange claim and re-scope to dipole/passivation-only mechanism with explicit disclosure.
Feasibility: Transport falsifiability is strengthened by making superexchange a *distance-scaling* claim rather than a temperature-activation inference. Exponential conductance decay with precisely quantified RP thickness (n=1–3; ellipsometry+GIWAXS calibrated) is a decisive observable that is difficult to mimic by simple Marcus hopping alone across a fixed barrier, especially when combined with bias-dependent admittance constraints and ultrafast hole-transfer kinetics that are weakly temperature dependent.

Spacer risk (CTC, Fermi-level pinning, Voc loss) is explicitly bounded by a three-layer screening gate: (i) DFT rejection of integer charge transfer propensity, (ii) UPS/IPES measured in dark and under illumination to reveal pinning/photoinduced effects, and (iii) sensitive sub-gap probes (PDS + sub-gap EQE) plus QFLS-vs-density to quantify any increase in interface recombination velocity. This converts “avoid mid-gap traps” into measurable acceptance thresholds.

Ni chemistry is de-risked by (i) replacing humidity/base hydroxylation with a low-water alkoxide-hydrolysis route in orthogonal solvent to minimize perovskite attack, (ii) pre-defining acceptable Ni speciation and proving it by complementary operando XAS (LCF), ex situ Ni 2p XPS shake-up analysis, and ToF-SIMS detection of Ni–X fragments, and (iii) enforcing sub-percolation loading verified by c-AFM so Ni does not become an electronic shunt. This addresses the reviewer concern that “few-Å clusters” are ill-defined by shifting emphasis from nuclearity claims to *speciation + loading window + spatial confinement* that can be reproducibly verified.

The utilization ratio metric becomes experimentally well-conditioned by moving its extraction away from buried PSC interfaces into dedicated metal/RP:Ni/metal and symmetric HTL/RP:Ni/HTL structures where faradaic signatures can be isolated from perovskite ionic currents. This mirrors the logic in high-utilization catalysts: accessibility and reversibility are operationally quantified, then correlated to device stabilization, rather than inferred from ill-conditioned buried measurements.

Finally, the proposal maintains coherence with the original concept chain while integrating reviewer-mandated controls (chelating-no-Ni, Ni-without-hydrolysis, inert hydroxide/oxide analog) to disentangle redox buffering from passive ion scavenging/physical blocking. The combined approach preserves the core objective—simultaneous FF and Voc gains—while adding explicit stop/go criteria to prevent post hoc mechanism assignment.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in engineering resolution and in pre-registered falsification logic for the superexchange claim (distance-scaling + weak T-dependence + bias-stability constraints). That said, several key deductions remain. (i) The central mechanistic discriminator—exponential conductance vs thickness—can still be mimicked by barrier tunneling through an insulator with thickness-dependent band bending or contact resistance artifacts; your current plan mitigates but does not decisively eliminate these confounds (e.g., independent extraction of barrier height and contact-limited contributions is not fully locked down). (ii) The “virtual-state–mediated relay without real CTC” hinge is conceptually plausible but under-specified quantitatively: you set strict sub-gap thresholds, yet do not provide a quantitative coupling/energy-detuning model connecting spacer EA (HOMO–LUMO gap alignment) to β and to the observed transfer kinetics, which weakens causal depth. (iii) The Ni(OH)2·x branch is chemically cautious, but the utilization-ratio construct risks being only loosely connected to halide/radical suppression at the buried PSC interface unless you define which redox couples are being buffered (I−/I2, Br−/Br2, superoxide, HTL radical cations) and demonstrate that Ni redox potential aligns under device-relevant quasi-Fermi-level splitting; otherwise it can devolve into an empirical additive. (iv) The target concept chain includes MOF and electrocatalytic activity; MOF is not actually instantiated, and “electrocatalytic activity” is inferred from reversible charge (U) rather than linked to measured interfacial reaction kinetics relevant to degradation pathways.
hypothesis_summary: A 2D perovskite surface cap with a π-acceptor spacer enables virtual-state–mediated superexchange charge transport, boosting conductance and voltage, while sub-percolation nickel hydroxide decoration provides interfacial redox buffering to suppress degradation.

original_chain: Carnosine -> Hydroxyl radical (OH) -> Piezoelectric response -> Singlet oxygen (^{1}O_{2}) -> Power density -> Redox chemistry
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A carnosine-anchored, nitroxide-terminated interfacial reconstruction layer can be engineered to (i) convert the 3D perovskite surface into a verifiable quasi-2D Ruddlesden–Popper-like (RP-like) slab of predefined thickness (≈1–5 nm) and (ii) act as a stoichiometrically bounded, regenerable redox buffer that suppresses interfacial ROS-triggered halide/organic oxidation, thereby increasing maximum-power-point (MPP) stabilized power density retention. Mechanistic rationale addressing reviewer limitations: (1) Strain node reframed and falsified: instead of asserting intrinsic piezoelectricity, we treat bending as a controlled accelerator of (a) ion migration and (b) interfacial redox/permeation via microcracks/permeability changes. We will only invoke flexoelectric/piezopotential contributions if directly observed as strain-dependent surface-potential signatures (KPFM/Kelvin probe under bending) that correlate with ROS formation and degradation. (2) TEMPO “ROS-gate” is kinetically/stoichiometrically constrained: TEMPO will be immobilized (no dopant-like diffusion) and monitored operando by EPR to quantify its nitroxide fraction over time. Its function is defined as a reversible one-electron redox reservoir (TEMPO•/TEMPO+) that intercepts oxidizing equivalents at the surface and suppresses the propagation steps that generate or amplify 1O2/OH-driven perovskite oxidation. We will explicitly bound side reactions by tracking iodine speciation (I−/I3−/IOx) and ensuring TEMPO does not catalyze iodine redox cycling. (3) RP-like formation is treated as an experimentally testable structural claim with pre-registered diffraction/chemical signatures and benchmarks: we will define GIWAXS peak positions/intensity ratios expected for n=1–3 RP-like phases and corroborate by FTIR/solid-state NMR/XPS depth profiling and a canonical ammonium-spacer RP reference. If those signatures fail, the hypothesis collapses to “coordination-only passivation + redox buffer” and performance/stability will be interpreted accordingly (explicit go/no-go criteria).
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration of falsifiable discriminators (before fabrication)
0.1 Define three success tiers with quantitative thresholds:
  Tier A (full claim): RP-like slab + intact nitroxide + improved stability. Criteria: (i) GIWAXS shows new low-q RP-like features + shifted/quantized out-of-plane periodicity consistent with n=1–3 relative to RP benchmark; (ii) depth profiling indicates an enriched carnosine/TEMPO-containing surface layer confined to ≤10 nm; (iii) operando nitroxide EPR retains ≥50% of initial nitroxide signal after 250 h MPP in air; (iv) ≥2× increase in T80 of PMPP in air (relative control).
  Tier B (partial): no RP-like diffraction, but clear coordination + redox buffering. Criteria: (i) FTIR/NMR/XPS show Pb–N(imidazole) coordination + reduced Pb0/Iox; (ii) nitroxide EPR retention and iodine speciation show non-catalytic behavior; (iii) ≥1.5× T80.
  Tier C (fail): nitroxide consumed rapidly (<20% remaining at 100 h) or iodine cycling enhanced, or Rs penalty >0.5 Ω·cm² with no stability gain.

Step 1 — Device and materials platform (baseline + controls)
1.1 Baseline PSC stack (n–i–p): glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/HTL/Au. Target initial PCE >21%, with matched Voc deficit across batches (document via QFLS-PLQY).
1.2 Surface-treatment library (all processed from orthogonal solvent, identical thermal budget):
  A) Car–TEMPO conjugate (test).
  B) Carnosine-only (coordination without redox buffer).
  C) TEMPO-only analog (redox without anchoring/coordination; choose a neutral small molecule with comparable volatility).
  D) Imidazole-free peptide analog (anchors/sterics without Pb–imidazole coordination).
  E) Canonical cationic RP spacer benchmark (e.g., PEACl/PEAI or BA-based) to calibrate “true RP” GIWAXS and band-offset behavior.
  F) “Redox-inactive tether” control: Car–(alkyl) replacing TEMPO with similar size/dipole to isolate dipole/band-bending from redox.
1.3 Car–TEMPO synthesis and verification (expanded):
  - Confirm structure (1H/13C NMR, HRMS).
  - Confirm redox couple and stability: CV/DPV in non-aqueous electrolyte; report E1/2, ΔEp, and diffusion/film-confined behavior.
  - Quantify nitroxide fraction in films by CW-EPR (spin concentration calibration vs standard) before device integration.

Step 2 — Engineering a bounded interfacial layer (composition + thickness + electronic benignity)
2.1 Post-deposition reconstruction protocol (explicit parameter window):
  - Spin-coat Car–TEMPO from IPA:MeCN (e.g., 4:1 to 1:1; optimize to avoid perovskite dissolution) at 2000–4000 rpm for 20–40 s.
  - Concentration series: 0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 mg mL−1.
  - Anneal: 80 °C for 2 min (primary), plus 70/90 °C brackets to map kinetics.
  - Confinement target: ellipsometry/AFM step-height on masked coupons to quantify thickness (goal 1–5 nm; hard cap ≤10 nm).
2.2 Electronic impact constraint:
  - Extract Rs and recombination parameters from J–V + impedance under 1 sun at MPP bias. Go/no-go: ΔRs ≤0.3 Ω·cm² and no >10% loss in initial PMPP vs baseline.
2.3 Adhesion and mechanical integrity of the cap (before strain tests):
  - Cross-hatch/tape test on perovskite/HTL stacks; nano-scratch if available.
  - Contact angle mapping and surface energy estimation (cap uniformity proxy).

Step 3 — Proving (or falsifying) RP-like formation vs coordination-only passivation
3.1 GIWAXS (pre-defined assignments + benchmark calibration):
  - Measure out-of-plane linecuts and in-plane texture for baseline, Car–TEMPO, carnosine-only, and RP benchmark.
  - Pre-register expected features: (i) emergence of low-q periodicity peaks associated with layered spacing (compared directly to RP benchmark); (ii) relative intensity changes consistent with preferential orientation.
3.2 Chemical coordination signatures:
  - FTIR: imidazole ring mode shifts upon Pb coordination; compare carnosine-only vs imidazole-free analog.
  - Solid-state NMR (as available): 13C/15N (or DNP-enhanced if accessible) to detect coordinated imidazole environments; otherwise use XPS N 1s chemical shift mapping as a minimum.
3.3 Composition-depth profiling:
  - Angle-resolved XPS and/or ToF-SIMS to confirm a surface-confined layer: nitrogen (carnosine) and TEMPO fragments enriched at top surface, decaying into bulk over ≤10 nm.
  - Cross-sectional TEM/EELS to exclude gross intermixing and to assess continuity (no requirement of perfect crystallinity, but continuity must be demonstrated if RP-like claim is made).

Step 4 — Quantitative redox/ROS balance for the immobilized TEMPO gate
4.1 Define the redox accounting to be tested:
  - Inputs: photogenerated holes/electrons at the interface + O2/H2O ingress.
  - Competing pathways (to be discriminated): (i) O2 reduction/ROS generation at traps; (ii) direct oxidation of I−/organic cations; (iii) nitroxide-mediated interception.
  - Readouts: nitroxide fraction (EPR), iodine speciation (XPS/Raman/UV–vis), and ROS probes (SOSG/EPR spin trapping).
4.2 Operando/aged-state nitroxide integrity tracking:
  - Operando CW-EPR on dedicated thin-film stacks under controlled illumination and bias (MPP-relevant potential), at 45–65 °C in dry air and N2.
  - Ex situ EPR before/after 100 h and 500 h MPP stress to quantify irreversible loss.
  - Complement with NEXAFS (if available) or high-resolution XPS on N/O environments to detect conversion to oxoammonium/hydroxylamine-like states.
4.3 Rule out catalytic iodine redox cycling (mandatory control set):
  - Operando/ex situ iodine speciation: XPS I 3d (I− vs higher oxidation states), Raman for polyiodides (I3−), and UV–vis of extracted films (where feasible) to detect I3−/polyiodide signatures.
  - Compare Car–TEMPO vs Car–(alkyl) dipole control and TEMPO-only control. Go/no-go: Car–TEMPO must show reduced (not increased) I3−/IOx signatures relative to baseline at equal aging dose.
4.4 Direct ROS quantification near the interface:
  - SOSG on encapsulated optical coupons (glass/perovskite/cap) with identical illumination dose; report photon-flux-normalized 1O2 signal.
  - EPR spin trapping for •OH/superoxide-related intermediates on analogous stacks; normalize to absorption and film thickness.

Step 5 — Deconvoluting strain effects: permeability/cracking vs electrostatic (flexo/piezopotential) contributions
5.1 Strain protocol (explicit) on flexible devices:
  - Substrate: ITO/PET or ITO/PI; bending radius calibrated to 0–0.5% strain.
  - Apply cyclic bending (e.g., 10^3–10^4 cycles) combined with light soaking at MPP; record Voc, FF, Rs evolution.
5.2 Crack formation and delamination monitoring (to remove ambiguity):
  - In situ optical microscopy during bending (crack onset density vs strain).
  - AFM topography before/after cycling for microcracks/roughness change.
  - Adhesion re-test post-bending.
5.3 Permeability proxies (oxygen/water ingress sensitivity):
  - Track water contact angle drift and photoluminescence quenching under controlled O2/H2O exposure.
  - If available, use Ca test (calcium corrosion) on separately prepared barrier stacks to compare relative WVTR/OTR proxies between caps.
5.4 Electrostatic signature test (only if present, to justify “piezo/flexo” node):
  - KPFM (or scanning Kelvin probe) mapping under controlled bending to detect strain-dependent surface potential/band-bending changes.
  - Correlate any observed Δsurface potential with ROS probe signal (SOSG/EPR) and degradation rate. If no reproducible Δpotential beyond noise, interpret strain effects purely as mechanical/permeation/ionic acceleration.

Step 6 — Performance/stability endpoints linked to ‘power density’
6.1 Standard PV metrics:
  - J–V forward/reverse, stabilized MPP tracking, and PMPP/area (power density) under 1 sun.
  - Report hysteresis index, ideality factor vs intensity, and temperature dependence.
6.2 Accelerated aging matrix:
  - 45–65 °C MPP in N2 and dry air (mandatory) plus controlled RH steps.
  - Encapsulated damp-heat screening (85/85) on mini-modules for barrier synergy.
6.3 Mechanistic linkage analysis:
  - Mixed-effects models across ≥25 devices/condition and ≥3 batches.
  - Regression linking PMPP decay to (i) nitroxide EPR decay, (ii) iodine oxidation markers, (iii) ROS probe signals, and (iv) crack density/permeability proxies under strain.

Step 7 — Scale-up compatibility
7.1 Slot-die/meniscus coating of Car–TEMPO on 1–10 cm² devices.
7.2 Uniformity criteria: spatial PL mapping, sheet resistance stability (no added series resistance gradients), and ToF-SIMS spot checks for nitrogen/TEMPO fragment uniformity.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing the “piezoelectric response” ambiguity with hard discriminators
Perovskite bending degradation can be dominated by ionic motion and mechanically induced permeability/cracking rather than true piezoelectric polarization. This proposal now treats strain as a controlled accelerator with mandatory measurements of crack formation, adhesion loss, and permeability proxies. Flexoelectric/piezopotential contributions are not assumed; they are tested directly via strain-dependent surface-potential mapping (KPFM/Kelvin probe under bending) and only used in interpretation if a reproducible Δsurface potential correlates with ROS generation and degradation kinetics.

2) Kinetic/redox closure for TEMPO under PSC operating conditions
The ROS-gating function is reformulated as an immobilized, regenerable redox buffer rather than an unbounded “ROS scavenger” claim. Feasibility hinges on two measurable conditions: (i) operando/ex situ EPR must show that a substantial fraction of nitroxide persists under illumination/bias, consistent with regeneration; (ii) iodine speciation must show suppression (not enhancement) of I3−/IOx signatures, ruling out catalytic iodine redox cycling. By including TEMPO-only and redox-inactive dipole/steric controls, we can separate anchoring, dipole/band-bending, and true redox-buffer effects.

3) RP-like formation is made testable rather than asserted
Because carnosine is non-ammonium and may not spontaneously yield a textbook RP lattice, we predefine structural expectations and introduce a canonical ammonium RP spacer as a calibration benchmark. GIWAXS is complemented by coordination-specific spectroscopy (FTIR/solid-state NMR or XPS chemical shifts) and depth profiling to determine whether the interfacial layer is (a) a true layered RP-like slab, (b) a mixed coordination complex, or (c) merely molecular passivation. The proposal remains scientifically valuable under Tier B (coordination + redox buffering) even if Tier A (RP-like slab) fails, preserving logical closure.

4) Coherence with the concept chain and literature assets
The proposal preserves the core chain: controlling redox chemistry to protect stabilized power density, while translating “ROS generation/quenching” logic (Asset 1) and “redox-engineered performance” logic (Asset 2) into a perovskite-native interface architecture without catalytic metal centers. The revised plan tightens causal inference by directly measuring ROS, interfacial redox state (iodine/Pb), and nitroxide integrity, and by deconvoluting mechanical strain pathways that could otherwise masquerade as electrostatic/piezo effects.
final_critique: Methodological execution is strong: the proposal pre-registers falsifiable structural discriminators (GIWAXS benchmarks, depth profiling), constrains interfacial thickness, and uses operando EPR to close the redox-accounting loop—rarely done rigorously in interfacial additive work. The major scientific risk is the Tier-A claim: converting a 3D halide perovskite surface into a well-defined 1–5 nm “RP-like slab” using a non-ammonium, zwitterionic peptide (carnosine) is chemically under-justified; even if GIWAXS shows low-q features, distinguishing true RP stacking from surface texturing/solvent-induced reorganization will be difficult without decisive cross-sectional structural proof (e.g., lattice-resolved STEM with layer periodicity and composition contrast). The TEMPO gate logic is plausible, but the proposal does not fully specify the thermodynamic alignment (TEMPO•/TEMPO+ potential vs perovskite hole quasi-Fermi level, vs iodide/iodine couples) that determines whether TEMPO will be regenerative or simply sacrificial; without that, EPR retention could reflect kinetic isolation rather than functional buffering. The strain/piezo node is handled responsibly (conditional), but it becomes peripheral to the core mechanism; if piezo/flexo signals are absent, the concept chain element is effectively unused rather than integrated.
hypothesis_summary: A carnosine-anchored, nitroxide-terminated surface layer forms a thin quasi-2D perovskite slab and acts as a regenerable redox buffer to block ROS-driven oxidation, boosting solar cell stability.

original_chain: Piezoelectric response -> Open-circuit voltage (Voc) -> Flexible perovskite solar cells -> Mechanical stability -> Bending cycles -> J-V curves -> EIS (electrochemical impedance spectroscopy) -> Hysteresis
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: If curvature in flexible inverted perovskite solar cells produces a *quantifiable* bending-induced electrostatic potential swing (Δφbend) across the absorber—arising from strain-gradient piezo/ flexoelectric polarization in the perovskite + curvature-amplified contact asymmetry—then this Δφbend will modulate the ionic electrochemical potential (μion) and interfacial band bending at the HTL-side, increasing low-frequency ionic capacitance (Cion), recombination activation, and J–V hysteresis, thereby degrading Voc under cycling. Embedding a *buried, sparse, vertically oriented* ferroelectric nanolaminate layer (sub-percolation platelet network) at a designed depth (100–250 nm from the HTL) will act as an internal electrostatic clamp that reduces ∂φ/∂κ (electric potential sensitivity to curvature κ) by (i) providing a high effective dielectric susceptibility χeff and (ii) adding a switchable remanent polarization Pr that can be oriented to oppose the curvature-induced field at the HTL-side. The hypothesis is falsifiable via (A) predicted Δφbend(κ) from an electromechanical stack model; (B) a required χeff/Pr threshold for a targeted suppression factor S = Δφbend,control/Δφbend,laminate; and (C) polarity dependence: reversing the ferroelectric dipole should *invert* the sign or increase the magnitude of Δφbend and hysteresis if screening—not generic passivation—is responsible. The refined approach overcomes feasibility concerns by (1) using platelets and passivation designed to retain switching (minimized depolarization via controlled shell thickness and partial screening), (2) aligning platelets with a demonstrably out-of-plane field geometry/dielectrophoresis rather than in-plane AC fields, (3) separating ferroelectric switching from ionic motion through blocking-layer test structures and time/frequency/temperature discrimination, and (4) employing matched-chemistry nonpolar platelet controls to isolate electrostatics from trap passivation.
Plan: PHASE 0 — Quantitative model + go/no-go gates (mandatory before full device campaigns)
0.1 Stack mechanics: compute neutral axis (z0) and strain profile εxx(z)=κ(z−z0) for the full flexible stack (PI / TCO or Ag-mesh/IZO / HTL / perovskite / ETL / top electrode / encapsulation). Use measured layer thicknesses and elastic moduli (nanoindentation or literature) to locate z0; report uncertainty. Define curvature κ=1/R for R=3,5,10 mm.
0.2 Electromechanical-to-electrostatic mapping (order-of-magnitude + FEM):
  • Baseline source term: represent bending-induced polarization density as Pbend(z)=μβend·∂ε/∂z ≈ μeff·κ (flexoelectric-like term) plus a possible piezo-like term if texture/strain breaks centrosymmetry locally. Use μeff as an extracted parameter from dedicated bending-KPFM measurements on pristine films (Phase 1), not assumed.
  • Solve Poisson with mobile-ion screening limits: bracket two regimes—(i) fast electronic screening/slow ionic (short-time, ‘frozen ions’), (ii) partial ionic screening (long-time). Implement as an effective Debye length λD,ion fitted from EIS/impedance spectroscopy of pristine devices. Outcome: predicted Δφbend at HTL-side and its relaxation time.
