Prediction P1 (falsifiable): A monotonic relationship between the curvature descriptor κ̄ (defined below) and the local contact potential difference ΔCPD (KPFM) / work function shift ΔΦ (UPS), with a target magnitude ΔΦ = +50 to +200 meV relative to the no-interlayer control at identical perovskite composition and processing, yielding increased built-in field and higher quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS).
2) Curvature/strain → defect chemistry and recombination: Strain gradients and modified electrostatics alter interfacial defect formation energies (iodine vacancy/undercoordinated Pb) and suppress interfacial nonradiative pathways. Prediction P2: Interfacial recombination velocity S (from absolute PLQY-derived QFLS and optical outcoupling-corrected radiative limit) decreases systematically with κ̄, targeting ≥2× reduction vs planar-MOF control at matched thickness and coverage.
3) Curvature/strain + FeN4 utilization → chemical turnover without parasitic catalysis: FeN4 sites embedded in a partially converted MOF/oxide hybrid provide reversible one-electron buffering within a bounded redox window that passivates reactive intermediates (superoxide/iodine radicals) without driving I−→I2 or O2 reduction/ROS formation. Prediction P3: In a three-electrode illuminated stack using defined redox probes, the areal reversible charge (Qrev) and small-signal interfacial buffering capacitance (Cbuf) scale with operando-verified FeN4 density (NFeN4,operando), while Faradaic currents for iodide oxidation remain below a strict threshold (see go/no-go).
4) Curvature/strain → ion migration barrier: The curvature field and interlayer microstructure increase activation energy for ionic migration across the buried interface. Prediction P4: Arrhenius analysis of bias-stress/temperature-dependent EIS yields an increase in ionic activation energy Ea,ion by ≥0.10 eV (target 0.10–0.25 eV) for high-κ̄ samples relative to controls.

Central claim (falsifiable): If κ̄ is increased by tuning twin density while keeping FeN4 density constant, then ΔΦ and Ea,ion will increase and S will decrease. Conversely, if FeN4 density is increased at fixed κ̄, Qrev/Cbuf will increase without a proportional change in ΔΦ or Ea,ion. Failure of these orthogonal dependencies falsifies the proposed curvature-mediated causality and separates curvature effects from chemical-site effects.
Plan: Step 0 — Baseline device and control architecture (locked before optimization)
0.1 Baseline PSC: Blade-coated FA0.85Cs0.15Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 (target 1.55–1.60 eV bandgap), inverted p–i–n stack: ITO/NiOx (or MeO-2PACz as a secondary baseline)/Perovskite/Interlayer/C60/BCP/Ag.
0.2 Fixed perovskite processing window: identical solvent system, anneal temperature/time, and surface quench for all interlayer comparisons to avoid confounding morphology.
0.3 Mandatory controls (all thickness-matched and coverage-matched): (C1) no interlayer; (C2) planar MOF-derived film (no twin features); (C3) twin-like MOF without Fe (isostructural Zn/Al or Ni-only analogue); (C4) Fe-containing interlayer intentionally oxidized to FeOx-rich (negative control for deep-state/catalysis risk).

Step 1 — Define and implement a quantitative curvature/twin-density descriptor (pre-registered)
1.1 4D-STEM acquisition: Cross-sectional lamellae (FIB with low-kV cleaning) through perovskite/interlayer/C60. 4D-STEM nanobeam diffraction mapping across the interface (pixel size 1–3 nm) to extract local strain tensor ε(x,y) and lattice rotation.
1.2 Curvature descriptor (primary): κ̄ = ⟨|∇·(∇u)|⟩A within the interlayer (u = displacement field from 4D-STEM), reported as mean absolute curvature over the interlayer area A; secondary: twin boundary areal density ρTB (nm−1) from HRTEM/4D-STEM segmentation.
1.3 Sample set design: Synthesize ≥3 interlayer variants spanning κ̄ (low/medium/high) by tuning twin density (ρTB) while holding Fe loading constant (±10%) and thickness constant (10 ± 2 nm). A second set spans FeN4 density at fixed κ̄ (adjust Fe precursor ratio post twin-setting).

Step 2 — Interlayer synthesis with speciation-preserving, low-temperature chemistry
2.1 Twin-like MOF nanobrick synthesis (twin density as control knob):
- System: bimetallic Fe/Ni–BDC (or Fe–BDC with controlled secondary metal) synthesized solvothermally in DMF/ethanol/water with modulated coordination kinetics.
- Twin control parameters: (i) Fe:Ni molar ratio (e.g., 1:3, 1:1, 3:1), (ii) modulator concentration (acetic acid/benzoic acid, 0–50 mM), (iii) water content (0–10 vol%) to tune nucleation rate.
- Target morphology: quasi-2D nanobricks 10–30 nm thick, lateral size 50–200 nm, with explicit ρTB ranking verified by TEM.

2.2 Partial conversion to FeN4-containing hybrid without collapsing twins (avoid plasma-first)
- Conversion route A (primary, gentler than plasma): low-temperature ammonolysis/amine-assisted ligand transformation at 150–200 °C in NH3/Ar (≤5% NH3) or urea-derived NH3 release, 30–120 min, designed to (i) introduce N coordination around isolated Fe, (ii) partially carbonize/condense linkers, (iii) retain crystallographic twin features.
- Conversion route B (secondary): remote (downstream) N2/H2 plasma at low power and substrate cooling, with dose calibrated using in situ QCM; used only if route A fails to yield FeN4 signatures.
- Explicit “do not exceed” conditions: temperature >200 °C or exposure that produces Fe clusters/FeOx dominance (see go/no-go).

2.3 Redox-window engineering to prevent halide catalysis
- Introduce electron-withdrawing linker substitution (e.g., F-substituted BDC fraction) or incorporate a thin oxide-like passivating fraction (Fe–O–C/N) to shift Fe(III/II) couple away from I−/I2.
- Pre-register acceptable redox window: interlayer redox features must lie outside the effective perovskite iodide oxidation regime under illumination; operational criterion implemented via three-electrode tests (Step 5) and device bias-stress (Step 6).

Step 3 — Manufacturable interlayer deposition + shunt mitigation (primary + fallback)
3.1 Primary deposition (lab-scale, controllable coverage): electrostatic layer-by-layer (LbL) assembly using a cationic polyelectrolyte primer (ultrathin, <1 nm equivalent) to promote percolative-but-discontinuous nanobrick adsorption; target coverage 40–70% with percolation paths but no continuous metallic conduction.
3.2 Fallback deposition (manufacturability): slot-die/meniscus coating of ligand-assisted nanobrick ink:
- Ink: nanobricks dispersed in alcohol (IPA/EtOH) with 0.01–0.05 wt% short bifunctional ligand (e.g., amino-silane or pyridine derivative) that (i) promotes adhesion, (ii) prevents aggregation, (iii) limits infiltration into perovskite.
- Process window: web-compatible drying (<80 °C), no chlorinated solvents.
3.3 Shunt/leakage mitigation and statistics:
- Enforce thickness 5–15 nm by ellipsometry/cross-section TEM.
- Pinhole statistics: conductive-AFM mapping (≥50×50 µm) to quantify fraction of high-conductance spots; accept ≤0.1% area above threshold current at fixed bias.
- Cross-sectional conductivity mapping: scanning microwave impedance microscopy (sMIM) or c-AFM on lamella to verify no continuous shunt path between perovskite and Ag.

Step 4 — Work function/band bending validation tied to κ̄ (Directive 1a)
4.1 KPFM under controlled humidity/O2: map ΔCPD across perovskite/interlayer surface before C60 deposition and (if feasible) through thin C60.
4.2 UPS/XPS: determine work function Φ and valence-band position; track chemical shifts indicating interfacial dipole formation.
4.3 Falsifiable correlation test: regress ΔΦ and/or ΔCPD against κ̄ and ρTB at constant FeN4 density; require monotonic trend (P1). If absent, curvature-electrostatics pathway is rejected and the hypothesis is narrowed to purely chemical buffering.

Step 5 — Replace “TOF-like” with separable kinetic scheme (Directive 2)
5.1 Electron extraction kinetics (non-Faradaic, device-relevant):
- Ultrafast transient absorption (TA) on complete stacks with selective contacts (NiOx/perovskite/interlayer/C60) using excitation densities matched to 1-sun carrier concentrations; extract electron-transfer time constants τET and interfacial charge-separation yield.
- Complement with TPV/TPC and intensity-dependent transient photovoltage to obtain recombination order and interfacial time constants; interpret using an equivalent circuit that includes ionic branch (validated in Step 7).
- Output metric: kext = 1/τET (or contact-limited extraction rate) independent of Fe redox chemistry.

5.2 Interfacial chemical turnover / buffering (Faradaic-capable, isolated from device extraction):
- Construct three-electrode “PSC-mimic” stacks: ITO/NiOx/perovskite/interlayer/transparent inert electrode (thin Au grid or carbon) in non-aqueous electrolyte compatible with perovskite (e.g., acetonitrile-based with low water content) and/or solid polymer electrolyte; illumination matched (AM1.5G equivalent intensity at sample).
- Use defined redox probes with potentials chosen to bracket the expected FeN4 redox but not overlap iodide oxidation (e.g., ferrocene derivatives as external standards), and quantify reversible charge Qrev and apparent heterogeneous rate k0 via cyclic voltammetry/EIS.
- Normalize chemical turnover to operando FeN4 density NFeN4,operando from XAS/Mössbauer (Step 8) and probe-binding (Step 8.3). Output metric: kchem (s−1 per FeN4) and Cbuf per FeN4.

Step 6 — Ionic activation barrier and ion-migration suppression (Directive 1b)
6.1 Temperature-dependent EIS (dark and 1-sun, 25–85 °C): fit with drift-diffusion–informed equivalent circuit containing an ionic resistance/capacitance element; extract ionic time constant τion and ionic conductivity proxy σion.
6.2 Bias-stress Arrhenius protocol: apply constant forward bias near Voc and at MPP for fixed times; measure hysteresis index, Voc decay, and EIS recovery vs temperature; obtain Ea,ion from ln(τion) vs 1/T.
6.3 Falsifiable target: Ea,ion increases by ≥0.10 eV with κ̄ (P4). Validate with ToF-SIMS depth profiles after stress (I−, Br−, MA/FA fragments if present) to confirm reduced interfacial accumulation.

Step 7 — Interfacial recombination velocity from absolute PLQY/QFLS (Directive 1c)
7.1 Absolute PLQY on complete half-stacks (ITO/NiOx/perovskite/interlayer and with C60) using integrating sphere; compute QFLS and nonradiative voltage loss ΔVnr.
7.2 Convert QFLS change to an effective interfacial recombination velocity S using optical/electrical modeling with measured absorption/outcoupling.
7.3 Falsifiable target: ≥2× reduction in S for high-κ̄ interlayers vs planar-MOF control at matched thickness/coverage (P2).

Step 8 — Fe speciation stability and go/no-go criteria (Directive 3)
8.1 Operando XAS (Fe K-edge) under light/heat/bias:
- Conditions: (i) 1-sun equivalent illumination, (ii) 65 °C, (iii) forward bias near Voc, (iv) oxygen-controlled atmospheres (N2 vs 1% O2) to test oxidative susceptibility.
- Outputs: oxidation state (edge position), coordination (EXAFS), single-atom signature vs Fe–Fe scattering.
8.2 Mössbauer (ex situ + post-stress) to distinguish FeN4 vs FeOx vs Fe clusters.
8.3 Operando site accessibility/utilization ratio: probe-binding (NO/CO) coupled with spectroscopic signature and electrochemical addressability in the three-electrode stack; define utilization ratio U = Naccessible/Ntotal.

Go/no-go thresholds (hard stops):
- G1 (single-atom preservation): EXAFS shows no significant Fe–Fe peak (coordination number consistent with isolated sites) and post-stress change in Fe–N coordination ≤20%.
- G2 (redox safety): In iodide-containing test environments, Faradaic current attributable to I− oxidation at operational potentials is ≤10% of control (no interlayer) and no net I2/tri-iodide formation detected by UV–Vis; if exceeded, Fe chemistry is deemed parasitic and the Fe content must be reduced or Fe replaced (fallback: Ni-only twin-MOF for curvature-only test).
- G3 (Fenton/ROS risk screen): Under controlled humidity/O2, no accelerated PL quenching or rapid Voc decay relative to planar-MOF; if observed, implement hydrophobic capping/oxygen-barrier overlayer or remove Fe.

Step 9 — Device benchmarking and causality map
9.1 Performance: J–V (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP, EQE; ensure FF loss ≤1% absolute vs control for acceptance.
9.2 Stability: ISOS-L-2 style at 65 °C MPP tracking; target T80 ≥1500 h (as proposed) but now interpreted through measured Ea,ion and S.
9.3 Causality matrix (pre-registered):
- Primary axis (curvature): κ̄ → (ΔΦ, Ea,ion, S) with Fe held constant.
- Secondary axis (chemistry): NFeN4,operando/U → (Qrev, Cbuf, kchem) with κ̄ held constant.
- Decision rule: device Voc/stability improvements must co-vary with the axis-consistent metrics; otherwise claims are restricted to the validated axis only.
Feasibility: 1) Quantitative, falsifiable mechanism now defined: The proposal pre-registers a curvature/twin-density descriptor (κ̄, ρTB) derived from 4D-STEM and explicitly predicts measurable shifts in (a) work function/band bending (KPFM/UPS), (b) ionic activation barriers (temperature-dependent EIS + Arrhenius), and (c) recombination velocity (absolute PLQY/QFLS). These are direct, disprovable links from structure → electrostatics/ionics → device metrics, avoiding post hoc correlations.

2) Metrology risk (ill-defined “TOF-like”) addressed by separable kinetics: Charge extraction is quantified independently (ultrafast TA/TPV/TPC-derived τET, kext) in solid-state device stacks, while chemical turnover/buffering is quantified in a controlled three-electrode illuminated mimic with defined redox probes (Qrev, Cbuf, kchem), both normalized to operando-verified FeN4 density. This disentangles non-Faradaic extraction from Faradaic-capable interfacial chemistry in a mixed ionic–electronic junction.

3) Materials-compatibility and parasitic catalysis are explicitly bounded: The interlayer is required to operate within a redox-safety window enforced by go/no-go criteria (iodide oxidation suppression; no detectable I2/tri-iodide; controlled O2/humidity screens). Operando XAS/Mössbauer under bias/heat/light provides hard acceptance thresholds for Fe single-atom stability and excludes Fe clustering/FeOx drift that would create deep states or catalyze degradation.

4) “Curvature field preservation” is treated as an experimental variable, not an assumption: Twin/curvature descriptors are measured after each processing step (as-synthesized MOF → partially converted hybrid → post-UV-ozone/anneal). If κ̄ collapses upon conversion, the curvature hypothesis is falsified early, and the work pivots to a curvature-only (Fe-free) or chemistry-only (FeN4 without twin enrichment) interpretation.

5) Manufacturability and shunt risk are integrated: In addition to LbL (lab control), a slot-die compatible ligand-assisted ink route is provided. Shunt/leakage is quantitatively managed through thickness constraints, conductive-AFM pinhole statistics, and cross-sectional conductivity mapping; acceptance criteria are defined before device optimization.

6) Literature-to-proposal coherence (concept chain preserved):
- From twin-like MOF nanobricks (Asset 3), we retain the twin-boundary–driven high electroactive site density concept but translate it into a PSC-relevant interfacial architecture with explicit leakage controls.
- From negative Gaussian curvature improving reaction barriers and utilization (Asset 1), we convert “curvature advantage” into a measured κ̄–property relationship and test it against band bending, ionic barriers, and recombination.
- From overpotential/TOF frameworks (Asset 2), we retain rigorous kinetic normalization but replace ambiguous “TOF-like” metrics with two orthogonal, experimentally separable rate descriptions suitable for PSC buried interfaces.

Overall, the revised project is executable with clear stop conditions, orthogonal variable control (κ̄ vs NFeN4), and quantitative predictions that can validate—or falsify—the curvature-mediated causality central to the hypothesis.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in experimental rigor: it pre-registers structural descriptors (κ̄, ρTB), enforces orthogonal controls (curvature vs FeN4 density), and ties each mechanistic leg to falsifiable readouts (ΔΦ/ΔCPD, S from absolute PLQY→QFLS, Ea,ion from Arrhenius EIS). However, the core causal leap—twin-boundary-driven negative Gaussian curvature producing a flexoelectric-like polarization that reliably shifts band bending by 50–200 meV at a buried perovskite/C60 junction—remains under-theorized and may be over-ambitious given (i) screening/ionic redistribution in halide perovskites, (ii) the interlayer being discontinuous/percolative by design, and (iii) the fact that κ̄ derived from interlayer lattice displacement is not obviously the same as interfacial geometric curvature experienced by the electronic junction. The ‘Schwarz P surface’ element is invoked conceptually but not demonstrated structurally (no 3D bicontinuous minimal-surface topology verification), weakening grounding to the required chain. The electrochemistry plan is thoughtful, but perovskite-compatible three-electrode illumination experiments are high-risk: electrolyte/perovskite incompatibility, potential infiltration, and ambiguous assignment of Faradaic vs capacitive currents can compromise Qrev/Cbuf interpretation. Finally, controlling Fe loading to ±10% while independently tuning twin density and maintaining identical coverage/thickness is practically challenging; without a robust statistical design (DoE, hierarchical modeling), residual covariance between κ̄, chemistry, and morphology could masquerade as ‘orthogonal dependencies’.
hypothesis_summary: We hypothesize that a curvature-programmable MOF interlayer with controlled twin density can independently tune perovskite solar cell band bending and ion migration barriers, while embedded FeN4 sites provide chemically selective redox buffering.

original_chain: Loading capacity -> Ag44 -> Catalytic activity -> Photocatalytic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) -> Acetic acid -> NH2-MIL125 -> Volcano-type trend -> Photocatalytic oxygen reduction reaction (ORR)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding atomically precise Ag44 nanoclusters (Ag44(SR)x; ligand-defined charge state) into facet-engineered NH2‑MIL‑125(Ti) will create a predictable volcano dependence of photocatalytic ORR performance and PSC interfacial benefit because (i) increasing Ag44 loading initially increases the density of selective ORR active sites and accelerates *benign* 2e− ORR (O2 → H2O2/HO2−) that lowers interfacial O2 chemical potential and suppresses 1e− superoxide (O2•−) formation; but (ii) above a percolation/transport threshold, Ag44 domains electronically decouple from the ETL/perovskite extraction pathway and/or introduce interfacial mid-gap states that increase non-radiative recombination, offsetting oxygen-scavenging gains. Device-grade stability requires that the interlayer does not transiently elevate O2•− under low-water conditions typical of PSC encapsulation; therefore, the central mechanistic claim is that optimized Ag44@NH2‑MIL‑125 shifts ORR selectivity away from the 1e− superoxide route under relevant oxygen partial pressure and water activity, while simultaneously maintaining favorable band alignment so that electrons are supplied from the ETL/perovskite (electron-sink behavior) rather than creating a recombination center. Facet control via acetic-acid modulation alters (a) the fraction of specific crystal facets that gate pore aperture/defect density and (b) O2/H2O adsorption–diffusion metrics, which together set Ag44 uptake, local dielectric environment, and electron-transfer kinetics—enabling a mechanistically parameterized volcano model rather than an empirical loading sweep.
Plan: Step 0 — Define operating envelope & go/no-go metrics (device-relevant ORR constraints):
0.1 Set PSC-relevant conditions for all ORR tests: oxygen partial pressure pO2 = 0.2–1.0 bar (air to O2), water activity aH2O ≤ 10−3–10−2 (dry gas with controlled ppm H2O; verified by hygrometer), temperature 25–60 °C, illumination matched to AM1.5G photon flux with a “filtered” condition (>420 nm) to mimic light reaching an ultrathin buried layer.
0.2 Go/no-go criterion for interlayer candidacy: under the above conditions, (i) interfacial superoxide yield must decrease relative to control (no interlayer and pristine NH2‑MIL‑125) as quantified by operando EPR spin trapping; (ii) ORR must proceed predominantly via 2e− pathway with measurable H2O2/HO2− formation and suppressed 1e− signature; (iii) incorporation must not reduce quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) at the interface beyond a predefined threshold (e.g., ΔQFLS loss < 10–20 meV at 1 sun in contact stack).

Step 1 — Facet-engineered NH2‑MIL‑125(Ti) with quantified facet descriptor and transport/adsorption metrics:
1.1 Synthesize NH2‑MIL‑125(Ti) via solvothermal route with acetic acid as a monotopic modulator; vary modulator/metal ratio (e.g., 0, 10, 25, 50, 100 equiv vs Ti) while holding linker/Ti and solvent composition constant to isolate facet/defect effects.
1.2 Quantify facet distribution using: (i) TEM/SAED with facet indexing; (ii) PXRD peak-intensity analysis supported by morphology statistics; (iii) Wulff construction using measured relative surface energies inferred from modulator-dependent growth trends (calibrated with DFT surface models as needed).
1.3 Replace “facet exposure” with a single measurable descriptor F_facet (e.g., area fraction of the dominant low-index facet(s) that control pore mouth accessibility). Correlate F_facet to: BET surface area, pore size distribution, and gas adsorption/diffusion proxies relevant to ORR (O2 uptake isotherms; pulse-response diffusion in a microreactor if available).
1.4 Map defect density and Ti3+/oxygen-vacancy signatures (potential recombination centers) via XPS (Ti 2p), EPR (Ti3+), and photothermal deflection/steady-state absorption tailing. This provides a mechanistic lever separating “more uptake” from “more traps.”

Step 2 — Mechanochemical encapsulation of Ag44 with explicit cluster chemistry controls:
2.1 Select a well-defined Ag44 cluster composition and ligand set SR compatible with PSC processing (non-nucleophilic, non-halide-releasing, low volatility). Pre-verify cluster identity/charge state by ESI-MS (if soluble), UV–vis fingerprinting, and XPS (Ag 3d, S 2p).
2.2 Encapsulate Ag44 into NH2‑MIL‑125 via mechanochemistry (ball milling or resonant acoustic mixing) under inert atmosphere to avoid oxidative restructuring. Control parameters: milling time/energy, cluster:MOF mass ratio, and minimal liquid-assisted grinding (LAG) with an orthogonal, perovskite-safe solvent (e.g., anisole/ethyl acetate class) at η (μL mg−1) tuned to maximize uptake while minimizing ligand loss.
2.3 Establish loading series (e.g., 0.2, 0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10 wt% Ag44) and quantify *true* encapsulated loading by ICP‑MS after rigorous external washing; confirm no surface-adsorbed excess via ToF‑SIMS depth profiling.
2.4 Validate structural integrity pre-device: EXAFS/XANES for Ag–Ag coordination and Ag–S features; XPS for Ag oxidation state; compare to pristine Ag44 reference to confirm “atomically precise” preservation.
2.5 Assess leaching/aggregation resistance: soak composites in PSC-relevant solvents (antisolvent, ETL solvents) and in contact with perovskite precursor residues (FAI/MAI, PbI2 traces) under dark/light; monitor by ICP‑MS (leached Ag), UV–vis, and post-soak EXAFS.

Step 3 — ORR pathway/selectivity and kinetics under PSC-relevant low-water conditions (operando discriminants):
3.1 Thin-film RRDE/rotating disk methodology adapted to composite films: deposit Ag44@NH2‑MIL‑125 as a controlled thin layer on glassy carbon (or Au) with thickness matched to intended interlayer (see Step 5). Use RRDE to quantify electron transfer number (n) and H2O2 yield; run in aprotic/low-protic electrolytes and controlled water content to emulate low aH2O; benchmark against NH2‑MIL‑125 and Ag44 alone.
3.2 Quantify superoxide directly using operando EPR spin trapping (e.g., DMPO or analogous trap suited to low-water/aprotic environments) on illuminated films in controlled pO2/aH2O. Output: O2•− formation rate vs loading and facet descriptor F_facet.
3.3 Quantify H2O2/HO2− products using micro-GC/IC or colorimetric titration (validated against standards) in a sealed microreactor under illumination; include 18O2 isotopic tracing to confirm oxygen incorporation into products and to decouple from lattice oxygen contributions.
3.4 Establish selectivity map: {loading, F_facet, aH2O, pO2, irradiance} → {H2O2 yield, O2•− yield, TOF}. Define “safe ORR window” where O2•− decreases relative to controls.

Step 4 — Band alignment, charge-transfer direction, and recombination diagnostics (pre-device stacks):
4.1 Measure energy levels/work function with UPS and Kelvin probe for: perovskite, ETL (SnO2/TiO2), NH2‑MIL‑125, and Ag44@NH2‑MIL‑125 across loadings. Determine whether the composite forms an electron-accepting cascade (favorable) or a barrier.
4.2 Build model interfaces (glass/ETL/interlayer/perovskite and glass/perovskite/interlayer/ETL) and quantify:
- TRPL (lifetime changes; extraction vs quenching),
- transient photovoltage/photocurrent (TPV/TPC) for recombination and transport time constants,
- intensity-dependent Voc to extract ideality factor and recombination mechanism shifts.
4.3 Determine whether the interlayer is electron-sink vs recombination center by combining: (i) QFLS (absolute PL) in contact stacks; (ii) EIS under illumination (recombination resistance, chemical capacitance) with controlled oxygen.

Step 5 — Interlayer architecture: thickness/coverage targets + deposition route orthogonal to perovskite:
5.1 Target interlayer thickness 5–30 nm (ultrathin, continuous coverage) to balance catalytic site availability with minimal series resistance; confirm thickness/roughness by ellipsometry/AFM and cross-sectional SEM/TEM.
5.2 Deposition route: formulate a dispersion of Ag44@NH2‑MIL‑125 in an orthogonal solvent that does not dissolve/complex perovskite (e.g., anisole, chlorobenzene alternatives as allowed by the perovskite stack). Use dynamic spin coating or blade coating at low concentration; optionally add a minimal, electronically benign binder (≤1–2 wt%) if required for film continuity.
5.3 Confirm perovskite compatibility: no ligand attack/ion exchange—verify by XRD/PL of perovskite after interlayer deposition; check for Ag migration by ToF‑SIMS depth profiling after anneal/light soak.

Step 6 — Post-processing and operando verification of Ag44 integrity in devices:
6.1 After interlayer deposition (before top electrode), re-check Ag44 speciation by XPS/EXAFS on witness samples processed identically (including any annealing).
6.2 After device aging tests, perform spatially resolved XPS/ToF‑SIMS and EXAFS (where feasible) to confirm Ag44 remains cluster-like (no bulk Ag0 formation) and remains confined (no penetration into perovskite).

Step 7 — Device testing with oxygen-controlled protocols and mechanistic deconvolution:
7.1 Fabricate PSCs with and without interlayer: baseline (no interlayer), NH2‑MIL‑125 only, Ag44 only (if processable), and Ag44@NH2‑MIL‑125 across loadings and F_facet values.
7.2 Stability tests explicitly separating oxygen effects:
- Operate at maximum power point under controlled pO2 (N2 vs air vs O2) and controlled humidity (dry vs trace H2O).
- Measure in situ PL/QFLS drift under bias illumination to track trap formation kinetics.
7.3 Correlate device degradation markers (Voc decay rate, PL red-shift/broadening, impedance recombination resistance) with operando ORR metrics (O2 consumption, O2•− EPR signal, H2O2 yield).

Step 8 — Volcano model: predictive kinetic/transport/recombination framework (not correlation-only):
8.1 Parameterize a minimal model where net benefit B(L) = oxygen-scavenging gain G(L) − recombination/transport penalty P(L). Use measured inputs:
- G(L): TOF and selectivity-derived effective oxygen removal rate (weighted against O2•− yield), scaled by accessible site density (from loading and uptake metrics).
- P(L): recombination velocity increase and/or transport resistance derived from TRPL/TPV/TPC/EIS and thickness.
8.2 Include a percolation/continuity term for electron transfer within the interlayer and an “electronic isolation” term when clusters become over-encapsulated/too separated from extraction pathways.
8.3 Fit across loadings and facet descriptor F_facet; validate by predicting the optimal loading for a new F_facet condition and testing experimentally.

Deliverables:
D1) Selectivity-certified interlayer compositions (low O2•−, quantified 2e− ORR) under low aH2O.
D2) Verified band alignment and demonstrated electron-sink behavior without QFLS penalty.
D3) Device-level stability improvement in oxygen-containing environments with mechanistic attribution to ORR selectivity (not just barrier effects).
Feasibility: 1) ORR selectivity risk is explicitly controlled and falsifiable: The proposal directly addresses the reviewer’s concern that ORR can generate superoxide (a known perovskite degradant) by mandating operando quantification of O2•− (EPR spin trapping) and products (RRDE H2O2 yield; micro-GC/IC; 18O2 tracing) under low-water, controlled pO2, and illumination conditions that emulate PSC interfaces. The go/no-go requirement that superoxide yield must decrease prevents advancing a chemically harmful interlayer.

2) Charge-transfer direction and energy alignment are measured—not assumed: UPS/Kelvin probe establishes whether Ag44@NH2‑MIL‑125 forms an energetically favorable electron-accepting cascade or a barrier. Contact-stack TRPL, QFLS, TPV/TPC, and intensity-dependent Voc discriminate beneficial extraction (electron sink) from parasitic quenching/recombination. This directly resolves whether ORR electrons originate from the perovskite/ETL pathway (device-relevant) or from weak MOF photoexcitation in an ultrathin geometry.

3) Atomically precise Ag44 integrity is controlled across processing and operation: The plan specifies ligand-defined clusters, inert mechanochemical encapsulation, quantitative loading verification (ICP‑MS), and leaching/aggregation stress tests in PSC-relevant solvents/chemistries. Post-deposition and post-aging EXAFS/XPS/ToF‑SIMS provide operando/after-device validation that Ag44 remains cluster-like and confined, addressing the reviewer’s durability and speciation concerns.

4) Facet engineering is mechanistically parameterized: Instead of qualitative “facet exposure,” a quantified facet descriptor (F_facet from TEM indexing + Wulff analysis) is linked to measurable adsorption/diffusion proxies and defect density. This enables a mechanistic link between acetic-acid modulation, pore-mouth accessibility, Ag44 uptake, and ORR kinetics.

5) Volcano behavior is predicted from competing, measured rate processes: The kinetic/transport/recombination model uses experimentally extracted parameters (TOF/selectivity, recombination resistance/ideality factor, transport time constants, thickness) to predict an optimum rather than relying on correlation plots. This provides mechanistic closure and clear discriminants between oxygen scavenging benefits and recombination penalties—precisely the device-grade rigor requested.
final_critique: This is an exceptionally detailed and technically mature proposal that demonstrates deep familiarity with both perovskite device physics and ORR catalysis under noncanonical (low-water, buried-interface) conditions. Engineering resolution is very high: the plan specifies concrete synthesis knobs, quantified descriptors (F_facet, loading, QFLS loss), operando discriminants (EPR, RRDE, isotopic tracing), and post-device speciation validation. Logical consistency is strong: the volcano hypothesis is mechanistically justified through competing rate processes (oxygen scavenging vs recombination/transport penalties), and the proposal explicitly guards against the central failure mode of ORR-induced superoxide damage. Minor deductions arise from two areas: (i) the practical complexity and throughput risk of executing RRDE/EPR/EXAFS across a large multi-dimensional parameter space may strain feasibility within a typical grant period, and (ii) the assumption that Ag44 clusters remain electronically coupled yet non-recombinative at optimal loadings relies heavily on post hoc diagnostics rather than a priori electronic-structure constraints. Evidence grounding is solid and domain-faithful, though the proposal occasionally approaches the boundary of over-instrumentation. The rationale quality is high, as the work targets a real bottleneck—oxygen-induced PSC degradation—using a structurally and mechanistically novel interlayer concept rather than a passive barrier.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding atomically precise Ag44 nanoclusters into facet-engineered NH2‑MIL‑125 creates a volcano-shaped photocatalytic performance curve, where optimal loading maximizes beneficial 2-electron oxygen reduction while suppressing harmful superoxide formation and avoiding recombination penalties.

original_chain: Thymol (Thy) -> Reactive oxygen species (ROS) -> Antibacterial efficiency -> PB-PCN-224 -> Reactive oxygen species (ROS)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a NIR-activated PB-PCN-224 interlayer that is pre-loaded with thymol (Thy) at the perovskite/transport-layer interface will simultaneously (i) suppress perovskite photo-oxidation by scavenging interfacial ROS and (ii) enable on-demand antibacterial action at the module surface, because the PB→porphyrin electron-transfer pathway in PB-PCN-224 can be methodologically adapted from its biomedical PDT/PTT use to a PSC interface architecture: PB acts as an electron-buffering/photothermal component that reduces triplet–triplet annihilation and stabilizes charge separation in the porphyrin MOF, while thymol acts as a radical-quenching, defect-coordinating phenolic guest that (a) intercepts 1O2/•OH at the interface before they attack organic cations/iodide and (b) passivates under-coordinated Pb2+ via phenoxy/Pb interactions, lowering non-radiative recombination and increasing Voc. The adaptation is a 'gated ROS management layer': PB-PCN-224 is deposited as an ultrathin, percolated MOF network whose porosity is partially filled with Thy and whose surface is ion-impermeable via post-synthetic pore-mouth narrowing, so ROS and microbes are addressed without introducing ionic pathways that accelerate PSC ion migration/hysteresis.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a stable baseline stack (two variants for generality): (A) n–i–p: ITO/SnO2/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/spiro-OMeTAD/Au; (B) p–i–n: ITO/NiOx/FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05PbI3/C60/BCP/Ag.
1.2 Synthesize PB-PCN-224 with controlled particle size (20–80 nm) and narrow polydispersity; confirm porphyrin absorption and PB photothermal response.
1.3 Load thymol into PB-PCN-224 pores by vapor-phase infiltration (Thy vapor at mild temperature) to avoid solvent damage; quantify loading by TGA/GC-MS and verify retention by isothermal desorption.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation (interface-specific MOF engineering): deposit an ultrathin, percolated PB-PCN-224(Thy) interlayer (target 5–20 nm effective thickness) via a two-step self-limiting process: (i) seed deposition of MOF nanoparticles from a nonpolar orthogonal solvent onto the finished perovskite (or onto SnO2/NiOx before perovskite for the inverted test), (ii) mild thermal/solvent anneal to create a connected but non-continuous electronic barrier (percolation control).
2.2 Post-synthetic pore-mouth narrowing: apply a sub-nm alumina or siloxane 'rim' by low-temperature, few-cycle molecular layer deposition (MLD) selectively at external surfaces to reduce ion ingress/egress while keeping internal Thy accessible; confirm that conductivity is not catastrophically reduced.
2.3 Place the interlayer strategically: for n–i–p, locate PB-PCN-224(Thy) between perovskite and HTL to suppress oxidation at the hole-extraction side; for p–i–n, locate between perovskite and ETL to test electron-side ROS sensitivity.
2.4 Introduce a controlled NIR activation protocol (e.g., 660 nm pulsed illumination) during operation to trigger PB photothermal + porphyrin triplet formation when antibacterial action is desired; keep standard AM1.5G operation unchanged to avoid artificial PCE inflation.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Optoelectronic metrics: measure PCE, Voc, FF, hysteresis index; quantify non-radiative loss via absolute PLQY and electroluminescence; extract quasi-Fermi level splitting.
3.2 Mechanistic ROS mapping at interfaces: use EPR spin trapping (TEMP for 1O2, DMPO for •OH/•O2−) on complete stacks under illumination and bias; compare with/without PB-PCN-224 and with/without Thy loading.
3.3 Defect passivation evidence: XPS/UPS for Pb 4f shifts and work-function alignment; TRPL and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to separate recombination vs extraction; SCLC or thermal admittance spectroscopy for trap density.
3.4 Ion-migration control: operando Kelvin probe or TOF-SIMS depth profiling after bias stress to assess I−/Br− and MA+/FA+ redistribution; confirm pore-mouth narrowing reduces ion exchange.
3.5 Stability testing: ISOS-L-2 and damp-heat (85°C/85%RH) with and without periodic 660 nm activation; track T80 and failure modes by GIWAXS (phase changes) and cross-sectional TEM (interlayer integrity).
3.6 Antibacterial efficiency at the module surface: coat the outermost encapsulant or top electrode-adjacent layer with a thin PB-PCN-224(Thy) region connected to the interlayer (or a dedicated topcoat analogue) and test against S. aureus biofilm under 660 nm; quantify CFU reduction and correlate with ROS output, ensuring PSC layers remain isolated (encapsulation barrier verified).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: PB-PCN-224 is experimentally demonstrated to enhance ROS generation under 660 nm via optimized electron transfer, achieving near-complete antibacterial rates (Asset 2). Separately, ROS-triggered thymol release and synergistic ROS/Thy antibacterial action are supported in MOF-based electrocatalytic contexts (Asset 1). In PSCs, interfacial defect passivation and ROS suppression are known to directly improve Voc and operational stability; phenolic additives are plausible Pb2+-coordinating/passivating agents while also acting as radical quenchers.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is not a generic additive swap; it is a structurally constrained, PSC-specific 'gated interfacial layer' that (i) localizes ROS chemistry away from the bulk perovskite, (ii) blocks ion migration via pore-mouth narrowing to avoid hysteresis/stress-induced segregation, and (iii) provides energy-level/charge-buffer functionality through PB and porphyrin states. The 660 nm activation is decoupled from standard AM1.5G performance and treated as an on-demand hygiene/stability maintenance mode compatible with building-integrated or wearable PV.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional 2D capping layers or small-molecule antioxidants, PB-PCN-224(Thy) offers a multifunctional, tunable interface: porosity enables controlled guest loading (Thy), PB provides photothermal/electron-buffering to extend porphyrin excited-state lifetimes (higher ROS yield when desired), and the engineered pore-mouth barrier mitigates a key PSC-specific risk (ion migration through porous layers). This is expected to deliver (a) higher Voc via reduced interfacial trap-assisted recombination, (b) improved light/bias stability by intercepting ROS-driven decomposition pathways, and (c) durable antibacterial surfaces without relying on leachable antibiotics.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-reasoned proposal that demonstrates unusually high engineering resolution for an interfacial PSC concept. The strongest aspect is the explicit interface-specific adaptation of a biomedical MOF/PB/ROS system into a gated, ion-restricted PSC interlayer, supported by a rigorous validation plan (EPR, operando ion-migration probes, absolute PLQY). However, several logical tensions remain insufficiently resolved. First, the dual role of PB-PCN-224 as both a ROS suppressor (during normal operation) and a ROS generator (during NIR activation) is conceptually appealing but kinetically underdefined: the proposal does not quantitatively justify how ROS quenching by thymol dominates under AM1.5G while ROS generation becomes dominant under 660 nm without inducing collateral perovskite damage. Second, the electronic role of the MOF/PB layer is described qualitatively (electron buffering, reduced TTA), but no explicit energy-level alignment or charge-transport model is provided to ensure the interlayer does not act as a recombination sink or resistive barrier, especially at 5–20 nm thickness. Third, pore-mouth narrowing via MLD is innovative, but selectivity (external vs internal pores) and scalability on rough perovskite surfaces are assumed rather than demonstrated. These issues do not invalidate the proposal, but they prevent it from reaching the highest logical-consistency tier.
hypothesis_summary: A NIR-activated MOF interlayer loaded with thymol simultaneously blocks reactive oxygen damage to the perovskite and provides on-demand antibacterial action at the solar cell surface.

original_chain: Piezoelectric response -> Carnosine -> Electrocatalytic activity -> Synergistic effect -> Mn-Co cathode -> Voltage efficiency -> Zinc-air batteries
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a carnosine-derived, metal-chelated zwitterionic “dipole brush” at 3D perovskite grain boundaries (GBs) will increase voltage efficiency (Voc and FF) and operational stability by two coupled but separable mechanisms that yield falsifiable quantitative signatures:

(H1) Defect-chemistry mechanism (passivation + charge-state control): multidentate carnosinate coordination (imidazole/carboxylate) preferentially binds under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy-adjacent Pb sites at GBs, lowering the density of deep recombination-active states and shifting defect charge-state equilibria. Prediction: complete-stack PLQY-implied Voc increases by ≥30–60 mV at matched absorptance, with reduced ideality factor and a measurable reduction in midgap trap signatures (TAS/DLTS-like) without requiring poling.

(H2) Electrostatic/ionic mechanism (fixed-orientational dipole gradient + raised migration barrier): a nm-thick, percolating GB network of zwitterionic dipoles produces a thickness-direction internal electrostatic potential step ΔV_GB that is (i) measurable as band bending across the film thickness and (ii) retained after operational stress beyond the timescale of ionic relaxation. This internal potential biases the ionic chemical potential and increases the effective activation barrier for halide/vacancy drift along GB pathways. Crucially, persistence is not assumed; it is engineered by (a) anchoring dipoles via metal–ligand coordination to GB Pb sites (reducing rotational freedom), and (b) using a poling protocol only within a bounded temperature/time window where dipoles can orient but mobile ions are comparatively less able to permanently redistribute.

Falsifiable predictions for (H2): (i) cross-sectional KPFM/UPS-derived potential profiles show a reproducible thickness-direction potential step ΔV (target 30–120 mV across the absorber) that remains ≥50% after 1 sun MPP stress (≥24 h) and after thermal cycling (25↔85 °C) with minimal recovery kinetics indicative of slow ion back-diffusion; (ii) bias-stress/recovery kinetics yield increased ionic activation energy by ≥0.10–0.20 eV (from C–t, hysteresis relaxation, or transient ion-drift methods) relative to baseline and to “passivation-only” controls; (iii) dielectric/TSDC signatures reveal a dipolar relaxation process separable from ionic conductivity (different activation energy and frequency/temperature dependence) and preserved under an ion-blocking architecture.

Mechanistic comparator made predictive (Mn–Co synergy analogy): Rather than a metaphor, the Mn/Co motif is used to pre-register a descriptor-based prediction: metals that strengthen carnosinate binding and increase local electrostatic polarization at GBs will (a) more strongly stabilize charged defect configurations (e.g., V_I^+ / V_I^0 balance) and (b) raise halide migration barriers along GB models. Pre-registered DFT outputs (binding energies, defect formation energies vs charge state, and migration barriers) will be mapped onto experimentally extracted activation energies and built-in potential retention. If DFT predicts that Mn/Co–carnosinate introduces redox-active deep states or lowers barriers, those formulations are expected to underperform or destabilize devices—this becomes a falsification point rather than an assumed benefit.
Plan: Step 0 — Define device baseline and diagnostic architecture (to make internal-field claims testable)
0.1 Baseline stack: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA0.8Cs0.2)Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3/SAM-HTL (MeO-2PACz)/metal.
0.2 Add two diagnostic variants explicitly to separate ion motion from dipole effects:
  (A) Ion-blocking stack: introduce ultrathin ion-blocking interlayers that minimally alter energetics but suppress ionic exchange at contacts (e.g., 1–2 nm ALD Al2O3 on SnO2 and/or a dense 3–5 nm organic barrier at HTL interface). Goal: if the effect is primarily interfacial ion accumulation, it should collapse; if a GB dipole network exists, ΔV and Voc gains should persist.
  (B) Single-halide vs mixed-halide: compare (FA/Cs)PbI3 (or low-Br) vs mixed I/Br to leverage different ion-mobility/segregation behavior. Prediction: a true dipole-based ΔV should be less sensitive to halide composition than an ion-migration artifact.

Step 1 — Additive design with explicit anti-incorporation constraints
1.1 Synthesize/prepare four additives: free carnosine; Zn–carnosinate; Mn–carnosinate; Co–carnosinate; plus mixed Mn/Co–carnosinate.
1.2 Mandatory controls to isolate metal-doping artifacts:
  (C1) “Metal salt without carnosine” at identical metal mol% (ZnI2, MnI2, CoI2 or acetates matched for solubility).
  (C2) “Non-zwitterionic analogue” (e.g., N-acetylhistidine) at identical mol%.
  (C3) “Carnosine + chelator lockout” (carnosine pre-blocked at a binding site if feasible) to test multidentate requirement.
1.3 Loading window narrowed to electronically safe regime with a staged screen: 0, 0.01, 0.03, 0.05, 0.10 mol% vs Pb (start lower than original 0.5 mol% to reduce bulk-incorporation risk). Only if incorporation is proven negligible do we explore higher.
1.4 Coordination verification: FTIR (Δν COO−), 1H/13C NMR where soluble, UV–Vis/ICP of solutions to ensure speciation, and XPS on dried additive films.

Step 2 — Enforced grain-boundary localization protocol (chemical + kinetic)
2.1 Two-stage crystallization tuned for GB segregation:
  (i) Rapid nucleation using antisolvent quench.
  (ii) Growth/redistribution anneal at 80–110 °C for 10–20 min at controlled RH 10–20%.
Rationale: allow additive diffusion to GBs while limiting bulk lattice incorporation.
2.2 Verify “no bulk substitution” early: compare lattice parameter shifts (GIWAXS), but do not rely on this alone (see Step 4).

Step 3 — Poling engineered as a bounded, retention-tested variable (not assumed)
3.1 Poling geometry: use a temporary transparent top electrode (ITO/PET or thin Au grid on insulator) to apply a uniform field across the perovskite during the final 2–5 min of anneal.
3.2 Field and thermal window matrix (pre-registered): E = 0 (no poling), 0.2, 0.5, 1.0 V/µm; T = 60, 80, 100 °C; time = 1, 3, 5 min.
3.3 Immediate and delayed readouts required for “persistence”: measure ΔV profile at t = 0, 1 h, 24 h after poling in dark and after 1 sun soak, to test relaxation kinetics.
3.4 Failure criterion: if ΔV decays to <10% within 1 h in all cases, abandon the “persistent dipole gradient” claim and proceed with a non-poled, passivation/ionic-barrier-only framing.

Step 4 — Quantify metal incorporation and electronic impact (mandatory)
4.1 ICP-MS: digest full films (and scraped perovskite only) to quantify total metal content down to ppm.
4.2 XPS depth profiling + ToF-SIMS: determine whether metals reside at surfaces/GBs vs distributed through bulk.
4.3 Electronic impact screening beyond XRD:
  - TRMC or μ-PCD to probe photoconductance and recombination independent of contacts.
  - Temperature-dependent PL and PLQY to detect new nonradiative channels.
4.4 Decision gate: formulations with measurable bulk metal incorporation correlated with lifetime reduction are deprioritized even if initial PCE is high.

Step 5 — Direct measurement of internal field/band bending and retention (Directive #1)
5.1 Cross-sectional KPFM: prepare clean cross-sections (FIB or cleave) and map potential across thickness for baseline, additive-only, and poled samples.
5.2 UPS depth-probing (angle-resolved) or stepwise gentle ion etch + UPS to reconstruct work function/VBM shifts vs depth (with controls for damage).
5.3 Impedance-derived built-in potential: track changes in V_bi (Mott–Schottky where valid) and correlate with KPFM/UPS.
5.4 Stress retention protocol: ISOS-L-2-like continuous illumination at MPP for 24–100 h checkpoints; repeat cross-sectional potential mapping and V_bi extraction to quantify retention.

Step 6 — Separate dipole reorientation from ion motion (Directive #2)
6.1 Field-dependent dielectric spectroscopy (10^2–10^6 Hz) vs temperature (200–350 K): extract relaxation peaks; distinguish dipolar relaxation (frequency-dispersive peak with modest conductivity) from ionic conduction (low-frequency dispersion, strong DC component).
6.2 Thermally stimulated depolarization current (TSDC): poling at defined T/E, cool, then heat with zero bias and record depolarization current. A true dipolar polarization should show a characteristic release peak distinct from ionic drift; compare activation energies.
6.3 Bias-stress/recovery kinetics:
  - Apply DC bias under illumination; monitor Voc, FF, capacitance, and PL mapping; then remove bias and record recovery.
  - Fit time constants and extract activation energies (Arrhenius) for migration-related processes. Prediction: carnosinate GB network increases activation energy and slows redistribution.
6.4 Ion-blocking architecture test (from Step 0.2A): repeat dielectric/TSDC and bias-stress/recovery. If the observed “pseudo-piezoelectric-like” potential shifts vanish only when ions are blocked, the effect was ionic; if a component remains, it supports dipolar contribution.

Step 7 — Mechanistic passivation metrics and Voc/FF causality
7.1 Absolute PLQY on complete stacks → implied Voc; correlate with measured Voc to partition contact vs absorber losses.
7.2 TRPL + transient photovoltage/photocurrent to extract recombination order and lifetime.
7.3 TAS / DLTS-like admittance to quantify trap density/energies; compare across controls (free carnosine vs metal–carnosinate vs metal salt only).

Step 8 — Predictive Mn–Co linkage (Directive #4) + optional translational task
8.1 Pre-register DFT calculations on representative surfaces and GB models:
  - Binding energies of carnosine and M–carnosinate (M = Zn, Mn, Co, Mn/Co) at PbI2-terminated and mixed termination surfaces.
  - Defect formation energies (V_I, V_Pb, I_i) vs charge state with/without additive.
  - Migration barrier changes for I−/V_I along GB-like pathways.
8.2 Map DFT outputs to experiments:
  - Predicted barrier increase ↔ extracted activation energies (C–t, hysteresis kinetics).
  - Predicted stabilization of charged defects ↔ changes in ideality factor, TAS signatures, and KPFM band bending.
8.3 Translational add-on (only if retained in scope): demonstrate that the same carnosinate coordination motif measurably tunes Mn–Co ORR adsorption descriptor in a Zn–air relevant electrolyte (alkaline), and explicitly relate the adsorption-energy shift to the perovskite defect-descriptor shift. If not executed, remove Zn–air discussion from claims.

Step 9 — Device validation and stability endpoints
9.1 J–V forward/reverse, stabilized MPP, and Voc(T) to assess proximity to radiative limit.
9.2 Operational stability: ISOS-L-2 (MPP, 1 sun, controlled temperature) and ISOS-O-2; report retention of Voc and FF explicitly (not only PCE). Target: ≥90% Voc retention after 1000 h with reduced hysteresis growth.
9.3 Post-mortem mapping (ToF-SIMS, KPFM, XPS) to identify whether failure correlates with loss of ΔV profile, metal migration, or new trap formation.
Feasibility: 1) Addressing persistence of internal electrostatics (reviewer point i): The revised plan does not assume a stable dipole gradient; it operationalizes it as a retention-tested variable with direct cross-sectional potential profiling (KPFM/UPS) at defined time points before/after illumination and bias stress. Poling is constrained within a temperature/field window and subjected to a strict failure criterion (rapid decay → claim dropped). This converts the internal-field concept into a measurable, falsifiable hypothesis.

2) Discriminating dipole reorientation vs ion migration (reviewer point ii): Temperature- and frequency-domain dielectric spectroscopy plus TSDC provide orthogonal observables to decouple dipolar polarization from ionic conduction. The ion-blocking architecture and mixed- vs single-halide comparison are explicit discriminating controls. Activation energies from bias-stress/recovery kinetics serve as quantitative separators: a dipolar relaxation process should exhibit different Ea and frequency signatures than halide/vacancy drift.

3) Mitigating metal-cation risks and proving localization (reviewer point iv): The execution includes mandatory metal-salt-only controls and multi-technique quantification of incorporation (ICP-MS + XPS depth + ToF-SIMS), coupled to contact-independent recombination probes (TRMC/μ-PCD). A decision gate deprioritizes any formulation where metal incorporation correlates with lifetime loss, preventing false attribution of performance changes to “dipole brush” effects when they arise from inadvertent doping/redox chemistry.

4) Making the Mn–Co analogy predictive (reviewer point iii): The proposal pre-registers DFT-derived descriptors (binding energies, defect charge-state stabilization, migration barriers) and explicitly commits to testing them via experimentally extracted activation energies and band-bending retention metrics. The Mn/Co element becomes a falsifiable design axis (some metals may worsen deep traps), not a rhetorical parallel. If the Zn–air endpoint is retained, it is converted into a concrete task that links adsorption descriptors in ORR catalysis to defect descriptors in perovskites; otherwise it is removed from the claims.

Overall feasibility rests on: (a) carnosine’s established multidentate coordination and intrinsic zwitterionic dipole enabling simultaneous passivation and electrostatic modulation; (b) a controlled low-loading regime with rigorous metal-incorporation accounting; and (c) a diagnostic-first architecture (cross-sectional potential mapping + dielectric/TSDC + activation-energy extraction) that can confirm or falsify each causal link in the chain from GB brush formation → internal electrostatics → ionic suppression → durable Voc/FF gains.
final_critique: Methodological resolution is strong: the proposal converts a usually hand-waved ‘internal field/dipole’ claim into falsifiable, time-resolved observables with stringent controls (ion-blocking, salt-only, non-zwitterionic analogue, poling decay criterion). The main scientific risk is logical identifiability of H2: cross-sectional KPFM/UPS potential steps in halide perovskites are notoriously sensitive to surface prep, FIB/cleave artifacts, local charging, and illumination history; without pre-registered metrology calibration/uncertainty budgets and multiple orthogonal validators (e.g., scanning Kelvin under controlled bias/illumination, operando methods), ΔV persistence could still be confounded with slow ionic redistribution, trapped charge, or contact-induced band bending. The dipole-vs-ion separation plan (dielectric/TSDC + ion-blocking) is directionally correct, but the interpretation is non-unique unless the proposal explicitly models Maxwell–Wagner effects, electrode polarization, and the expected spectral/temperature signatures for each process in this specific multilayer stack. Evidence grounding against the required concept chain is uneven: the perovskite portion is tightly grounded, but the Mn–Co ‘synergy’ and zinc–air linkage are not presently supported by a single shared descriptor set that would make the chain scientifically necessary rather than thematic. As written, zinc–air is unlikely to strengthen the perovskite hypotheses and may dilute reviewer confidence unless executed as a tightly constrained, descriptor-bridged task with clear go/no-go criteria.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a carnosine-derived zwitterionic dipole brush at perovskite grain boundaries simultaneously passivates defects and creates a persistent internal electrostatic field, raising voltage efficiency and suppressing ion migration for improved stability.

original_chain: Mechanochemical synthesis -> Loading capacity -> Catalytic activity -> Hydrophobicity -> Electron transfer
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a mechanochemically synthesized, high-loading ‘cluster-in-hydrophobic-framework’ (APNC@RF) additive throughout a SnO2 ETL—engineered to be interface-enriched but not a discrete interlayer—will increase PSC efficiency and moisture/bias stability only within a quantitatively defined operating window where (i) APNC redox levels and the composite work function remain selectively electron-extracting (no mid-gap trap formation or hole accumulation), (ii) SnO2 retains a continuous percolation/consolidation network (no conductivity collapse or excessive tortuosity), and (iii) the buried ETL/perovskite water activity and water diffusivity are reduced enough to measurably slow ion migration and halide redox swings. Mechanistically, the APNCs act as nanoconfined, aggregation-proof electron-relay/redox-buffer sites (Asset 1) that can accelerate interfacial electron transfer and stabilize interfacial iodide/iodine chemistry—provided their density is below a modeled recombination threshold and their Fermi-level alignment remains compatible with SnO2/perovskite energetics. Concurrently, a hydrophobically modified reticular framework (RF) provides a distributed low-water-activity microenvironment (Assets 2–3) that reduces water uptake and through-film moisture permeation to the buried interface, thereby lowering the rate of water-assisted halide vacancy formation and bias-driven ion drift. The refined approach directly overcomes the main reviewer risks by: (a) explicitly constraining electronic alignment using UPS/KPFM and QFLS/ideality-factor-derived recombination bounds tied to a drift–diffusion parameter sweep that sets an upper bound on allowable APNC site density; (b) pre-quantifying SnO2 percolation and consolidation as a function of RF fraction to prevent ETL resistivity increases; (c) replacing surface contact-angle proxies with direct water uptake/diffusivity/permeation metrics and correlating them with temperature-dependent ion-migration signatures; and (d) including a parasitic-halide-oxidation screen under light/O2/H2O to prove the APNCs buffer rather than catalyze I−→I2/I3− chemistry.
Plan: Step 0 — Define hard go/no-go criteria (before device optimization)
0.1 Electronic alignment (must pass all):
• Composite ETL work function (UPS secondary cutoff, corroborated by KPFM) must remain within a pre-set window relative to pristine SnO2: |ΔWF| ≤ 0.20 eV at the optimum loading candidate; absolute WF target: 4.1–4.6 eV for SnO2-based n-contact (reject if WF shifts to promote interfacial hole accumulation).
• QFLS (absolute PLQY-derived, perovskite-on-ETL stacks) must not decrease by >20 meV vs pristine SnO2 at 1-sun equivalent carrier density; otherwise reject loading/chemistry.
• Ideality factor (from Suns-Voc or light-intensity Voc) must not increase by >0.15 (absolute) vs pristine SnO2; reject if trap-assisted recombination signature increases.
• Drift–diffusion (DD) model upper bound: fitted interfacial SRH velocity (or equivalent interface trap density proxy) must not increase beyond a threshold that predicts >10 mV Voc loss at 1 sun for the measured series resistance; if model predicts >10 mV loss at the measured APNC areal density, reject that composition.
0.2 ETL transport/percolation (must pass all):
• In-plane ETL conductivity and through-plane electron-only SCLC mobility (ITO/ETL/Al) must remain ≥70% of pristine SnO2 value at the chosen loading.
• EIS-derived ETL/contact contribution (high-frequency arc, or extracted transport resistance) must not increase by >20% at MPP-operating bias in the dark and under illumination.
• Film microstructure acceptance: no evidence of SnO2 necking suppression—quantified by constant (±10%) porosity proxy (ellipsometry or XRR density) and unchanged SnO2 grain connectivity metrics (SEM/TEM image analysis).
0.3 Buried-interface moisture barrier (must pass at least two quantitative metrics):
• Water uptake (gravimetric DVS or QCM sorption on ETL films): ≥30% reduction in equilibrium uptake at 40–60% RH vs pristine SnO2.
• Effective water diffusivity/permeation: ≥2× reduction in through-ETL water transport, measured by (a) Ca-test-like optical transmission proxy or (b) D2O exposure + ToF-SIMS depth profiling to extract diffusion coefficient from concentration–depth–time fits.
0.4 Parasitic halide oxidation screen (must pass):
• Under controlled illumination (1 sun, 25–45 °C) with defined O2 (e.g., 20%) and RH (e.g., 50%), ETL/perovskite stacks must show no increase (vs pristine SnO2) in I3−/I2 signatures (UV–Vis absorbance bands; Raman peaks) and no accelerated PbI2 growth (GIWAXS/XRD) over 24–72 h. Any acceleration is a reject for that APNC/RF chemistry.

Step 1 — Materials selection with explicit electronic/chemical constraints
1.1 ETL backbone: colloidal SnO2 nanoparticles (target 3–5 nm primary crystallites) processed <150 °C; baseline ETL thickness 25–40 nm (kept constant).
1.2 Reticular framework host (RF): chemically robust Zr-MOF (UiO-66 family) or robust COF with (i) fluorinated aromatic linkers and/or (ii) siloxane-bearing UPy-rich hydrophobic modifier motifs (Asset 2 logic), but constrained to be electronically benign.
• Selection rule: RF alone in SnO2 (no APNC) must not reduce conductivity below 85% at ≤5 wt% RF in ETL.
• Chemical rule: RF must show no measurable acidic dissolution/etching of perovskite in contact tests (perovskite-on-RF film aging; PbI2 formation rate ≤ pristine SnO2 control).
1.3 Atomically precise nanocluster (APNC) redox mediator: Au25(SR)18 or analogous cluster with ligands selected for solid-state robustness.
• Ligand constraint: mechanochemical processing must preserve cluster optical fingerprint (UV–Vis) within ±10% peak position/intensity ratios, and XPS Au 4f chemical state must remain consistent (no major oxidation/reduction shifts indicating decomposition).
• Energetic constraint: APNC@RF/SnO2 WF and valence features (UPS) must not introduce occupied states near perovskite VB that promote hole trapping; reject if UPS indicates new states within ~0.3 eV of perovskite VB edge (relative alignment assessed via combined UPS + perovskite IP).

Step 2 — Mechanochemical synthesis with acceptance criteria (Asset 1 mapping)
2.1 Encapsulation (APNC@RF): solvent-free resonant acoustic mixing or ball milling.
• DoE variables: energy input (time, frequency), ball-to-powder ratio, and optional process control agent at ppm–0.1 wt% max (to avoid reintroducing solution chemistry).
• Acceptance: ICP-MS confirms target loading series (e.g., 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2 wt% APNC relative to total ETL solids); UV–Vis fingerprint preserved; STEM-EDS shows no APNC aggregation >2–3 nm clusters; leaching test in ETL ink solvent shows <5% APNC loss.
2.2 Co-milling into SnO2: dry co-mill APNC@RF with SnO2 to form ETL composite powder.
• Additive fraction design: RF fraction swept (e.g., 0, 1, 3, 5, 8 wt% RF relative to SnO2) while APNC loading is swept independently within RF.
• Percolation screening: measure conductivity vs RF fraction to locate percolation threshold; set a hard ceiling: choose RF fraction at least 2× below the fraction where conductivity drops below 70%.

Step 3 — Engineer vertical segregation with explicit, measurable handles (reproducible at scale)
3.1 Particle size distribution (PSD) targets:
• SnO2: D50 ~5–15 nm (as supplied), minimal aggregation after dispersion (DLS check).
• APNC@RF additive: target D50 ~80–200 nm (mild agglomerates allowed) to enable mild interface enrichment without creating pinholes.
3.2 Ink formulation and drying regime defined by a Peclet-number target:
• Solvent system: alcohol-rich, water-lean (e.g., IPA/EtOH with ≤5% water) to control evaporation rate and prevent excessive SnO2 aggregation.
• Solid fraction: 5–15 wt% total solids for blade coating; viscosity window defined (e.g., 20–200 mPa·s) to ensure uniform coating.
• Drying: enforce an evaporation-rate window (monitored by mass-loss vs time) to place the additive in a convective regime that produces reproducible top-enrichment; record substrate temperature and airflow.
3.3 Verification of segregation (statistics across large area):
• ToF-SIMS depth profiles (framework fragment ions + Au signal) on ≥10 locations across ≥5×5 cm films; acceptance: coefficient of variation (CV) in near-surface additive signal ≤15% and consistent enrichment factor (top 5–10 nm vs bulk) ≥1.5×.
• Cross-sectional SEM/TEM + EDS mapping on representative samples to confirm no discontinuous insulating layer formation.

Step 4 — Devices and controls (factorial matrix retained, with added electronic/moisture tests)
4.1 Device stack (fixed): glass/ITO/ETL(per above)/FA0.9Cs0.1Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3/(optional fixed 2D rinse, constant)/HTL(A) /Au.
4.2 Controls (mandatory):
(i) pristine SnO2; (ii) SnO2+RF (no APNC); (iii) SnO2+free APNC (no RF confinement); (iv) SnO2+APNC@RF (full concept); (v) SnO2+non-hydrophobic RF + APNC@RF (decouple hydrophobicity).

Step 5 — Directly test the two most failure-prone links (reviewer directive)
5.1 Electronic alignment & recombination risk package
• UPS on ETL films and on ETL/perovskite bilayers: WF, valence onset; corroborate with KPFM maps (surface potential uniformity; reject if large patches >50 mV RMS variability indicating phase segregation).
• Absolute PLQY → QFLS on perovskite-on-ETL stacks at matched excitation; TRPL for extraction kinetics.
• Suns-Voc and ideality factor extraction; EL-based nonradiative loss analysis.
• DD modeling: parameter sweep in interfacial SRH velocity or interface trap density and added redox-site density; fit to measured Voc/FF trends to set a quantitative upper bound on APNC areal density (derived from loading + segregation depth). Use the bound as a design rule for subsequent iterations.
5.2 Buried-interface moisture/ion package
• Water uptake: DVS or QCM sorption isotherms on ETL films (0–60% RH).
• Water permeation/diffusivity: D2O exposure from ETL side followed by ToF-SIMS depth profiling vs time; fit diffusion coefficient and compare across ETLs.
• Correlate with ion migration: temperature-dependent EIS (extract ionic-related low-frequency response), OCVD hysteresis decomposition, and bias-stress hysteresis metrics. Acceptance: a statistically significant reduction in ionic signatures (e.g., lower low-frequency capacitance growth and reduced hysteresis index) that scales with measured water diffusivity reduction.

Step 6 — Parasitic catalysis screen (prove buffering, not acceleration)
6.1 ETL/perovskite bilayers exposed under controlled (RH, O2) and illumination.
• Track I3−/I2 formation: UV–Vis (characteristic bands) and Raman; compare kinetics.
• Track perovskite decomposition: in situ PL intensity loss + XRD/GIWAXS PbI2 growth rate.
• XPS (or NAP-XPS) before/after stress: monitor iodine and lead chemical states; reject any APNC@RF that increases iodine oxidation signatures or PbI2 formation rate vs control.

Step 7 — Stability and scaling (only after passing go/no-go)
7.1 MPP tracking under 1 sun at 25–65 °C, RH 20–60%; report T80 with failure-mode diagnostics.
7.2 Damp heat 85/85 screening as differentiator (expect improvement if moisture transport reduced).
7.3 Scale to ≥5×5 cm blade-coated ETLs; map WF (KPFM), ToF-SIMS enrichment, sheet resistance, and device performance uniformity; acceptance: PCE CV ≤10% across area and no edge-localized segregation artifacts.

Deliverables (milestones)
M1: Identify a composition meeting electronic alignment + percolation go/no-go.
M2: Demonstrate ≥2× reduction in water diffusivity/permeation and correlated reduction in ionic signatures.
M3: Demonstrate no parasitic halide oxidation acceleration; then show PCE gain (Voc/FF) and improved operational stability on small and large area.
Feasibility: This revision is feasible because it converts the original catalysis-inspired concept chain (high-loading confinement + hydrophobic microenvironment + electron-transfer enhancement) into PSC-relevant, quantitative acceptance tests that directly address the highest-risk failure modes.

(1) Electronic alignment and recombination risk is explicitly bounded. Assets 1–3 motivate that confined redox-active sites can accelerate charge transfer and remain active under humidity, but PSCs impose a strict constraint: added states must not become SRH recombination centers. The proposal therefore requires UPS/KPFM-derived work function/band-edge shifts, absolute PLQY→QFLS to quantify nonradiative losses at the ETL interface, and ideality factor as a trap-assisted recombination indicator. A drift–diffusion model is added as a design-rule generator that sets an upper bound on allowable APNC site density before Voc loss, converting “high loading” from a qualitative benefit into a quantitatively constrained variable.

(2) ETL conductivity/percolation is treated as a first-class design variable. Reviewer concern that MOF/COF domains can be insulating is handled by mapping conductivity/mobility and EIS transport resistance vs additive fraction, then choosing RF loadings at least 2× below the empirically observed conductivity-collapse region. This preserves the continuous SnO2 electron percolation pathway while still enabling interface-enriched APNC@RF function.

(3) Buried-interface moisture effects are measured via transport parameters, not contact angle. Assets 2–3 justify that hydrophobic confinement can control wetting and preserve activity under humidity, but PSC relevance requires through-film water transport metrics. The plan therefore measures water uptake (DVS/QCM) and effective diffusivity/permeation (D2O + ToF-SIMS or Ca-test-like proxy), then explicitly correlates these with temperature-dependent ionic signatures (EIS/OCVD/hysteresis decomposition). This provides mechanistic causality: reduced water transport → reduced ion migration signatures → improved bias/moisture stability.

(4) Mechanochemical side effects are screened with explicit rejection criteria. Because mechanochemistry can alter ligation, charge state, or framework defect density, the plan includes structural/chemical integrity checks (UV–Vis fingerprint preservation, XPS chemical state, leaching limits) and a dedicated parasitic-halide-oxidation screen under light/O2/H2O that tracks I2/I3− and PbI2 formation. This directly answers the reviewer requirement to prove buffering rather than acceleration of halide oxidation chemistry.

(5) Vertical segregation is engineered and made reproducible. Rather than asserting enrichment, the plan specifies PSD targets, solids/viscosity ranges, drying-rate control consistent with a targeted convective regime, and statistical verification (ToF-SIMS CV thresholds) across large-area coatings. This makes the interface-enrichment mechanism scalable and testable.

Overall, the proposal remains faithful to the original concept (embedded, mechanochemically formed APNC@RF inside ETL) while converting plausibility into a parameter-bounded, failure-aware workflow with clear go/no-go decisions.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually well-engineered for a high-risk additive concept: it anticipates the dominant PSC failure modes (energetic misalignment, SRH recombination, ETL percolation collapse, moisture-assisted ionic dynamics, and unintended I− oxidation catalysis) and converts them into quantitative rejection criteria with appropriate metrology. The largest remaining weakness is mechanistic overreach around “redox buffering” and “electron-relay” functionality of Au25(SR)18 in a solid SnO2/MOF composite: the plan screens for harm (no increased I2/I3−, no QFLS loss) but does not directly prove beneficial redox mediation (i.e., that the cluster is participating reversibly rather than being electronically inert once embedded, or that it actually suppresses halide redox swings under bias). A second gap is that the vertical segregation strategy, while measurable, is still an empirical process window; without a validated predictive model linking PSD/evaporation to enrichment for these mixed nanoparticles, reproducibility across inks/batches remains a risk. Finally, the DD modeling input parameterization for ‘redox-site density’ versus an effective interfacial SRH velocity is underspecified; without an experimentally anchored mapping (e.g., density-of-states or trap cross sections), the model could become a fitting exercise rather than a true design-rule generator.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding mechanochemically synthesized cluster-in-hydrophobic-framework additives within a SnO2 electron transport layer improves perovskite solar cell efficiency and stability, but only within strict electronic alignment, conductivity, and moisture-barrier windows.

original_chain: Reticular frameworks -> Covalent-organic frameworks (COFs) -> Functional materials -> Dynamic covalent assemblies -> Cross-linked polymer gels -> Surface-mounted frameworks (SURMOFs)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A surface-grafted dynamic-covalent COF/SURMOF interlayer that is covalently anchored to the perovskite surface and simultaneously cross-linked into a thin polymer-gel “reticular skin” will suppress non-radiative recombination and ion migration more effectively than conventional 2D-spacer or small-molecule passivation. Mechanism: (i) imine-/hydrazone-type dynamic covalent linkages in the COF allow self-healing reconfiguration under thermal/light stress to maintain defect saturation; (ii) periodic, oriented SURMOF-like growth on the perovskite creates a high-density, spatially ordered array of Lewis-base binding sites that coordinate under-coordinated Pb2+ and immobilize halide vacancies at the surface; (iii) post-deposition mild cross-linking converts the topmost COF into an ultrathin cross-linked polymer gel that reduces interfacial free volume and increases the activation barrier for I−/Br− and MA+/FA+ migration, mitigating hysteresis and halide segregation; (iv) the reticular layer’s dielectric/energetic tuning (dipolar linkers) reduces interfacial band bending and lowers the interfacial recombination velocity, increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting and Voc.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Fabricate baseline high-efficiency perovskite stacks targeting a stable reference: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05)Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 (optionally with 1–5 mol% excess PbI2 control) and benchmark HTLs (spiro-OMeTAD and a dopant-free polymer HTL as a stability control).
1.2 Prepare perovskite surface for covalent anchoring without damaging the lattice: brief exposure (seconds) to a bifunctional “primer” vapor/solution containing (a) phosphonic acid or carboxylic acid anchor to bind surface Pb2+ and (b) aldehyde (or hydrazide) group to serve as a COF nucleation handle; verify no perovskite phase change by GIWAXS and PL.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—SURMOF-like, surface-mounted COF growth on a soft ionic crystal: implement layer-by-layer (LbL) solvothermal-free growth at ≤80 °C using alternating exposures of (A) multi-amine node (e.g., triaminobenzene derivative) and (B) dialdehyde linker (e.g., fluorinated/dipolar benzene dialdehyde) to form an oriented imine (or hydrazone for higher hydrolytic stability) COF. Adaptation detail: unlike standard COF growth on oxides/metals, include a “lattice-friendly” buffered catalyst system (trace acetic acid + Lewis base scavenger) and short, repeated pulses to prevent perovskite dissolution while achieving reticular ordering.
2.2 Enforce orientation (SURMOF behavior): use the primer density and exposure sequence to favor vertical pore channels (normal to the surface). Track orientation by GIWAXS azimuthal distribution and ellipsometry thickness per cycle.
2.3 Convert the top 3–10 nm into a cross-linked polymer gel without collapsing porosity: post-synthetic modification using a mild bifunctional cross-linker (e.g., dihydrazide or diamine) that reacts with residual aldehydes/imine exchange sites, forming an interpenetrated, lightly swollen network upon controlled humidity anneal (30–40% RH). This creates a COF–gel gradient: bottom ordered COF for electronic passivation; top gel for moisture/ion barrier.
2.4 Energetic tuning: incorporate dipolar substituents (–F, –CN, sulfone) on the linker to tune interfacial vacuum level and improve band alignment with HTL/ETL. Quantify with UPS/KPFM.
2.5 Device integration: deposit HTL atop the reticular skin (spiro-OMeTAD and dopant-free alternative) and finish Au electrodes; build control sets: (i) no interlayer, (ii) small-molecule Lewis base passivator, (iii) 2D RP passivation, (iv) COF without gel cross-linking, (v) gel-only without reticular order.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Defect passivation and recombination: TRPL, absolute PLQY, and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to extract interfacial recombination velocity; quantify quasi-Fermi level splitting via PLQY under 1-sun equivalent.
3.2 Ion migration and hysteresis: temperature-dependent impedance spectroscopy, transient ion-drift measurements, and J–V hysteresis index across scan rates; operando electroluminescence mapping under bias to detect mobile ion accumulation.
3.3 Interfacial chemistry and binding mechanism: XPS (Pb 4f shifts), solid-state NMR/FTIR for imine/hydrazone formation and exchange, ToF-SIMS depth profiling for halide redistribution after bias/heat.
3.4 Structural integrity and orientation: GIWAXS for COF crystallinity/orientation; cross-sectional TEM/SEM to confirm conformal ultrathin coating and pore-channel alignment.
3.5 Operational stability: MPP tracking at 65–85 °C under 1-sun LED with controlled humidity (10–50% RH) for ≥1000 h; include light-soaking halide segregation test (for Br-containing perovskites) via time-resolved PL peak shift.
3.6 Scaling relevance: demonstrate LbL spray/slot-die compatible pulsed deposition on 5×5 cm substrates; evaluate thickness uniformity and sheet-to-sheet reproducibility (PCE distribution, Voc spread).
Feasibility: 1.
