Feasibility: 1) Causality and falsifiability of curvature effects: The revised plan converts the curvature→strain→electronic-structure→adsorption→activity chain into measurable descriptors (K-distributions; εij from 4D-STEM/GPA; ΔΦ/valence shifts; operando XAS edge/white-line shifts; DFT-derived ΔG(*OH/*O/*OOH)). Curvature-matched controls with ECSA/roughness matched (±10%) directly address the reviewer’s concern that apparent gains could be ECSA/mass-transport artifacts.
2) Reconstruction-aware active-phase assignment: Because FeP/CoP will oxidize/reconstruct under OER, the proposal no longer assumes static “phosphide interface” activity. Operando Fe/Co K-edge XAS, operando/quasi-operando XPS, identical-location STEM, and H2^18O + DEMS are built in to identify the working surface (phosphide vs (oxy)hydroxide), quantify Fe dispersion retention, and test for lattice-oxygen participation. Success criteria for single-atom retention (EXAFS coordination bounds + microscopy) are explicitly stated, preventing misassignment.
3) Device-level engineering completeness for perovskite-driven PEC: The PV–PEC coupling is specified as an engineered recombination/interconnect with measurable contact resistivity targets and band-alignment verification (UPS/KPFM + impedance). The alkaline barrier is upgraded to a pinhole-tolerant multilayer nanolaminate with pre-integration leakage and permeation diagnostics, directly addressing the pinhole/grain-boundary failure mode. Encapsulation and electrolyte isolation are verified in situ (tracer/marker tests), not only post-mortem.
4) Voltage/energy budget and practical operating window: A required voltage budget is explicitly included and tied to target jop (10–20 mA cm−2). This prevents an underpowered PV demonstration and provides a clear decision rule for switching to a tandem PV if needed, maintaining the proposal’s central innovation (curvature-engineered external catalytic back-electrode) while ensuring a credible route to sustained operation.
5) Literature/empirical grounding aligned to assets: The approach leverages (i) curvature-enhanced catalytic site utilization and barrier lowering (negative Gaussian curvature concept; Asset 1), (ii) single-atom/dual-site electronic synergy in oxygen electrocatalysis (Asset 2), and (iii) heterostructure/interface-driven OER improvements informed by DFT and experimentally validated overpotential reductions (Asset 3), but now framed in a reconstruction-aware manner that is standard for transition-metal phosphides under anodic bias.
final_critique: Methodological definition and falsifiability are strong (pre-registered curvature/strain/electronic/kinetic descriptors; ECSA-matched controls; reconstruction-aware operando plan). The main scientific risk is attribution: under OER, phosphides reconstruct into (Fe,Co)OOH-like phases whose catalytic energetics are dominated by local coordination, Fe incorporation level, and hydration/anion effects; the proposal assumes curvature-imprinted strain fields persist in (oxy)hydroxide motifs and remain the dominant causal variable beyond morphology and transport, but does not yet specify how strain will be demonstrated in the reconstructed phase (not the pre-OER phosphide) or how curvature effects will be disentangled from curvature-driven differences in reconstruction kinetics/composition (Fe uptake, P leaching, crystallinity, hydration) that can independently shift activity and XAS signatures. The DFT plan is directionally appropriate but may be under-realistic: strained slab models of FeP/CoP interfaces may not predict adsorption energetics of the true operating (oxy)hydroxide surface; without explicit reconstructed-phase models (and/or grand-canonical/Pourbaix-informed surface states), the computed ΔG(*OH/*O/*OOH)–strain linkage risks becoming non-diagnostic. On the device side, the voltage-budget discussion is thoughtful, but the half-cell PV-driven OER constraint (VMPP vs required anodic potential at 10–20 mA cm−2 including iR and junction drops) is tight for a single 1.7–1.8 eV perovskite; the contingency to tandem is good, yet the proposal’s primary success narrative should be framed around a tandem-compatible pathway to avoid an underpowered demonstration. Finally, several key acceptance criteria remain difficult: matching ECSA within ±10% across radically different topologies is nontrivial (Cdl can be chemistry-dependent; UPD proxies are not universally valid), and Kelvin probe/UPS ex situ work-function shifts may not track the operando interface relevant for OER.
hypothesis_summary: Negative Gaussian curvature in FeP–CoP interfaces creates strain that electronically tunes reconstructed Fe–Co oxyhydroxide active sites, lowering OER overpotential while a decoupled perovskite PV and pinhole-tolerant barrier maintain device stability.

original_chain: Half-wave potential -> Electrochemical accessible surface area (EASA) -> COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900 -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Selectivity for oxidation -> Porous crystalline materials
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: An ultrathin (3–15 nm) COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900 interfacial nanolayer inserted between FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 and the HTL will increase Voc and operational stability by functioning as a quantitatively designed “redox buffer + pore-gate + defect-passivation” interface. Mechanistically, (i) the MOF-confined Fe–N4 centers provide a reversible Fe(III)/Fe(II) reservoir that can accept holes under illumination (oxidative charging) and preferentially intercept oxidizing equivalents that would otherwise drive formation/accumulation of I0/I2/I3− at the buried interface; (ii) the porous crystalline scaffold provides high electrochemically accessible surface area (EASA) to maximize areal density of passivation/charge-buffering sites and to distribute local redox events (avoiding hot spots that accelerate halide vacancy generation); and (iii) pore apertures and surface termination are tuned to allow rapid transport/uptake of small iodine/oxygen species (I2, I3−, O2) while suppressing uptake of representative HTL dopants/additives (tBP, Co(III) complexes and bulky anions), thereby reducing dopant-driven interfacial corrosion without introducing a hole-extraction barrier. 

Falsifiable design rules tie the ORR-derived Fe–N redox potential to device-relevant energetics: we explicitly target the iodine couples I−/I3− and I−/I2 (and secondarily O2/O2−) at the perovskite/HTL interface. Thermodynamic feasibility is tested by translating redox energies onto the vacuum scale and comparing them against perovskite/HTL quasi-Fermi levels under operating bias/illumination. The hypothesis is confirmed only if (a) operando spectroscopy shows reversible Fe(III)↔Fe(II) cycling accompanied by suppression of interfacial polyiodides, (b) quantified redox capacity (C cm−2) exceeds the measured/estimated iodine oxidative flux during stress tests, and (c) transport/recombination metrics demonstrate no added contact barrier or shunt pathway across the thickness/percolation window.
Plan: Step 0 — Quantitative electrochemical targeting and energy-scale translation (device-relevant grounding)
0.1 Identify targeted couples and map potentials to vacuum level. Target couples: (A) I−/I3− and (B) I−/I2 as primary iodine oxidation equilibria at the perovskite/HTL interface; (C) O2/O2− as a secondary oxidative pathway (particularly under ISOS-O-1). For each couple, tabulate E° vs NHE/RHE from literature and convert to absolute energy vs vacuum using E(abs, eV) ≈ −(4.44 + E vs NHE) (and adjust for RHE↔NHE at pH where relevant). Measure the perovskite valence-band maximum and work function (UPS) and determine the illuminated hole quasi-Fermi level splitting (from absolute PLQY/EQEEL). The design criterion is: the interlayer Fe(III)/Fe(II) formal potential (converted to eV vs vacuum) must sit within the energetic window accessible to holes at the interface under operating conditions (1 sun, near-MPP and near-Voc) so that the Fe–N sites can be oxidatively charged without requiring additional overpotential that would impede hole extraction.
0.2 Define success/failure thresholds (pre-registered). Success requires: (i) ≥30% reduction in interfacial I3−/polyiodide spectral signatures after stress (relative to control) at constant exposure, (ii) measurable reversible Fe oxidation-state swing under bias/light (Δ(FeIII/FeII) in operando XPS/XANES), and (iii) no increase in contact resistivity beyond 10% at the optimum thickness.

Step 1 — Interlayer synthesis with explicit pore-gating targets and chemistry
1.1 Synthesize COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900 nanoplates with controlled thickness distribution (target 5–15 nm median; reject batches >25 nm median by AFM/TEM). Confirm porosity and aperture distribution via N2 sorption (BET, pore size distribution) and verify structural integrity by PXRD.
1.2 Define pore-gating targets and termination chemistry. Establish an aperture/transport target window of ~3.4–6 Å (small-molecule/ion accessible) by selecting MOF-900 modulation and surface termination (e.g., partial pore-mouth functionalization with sterically demanding but electronically benign groups) while keeping internal Fe–N accessibility. Explicit gating objective: allow diffusion/uptake of I2 (~5–6 Å kinetic diameter) and small anions (I3− effective size dependent on solvation) while suppressing uptake of larger/less mobile dopant complexes (e.g., Co(III) TFSI-based complexes) and reduce tBP uptake by hydrophobic/steric termination. Because Li+ is intrinsically small and cannot be sterically excluded reliably, mitigation is re-framed: reduce Li+ residence at the perovskite by preferentially sequestering/neutralizing oxidative iodine species that accelerate Li+-driven degradation, and (if needed) add an additional ultrathin dipolar capping (≤1 nm) atop the MOF to slow Li+ penetration (tested as an optional sub-aim).
1.3 Verify chemical state of Fe–N sites pre-integration. Use XPS (Fe 2p, N 1s), Mössbauer/EPR (if available) to confirm Fe–N coordination and baseline Fe oxidation state distribution; quantify site density (mol Fe cm−2) from areal mass loading and Fe wt% (ICP-OES).

Step 2 — Device integration with transport-safe thickness/percolation window
2.1 Fabricate baseline n–i–p PSCs: glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/interlayer/HTL/Au. Perovskite: FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 on compact SnO2; target thickness 450–650 nm.
2.2 Deposit COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900 by orthogonal solvent processing with strict dissolution controls (in situ ellipsometry/UV–vis to confirm no perovskite bleaching). Thickness series: 0 (control), 3, 5, 8, 12, 20 nm (AFM step height and cross-sectional SEM/TEM). Define continuity/percolation by conductive-AFM and TEM: the layer must be continuous but not thick enough to create a tunneling barrier.
2.3 Energy-level alignment and dipole assessment: UPS (work function, valence onset) and Kelvin probe (surface potential) on perovskite vs perovskite+interlayer, then after HTL coating. Design rule: interlayer-induced vacuum level shift (ΔWF) must not push the perovskite/HTL hole-extraction barrier >0.2 eV (otherwise revise termination or thickness).

Step 3 — Proving (or falsifying) redox buffering: chemical fate, reversibility, and capacity
3.1 Operando/near-operando spectroscopy to identify iodine and Fe states.
• Operando XPS on functioning stacks (simplified architecture enabling access): build a thin Au grid top-contact or semitransparent electrode to allow biasing during XPS; alternatively perform bias-and-light “freeze-quench” near-operando XPS at defined states (dark, 1 sun open-circuit, MPP bias) within minutes to minimize relaxation artifacts. Track I 3d (I− vs I0/I2 vs polyiodide components), Fe 2p (FeII/FeIII), and N 1s (Fe–N vs protonated/oxidized N).
• XANES/EXAFS at Fe K-edge (ex situ after controlled electrochemical charging under defined potentials in a three-electrode solid-state cell, and after device stress) to confirm reversible Fe coordination environment and rule out irreversible Fe aggregation.
3.2 Quantify redox buffering capacity (C cm−2) and compare to iodine flux.
• Build a dedicated solid-state electrochemical test structure: ITO/perovskite/COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900/ion-blocking inert top electrode (e.g., Au) configured for chronoamperometry with a defined reference (micro-reference electrode or calibrated pseudo-reference) to integrate charge associated with Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycling (after subtracting capacitive background from Fe-free controls). Capacity metric: Qredox per unit area until Fe sites saturate.
• Independently estimate/measure iodine-related oxidative charge flux under ISOS-L-2 and ISOS-O-1 via (i) time-integrated interfacial polyiodide growth rate from spectroscopy, and/or (ii) ToF-SIMS-measured iodine redistribution combined with charge neutrality constraints. Success criterion: Qredox ≥ 5× expected iodine oxidative flux over the stress duration used for stability claims.
3.3 Identify binding motif and reversibility of iodine capture. Use ToF-SIMS depth profiling and angle-resolved XPS to locate iodine accumulation (confined to interlayer vs penetrating perovskite). Use Raman/UV–vis of extracted interlayers (if possible) to detect I3− signatures. Demonstrate partial regeneration by applying reducing bias/dark recovery and showing reversal of Fe oxidation state and reduction in polyiodide signal.

Step 4 — De-risking recombination and transport penalties (quantitative)
4.1 Contact resistivity and series resistance vs thickness.
• Transfer length method (TLM) using patterned test structures: perovskite/interlayer/HTL with varying electrode spacings to extract specific contact resistivity (ρc) at the buried interface; cross-check with J–V-derived Rs.
• Criterion: identify an optimum thickness range where ρc does not increase >10–20% relative to no-interlayer while stability gains persist.
4.2 Recombination/trap diagnostics to rule out new trap-assisted pathways.
• Absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi-level splitting (QFLS) on full stacks (perovskite ± interlayer ± HTL) to quantify non-radiative loss changes.
• TPV/TPC to separate recombination lifetime and extraction time constants.
• SCLC or thermal admittance spectroscopy on hole-only devices (ITO/PEDOT:PSS/perovskite/interlayer/HTL/Au or analogous) to extract trap density changes attributable to the interlayer.
4.3 Impedance spectroscopy with constrained equivalent-circuit fitting. Measure EIS at multiple biases (near Voc and near MPP) under 1 sun to separate transport resistance (Rtr) from recombination resistance (Rrec) and interfacial capacitances; compare across thickness series and across controls.

Step 5 — Making pore-gating concrete: diffusion/uptake tests for dopants vs iodine species
5.1 Uptake/diffusion measurements on standalone films.
• Quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) with COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900 films exposed to vapors/solutions of (i) I2 (or I2-generating conditions), (ii) tBP, (iii) LiTFSI, and (iv) representative Co(III) dopant complex; quantify uptake kinetics and equilibrium mass.
• Complement with ellipsometric swelling and FTIR (tBP signatures) to identify penetration.
5.2 Device-relevant depth profiling.
• ToF-SIMS on stressed devices to quantify Li+, TFSI− fragments, Co-containing fragments, and iodine distribution across HTL/interlayer/perovskite. Success criterion: reduced penetration of bulky dopant signatures and reduced iodine accumulation inside the perovskite bulk for the Fe-containing porous interlayer relative to non-porous controls.

Step 6 — Controls that decouple porosity/EASA from redox chemistry (mandatory)
6.1 Fe-free porous control: COP-TPP@MOF-900 (no Fe) to isolate porosity/passivation without redox buffering.
6.2 Collapsed/non-porous analog: densified COP-TPP(Fe)@MOF-900 (pore-collapsed by controlled thermal/solvent treatment while retaining similar surface chemistry) to isolate Fe redox without pore transport.
6.3 Redox-matched but non-porous Fe-porphyrin layer: planar Fe-porphyrin polymer/film with comparable Fe loading and formal potential, but lacking MOF porosity/EASA, to test whether confinement/EASA is required.
6.4 Inert MOF interlayer: MOF-900 without COP/Fe to benchmark purely dielectric/porous effects.

Step 7 — Operational stability and degradation-pathway attribution
7.1 ISOS protocols: ISOS-L-2 (continuous light, controlled temperature), ISOS-O-1 (ambient oxygen exposure) plus MPP tracking. Report T80 and T95, and correlate with chemical signatures (I speciation, Fe oxidation state) and electrical metrics (Rrec, Rs).
7.2 Competing degradation pathways: monitor Pb0 formation (XPS Pb 4f), halide segregation (PL peak shifts under illumination), and metal electrode migration (ToF-SIMS Au) to ensure observed benefits map specifically to suppressed interfacial oxidation/iodine chemistry rather than unrelated effects.
Feasibility: 1) Thermodynamic and device-relevant electrochemical feasibility: The reviewer concern (RHE potential not mapped to device energetics) is addressed by explicitly converting targeted iodine/oxygen redox couples and the Fe(III)/Fe(II) formal potential to an absolute (vacuum) energy scale and comparing them against experimentally measured perovskite/HTL work functions and quasi-Fermi levels under illumination/bias (UPS + PLQY-derived QFLS). This yields a go/no-go criterion for whether Fe–N sites can be oxidatively charged (and thus buffer oxidizing equivalents) without imposing an extraction barrier.

2) Chemical fate, reversibility, and capacity are explicitly measurable and compared to flux: The proposal now defines what “immobilize iodine” means in falsifiable terms—suppression of I0/I2/I3− accumulation at the buried interface and preferential localization within the interlayer—verified by operando/near-operando XPS (I 3d, Fe 2p, N 1s) and supported by Fe K-edge XANES/EXAFS. Redox buffering capacity is quantified as integrated charge per area (C cm−2) associated with Fe(III)/Fe(II) cycling in a defined solid-state electrochemical architecture with appropriate controls to remove capacitive/ionic-migration artifacts. Capacity is then benchmarked against measured/estimated iodine oxidative flux during ISOS stress, turning the selectivity narrative into a quantitative mass/charge-balance argument.

3) Transport/recombination risks are de-risked by thickness-window mapping and separable metrics: Because a redox-active interlayer could introduce traps/shunts, the plan includes a thickness series with (i) TLM-derived specific contact resistivity, (ii) TPV/TPC extraction/recombination kinetics, (iii) SCLC/trap-density determination, and (iv) bias-dependent EIS fits that separate transport resistance from recombination resistance. Acceptance criteria (e.g., ≤10–20% increase in ρc at optimal thickness; no reduction in Rrec; improved QFLS) explicitly prevent overfitting stability improvements that come at the cost of charge extraction.

4) Pore-gating is made concrete with apertures, termination goals, and uptake/diffusion tests: Rather than asserting steric exclusion, the proposal defines a targeted aperture regime and directly tests uptake/penetration using QCM and ToF-SIMS for representative HTL dopants/additives (tBP, LiTFSI, Co(III) complexes) versus iodine species. The plan also acknowledges that Li+ cannot be reliably sterically excluded and reframes the gating objective accordingly, preventing an unsupported claim.

5) Controls unambiguously decouple porosity/EASA from redox chemistry: The mandatory set of Fe-free porous, pore-collapsed Fe-containing, and redox-matched non-porous Fe-porphyrin controls provides a clean causal test: (i) if only Fe-containing porous layers suppress polyiodides and improve stability without transport penalty, the mechanism requires both redox activity and porosity/EASA; (ii) if Fe-containing non-porous performs similarly, porosity is not essential; (iii) if Fe-free porous performs similarly, redox buffering is not the dominant lever. This structure directly addresses the reviewer’s demand for falsifiability.

6) Alignment with literature assets while remaining PSC-specific: The proposal leverages Asset 1’s core insight—MOF-confined Fe–N sites yield high EASA and shifted redox behavior—without over-claiming ORR equivalence to PSC chemistry; instead it uses those properties as tunable design parameters whose relevance is tested via iodine/oxygen couples and operando spectroscopy. Asset 2’s confinement-driven selectivity is translated into experimentally verifiable pore-gating/uptake behavior for PSC additives and reactive halogen species.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-structured proposal that directly addresses common reviewer objections in perovskite interfacial chemistry (energetic mismatch, unverifiable 'passivation' claims, and transport penalties). Engineering resolution is high: the plan specifies thickness windows, acceptance thresholds, operando techniques, and quantitative capacity metrics rather than qualitative stability narratives. Logical consistency is strong, with a coherent mechanism linking Fe–N redox buffering, EASA, and pore-mediated selectivity to suppression of iodine-driven interfacial degradation. Minor deductions arise from residual experimental risk: operando XPS/XANES under bias in PSC-relevant stacks is technically challenging and may limit throughput, and the solid-state electrochemical capacity measurements rely on careful subtraction of ionic/capacitive artifacts that can be nontrivial. Evidence grounding is excellent; the concept chain is respected without importing irrelevant ORR claims, although the dependence on literature iodine redox potentials under ill-defined interfacial chemical potentials introduces some uncertainty. The rationale quality is high: the work does not merely insert a MOF interlayer but reframes stability as a charge-balance problem with falsifiable design rules. Overall, this is near the upper bound for methodological depth and falsifiability in PSC interface proposals.
hypothesis_summary: An ultrathin MOF-confined Fe–N₄ nanolayer acts as a redox buffer and pore-gate at the perovskite/HTL interface, suppressing iodine-driven degradation to boost voltage and stability.

original_chain: Modulation depth -> Ni3(HHTP)2 -> Charge transfer -> Specific capacitance -> Capacitance retention rate -> Specific capacitance -> Electrode material
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding an ultrathin, redox-active Ni3(HHTP)2 coordination-nanosheet interlayer (1–5 nm) at the perovskite/metal electrode interface will simultaneously (i) increase effective interfacial modulation depth of the interfacial electric field under illumination/bias, and (ii) raise the interfacial specific capacitance with high capacitance retention, thereby suppressing ion-accumulation-driven band bending and interfacial non-radiative recombination. Mechanistically, the conjugated MOF provides a high-density, fast Ni(II/III)-mediated pseudocapacitive charge-buffering pathway plus a porous, π-conjugated transport network that lowers charge-transfer resistance (Rct) while spatially redistributing ionic space charge; this converts slow, hysteretic ion-electrode charge storage into rapid, electronically buffered interfacial charging with improved stability. Methodological adaptation: instead of using Ni3(HHTP)2 as a bulk electrode additive (common in supercapacitors) or a thick film, we will (a) grow a wafer-scale coordination-nanosheet directly on the metal electrode by electrochemical interfacial polymerization to enforce epitaxial-like contact and minimal series resistance, and (b) cap it with a 0.5–1 nm ALD Al2O3 ‘ion-sieve’ to preserve electronic tunneling while limiting halide/metal diffusion; this dual-layer transforms the PSC metal contact into a charge-transfer-optimized, high-capacitance, retention-stable “pseudocapacitive electrode skin.”
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Fabricate baseline inverted PSCs (glass/ITO/SAM-based HTL or NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag) and regular n–i–p PSCs (glass/FTO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au) to test universality; use a mixed-cation perovskite (FA/Cs, I/Br) with controlled surface termination (post-treatment to enrich PbI2 or FA-iodide as needed).
1.2 Prepare control electrodes: bare Ag/Au; Ag/Au + Al2O3 (0.5–1 nm); Ag/Au + physically transferred Ni3(HHTP)2 film (thicker, 10–30 nm) to decouple thickness/contact effects.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Direct growth of Ni3(HHTP)2 coordination-nanosheets on metal electrode:
- Deposit 1–2 nm Ti (or Cr) adhesion only where necessary; keep work-function perturbation minimal.
- Use electrochemical interfacial polymerization: immerse Ag/Au in ethanolic HHTP solution; apply controlled potential pulses in Ni2+ electrolyte to nucleate and self-limit a nanosheet layer (target 1–5 nm). Tune growth via pulse width/duty cycle to control areal coverage and avoid insulating agglomerates.
- Rinse and mild anneal (<120 °C) to stabilize coordination without damaging underlying layers.
2.2 Ion-sieve capping without killing charge transfer:
- Deposit ALD Al2O3 at low temperature (≤80–90 °C) for 3–8 cycles (0.5–1.0 nm). This is intentionally below typical blocking-layer thickness to allow electron tunneling/thermionic transport while reducing halide ingress and metal migration.
2.3 Integrate into PSC stacks:
- For inverted devices: apply Ni3(HHTP)2/Al2O3 skin onto Ag cathode prior to deposition, or alternately onto ITO prior to organic layers to test polarity-dependent effects.
- For regular devices: integrate at Au/HTL interface (Au-side growth) or at perovskite/HTL using a transfer-assisted nanosheet if electrochemical growth is incompatible; keep the key test as the metal-contact skin.
2.4 Quantify ‘modulation depth’ in PSC-relevant terms:
- Define modulation depth as relative swing of interfacial field/photovoltage under a small AC perturbation: MD = (ΔVinterface or ΔEinterface)/(baseline) extracted from intensity-modulated photovoltage spectroscopy (IMVS) and bias-dependent electroabsorption/photothermal deflection where feasible.
- Map bias- and light-intensity-dependent impedance to extract interfacial capacitance (Cint), recombination resistance (Rrec), and charge-transfer resistance (Rct).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Charge transfer and capacitance metrics:
- EIS (10 mHz–1 MHz) under dark and 1-sun at multiple biases; fit with physically constrained equivalent circuits separating geometric capacitance, ionic accumulation capacitance, and pseudocapacitive contributions.
- Mott–Schottky and transient ion-drift measurements to quantify reduction in mobile-ion-induced interfacial charge density.
- Galvanostatic intermittent titration-like small-signal protocol on completed devices to probe capacitance retention under repeated bias cycling (e.g., ±0.2 V around MPP for 10^4 cycles), defining capacitance retention rate = Cint(after)/Cint(initial).
3.2 Device-level outcomes:
- J–V hysteresis index vs scan rate; stabilized MPP tracking for ≥100 h.
- PLQY and time-resolved PL at the perovskite interface (with partial stacks) to quantify non-radiative recombination suppression; target Voc increase explained via quasi-Fermi level splitting.
- ToF-SIMS depth profiling after aging to test halide/Ag migration suppression by Al2O3-capped Ni3(HHTP)2.
3.3 Mechanistic falsification tests:
- If improvements arise only with thick MOF layers, the mechanism is series-resistance filtering rather than pseudocapacitive buffering; enforce thickness series to pinpoint optimum.
- Replace Ni3(HHTP)2 with Cu3(HHTP)2 or an insulating MOF analogue to separate ‘conjugation/charge transfer’ from ‘porosity-only’ effects.
- Temperature-dependent EIS to distinguish electronic activation from ionic relaxation; expect reduced low-frequency ionic arcs and lower apparent ionic capacitance while maintaining/increasing Cint at intermediate frequencies due to pseudocapacitance.

Success criteria: (i) reduced Rct by ≥30% and reduced hysteresis index by ≥50% relative to controls; (ii) increased intermediate-frequency Cint without increased series resistance; (iii) capacitance retention rate ≥90% after 10^4 bias cycles; (iv) improved operational stability (T80 at MPP) by ≥2× with unchanged or improved PCE.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Ni3(HHTP)2 in ultrathin vdW heterostructures exhibits enhanced charge transfer and electron cloud extension (supporting fast interfacial carrier exchange and field responsiveness), while MOF-derived electrode concepts show that improved charge transfer lowers electron-transfer resistance and boosts specific capacitance with high cycling durability—an analogue for interfacial charge-buffering in PSCs.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC instability and hysteresis are strongly linked to ionic space-charge accumulation and metal-contact reactions. Converting the metal contact into a high-capacitance, fast charge-transfer ‘buffer’ layer is a direct interface-engineering approach: it reshapes interfacial band bending dynamics (modulation depth), reduces recombination at the contact, and limits ion/metal diffusion via the ultrathin ALD ion-sieve.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with standard SAMs or polymer interlayers that mainly tune work function, the Ni3(HHTP)2 nanosheet adds an electronically accessible pseudocapacitive reservoir that dynamically stabilizes the interfacial potential under operation, enabling higher capacitance retention under repeated bias/light cycling. Relative to thicker carbon/MOF composites, the self-limited nanosheet + sub-nm ALD cap preserves low series resistance and is compatible with low-temperature, scalable electrode processing.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-justified proposal that goes beyond work-function tuning to address ion-driven interfacial instability via a pseudocapacitive buffering mechanism. The engineering plan is unusually detailed for a PSC interfacial study, with credible growth control, control experiments, and falsification logic. However, several points limit a near-perfect score: (i) the electrochemical interfacial polymerization of Ni3(HHTP)2 on noble metals at the 1–5 nm regime is nontrivial, and uniformity/defect tolerance across wafer-scale electrodes is assumed rather than quantitatively risk-managed; (ii) the assumption that 0.5–1 nm Al2O3 simultaneously blocks halide diffusion yet preserves low-Rct tunneling is plausible but not rigorously bounded (no tunneling-length or barrier-height estimates are provided); and (iii) the definition of ‘modulation depth’ is conceptually interesting but somewhat bespoke, risking ambiguity in interpretation relative to standard PSC interfacial field metrics. These issues do not invalidate the concept but introduce execution and interpretability risk.
hypothesis_summary: An ultrathin Ni₃(HHTP)₂ nanosheet interlayer with an Al₂O₃ ion-sieve cap transforms the perovskite/metal electrode interface into a pseudocapacitive buffer that suppresses ion-driven band bending and non-radiative recombination.

original_chain: Oxygen reduction reaction -> Superionic functionalized bio-cellulose electrolyte -> Oxygen reduction reaction -> Half-wave potential -> Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) -> Layered double hydroxides (LDHs) -> Nanoreactors -> Covalent-organic frameworks (COFs)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that an ORR-quenched, ion-stabilized perovskite interface can be realized by replacing conventional organic passivation layers with a structurally novel, electronically inert “redox/ion sink laminate” composed of (i) an ultrathin LDH nanosheet layer whose interlayer galleries are preloaded with peroxide/superoxide-trapping anions and (ii) a COF overlayer grown as a self-limiting 2D skin via interfacial polymerization on top of the LDH, while (iii) a superionic functionalized bio-cellulose electrolyte is used only as an edge-seal/encapsulant ionic buffer (not as an interlayer). Mechanistically, the LDH provides fast anion-exchange to capture O2•−/HO2− and immobilize migrating halides (I−/Br−) at the interface, while the COF skin acts as a molecular sieve that limits O2/H2O access and suppresses electron-leakage-driven ORR by reducing local O2 adsorption/transport to catalytic sites. The combined effect is a measurable negative shift and reduced magnitude of the interfacial ORR half-wave potential (E1/2) on perovskite-adjacent model electrodes, coupled with reduced interfacial ionic accumulation, thereby increasing Voc (via lower non-radiative recombination) and operational lifetime under oxygen/light stress. The methodological adaptation is the use of a bilayer formed by sequential, substrate-confined assembly: Langmuir–Schaefer deposition of single/few-layer LDH nanosheets as a pinhole-minimized ionic/redox sink followed by room-temperature interfacial polymerization to create a thickness-limited COF barrier—distinct from nanoreactor growth within LDH galleries and distinct from mixed composite interlayers.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Baseline PSC: Use a high-Voc, oxygen-sensitive composition such as FA0.85Cs0.15Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3 in an n–i–p stack (ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au). Keep SnO2 processing fixed to isolate interfacial effects.
1.2 LDH selection and preloading: Synthesize colloidally stable, single/few-layer LDH nanosheets (e.g., MgAl-LDH or ZnAl-LDH) via exfoliation. Preload interlayers with ROS-reactive anions (e.g., iodide/thiocyanate-derived redox buffers, or phenolate/quinone-type anions chosen for fast O2•−/HO2− quenching) using controlled anion exchange; quantify loading by ion chromatography and XPS.
1.3 COF monomer design for electronic benignity: Choose a COF chemistry with low trap density and minimal Lewis basicity toward Pb2+ (e.g., β-ketoenamine COF with carbonyl-rich linkers to weakly coordinate undercoordinated Pb without strong chemical etching). Pre-screen monomers for solvent orthogonality to perovskite.
1.4 Superionic functionalized bio-cellulose electrolyte (SFBC) as sealant: Prepare SFBC with tethered imidazolium/sulfonate groups and controlled water activity (add hygroscopic salt only in a separated edge-seal region). Target high ionic conductivity for buffering external ionic contaminants at device perimeter while maintaining low electronic conductivity.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 LDH laminate formation (non-nanoreactor, non-composite): Form a continuous LDH nanosheet laminate (2–10 nm total) on top of SnO2 by Langmuir–Schaefer transfer or electrophoretic deposition. Key adaptation: optimize nanosheet packing density and orientation to minimize pinholes while keeping series resistance low. Verify coverage by AFM, SEM, and conductive-AFM mapping.
2.2 Self-limiting COF skin by interfacial polymerization: Grow a COF overlayer (nominally 3–8 nm) directly on the LDH laminate via room-temperature interfacial polymerization (aqueous/organic interface or vapor–solid interface) so that growth is limited by monomer diffusion through the forming COF. Key adaptation: exploit LDH surface hydroxyls as nucleation anchors to promote uniform COF wetting without infiltrating the perovskite.
2.3 Perovskite deposition and crystallization control: Deposit perovskite on SnO2/LDH/COF using antisolvent or gas-quench methods adjusted for the modified surface energy. Tune nucleation density via brief surface conditioning (e.g., mild UV-ozone on COF or a sub-monolayer ammonium halide primer) to preserve large grains while preventing interfacial voids.
2.4 SFBC edge-seal integration: Apply SFBC as an edge-seal/encapsulant layer after electrode deposition, spatially separated from the active area by a patterned inert barrier. Purpose: buffer ion ingress/egress at edges and stabilize interconnect regions without adding interfacial electronic barriers.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Direct ORR metrics at relevant interfaces: Build model electrodes (ITO/SnO2, ITO/SnO2/LDH, ITO/SnO2/LDH/COF; plus perovskite-coated variants protected with ultrathin inert overlayers to enable electrochemistry). Use rotating disk electrode measurements in O2-saturated electrolyte to extract ORR E1/2 and kinetic current; confirm that LDH/COF reduces ORR activity (more negative E1/2 and lower limiting current) relative to controls.
3.2 ROS detection under illumination: Quantify superoxide formation using operando EPR spin trapping and/or fluorescent ROS probes in controlled O2 environments. Correlate ROS suppression with LDH anion identity (anion-exchange dependence test).
3.3 Ion migration and hysteresis: Use bias-stress J–V hysteresis, impedance spectroscopy (ionic capacitance), and Kelvin probe force microscopy under bias/light to map interfacial ionic accumulation. Use ToF-SIMS depth profiling (I−/Br− distribution; Au diffusion) pre/post stress.
3.4 Recombination and Voc mechanism: Measure absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi level splitting on perovskite films grown on each interface; perform TRPL and Suns–Voc to separate transport losses from non-radiative recombination. Validate that the laminate increases Voc without FF penalty.
3.5 Stability protocols with oxygen specificity: Run ISOS-O and ISOS-L protocols with controlled O2 partial pressure (0–21%) and humidity (10–30% RH) at 60–85 °C. Track T80 and identify degradation signatures (Pb0 by XPS; halide loss by XRF; phase changes by GIWAXS). Use post-mortem mapping to confirm that failures shift from oxygen-driven interfacial degradation to other modes.
3.6 Falsification/controls: Compare against (i) COF-only skin on SnO2, (ii) LDH-only laminate without ROS-trapping anions, (iii) LDH laminate with non-reactive anions, (iv) standard SAM passivation. Demonstrate that both (a) LDH anion-exchange chemistry and (b) COF molecular sieving are required to suppress ORR E1/2 and improve operational stability simultaneously.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: ORR half-wave potential is a quantitative descriptor of oxygen electrochemistry and can be mapped on model electrodes; ROS (superoxide/peroxide) are known drivers of oxygen/light-induced perovskite degradation. LDHs offer rapid, reversible anion exchange and can immobilize/intercept anionic species; COFs can be synthesized as ultrathin, continuous films by interfacial polymerization and can act as selective diffusion barriers. Prior electrocatalysis literature links confinement/architectures to ORR kinetics (E1/2 shifts), enabling translation to ORR suppression (anti-catalysis) at PSC interfaces.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC stability bottlenecks include oxygen-assisted interfacial redox and halide/vacancy migration that elevates recombination and accelerates decomposition. The proposed laminate specifically targets (i) oxygen access/activation (COF sieve suppresses O2 transport and adsorption) and (ii) anionic species stabilization (LDH traps ROS and halides via exchange), while preserving electron extraction because the layers are ultrathin, electronically insulating but not thick enough to cause large tunneling barriers. Using SFBC as an edge-seal (not in the active interface) leverages its ionic buffering without risking moisture-assisted degradation.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike conventional passivators that mainly bind Pb defects or add hydrophobicity, this approach introduces a measurable electrochemical design target (lower ORR E1/2 and ROS yield) coupled to ionic stabilization (anion exchange). Unlike the rejected concept, it avoids nanoreactor-in-LDH COF growth and avoids mixed SFBC/COF@LDH composite interlayers; instead it uses sequential, substrate-confined assembly (LDH laminate + self-limited COF skin) to achieve pinhole-minimized coverage with controllable thickness, compatible with scalable deposition (Langmuir–Schaefer/EPD and interfacial polymerization).
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and unusually well-articulated proposal with strong alignment between hypothesis, methodology, and validation metrics. The use of ORR half-wave potential as an anti-catalytic design target at perovskite-adjacent interfaces is original and scientifically defensible. The sequential LDH/COF laminate concept is logically coherent and addresses known oxygen-assisted degradation and ionic migration bottlenecks in PSCs. Minor score deductions arise from (i) residual uncertainty about the electronic benignity of ROS-reactive anions within LDH galleries under prolonged bias/light stress (possible redox cycling or unintended halide exchange dynamics), and (ii) the practical risk that even 3–8 nm COF skins introduce interfacial dipoles or tunneling barriers that could subtly affect electron extraction, which is acknowledged but not quantitatively bounded. The SFBC edge-seal concept is sensible but peripheral to the core mechanistic claim and slightly overdeveloped relative to its scientific leverage.
hypothesis_summary: We hypothesize that a layered LDH/COF interface can suppress oxygen reduction and trap halides, boosting perovskite solar cell voltage and stability.

original_chain: Negative Gaussian curvature -> FeN4 coordination -> Bicontinuous structure -> Specific surface area -> Ce-MOF-1 -> Ce-MOF/CNT composite -> Electrochemical impedance spectra (EIS) -> Ce(IV)-cluster nodes
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A curvature-programmable, electrically benign Ce-MOF-1-derived interfacial “chelator-skin” grown as a self-limited monolayer on a pre-formed bicontinuous CNT gyroid scaffold—and subsequently converted into a Ce(IV)-cluster-node-rich, linker-condensed inorganic-organic network—will suppress interfacial non-radiative recombination and ion-migration-driven hysteresis in perovskite solar cells without adding a transport barrier. Mechanism: (i) negative Gaussian curvature in the bicontinuous scaffold increases accessible Ce(IV)-cluster node density per projected area at fixed thickness, raising the probability of halide capture and under-coordinated Pb passivation; (ii) Ce(IV)/Ce(III) redox buffering neutralizes photoinduced interfacial oxidants and stabilizes the perovskite surface stoichiometry, reducing defect formation under bias/illumination; (iii) the CNT bicontinuous network provides the only long-range electronic percolation pathway, while the Ce-MOF-1-derived skin remains electronically thin and ion-adsorbing, thereby decoupling ‘chemical functionality’ from ‘charge transport’. Methodological adaptation: rather than templated MOF growth or thick MOF/CNT coatings, we will (A) fabricate a negative-Gaussian-curvature CNT gyroid using a removable block-copolymer gyroid template and (B) perform a vapor-phase, self-limiting coordination infiltration (molecular-layer-infiltration-like) to deposit an ultrathin Ce-MOF-1 skin only on CNT surfaces, followed by a mild linker-condensation step to lock Ce(IV)-cluster nodes and prevent MOF swelling/dissolution during perovskite processing. FeN4 coordination is introduced as a sparse, covalently tethered interfacial ROS-quenching motif on the CNT gyroid (prior to Ce deposition) to intercept O2•–/I2-like species under operation while remaining optically and electronically non-parasitic.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1. Device platforms (two polarity tests):
   1.1 n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au.
   1.2 p–i–n: glass/ITO/NiOx/perovskite/C60/BCP/Ag.
2. Baseline perovskite absorber (one well-controlled reference composition for all comparisons): FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3, fixed antisolvent and anneal; quantify baseline Voc deficit (via EQEEL), trap density (SCLC on electron-only/hole-only stacks), and baseline EIS signatures (ionic arc magnitude, recombination resistance).
3. Define target interlayer requirements before synthesis: optical loss <1% in 450–800 nm, added series resistance <0.3 Ω·cm2, interlayer thickness (effective) 5–15 nm while maximizing chemically accessible Ce sites.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
4. Build a negative-Gaussian-curvature bicontinuous CNT gyroid scaffold (architectural adaptation distinct from cubosomes):
   4.1 Deposit a thin block-copolymer gyroid template (e.g., PS-b-PMMA gyroid-forming composition) on SnO2 (or on top of perovskite when used as a top interlayer; see Step 7 variants). Induce gyroid phase via solvent-vapor annealing to yield a continuous, periodic bicontinuous morphology.
   4.2 Infiltrate CNTs selectively into one gyroid domain using differential wetting (CNT dispersion engineered with surfactant/solvent selectivity). Lock CNT connectivity by brief photonic or low-temperature chemical crosslinking (no high-T sintering).
   4.3 Remove the polymer template with orthogonal solvent/plasma conditions validated not to damage SnO2/NiOx (performed on transport-layer-only substrates; for perovskite-facing layers use a ‘sacrificial-on-carrier’ transfer described in Step 7).
   4.4 Verify gyroid/Schwarz-type bicontinuity and negative Gaussian curvature by GISAXS (gyroid reflections) and electron tomography on dummy samples.
5. Introduce sparse FeN4 coordination on CNT surfaces (without forming an electrocatalyst layer):
   5.1 Covalently graft pyridinic-N ligands onto CNTs (diazonium or amidation route) at low coverage.
   5.2 Coordinate Fe to form isolated FeN4 motifs using a macrocycle-free, surface-confined chelation (Fe salt + tetradentate N-ligand motif on CNT); confirm single-site character with XAS (Fe K-edge) on thicker witness films.
   5.3 Set Fe areal density below the threshold of parasitic absorption and shunting (calibrate via sheet resistance + optical transmission).
6. Self-limited Ce-MOF-1 “chelator-skin” deposition by vapor/solution sequential infiltration (key methodological adaptation):
   6.1 Perform alternating exposures of Ce(IV) precursor (e.g., Ce(IV) β-diketonate or Ce ammonium nitrate in low-activity solvent) and Ce-MOF-1 linker vapor/solution pulses to deposit a conformal, sub-nanometer-per-cycle coordination layer only on CNT surfaces (no free MOF crystallites).
   6.2 Stop after achieving an estimated 2–6 nm equivalent thickness (monitored by quartz crystal microbalance on witness sensors and by XPS attenuation).
   6.3 Mild linker-condensation/partial inorganic densification: brief thermal (≤120 °C) or UV-assisted step to crosslink linkers and stabilize Ce(IV)-cluster nodes, intentionally reducing framework swelling while retaining accessible Lewis-acid sites.
   6.4 Optional: tune Ce(IV)/Ce(III) ratio by controlled ozone-free oxidizing/reducing pulses (e.g., mild benzoquinone for oxidation avoidance; gentle reductant vapor for partial Ce(III)) to optimize redox buffering without inducing iodide oxidation.
7. Interface placement variants (performed without direct templating on the perovskite to avoid solvent incompatibility):
   7.1 Bottom interlayer (electron side): ITO/SnO2/(gyroid CNT–FeN4@Ce-MOF-1-skin)/perovskite.
   7.2 Top interlayer (hole side): fabricate the gyroid CNT–FeN4@Ce-MOF-1-skin on a sacrificial carrier (e.g., water-soluble polymer), then dry-transfer laminate onto perovskite before HTL deposition to avoid exposing perovskite to template-removal steps.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
8. Structural/chemical proof of the intended coordination and nodes:
   8.1 XPS/UPS: Ce3+/Ce4+ ratio; Pb 4f and I 3d shifts indicating coordination/passivation; work function alignment changes.
   8.2 XAS (Ce L-edge; Fe K-edge) on witness samples to confirm Ce(IV)-cluster node environment and FeN4 coordination.
   8.3 Quantify accessible site density: electrochemical double-layer capacitance (Cdl) on conductive analog electrodes + Kr adsorption on scraped films (where feasible) as proxies for effective specific surface area.
9. Optoelectronic and interfacial recombination metrics:
   9.1 Steady-state PL and TRPL of perovskite on modified ETL/HTL stacks to extract surface recombination velocity trends.
   9.2 Absolute PLQY and implied Voc to decouple optical improvements from contact resistance.
   9.3 Transient photovoltage/photocurrent (TPV/TPC) to assess recombination kinetics and extraction.
10. EIS-centered mechanistic verification (core readout):
   10.1 Perform light-intensity-dependent EIS (0.1–1 sun) at biases from short-circuit to near Voc; use a physically constrained equivalent circuit separating electronic transport, interfacial recombination, and ionic polarization (include a dedicated low-frequency ionic branch).
   10.2 Success signatures: increased recombination resistance (Rrec) near Voc; reduced low-frequency capacitance growth and/or increased ionic relaxation frequency (suppressed ion accumulation); unchanged or reduced charge-transfer/transport resistance associated with the selective contact (no added barrier).
   10.3 Temperature-dependent EIS (200–330 K) to extract activation energies for ionic polarization; expect increased activation energy and reduced ionic capacitance for treated interfaces.
11. Ion-migration and chemical stability tests:
   11.1 ToF-SIMS depth profiling after bias stress to quantify iodide/bromide accumulation at interfaces.
   11.2 Operando XPS (or near-ambient XPS on model stacks) under illumination/oxygen to evaluate whether FeN4 reduces superoxide-linked interfacial oxidation markers.
12. Device benchmarks and falsification controls:
   12.1 Controls: (i) planar CNT film (no gyroid), (ii) gyroid CNT without Ce skin, (iii) gyroid CNT@Ce skin without FeN4, (iv) Ce skin on planar CNT, (v) FeN4 on gyroid CNT without Ce, (vi) conventional small-molecule passivator (reference).
   12.2 Targets: Voc gain ≥40 mV and/or reduction in Voc deficit by ≥10%; hysteresis index reduced by ≥50%; FF maintained within ±1% absolute vs baseline; operational T80 (MPP tracking, ISOS-L-2) improved ≥2×; EIS signatures match Step 10 success criteria.

Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 1 establishes that negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous architectures dramatically increase specific surface area and improve utilization of FeN4-type sites; translating this to PSC interfaces predicts higher density of chemically active passivation/ion-capture sites at fixed thickness. Asset 2 shows Ce-MOF/CNT composites reduce interfacial impedance (EIS-visible) and leverage Ce(IV)-cluster nodes for strong adsorption/catalysis; in PSCs the analogous function is halide coordination, Pb-defect passivation, and interfacial redox buffering.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC losses are dominated by interfacial non-radiative recombination and ion accumulation at selective contacts. A self-limited Ce-MOF-1-derived skin provides high-density Lewis-acid sites and redox buffering directly at the contact, while the CNT gyroid ensures that electronic transport is not forced through an insulating MOF. The gyroid’s bicontinuous geometry provides curvature-amplified accessible area without the thickness penalty that typically degrades FF.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to the rejected ‘templated MOF growth’ approach, this strategy is structurally novel: (i) the bicontinuous architecture is created first as a CNT gyroid (transport backbone), (ii) Ce-MOF-1 functionality is added as an ultrathin, conformal, self-limited skin (not a porous bulk film), and (iii) a linker-condensation stabilization step converts the MOF-like skin into a solvent-robust node-rich chelator network compatible with perovskite processing and long-term bias/illumination. This decoupling of conductivity (CNT) from chemistry (Ce nodes + sparse FeN4) is designed to yield EIS-proven interfacial improvements without incurring a transport barrier.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and technically mature proposal with clear command of both perovskite interfacial physics and advanced nanostructured materials synthesis. The engineering plan is detailed down to curvature verification, infiltration limits, redox-state tuning, and falsifiable EIS signatures. Logical consistency is strong: the decoupling of electronic percolation (CNT gyroid) from chemical functionality (Ce(IV) nodes and sparse FeN4) is well justified and directly addresses the transport–passivation tradeoff that plagues MOF-based interlayers. Minor deductions arise from cumulative execution risk rather than conceptual flaws: (i) the block-copolymer gyroid fabrication, CNT selective infiltration, and defect-free transfer to perovskite stacks represent a long, failure-prone process chain; (ii) the assumption that a partially condensed Ce-MOF-1 skin simultaneously preserves high Lewis acidity, redox buffering, and complete electronic benignity is plausible but not yet quantitatively bounded; and (iii) FeN4 stability and true single-site behavior under halide-rich PSC bias conditions remain an open variable despite good proposed controls. These are risks of ambition, not of weak reasoning.
hypothesis_summary: A curvature-engineered, ultrathin Ce-MOF-1-derived chelator skin on a bicontinuous CNT gyroid scaffold suppresses interfacial recombination and ion-migration hysteresis in perovskite solar cells without adding a transport barrier.

original_chain: Tribo-piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) -> Zn-Car_MOF -> Open-circuit voltage (Voc) -> Photochemical energy conversion -> Electron transport layer (ETL) -> Nanophotonics -> Surface plasmons -> Plasmonic nanoparticles
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a plasmonic-nanoparticle–decorated Zn-Car_MOF interlayer inside (not merely on top of) the ETL will simultaneously increase Voc and stabilize perovskite solar cells by a dual mechanism: (i) nanophotonic near-field enhancement and plasmon-induced hot-electron injection into the ETL raises the electron quasi-Fermi level and accelerates electron extraction, lowering interfacial carrier density and suppressing non-radiative recombination; (ii) the piezoelectric Zn-Car_MOF, when mechanically biased by an integrated tribo-piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) during operation, generates a dynamic interfacial polarization field that acts as an adaptive ‘ferroelectric-like’ dipole, increasing the built-in potential and further reducing interfacial recombination velocity. The methodological adaptation is to convert the ETL from a passive extractor into an actively biased, nanophotonic–piezoelectric ‘field-programmable ETL’ by structurally (a) forming a MOF-to-oxide infiltrated composite ETL scaffold and (b) electrically coupling it to a TPHG so that mechanical micro-strain periodically modulates the ETL/perovskite band bending without introducing DC leakage or chemical dopants.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1. Choose a high-Voc perovskite baseline (e.g., FA/Cs mixed-cation, I/Br mixed-halide, ~1.55–1.60 eV) and a low-hysteresis device stack (glass/ITO/SAM or compact layer/ETL/perovskite/HTL/Au).
2. Select an oxide ETL that tolerates interfacial modification (SnO2 preferred for low-temperature processing and reduced UV instability). Prepare a reference ETL (spin-coated SnO2 colloid or ALD-SnO2).
3. Synthesize Zn-Car_MOF with controlled crystal size (20–100 nm) and verify piezoelectric response via PFM (d33 mapping) and dielectric spectroscopy.
4. Prepare plasmonic nanoparticles (Au nanospheres 20–40 nm or Ag@SiO2 core–shell to avoid halide corrosion). Tune LSPR to overlap perovskite absorption edge (650–800 nm) to maximize near-field intensity at the perovskite/ETL interface.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
1. Build a composite ‘infiltrated ETL’: deposit a thin porous SnO2 (or mesoporous SnO2) layer (30–80 nm). Infiltrate Zn-Car_MOF into the porous ETL (capillary infiltration from a MOF precursor solution followed by in situ crystallization) to form an oxide–MOF interpenetrating network rather than a discrete MOF film.
2. Decorate the MOF within the ETL with plasmonic nanoparticles by (a) anchoring metal seeds to Zn-Car_MOF carboxylate sites and (b) controlled growth to keep NPs spatially separated (>5–10 nm) from the perovskite to avoid direct metal/perovskite contact. Add an ultrathin insulating spacer if needed (1–2 nm Al2O3 by ALD or SiO2 shell) to suppress interfacial quenching while preserving near-field coupling.
3. Create a ‘field-programmable’ interface: engineer the top of the composite ETL with a dipole-forming surface termination (e.g., a thin ionic/cationic self-assembled monolayer on SnO2 and/or oriented Zn-Car_MOF domains) to maximize polarization alignment toward electron extraction.
4. Integrate the TPHG mechanically with the PSC module (laminated backplane or edge-mounted harvester) and electrically couple it through a rectifying/charge-limiting network (diode bridge + high-impedance coupling capacitor) so the nanogenerator produces a periodic bias or displacement current that polarizes the Zn-Car_MOF without causing steady-state DC injection. Calibrate mechanical excitation (frequency 1–200 Hz, pressure/strain matched to wearable or wind-induced vibration regimes).
5. Fabricate control devices: (i) baseline ETL; (ii) ETL+Zn-Car_MOF (no plasmonics, no TPHG); (iii) ETL+plasmonics (no MOF, no TPHG); (iv) ETL+Zn-Car_MOF+plasmonics (no TPHG); (v) full system with TPHG coupling.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
1. Quantify Voc gains and recombination changes: measure JV (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP, Suns-Voc, and ideality factor (n) vs light intensity to separate bulk vs interface recombination.
2. Mechanistic spectroscopy: TRPL and transient photovoltage/photocurrent to extract carrier lifetime and recombination velocity at the ETL/perovskite interface; impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to monitor interfacial charge-transfer resistance and recombination resistance under TPHG actuation on/off.
3. Nanophotonic verification: optical simulations (FDTD/RCWA) using measured NP distributions to compute near-field intensity at the interface; correlate with EQE enhancement spectra and LSPR position. Confirm hot-electron contribution by wavelength-dependent photocurrent under sub-bandgap/LSPR excitation and by inserting an ultrathin tunneling barrier to modulate injection.
4. Piezo/polarization verification: PFM under cyclic strain to confirm polarization switching/variation; Kelvin probe/UPS to track work-function and band bending shifts with TPHG actuation; measure Voc modulation amplitude and phase relative to mechanical drive to confirm electromechanical origin.
5. Stability and degradation: ISOS-L (continuous illumination at 60–85°C) and damp-heat testing; track ion migration via bias-stress hysteresis, ToF-SIMS for halide/metal diffusion, and operando PL mapping. Compare full system vs controls to determine whether dynamic polarization reduces interfacial defect growth and suppresses ion accumulation.
6. Scalability check: demonstrate blade-coated or slot-die SnO2 and MOF infiltration on ≥10 cm^2 substrates; evaluate uniformity via sheet resistance, optical haze, and spatially resolved JV/PL.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 3 supports plasmonic nanoparticles and surface plasmons as nanophotonic tools to enhance extraction and mitigate non-radiative recombination at transport-layer interfaces. Asset 2 establishes MOF composites as tunable interlayers/ETL modifiers that correlate with Voc via improved interfacial charge transfer and reduced recombination. Asset 1 demonstrates Zn-Car_MOF possesses strong piezoelectric output (high Voc under pressure) in a TPHG context, evidencing robust electromechanical polarization that can be repurposed as an interfacial field source.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Voc in PSCs is typically limited by interfacial non-radiative recombination and insufficient band bending at the ETL/perovskite junction. The adapted ETL converts Zn-Car_MOF piezoelectric polarization into a controllable interfacial dipole (increasing built-in potential and lowering interfacial carrier density), while plasmonic near-fields increase photogeneration and accelerate electron extraction specifically at the interface where recombination is most damaging. Infiltrating MOF into porous SnO2 is a structural adaptation that preserves electron percolation through SnO2 while adding polarization and chemical passivation sites without relying on unstable molecular dopants.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to static dipole layers or simple NP sprinkling, the proposed ‘field-programmable ETL’ provides (i) dynamic, mechanically driven modulation of band bending that can counteract time-dependent ion accumulation and interfacial trap activation; (ii) spatially localized nanophotonic enhancement that boosts interfacial collection without thickening the absorber; and (iii) a chemically buffered architecture (MOF inside ETL + NP spacing layers) that minimizes direct metal–halide contact, reducing plasmonic-induced corrosion. The control matrix and operando measurements are designed to attribute Voc and stability gains to specific mechanisms (hot-electron/near-field vs piezo-polarization vs passivation).
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-reasoned proposal that integrates nanophotonics, piezoelectric MOFs, and interfacial energetics in PSCs with uncommon depth. Engineering resolution is strong: the infiltrated ETL scaffold, NP spacing strategy, rectified high-impedance TPHG coupling, and comprehensive control matrix are all actionable and appropriate. Logical consistency is high but not flawless: the assumed magnitude and temporal stability of piezoelectric-induced band bending under realistic micro-strain conditions is not quantitatively bounded, and the coupling efficiency between TPHG displacement current and MOF polarization inside a conductive SnO2 matrix is under-theorized. Evidence grounding is solid; however, hot-electron injection claims remain somewhat speculative in oxide ETLs (SnO2) where energy relaxation is ultrafast, and near-field enhancement alone may dominate. The rationale is creative and addresses a genuine bottleneck (interfacial Voc loss and instability), but the proposal occasionally conflates dynamic polarization effects with quasi-ferroelectric behavior without establishing whether Zn-Car_MOF exhibits remanent polarization or merely strain-correlated piezopotential under load.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding plasmonic-nanoparticle–decorated piezoelectric MOF inside the electron-transport layer creates a field-programmable interface that uses nanophotonic enhancement and mechanically driven polarization to boost voltage and stabilize perovskite solar cells.

original_chain: Nanocomposites -> Mechanochemical synthesis -> Mg2(dobdc) -> Acid modulation -> High-concentration solvothermal synthesis -> pKa -> Ionothermal synthesis -> Salicylate frameworks
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A pKa-programmed acid-modulation strategy, implemented via mechanochemical pre-coordination of salicylate modulators into Mg2(dobdc) followed by ionothermal activation, will create a perovskite–MOF nanocomposite interphase that simultaneously (i) suppresses non-radiative recombination by Lewis-base chelation of under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy passivation and (ii) improves operational stability by immobilizing mobile ionic species (I−/Br−, MA+/FA+, and metal ions from electrodes) within a polar, size-selective MOF microenvironment. The key methodological adaptation is to replace conventional solution-phase additive/passivation (which suffers from inhomogeneous distribution and solvent-driven phase segregation) with a two-stage, solvent-minimized route: (1) mechanochemical synthesis of salicylate-modulated Mg2(dobdc) nanoparticles engineered to present a controlled density of free –COO−/–O− sites, and (2) ionothermal infiltration/activation that generates an ultrathin, perovskite-compatible interphase during film formation without introducing additional volatile solvents. Mechanistically, the salicylate pKa determines the equilibrium between (a) strongly chelating bidentate salicylate bound to Pb2+ at the perovskite surface (defect healing) and (b) salicylate anchored to Mg sites inside Mg2(dobdc) (ion-buffering and interphase robustness); tuning this balance yields an optimal interphase that increases quasi-Fermi level splitting (higher Voc) while reducing ion-migration-driven hysteresis and degradation under heat/light bias.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a high-performance baseline perovskite stack (e.g., n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au) using a mixed-cation mixed-halide absorber (FA/Cs, I/Br) to ensure relevance to state-of-the-art Voc and stability.
1.2 Prepare a salicylate modulator library spanning pKa and coordination strength: salicylic acid, 5-fluorosalicylic acid (lower pKa), and 5-methoxysalicylic acid (higher pKa). Define target pKa windows to bias (i) stronger deprotonation/chelation vs (ii) more neutral hydrogen-bonding.
1.3 Define the MOF target: Mg2(dobdc) nanoparticles (50–200 nm) with controlled surface terminations; establish three MOF states: pristine, salicylate-modulated (partially substituted at Mg sites), and “acid-primed” (excess free salicylate physically confined).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Mechanochemical synthesis (adaptation component A):
- Perform ball-milling of Mg source (e.g., MgO or Mg(OH)2) with H4dobdc and a calibrated amount of salicylic-acid derivative (modulator) under liquid-assisted grinding using a minimal, non-perovskite-damaging LAG agent (e.g., ethanol at μL mg−1 scale).
- Control modulation level by modulator:dobdc ratio and milling energy/time; aim to create missing-linker/defect-engineered Mg2(dobdc) that exposes coordinatively unsaturated Mg sites while retaining crystallinity.
- Post-milling, wash quickly to remove unbound modulator while preserving a designed fraction of confined salicylate; dry under mild vacuum.
2.2 Ionothermal activation (adaptation component B):
- Disperse mechanochemically made Mg2(dobdc)-salicylate nanoparticles into a low-volatility ionic liquid (IL) compatible with perovskite processing constraints (dry, aprotic; e.g., imidazolium-based with weakly coordinating anions). Use IL volume fractions that enable ultrathin interphase formation, not bulk IL retention.
- Apply the IL–MOF dispersion as a pre-layer on SnO2 (or as an ultralow loading additive to the perovskite precursor) and thermally treat at moderate temperature (e.g., 80–120 °C) to (i) activate/open pores, (ii) lock salicylate distribution, and (iii) promote intimate interfacial contact without conventional solvent swelling.
2.3 High-concentration solvothermal synthesis translation to film growth (adaptation component C):
- Fabricate perovskite films using high-concentration precursor inks to reduce solvent content and enhance nucleation control.
- Implement acid modulation during crystallization: add trace equivalents of the same salicylate derivative (matched pKa to MOF modulator) to the precursor to synchronize solution chemistry with the MOF interphase; this alignment is designed to prevent modulator leaching and ensure a continuous chemical potential from solution → grain boundaries → interface.
- Tune crystallization kinetics (antisolvent timing or gas-quench) to drive MOF nanoparticles preferentially to the buried interface or grain boundaries (depending on target), forming a percolation-limited nanocomposite interphase rather than a scattering-rich bulk composite.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Structural/chemical verification:
- PXRD/FTIR/solid-state NMR to confirm Mg2(dobdc) formation and salicylate incorporation mode (anchored vs free).
- XPS/UPS on perovskite films with/without MOF interphase to quantify Pb–O bonding signatures, halide vacancy-related shifts, and work-function alignment.
- ToF-SIMS depth profiling to locate salicylate and MOF distribution (buried interface vs bulk).
3.2 Optoelectronic mechanism tests:
- TRPL and absolute PLQY to extract non-radiative recombination reduction; compute implied Voc and compare to device Voc.
- SCLC or thermal admittance spectroscopy to quantify trap-density changes; EIS to assess interfacial recombination resistance and ion-migration signatures.
- Bias-stress hysteresis mapping and transient ionic drift measurements (e.g., chronoamperometry under light/bias) to test ion immobilization.
3.3 Device performance and stability:
- Compare PCE, Voc, FF, and hysteresis index across pKa series and modulation levels.
- Operational stability: ISOS-L (MPP tracking, 1 sun), ISOS-D (dark heat), and damp-heat (85 °C/85% RH if encapsulated), with failure analysis by cross-sectional SEM and chemical mapping.
3.4 Falsifiable decision criteria:
- Success is defined by simultaneous improvements: Voc increase ≥ 30 mV at matched Jsc, hysteresis reduction ≥ 50%, and T80 under MPP tracking improved by ≥ 2× vs control.
- Mechanism is supported if (i) Pb–O coordination signatures correlate with trap-density reduction and (ii) ToF-SIMS shows reduced halide/metal electrode migration into the absorber during stress.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Mechanochemical synthesis is proven to encapsulate and stabilize sensitive nanostructures in reticular frameworks, enabling solvent-minimized nanocomposite formation with high loading and preserved structure (supports scalability and stability). Separately, high-concentration solvothermal, mechanochemical, and ionothermal MOF synthesis literature demonstrates that acid modulation governed by pKa can tune crystallinity/porosity and generate new phases, including scalable Mg2(dobdc) production; this provides a validated handle for controlling modulator incorporation and defect density.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC performance is limited by interfacial trap-mediated recombination and ion migration. A salicylate-bearing Mg2(dobdc) interphase directly targets these by providing (i) chelating oxygen donors for Pb2+ defect passivation and (ii) a porous, polar scaffold that can immobilize mobile ions. Using ionothermal activation minimizes exposure of the perovskite to harmful solvents and enables formation of an ultrathin, conformal interphase compatible with scalable coating.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike conventional small-molecule passivators that can diffuse, desorb, or create insulating layers, the proposed MOF-anchored salicylate creates a mechanically robust, chemically buffered interphase with programmable binding strength (via pKa) and ion-capture capacity. The two-stage mechanochemical + ionothermal route addresses a key limitation—inhomogeneous additive distribution and solvent-driven variability—by pre-defining modulator location and density in a solid framework before film formation, enabling more reproducible Voc gains and longer operational stability at low additive loading.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-constructed proposal that demonstrates strong command of both perovskite interfacial physics and MOF chemistry. The engineering resolution is high: mechanochemical modulation, controlled defect engineering in Mg2(dobdc), and ionothermal interphase formation are articulated with actionable parameters (particle size, modulation ratios, temperature windows, validation metrics). Logical consistency is generally strong, especially in linking salicylate pKa to competitive binding equilibria between Pb2+ surface passivation and Mg–salicylate anchoring. However, the central mechanistic claim—that pKa alone can reliably program this equilibrium under the complex, non-equilibrium conditions of perovskite crystallization and ionothermal treatment—is somewhat overstated. Competing factors such as local dielectric environment, IL-specific coordination, kinetic trapping, and perovskite lattice strain are not sufficiently acknowledged or decoupled experimentally. Evidence grounding is solid: the proposal stays firmly within reticular chemistry, mechanochemistry, and perovskite device physics, without importing speculative concepts. Rationale quality is high and creative, addressing a real bottleneck (inhomogeneous, unstable passivation) with a structurally novel solution. The main weakness is not feasibility but mechanistic over-determination: too many coupled variables are implicitly attributed to pKa tuning without a clear hierarchy or orthogonal controls.
hypothesis_summary: A pKa-tuned salicylate–MOF interphase, made by solvent-minimized mechanochemical and ionothermal steps, simultaneously passivates perovskite defects and immobilizes mobile ions to boost voltage and stability.

original_chain: Stability enhancement -> Loading capacity -> Stability enhancement -> Hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) -> Catalytic efficiency -> Post-modification -> Hydrophobic pore nature
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Post-modifying a high-performing 3D FA/Cs mixed-halide perovskite with an ultrathin (≤10 nm), hydrophobic hydrogen-bonded organic framework (HOF) interlayer will improve Voc/FF and operational stability by (i) chemically passivating under-coordinated Pb2+ and halide-vacancy-rich surface/grain-boundary sites via directional carbonyl/pyridyl→Pb coordination and H-bonding and (ii) creating a low-water-activity, ion-confining pore microenvironment that increases the activation barrier for halide/FA migration without blocking electronic transport.

To address the reviewer concern about over-asserted “interfacial catalysis,” the charge-extraction enhancement is reformulated as a testable mediated interfacial hole-transfer model: redox-active guests confined inside the HOF pores can act as a reversible interfacial electron/hole relay only if (a) their frontier levels are energetically aligned (no barrier for hole extraction to the HTL), (b) the guest optical density at the working thickness produces negligible parasitic absorption, and (c) the interlayer remains in the tunneling/field-assisted transport regime (no series-resistance penalty). The hypothesis is falsifiable by extracting interfacial transfer rate constants and by control experiments that decouple hydrophobic barrier effects, chemical passivation, and any true redox-mediated transfer.

Key mechanistic expectation: a hydrophobic, π-conjugated, carbonyl-rich HOF (pore aperture 0.8–1.1 nm) anchored only within the top ~10–20 nm of the perovskite (top surface + accessible grain boundaries) will (1) reduce non-radiative recombination (lower interfacial trap-assisted recombination velocity) and (2) suppress bias-driven ionic redistribution, while maintaining low contact resistivity due to sub-10 nm thickness, partial coverage optimized below the percolation threshold for insulation, and favorable vacuum-level alignment confirmed by UPS/KPFM. Redox guests are optional and will be retained only if the mediated-transfer model yields faster interfacial kinetics without added recombination or absorption losses.
Plan: Step 0 — Define the “engineering-closed” HOF system (identity, metrics, acceptance criteria)
0.1 HOF identity (two-member design set to enable decisive controls):
• Hydrophobic HOF (target interlayer): HOF-CO/Py-R (a hydrogen-bonded framework built from a π-conjugated, carbonyl-rich core with peripheral pyridyl groups for Pb2+ coordination and external aryl/alkyl substituents to enforce hydrophobic pore walls). Target functional motifs per linker: ≥2 carbonyl O acceptors + ≥1 pyridyl N.
• Hydrophilic analogue control: HOF-CO/Py-OH (same backbone/pyridyl density but with polar –OH/–OEG substituents to raise water uptake and remove hydrophobic barrier while preserving coordination chemistry).
0.2 Measurable materials specifications (must be met before device integration):
• Crystallite size distribution (DLS + SEM): 20–80 nm (D50 ~40 nm) to enable grain-boundary access but avoid rough, thick films.
• Pore aperture (N2 sorption/QSDFT or CO2 sorption if ultramicroporous): 0.8–1.1 nm; BET surface area reported.
• Functional group density: quantified by elemental analysis/XPS (N:Pb binding proxy later) and solid-state NMR/FTIR (carbonyl/pyridyl signatures).
• Optical absorption (UV–Vis): extinction coefficient in 450–800 nm kept minimal; reject any HOF with significant absorption tail overlapping perovskite.

Step 1 — Baseline perovskite stack and reproducibility
1.1 Fabricate baseline n–i–p devices: glass/ITO/SnO2/FA0.85Cs0.15Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/HTL/Au.
• Perovskite deposition: anti-solvent engineering with controlled atmosphere (RH < 20%); target thickness 500–650 nm.
• HTL baseline: Spiro-OMeTAD (for comparability) and a dopant-lean polymeric HTL (secondary set to isolate interfacial effects).
1.2 Baseline diagnostics:
• Trap density / recombination: absolute PLQY, TRPL, TA (optional), thermal admittance spectroscopy.
• Ion migration baseline: bias-stress KPFM mapping (surface potential evolution), and transient ion-drift (current transient under step bias).
• Interface energetics: UPS (work function/valence onset) + KPFM (surface potential).

Step 2 — Closed-process HOF deposition (solvent system + loading targets + time/temperature)
2.1 Solvent selection using Hansen solubility parameters (HSP) to minimize perovskite interaction:
• Primary dispersion solvent for HOF nanocrystallites: anisole or chlorobenzene (low polarity; low hydrogen-bonding component).
• Additive limit: if dispersion requires a polar co-solvent (e.g., 0.5–2 vol% iPrOH or MeCN), quantify and cap below the perovskite dissolution threshold; verify by in situ reflectance/ellipsometry that the perovskite thickness does not change.
2.2 Deposition protocol (solution-assisted, solid-state anchoring; parameters fixed and logged):
• Dispersion concentration: 0.05–0.5 mg mL−1.
• Dynamic spin infiltration: 2000–4000 rpm, 20–40 s.
• Exposure time window (drop-to-spin delay): 0–10 s (series).
• Post-deposition anneal: 60–80 °C, 5–10 min in dry N2.
2.3 Targeted areal mass loading and thickness/coverage series:
• Areal loading quantified by QCM witness (flat Si/ITO witness placed alongside) or gravimetry on coupons: 5–50 µg cm−2.
• Thickness target: 2, 5, 8, 12 nm (ellipsometry on witness + cross-sectional TEM confirmation). Define “transport-safe” regime as contact resistivity not exceeding 2× baseline.
2.4 Anchoring chemistry verification (must show real coordination, not only physical adsorption):
• FTIR: carbonyl shift upon Pb2+ binding.
• XPS: Pb 4f chemical shift; N 1s shift consistent with pyridyl→Pb coordination.

Step 3 — Prove spatial placement, grain-boundary selectivity, and non-penetration (mandatory)
3.1 Cross-sectional ToF-SIMS depth profiling:
• Track HOF-specific fragments (e.g., CN−/CNO−/aromatic fragments) vs perovskite ions (I−/Br−/Cs+/FA+). Acceptance: HOF signal confined to top ≤20 nm with enhanced intensity along grain-boundary vertical features; negligible signal in the bulk mid-film.
3.2 XPS depth profiling (gentle cluster sputter):
• Confirm top-localized N/O enrichment with decay to baseline within ≤20 nm.
3.3 GIWAXS:
• Confirm HOF crystallinity signatures and ensure no new perovskite secondary phases; check that perovskite (100)/(110) textures remain unchanged.
3.4 TEM/EDS or STEM-EDS mapping:
• Map N/O signals at the interface and grain boundaries; confirm discontinuous ultrathin interlayer rather than thick insulating overlayer.

Step 4 — Energetic alignment and transport impact (mandatory quantitative metrics)
4.1 UPS + KPFM:
• Measure work function shift (ΔΦ) and valence band maximum relative to HTL. Criterion: no energetic cliff for hole extraction; interlayer-induced dipole should not increase hole barrier.
