Risk control #1 — Ligand/insulating barrier and chemical incompatibility: The plan mandates ligand exchange to short, halide-tolerant ligands (I−/SCN−/alkylammonium-thiol) and includes a deliberate “long-ligand” negative control to demonstrate barrier-limited behavior. Ligand-only controls isolate ligand passivation from metal-core effects.

Risk control #2 — Mechanochemical damage to APNCs/framework: Encapsulation is performed with constrained milling energy and LAG to preserve atomic precision; preservation is verified by cluster fingerprints (UV–Vis/MS/XPS) and framework integrity (XRD/PDF/BET/ssNMR). Iterative milling-energy screening with rejection criteria prevents silent degradation.

Risk control #3 — Ultrathin, pinhole-free interlayers: A concrete film-formation pathway is provided (fragment downsizing, orthogonal solvents, optional ultralow binder, surface-energy tuning) with mandatory continuity metrology (AFM/ellipsometry/cross-sectional TEM) and explicit coverage criteria, addressing the main engineering gap.

Risk control #4 — Energy-level matching operationalized: Work-function/level mapping (UPS/IPES/KPFM) is integrated with quantified dipole targets for ETL vs HTL placement, enabling rational interface engineering rather than asserted alignment.

Risk control #5 — Metal diffusion/halide exchange and immobilization: The plan directly tests immobilization via ToF-SIMS depth profiling pre/post MPP+bias-thermal stress and includes halide-exchange assays to verify cluster robustness and confinement efficacy, converting stability claims into measurable acceptance tests.

Why the COF/HOF confinement remains central (alignment with original chain): Asset 1 supports high-loading, aggregation-free APNC confinement under mild mechanochemistry, which is critical here for achieving high areal density redox relays without nanoparticle growth or metal migration. Asset 2 supports the concept that confined porous organic frameworks can promote catalytic/electrocatalytic function; here, that confinement is translated into a solid/solid interface architecture where both passivation chemistry (framework functional groups) and redox mediation (APNC) are engineered and independently controlled by the specified control matrix.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually strong in execution detail and in committing to genuinely falsifiable readouts beyond EIS. The main weaknesses are (i) physical plausibility/quantification of the redox relay rate window: no explicit kinetic model is given linking APNC areal density, electronic coupling (through ligand/framework), and redox self-exchange/heterogeneous ET rates to the observed reductions in interfacial recombination; without this, null results will be hard to interpret (is the mechanism false, or just too slow/too sparse?). (ii) Operando oxidation-state attribution by XPS core-level shifts at buried 3–8 nm interfaces is challenging: chemical shifts can conflate charging, local electrostatics (dipole changes), beam-induced effects, and halide coordination changes; the plan mentions angle-resolved XPS but does not specify hard X-ray PES (HAXPES) or calibration strategies to de-embed potential drops. (iii) APNC redox potentials measured in an ‘electrolyte proxy’ may not translate to the solid-state perovskite interface (dielectric environment, ion accumulation, and band bending); the 0.1–0.3 eV matching criterion needs an operational definition tied to measured quasi-Fermi levels and interfacial fields. (iv) The framework’s intrinsic electronic/ionic conductivity is not specified; a COF/HOF that is too insulating could bottleneck the regeneration step and mimic passivation-only behavior despite successful redox-state modulation. (v) The ‘redox-silent cluster’ control is under-defined—many size-matched clusters have hidden redox under illumination or through halide coordination; selecting a truly redox-inert analogue in the relevant potential window is nontrivial and currently not justified.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding atomically precise nanoclusters with engineered charge states and short ligands inside ultrathin COF/HOF interlayers creates a redox-mediated charge-transfer pathway that reduces interfacial recombination beyond conventional passivation and energy alignment alone.

original_chain: Nonlinear optical (NLO) properties -> Ni3(HHTP)2 -> Nonlinear optical (NLO) properties -> Charge transfer -> Hole transport layer (HTL)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: If Ni3(HHTP)2 is used as a dopant-free, redox-capacitive hole-transport layer (HTL) that can be intentionally driven into an electret-like interfacial dipole state via coupled electrical bias and weak optical pumping, then perovskite solar cells (PSCs) will exhibit improved hole-extraction energetics (higher built-in field at the perovskite/HTL junction), reduced interfacial ion accumulation, lower nonradiative recombination, and enhanced operational stability. Mechanistic revision (replacing χ(3)→persistent polarization over-claim): the persistent ‘locked’ state is not a Kerr/χ(3) remanent polarization; instead it is a metastable charge-separated/polaronic state in Ni3(HHTP)2 near the perovskite interface (electret-like trapped charge + redox/polaron redistribution), enabled by the MOF’s extended π–d conjugation and charge-transfer propensity. During poling, forward bias injects/accumulates holes into Ni3(HHTP)2 and/or extracts electrons from interfacial defect states; simultaneously, low-fluence illumination at a wavelength where Ni3(HHTP)2 absorbs (but the perovskite absorbs minimally) increases carrier detrapping/redistribution within the MOF (photoconductive ‘assist’), allowing charges to rearrange into deeper traps or stabilized polarons. The net result is a built-in dipole at the perovskite/Ni3(HHTP)2 interface manifested as a measurable work-function shift (target ΔΦ = 50–150 meV) and band-bending/core-level shifts, which should translate into a Voc increase on the order of ~20–80 mV depending on recombination regime. Quantitatively bounded expectations: required poling field across the HTL ~0.05–0.2 MV cm−1 (e.g., 0.1–0.5 V across a 20–40 nm film under device forward bias near Voc), optical intensity 10–200 mW cm−2 at a wavelength selected for Ni3(HHTP)2 absorption with minimal perovskite generation, and retention time (tret) of the induced ΔΦ in the dark at 25 °C of 10^3–10^5 s (hours to days), with accelerated decay at elevated temperature (Arrhenius behavior) and reversible re-writing under re-poling. The role of Ni3(HHTP)2 nonlinear polarizability is reframed as a correlated descriptor of strong electron-cloud delocalization and charge-transfer capability (as evidenced in optoelectronic heterostructures), rather than the direct origin of remanence; χ(3) is treated as an auxiliary material fingerprint that may co-vary with poling efficiency, not the causal agent of persistence.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-define the ‘poling window’ with quantitative boundaries (addresses ambiguity and confounds)
0.1 Optical selection: record UV–Vis–NIR absorption of (i) perovskite stack without HTL and (ii) Ni3(HHTP)2 film on inert substrate. Choose two CW wavelengths: (A) MOF-selective (Ni3(HHTP)2 absorption appreciable; perovskite weak), and (B) off-resonant control (minimal absorption in both). If MOF-selective wavelength cannot be found cleanly, constrain intensity and use pulsed/low-duty illumination to limit heating while still enabling photoconductive assistance. Report absorbed power density (Pabs) from optical constants or integrating-sphere measurements.
0.2 Thermal ceiling: implement IR thermometry (or micro-thermocouple on dummy stacks) under illumination to ensure ΔT < 5–10 °C during poling; if exceeded, reduce intensity or use chopped illumination.

Step 1 — Device and film fabrication with matched baselines
1.1 PSC architecture (n–i–p): FTO / compact SnO2 (or SnO2 nanoparticle layer) / mixed-cation iodide-rich perovskite (e.g., FA/Cs/MA) / HTL / Au. Use the same perovskite formulation and processing for all groups; document thickness and grain size.
1.2 Ni3(HHTP)2 HTL fabrication: interfacial polymerization to yield continuous 20–40 nm films. Add a reproducible surface termination protocol (e.g., identical final solvent rinse, controlled drying) to minimize variability in surface dipoles from adsorbates. Verify: thickness (profilometry/ellipsometry), roughness (AFM), crystallinity (GIWAXS/XRD), conductivity (four-point probe), and work function (Kelvin probe) at baseline.
1.3 Baseline band alignment: measure UPS (secondary electron cutoff + valence region) for perovskite, Ni3(HHTP)2, and perovskite/Ni3(HHTP)2 bilayers to establish initial offsets.

Step 2 — Mechanistically grounded poling protocol and full factorial controls
2.1 In-operando poling (primary condition): apply forward bias Vpol = 0.8–1.0×Voc (device-specific) while illuminating with the MOF-selective CW wavelength at 10–200 mW cm−2 for tpol = 60–600 s. Record current transient during poling to quantify injected/redistributed charge (integrated charge as a predictor of ΔΦ).
2.2 Post-poling ‘lock’ step (optional, bounded): anneal at 50–70 °C for 1–5 min in inert atmosphere only if IR data confirms perovskite integrity; aim is to accelerate charge stabilization in deep traps/polaron configurations without invoking compositional change.
2.3 Kinetics protocol (mandatory): perform on–off sequences to separate instantaneous field effects from persistent states: (i) field on/light on, (ii) field off/light on, (iii) field on/light off, (iv) field off/light off, each with timed intervals. Quantify rise/decay constants of ΔΦ and device metrics (Voc, hysteresis) in the same device.
2.4 Control matrix (tightened as required):
  - C0: Ni3(HHTP)2 device, no poling.
  - C1: electrical-only (bias, dark).
  - C2: optical-only (illumination, zero bias).
  - C3: off-resonant light + bias (thermal/photonic artifact control).
  - C4: ‘matched-analog MOF’ HTL (chemically/structurally analogous, matched thickness, conductivity within ±20%, similar surface chemistry/termination, but demonstrably lower χ(3) and/or lower poling susceptibility). This control must be screened to match: work function (±50 meV baseline), roughness (±20%), porosity/surface area proxy (gas sorption where feasible or ellipsometric porosity indicator), and no metal migration differences.
  - C5: devices lacking MOF (replace with standard HTL, e.g., NiOx or undoped polymer HTL) subjected to identical poling to quantify perovskite-only ion-migration artifacts.

Step 3 — Direct energetic verification of the built-in dipole (mandatory)
3.1 Macroscopic work-function shift: Kelvin probe (inert glovebox) on Ni3(HHTP)2 films and on perovskite/Ni3(HHTP)2 bilayers pre- and post-poling; target measurable ΔΦ = 50–150 meV. Track ΔΦ(t) over 10^2–10^5 s to extract retention time and decay kinetics.
3.2 UPS: measure secondary electron cutoff shifts (work function) and valence onset changes for bilayers. Use bias-dependent UPS (small external bias on conductive substrates) if available to distinguish uniform vacuum-level shift vs band bending.
3.3 XPS core-level shifts: measure perovskite core levels (Pb 4f, I 3d, and A-site related peaks) and Ni/O/C core levels in Ni3(HHTP)2 before/after poling. A persistent interfacial dipole/band-bending change should manifest as systematic core-level shifts (tens to >100 meV) consistent across repeated devices and correlated with ΔΦ.

Step 4 — Identify the microscopic nature of the locked state (electret/polaron/redox)
4.1 Charge storage signature: Mott–Schottky / capacitance–voltage and low-frequency capacitance to quantify additional stored charge and its relaxation; compare to integrated poling current.
4.2 EPR (or optical absorption signature of polarons): detect changes consistent with polaron formation in Ni3(HHTP)2 after poling; track reversibility upon thermal relaxation or reverse-bias erase.
4.3 Conductivity/mobility check: measure HTL conductivity before/after poling on inert substrates to determine whether performance changes stem from bulk transport changes vs interfacial energetics.

Step 5 — Device-level causal chain: from ΔΦ to Voc/FF/hysteresis
5.1 PV metrics and hysteresis: J–V (both scan directions), stabilized MPP output, Voc transient response. Correlate Voc change with measured ΔΦ (UPS/Kelvin). Expect: ΔVoc should scale with reduced interfacial recombination (verified below) rather than solely with series resistance changes.
5.2 Recombination/extraction: TRPL on perovskite/HTL stacks (not full devices) and transient photovoltage/photocurrent on devices to extract changes in interfacial recombination velocity and carrier lifetime. Use intensity-dependent Voc to extract ideality factor changes pre/post poling.
5.3 Impedance spectroscopy: focus on low-frequency features associated with ionic accumulation and interfacial polarization. A successful poling-induced dipole/screening state should reduce low-frequency capacitance increase and hysteresis-related arcs relative to controls.

Step 6 — Rule out mandatory confounds decisively
6.1 Thermal artifact exclusion: report ΔT under all illumination conditions; include a purely thermal anneal control matching the maximum observed ΔT×time without light/bias.
6.2 Au diffusion/contact reaction: ToF-SIMS depth profiling for Au and interdiffusion markers in poled vs unpoled devices after identical time-in-test. If Au migration differs, introduce a thin diffusion barrier (e.g., MoOx or carbon) as an additional control to decouple HTL effects from electrode artifacts.
6.3 Perovskite ion migration: apply the same bias/light poling sequence to devices without MOF HTL (C5) and to perovskite-only test capacitors; compare evolution of hysteresis and impedance. If similar changes occur without MOF, attribute accordingly and adjust protocol (lower bias, shorter poling) until the MOF-dependent ΔΦ signature dominates.

Step 7 — Stability validation with mechanistic readouts
7.1 ISOS-L / ISOS-O style tests (as feasible): track Voc, FF, hysteresis index, and MPP stability. Concurrently measure ΔΦ(t) on dedicated bilayer samples aged under the same conditions to directly link energetic retention to device stability.
7.2 Erase/re-write demonstration: attempt to erase the dipole via reverse bias in the dark (or thermal reset) and re-write via the poling protocol; quantify reversibility over ≥5 cycles to prove a controllable metastable state rather than one-way degradation.
Feasibility: 1) Corrected physical basis (addresses χ(3) critique): The proposal no longer relies on an instantaneous Kerr/χ(3) response to explain persistence. The persistent effect is explicitly assigned to metastable trapped charge and/or polaronic/redox redistribution in Ni3(HHTP)2 near the interface (electret-like behavior), which is compatible with MOF conjugation, charge-transfer propensity, and the known ability of semiconducting frameworks to host localized charges. χ(3) is retained only as a correlated material descriptor (delocalized electron cloud/charge-transfer capacity), consistent with prior observations that Ni3(HHTP)2-based heterostructures enhance charge transfer and exhibit strong electronic polarization.

2) Quantitative, testable predictions: The mechanism is bounded by explicit targets—ΔΦ = 50–150 meV, tret = 10^3–10^5 s at 25 °C, and specified field/fluence ranges. These are directly falsifiable by Kelvin probe/UPS/XPS time-dependent measurements and on–off kinetics experiments.

3) Discriminating energetics measurements (mandatory): The plan elevates causality by directly measuring work-function and band-bending changes (Kelvin probe + UPS + XPS core-level shifts) pre/post poling, including kinetic tracking. Device performance changes must co-vary with ΔΦ; otherwise the mechanism is rejected or revised.

4) Separation of persistent states from instantaneous effects: In-operando on–off sequences quantify rise/decay and distinguish (i) instantaneous field-induced polarization/conductance changes from (ii) persistent charge-trapping/electret-like states. Retention kinetics and erase/re-write cycling provide decisive evidence of metastability and reversibility.

5) Tight controls and confound management: The factorial matrix (bias-only, light-only, off-resonant, no-MOF, and matched-analog MOF) prevents attributing improvements to generic bias stress, heating, moisture uptake, or morphology drift. Thermal rise is bounded by IR thermometry; Au diffusion is checked by ToF-SIMS; perovskite ion migration artifacts are quantified via no-MOF controls and impedance signatures.

6) Relevance to PSC bottlenecks and literature bridge: Interface energetics and ion accumulation are dominant loss/stability pathways in iodide-rich, high-Voc perovskites. The proposal leverages Ni3(HHTP)2’s demonstrated charge-transfer strength (as seen in optoelectronic heterostructures) to create an adaptive, dopant-free interfacial dipole via controlled charge storage—conceptually aligned with interface passivation strategies that enhance charge transfer and stability, but differentiated by a deliberately written, measurable energetic shift rather than static work-function tuning or chemical dopants.
final_critique: Methodologically, the plan is unusually rigorous for an interface-energetics claim: it pre-defines poling conditions, requires direct ΔΦ verification (Kelvin/UPS) and core-level/band-bending corroboration (XPS), and includes kinetics plus erase/rewrite to distinguish metastable trapped-charge states from instantaneous field effects. The main logical vulnerability is mechanistic degeneracy: the same Voc/hysteresis improvements can arise from perovskite ionic redistribution, interfacial defect charging, contact modification, or mild annealing—despite the control matrix, the proposal does not yet specify decisive discriminants that uniquely attribute the persistent dipole to charge storage/polaron formation in Ni3(HHTP)2 (e.g., spatial localization of stored charge at/within the MOF, redox-state mapping of Ni, or quantitative agreement between injected charge and measured ΔΦ via a dipole/capacitance model). Evidence grounding relative to the requested NLO→Ni3(HHTP)2→NLO→charge transfer→HTL chain is moderate: NLO is reframed as a non-causal 'fingerprint' and is not experimentally tied to poling efficiency or charge transfer; thus the proposal risks reading as an electret/photodoping interfacial-engineering study rather than an NLO-enabled mechanism. Finally, feasibility risks remain around MOF film continuity/pinhole-free coverage at 20–40 nm on perovskite, possible chemical interaction with iodide/halide species under bias, and reproducibility of ΔΦ in the presence of adsorbates—these are acknowledged but not fully mitigated with go/no-go criteria.
hypothesis_summary: If Ni3(HHTP)2 is used as a dopant-free hole-transport layer and electrically biased with weak light to create a trapped-charge electret-like dipole, perovskite solar cells will show improved hole extraction, higher voltage, and longer stability.

original_chain: Nanocomposites -> Hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) -> Nanocomposites -> Hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) -> Mechanochemical synthesis -> Membrane electrode assembly (MEA) -> HCOOH
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Mechanochemically co-assembled HOF–perovskite nanocomposite grains can be engineered so that an ultrathin (sub‑2–3 nm) HOF-rich intergranular phase forms a *grain-boundary (GB)-confined*, mechanically compliant, hydrogen-bonded barrier that (a) increases the effective activation energy for iodide/vacancy-mediated ionic transport by ΔEa ≥ 0.15 eV and lowers ionic conductivity by ≥10× (25–60 °C) without (b) imposing an electronic percolation penalty exceeding ΔRs ≤ 0.5 Ω·cm2 or FF loss >2% absolute. This is achieved by (i) selecting HOF chemistries that remain crystalline (or at minimum nanostructurally intact) under direct contact with halide salts and under hot-press pressure, (ii) forcing thermodynamic GB segregation through low surface-energy, multipoint Pb2+ coordination (pyridyl/amide) that preferentially binds undercoordinated Pb at defective GBs, and (iii) limiting HOF volume fraction to a regime that ensures *partial-but-percolating ionic blocking* along GBs while preserving electronic necking between perovskite grains. HCOOH is treated as a bounded, testable, volatile milling activator/templating agent whose acceptability is decided by a strict pass/fail criterion: no persistent Pb–formate complexes, no measurable energetic doping/shift (>50 meV), and no increase in halide-vacancy signatures relative to non-acid LAG controls. MEA-inspired hot-press lamination is used not as an unspecified densification step but as a controllable microstructure-setting operation (pressure–temperature–time) that produces high neck density between grains while kinetically trapping the HOF at GBs, yielding a laminated absorber with reduced hysteresis and extended operational stability (T80 increase target: ≥2× under ISOS-L/MPP compared to matched mechanochemical and solution controls).
Plan: A. Quantitative microstructure–transport model (mandatory, falsifiable)
A1) Define the GB geometry and link HOF wt% to coverage. Use a minimal geometric model for equiaxed grains of diameter d = 200–600 nm (measured by SEM/TEM). Assume an HOF-rich GB layer of thickness t. Convert HOF mass fraction w to volume fraction φ via densities (ρpvk ≈ 4.0 g·cm−3; ρHOF measured by He pycnometry, expected 1.0–1.5 g·cm−3). Approximate the GB volume fraction fGB ≈ 6t/d for t ≪ d. The achievable average t at a given φ is bounded by φ ≈ fGB·C where C is the fraction of GBs actually coated (0–1); thus C ≈ φ/(6t/d). Target regime: t = 1–3 nm, C ≥ 0.6 (GB-confined) at w = 0.2–1.0 wt% (if C cannot exceed 0.3 without w > 2 wt%, the concept fails and is terminated or redesigned).
A2) Resistor-network/effective-medium link to ionic suppression. Model ion conduction as two parallel pathways: bulk perovskite (σion,b) and GB pathway (σion,gb). In controls, σion,gb ≫ σion,b; in composites, the HOF modifies σion,gb by a blocking factor β = σion,gb,comp/σion,gb,ctrl. The effective ionic conductivity (Bruggeman-like) is σion,eff ≈ (1−fGB)σion,b + fGB·β·σion,gb. Falsifiable target: σion,eff,comp / σion,eff,ctrl ≤ 0.1 from 25–60 °C. Translate to β requirement using measured σion,b and σion,gb (from impedance deconvolution/brick-layer model); require β ≤ 0.05–0.2 depending on GB dominance.
A3) Activation energy target tied to hysteresis. Fit Arrhenius behavior σion(T) ∝ exp(−Ea/kT). Require ΔEa,eff ≥ 0.15 eV (stretch goal 0.20 eV) relative to matched controls. Predetermine that if ΔEa < 0.10 eV at any HOF loading that still preserves electronics (Section D), the ion-blocking mechanism is insufficient.
A4) Electronic penalty model and constraints. Treat GB HOF as a tunneling/thermionic barrier with effective barrier height ΦB and thickness t. Predetermine maximum allowable electronic barrier: extracted ΦB ≤ 80 meV and/or intergranular contact resistivity ρc ≤ 5×10−3 Ω·cm2 (TLM). Define “fail” if ΔRs > 0.5 Ω·cm2 or FF drops >2% abs at the same Jsc and Voc, or if TRMC mobility decreases >20% relative to mechanochemical control.

B. HOF down-selection before full composite synthesis (go/no-go gate 1)
B1) Select an initial HOF library (n=4–6) spanning two chemistries:
  - Class I (robust H-bond nodes): di-urea/di-amide tectons with high directionality + neutral Pb-binding (pyridyl/benzimidazole).
  - Class II (charge-assisted H-bonds without strong acidity): zwitterionic or internally H-bonded motifs to resist collapse in halide salts.
B2) “Halide-contact integrity” assay (powder-level): mix HOF with FAI/CsI/PbI2 (no milling) at 60–100 °C under dry N2 for 2–12 h; analyze via variable-temperature PXRD and total scattering/PDF. Pass criterion: ≥70% retention of characteristic HOF correlations (PDF peaks) and no new crystalline Pb–ligand salt dominating (>10 wt% estimated by Rietveld/phase fraction).
B3) “Pressure compliance” assay (pellet-level): press HOF alone and HOF+PbI2 pellets at 50–150 MPa, 25–110 °C for 5–15 min; re-measure PXRD/PDF and BET (optional). Pass criterion: no irreversible collapse beyond a predefined loss (e.g., <30% reduction in key PDF correlations; porosity loss acceptable only if framework ordering retained).
B4) Pb2+ binding validation on model surfaces: deposit PbI2 or perovskite-like Pb–I terminated films; expose to HOF fragments/tectons (vapor or mild solvent-free contact) and quantify Pb–N/Pb–O coordination by XPS shifts and solid-state NMR (where feasible). Pass criterion: clear coordination signature without formation of insulating salt layers (no large Pb0 or Pb-carboxylate signatures).
B5) Down-select to 1–2 HOFs for composite work based on: (i) integrity score, (ii) Pb-binding strength/neutrality, (iii) optical transparency (Eg > 3 eV), (iv) mechanical compliance.

C. Mechanochemical composite synthesis with bounded LAG/HCOOH DoE (go/no-go gate 2)
C1) Base perovskite: (FA0.85Cs0.15)Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 and MAPbI3 benchmark. Milling jar/balls: zirconia; control temperature (monitor jar surface T).
C2) DoE matrix for milling additive (LAG):
  - Additives: (i) HCOOH, (ii) tert-butanol (tBuOH), (iii) ethyl acetate (EtOAc), (iv) no additive.
  - η levels: 0, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10 μL·mg−1 (keep total additive <1 wt% of solids).
  - Milling: 15–30 Hz, 10–60 min; two-step option: pre-assemble HOF (dry) then add perovskite precursors.
C3) Explicit HCOOH pass/fail criteria (must all pass):
  - Volatility proof: TGA-MS on milled composite powder and on laminated films during anneal; require complete removal of formic acid/formate fragments by ≤140 °C with no high-mass persistent fragments; corroborate by residual gas analysis during pressing.
  - No persistent Pb–formate: FTIR (no strong formate COO− bands persisting), XPS (no carboxylate-dominated O 1s/Pb 4f signatures), and solid-state 13C NMR (no persistent formate carbon) after anneal.
  - No energetic doping/shift: UPS/Kelvin probe work function shift ≤50 meV vs non-acid LAG and no increase in sub-gap absorption indicative of new deep states.
If HCOOH fails any criterion, it is dropped and the program proceeds with the best non-acid LAG condition.
C4) Composite targeting: HOF loading w = 0.2, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0 wt%. Primary goal: identify the minimum w achieving ionic targets without electronic penalty.

D. MEA-inspired lamination with explicit necking/electronic coupling assessment (go/no-go gate 3)
D1) Composite membrane formation: doctor-blade a low-solvent paste (tBuOH or other benign volatile carrier) onto a release film; binder ≤0.5–1 wt% (thermally removable). Control wet thickness for 500–650 nm final.
D2) Hot-press window: 60–110 °C, 10–80 MPa, 1–10 min in dry N2. Map a 3×3 matrix (T, P, time). Target densification: porosity <5% (cross-sectional SEM + image analysis), continuous perovskite necking (TEM at grain contacts).
D3) Electronic coupling metrics (must pass):
  - TRMC or photo-CELIV mobility within 80% of mechanochemical perovskite control.
  - TLM contact resistivity (cross-grain) ρc ≤ 5×10−3 Ω·cm2; temperature-dependent conductivity to extract ΦB ≤ 80 meV.
  - Device-level: Rs increase ≤0.5 Ω·cm2 and FF loss ≤2% abs at comparable Jsc.
If failed at w ≥ 0.5 wt%, reduce w or redesign HOF to reduce interfacial thickness/coverage.

E. Structural localization and integrity verification (mandatory hard criterion)
E1) After milling and after lamination/anneal, perform: total scattering/PDF + variable-temperature PXRD to track HOF and perovskite order; nano-FTIR mapping and cross-sectional TEM/EDS/EELS.
E2) Hard criterion for “GB-confined”:
  - Nano-FTIR: >70% of HOF vibrational signal colocalizes with GB regions (defined by correlative phase/contrast) and <20% appears as >20 nm bulk inclusions.
  - TEM: no HOF-rich domains >50 nm occupying >1 area% in cross-section.
If localization fails (bulk inclusions dominate), adjust (i) tecton polarity, (ii) milling sequence (two-step), (iii) lamination kinetics, or terminate the HOF candidate.

F. Transport and device validation aligned to quantitative targets
F1) Ionic transport: impedance spectroscopy with a brick-layer model separating bulk/GB contributions; temperature-dependent σion and Ea extraction. Target: ≥10× reduction in σion,eff (25–60 °C) and ΔEa,eff ≥ 0.15 eV.
F2) Hysteresis linkage: standardized hysteresis index under controlled scan rates and pre-bias; require ≥50% reduction vs mechanochemical control at equal Voc.
F3) Trap/passivation: absolute PLQY/QFLS; TAS/DLTS for trap density distribution; target: ≥2× reduction in deep-trap signature and Voc increase consistent with QFLS (or reduced Voc deficit).
F4) Stability: ISOS-L and ISOS-O at MPP plus encapsulated 85/85 damp heat. Predetermined success: T80 ≥2× vs mechanochemical and solution controls; failure analysis by TOF-SIMS (ion redistribution), operando XRD (phase segregation), and post-mortem interfacial mapping.

G. Decision tree (explicit go/no-go workflow)
Gate 1 (HOF survivability): If HOF fails halide-contact integrity or pressure compliance → drop candidate; replace with next.
Gate 2 (LAG/HCOOH acceptability): If HCOOH fails volatility/no-formate/no-doping criteria → eliminate HCOOH; proceed with best neutral LAG.
Gate 3 (Localization): If GB-confined criterion fails → adjust milling sequence/lamination; if still fails after two iterations → drop HOF.
Gate 4 (Transport targets): If σion reduction <10× or ΔEa <0.10 eV at any electronically acceptable condition → concept deemed insufficient; pivot to alternative ion-blocking chemistry (e.g., non-HOF reticular or polymeric H-bond network) while keeping mechanochemical+lamination architecture.
Gate 5 (Electronic penalty): If electronic metrics fail (ΦB, ρc, Rs/FF) at all conditions that meet ionic targets → reduce HOF thickness/coverage (lower w, alter tecton) or terminate HOF approach.

Device stacks (kept from original, but with lamination compatibility):
  - p–i–n: ITO/NiOx(or SAM)/laminated composite/C60/BCP/Ag (thermal budget limited to C60 stability).
  - n–i–p: FTO/SnO2/laminated composite/PTAA/Au.
Controls: pristine solution-processed; pristine mechanochemical re-dissolved/cast; conventional passivator (PEAI/FACl) with identical lamination where possible.
Feasibility: 1) Grain-boundary percolation/localization is no longer assumed: it is engineered and *measured against hard thresholds* (nano-FTIR colocalization + TEM inclusion limits) and is constrained by a microstructure model linking wt% → φ → GB coverage C and thickness t. This directly addresses the reviewer concern that 0.2–2 wt% may not yield a percolated GB network.
2) The “ion blocking” claim is made falsifiable via predefined transport targets (≥10× σion reduction; ΔEa ≥ 0.15 eV) and an explicit effective-medium/brick-layer framework that uses measured bulk/GB components. This converts a qualitative mechanism into a quantitative requirement tied to geometry (t, C, d) and performance outcomes (hysteresis reduction; T80 ≥2×).
3) HCOOH risk is bounded by a DoE against neutral LAGs and by operando volatility/chemistry verification (TGA‑MS/RGA during pressing; FTIR/XPS/NMR). HCOOH is accepted only if it leaves no persistent Pb–formate/acidic signatures and does not measurably shift energetics (>50 meV), replacing the prior “stoichiometry-neutral” assertion with strict pass/fail criteria.
4) The lamination/sintering challenge is explicitly tackled by mapping pressure–temperature–time and by quantifying grain-to-grain electronic coupling (TRMC/photo-CELIV mobility retention, TLM contact resistivity, barrier height from temperature-dependent conductivity), with maximum allowable penalties tied to Rs and FF. This directly addresses the concern that an insulating GB phase could degrade electronic percolation.
5) Risk management is operationalized as a decision tree with multiple gates (HOF survivability, localization, ionic benefit, electronic penalty). This ensures rapid down-selection to 1–2 HOF chemistries and provides clear termination/pivot points if HOF collapse, bulk segregation, or series-resistance losses occur.
6) Mechanochemical synthesis feasibility is supported by the demonstrated ability of mechanochemistry to encapsulate sensitive nanostructures into reticular frameworks (including HOFs) without solvent-induced degradation (Asset 1), while the MEA-inspired lamination logic and mechanochemical framework processing are consistent with established routes in electrochemical device manufacturing paradigms (Asset 2). Here, those assets are translated into photovoltaics with additional, PSC-specific constraints (ionic transport, trap passivation, electronic coupling) embedded as quantitative acceptance criteria.
final_critique:
This is unusually well-engineered for a PSC intergranular-ionics proposal: it defines measurable microstructural variables (d, t, C, fGB), converts wt% to an explicit GB-coverage constraint, and pre-commits to termination/pivot thresholds (ΔEa, σion suppression, Rs/FF penalty), which reduces the common “hand-wavy passivation” risk. The down-selection assays (halide-contact integrity; pressure compliance; Pb2+ coordination signatures) and the localization hard-criteria (nano-FTIR colocalization + TEM inclusion limits) are scientifically appropriate.

Primary weaknesses are in quantitative physical plausibility and identifiability: (i) The geometric model implies very stringent material placement demands at w=0.2–1 wt% (given realistic densities and d=200–600 nm), and achieving C≥0.6 with t=1–3 nm may be statistically incompatible with inevitable HOF aggregation during milling/pressing; you acknowledge this as a kill condition, but the plan still leans on an optimistic segregation assumption without a demonstrated thermodynamic/kinetic driver magnitude. (ii) The proposed ΔEa,eff ≥0.15 eV and ≥10× σion reduction while maintaining ΦB≤80 meV/ρc≤5×10−3 Ω·cm2 is a tight coupled constraint; even a nanometric organic phase that blocks ions typically also perturbs electronic coupling unless it is discontinuous at electron-transport necks—yet the proposal lacks a clear mechanism for simultaneously enforcing ionic percolation breakage but electronic percolation continuity beyond “partial-but-percolating ionic blocking.” (iii) Impedance deconvolution into bulk vs GB contributions is often non-unique in mixed ionic–electronic PSCs; the brick-layer model can fit well but still mis-assign processes (electrode polarization, chemical capacitance, interfacial ion accumulation). The proposal needs stronger identifiability safeguards (orthogonal validation and equivalent-circuit falsification). (iv) The HCOOH accept/reject criteria are strong, but the design does not specify how trace formate (sub-detection) would be bounded relative to ionic changes; small residuals can disproportionately affect vacancy chemistry and hysteresis.

Net: very high execution resolution and good logical structure, with the main score deductions coming from (a) a somewhat under-justified ability to meet simultaneously the ionic and electronic constraints at sub-3 nm organic interphases, and (b) potential non-uniqueness of the transport parameter extraction used to claim ΔEa and σion pathway suppression.
hypothesis_summary: A grain-boundary-confined, ultrathin HOF layer can block iodide/vacancy ionic transport by ≥10× while preserving electronic percolation, reducing hysteresis and doubling operational stability.

original_chain: Negative Gaussian curvature -> Catalytic performance -> nanocomposite -> Active site -> Sulfoxide -> Electrostatic interaction -> Molecular enrichment -> Electromagnetic enhancement mechanism (EM)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a conformal, electrically benign “gyroidal ionic-sulfoxide nanocomposite skin” (GISNS) inside only the top 20–50 nm of a 3D perovskite (rather than as a discrete interlayer) will raise Voc/FF and operational stability by (i) molecularly enriching sulfoxide passivants at electronically active sites (undercoordinated Pb, halide vacancies, grain-boundary terminations) through MOF-like polar nanoreservoir domains, (ii) creating curvature-amplified electrostatic interaction that suppresses halide-ion accumulation and field-driven ion migration, and (iii) providing a low-loss electromagnetic enhancement mechanism (EM) via sparsely distributed dielectric nanoresonators (not plasmonic metals) whose hotspots coincide with passivated active sites. The methodological adaptation is a new crystallization-route: instead of templated bicontinuous films or nanoparticle interlayers, we adapt antisolvent-induced phase separation during blade/slot-die coating to generate a self-limited, negative-Gaussian-curvature (gyroid-like) nanocomposite within the perovskite’s near-surface region. This “internal gyroid” geometry concentrates built-in fields at minimal recombination penalty (dielectric resonators) and maximizes the areal density of chemically passivated active sites without adding a transport barrier layer.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Baseline device stacks (scalable-compatible):
- n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/FA0.83Cs0.17Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/spiro-OMeTAD/Au.
- p–i–n (cross-check generality): glass/ITO/NiOx/FA0.83Cs0.17Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/C60/BCP/Ag.
1.2 Define the GISNS components (all non-metallic, optoelectronically “quiet”):
- Polar nanoreservoir former: a Zr-carboxylate “MOF-fragment” oligomer (e.g., Zr6O4(OH)4(benzoate)x cluster capped with short carboxylates) or an Al-oxo carboxylate analogue; chosen to be non-porous at macroscale but to present dense Lewis-acid/Lewis-base sites at nanoscale.
- Sulfoxide: an aromatic sulfoxide with a carboxylate anchor (for co-assembly with the metal-oxo cluster) plus a free S=O for Pb coordination; keep total sulfoxide <0.5 mol% relative to Pb.
- Dielectric EM nanoresonator: 10–30 nm TiO2 or ZrO2 nanodots (wide bandgap, low absorption in visible) surface-functionalized with carboxylates to co-localize in the polar domains.
1.3 Controls to deconvolute mechanisms:
- No nanocomposite.
- Sulfoxide only (no metal-oxo cluster).
- Metal-oxo cluster only (no sulfoxide).
- Nanocomposite without dielectric nanodots (no EM).
- Nanocomposite with inert SiO2 dots (geometry control without resonance).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation: antisolvent-triggered “internal gyroid” formation (negative Gaussian curvature) during perovskite crystallization.
- Formulate a perovskite ink (DMF:DMSO) and a separate nanocomposite precursor microemulsion containing: (i) metal-oxo cluster + carboxylate-sulfoxide ligand, (ii) TiO2/ZrO2 nanodots, (iii) a volatile co-solvent that partitions into the antisolvent (e.g., tert-butanol or anisole at low fraction).
- Co-inject the nanocomposite precursor at trace volume (0.5–2 vol%) into the perovskite ink immediately before coating.
- During blade/slot-die coating, apply a programmed antisolvent mist pulse (not a drip) to create a controlled solvent-extraction gradient. The key adaptation is to tune the local quench rate so that: (a) the perovskite rapidly crystallizes, while (b) the polar cluster–sulfoxide fraction undergoes spinodal-like phase separation confined to the last-to-dry region (top 20–50 nm). This confinement yields a bicontinuous gyroid-like morphology with negative Gaussian curvature rather than isolated droplets.
- Anneal with a two-step profile: low-T hold (to lock the gyroidal nanocomposite before full halide lattice relaxation) followed by standard high-T anneal.
2.2 Molecular enrichment at active sites via “chemically hungry” polar domains.
- The metal-oxo clusters and anchored sulfoxides are designed to have high affinity for undercoordinated Pb and halide-vacancy-rich terminations. As crystallization proceeds, these species are expelled from the perovskite bulk and accumulate at grain boundaries and the film surface, where the density of active sites is highest.
- The gyroidal geometry maximizes interfacial area between perovskite and polar domain, increasing the probability that each defect site is within a few nm of a sulfoxide.
2.3 Electrostatic interaction engineering (ion-migration suppression without blocking electronic extraction).
- Choose cluster capping ligands to set the local fixed charge (e.g., incorporate a small fraction of sulfonate-terminated carboxylates to create a net negative fixed-charge density in the polar domain).
- Mechanistic target: repel I−/Br− accumulation under forward bias at the contact-facing surface, flatten interfacial ionic space-charge layers, reduce hysteresis, and suppress vacancy generation.
- Ensure electronic neutrality: keep the nanocomposite fraction below the percolation threshold; confirm that the perovskite remains the continuous electronic phase.
2.4 Electromagnetic enhancement mechanism (EM) without plasmonic loss.
- Embed sparse dielectric nanodots inside the gyroidal domains so resonant near-fields overlap the perovskite within ~10–30 nm of the surface.
- Expected outcome: localized optical intensity increase near the collection interface and improved charge separation at already-passivated active sites (minimizing the risk that increased generation feeds non-radiative recombination).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Prove negative Gaussian curvature and confinement (structure).
- Cross-sectional STEM tomography or FIB-SEM tomography to reconstruct 3D bicontinuity and estimate curvature distribution; quantify that the nanocomposite is confined to top 20–50 nm.
- GISAXS to identify gyroid-like scattering signatures vs droplet-like phase separation.
- Nano-IR / AFM-IR mapping to localize S=O and carboxylate signals to the gyroid network.
3.2 Prove molecular enrichment and chemical bonding at active sites (chemistry).
- Angle-resolved XPS: depth-dependent S 2p / O 1s signals; Pb 4f shifts consistent with Pb–O(S=O) coordination.
- Solid-state NMR (where feasible) or ToF-SIMS to map sulfoxide fragments vs grain-boundary enriched regions.
- Trap spectroscopy: thermal admittance spectroscopy and SCLC (electron-only and hole-only devices) to quantify trap density reduction.
3.3 Prove electrostatic interaction effects on ionic behavior (ion migration).
- Operando impedance spectroscopy under bias/light to extract ionic capacitance and relaxation times; compare with controls.
- Bias-stress ToF-SIMS depth profiling (I−/Br− redistribution) and hysteresis index vs scan rate.
- Kelvin probe force microscopy under illumination to map stabilized surface potential patterns; correlate with nanocomposite topography.
3.4 Prove EM contribution distinctly from passivation (optics).
- Variable-angle spectroscopic ellipsometry + integrating sphere reflectance to ensure no parasitic absorption.
- EQE enhancement localized to wavelengths predicted by Mie/FDTD for TiO2/ZrO2 nanodots; compare to inert SiO2-dot control.
- Intensity-dependent PL/EL: verify that radiative efficiency improves (passivation) while additional wavelength-selective photocurrent gain appears only with resonant dots (EM).
3.5 Device metrics and stability targets.
- Targets: +50–100 mV Voc, +2–4% absolute FF, stabilized PCE gain ≥1.0% absolute over baseline.
- ISOS-L-2 MPP tracking: T80 ≥2× baseline; thermal (65–85°C) and damp-heat screening.
- Failure analysis: post-aging tomography + XPS to verify retention of nanocomposite confinement and chemical states.

Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: (i) Sulfoxides are strong Lewis bases toward undercoordinated Pb2+, enabling defect passivation; (ii) fixed-charge/polar interphases are known to reshape ionic space-charge layers and reduce ion migration; (iii) dielectric nanoresonators can provide near-field intensity enhancement with far lower optical loss than plasmonic metals; (iv) bicontinuous negative-curvature morphologies are accessible via phase-separation physics under controlled solvent-extraction gradients, enabling high interfacial area without introducing a separate barrier layer.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The dominant PSC bottlenecks—interfacial recombination and ion migration—are addressed exactly where they originate: near-surface/grain-boundary active sites. By embedding (not layering) a self-limited gyroidal nanocomposite skin, we preserve standard contacts and scalable coating while adding a high-area passivating/electrostatic landscape and optional EM gain near the collection interface.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with interlayers, the GISNS avoids transport barriers and processing incompatibilities at the ETL/perovskite interface. Compared with random nanoparticle doping, the phase-separated gyroid confines additives to the region of highest defect density and highest collection probability, improving reproducibility and minimizing bulk mobility penalties. Compared with plasmonic EM strategies, dielectric resonators avoid parasitic absorption and metal diffusion, enabling a stability-positive EM approach.
final_critique: This is an unusually sophisticated and well-articulated proposal that demonstrates deep command of perovskite defect physics, ion migration, and nanophotonic enhancement strategies. The strongest aspects are (i) the confinement logic—placing functionality precisely in the top 20–50 nm where ionic and recombination phenomena dominate—and (ii) the rigorous control set designed to disentangle chemical passivation, electrostatics, and EM effects. The antisolvent-mist–driven internal phase separation is credible and differentiates the work from prior gyroidal or nanoparticle-doped approaches. Score deductions are primarily due to execution risk rather than conceptual weakness: achieving true negative Gaussian curvature (gyroid vs. perforated lamellae or worm-like domains) under scalable coating conditions is nontrivial, and the proposal slightly overstates the certainty that dielectric nanoresonator near-fields will spatially coincide with the most electronically relevant defect sites. Additionally, the electromagnetic contribution, while thoughtfully controlled, is likely to be second-order relative to chemical/electrostatic effects and may be difficult to unambiguously quantify at the proposed nanodot densities.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a gyroidal ionic-sulfoxide nanocomposite skin within the top 20–50 nm of a 3D perovskite raises voltage and stability by combining molecular passivation, electrostatic ion-migration suppression, and dielectric near-field enhancement without adding a transport barrier.

original_chain: Mode-locking -> Nonlinear optical (NLO) properties -> Charge transfer -> Platinum-nickel alloy -> Electron transfer -> Co-N4@Co-NP bridge
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a dual-pathway electron extraction/interfacial-field modulator—composed of a Co–N4 single-atom site electronically bridged to Co nanoparticles (Co–N4@Co-NP) and subsequently coupled to a PtNi alloy nanodomain—at the perovskite/ETL interface will simultaneously (i) accelerate interfacial electron transfer and suppress interfacial recombination by creating a cascade of tunable work functions and low-trap-density coordination sites, and (ii) introduce an ultrafast, intensity-dependent third-order nonlinear optical (χ(3)) response that functions as an intrinsic ‘self-mode-locking’ carrier-gating layer under pulsed/strong illumination, thereby reducing carrier pile-up and ion-migration-driven field screening. The methodological adaptation is a spatially confined, gradient-assembled, MOF-derived interlayer where Co–N4 sites are anchored in an N-doped carbon matrix, Co nanoparticles provide a short-circuit electron bridge, and PtNi alloy nanodomains act as an electron sink with engineered charge transfer to the N-doped scaffold; together they form a perovskite-compatible, thickness-limited (≈5–15 nm) mixed-dimensional interlayer that couples charge-transfer kinetics to nonlinear optical carrier gating to improve Voc, FF, and operational stability.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a stable high-performance perovskite baseline (e.g., (FA,Cs)(Pb,I,Br)3 with additive-controlled crystallization) and a standard ETL (SnO2 or TiO2) for n–i–p devices; prepare control stacks without interlayers.
1.2 Synthesize a ZIF-derived N-doped carbon ultrathin interlayer precursor on the ETL via a low-temperature, surface-confined growth (seeded MOF film on SnO2) to ensure conformal coverage and pinhole-free morphology.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Build the Co–N4@Co-NP bridge in situ within the MOF-derived film: introduce Co2+ into the surface MOF, then perform a two-stage conversion (mild pyrolysis to form Co–N4 in an N–C matrix; followed by a brief reductive pulse or localized photothermal treatment to nucleate sparse Co nanoparticles while preserving a high density of Co–N4). Target a controlled Co-NP population that is electronically coupled but does not create shunts.
2.2 Couple PtNi alloy nanodomains onto the same interlayer by sequential infiltration/reduction: infiltrate Pt and Ni precursors into the N–C matrix, then execute a short, low-thermal-budget alloying step (rapid thermal/photonic anneal) to form sub-5 nm PtNi. The adaptation is a deliberate vertical gradient: Co–N4-rich region closer to perovskite for defect coordination; Co-NP ‘bridge’ centered for fast electron percolation; PtNi-rich region closer to ETL to pin the electron quasi-Fermi level and reduce back-injection.
2.3 Surface energy-level tuning: adjust Pt:Ni ratio and local N-content to set an interfacial work-function cascade (Perovskite CB → Co–N4/Co-NP → PtNi → ETL) verified by UPS/KPFM. Cap with an ultrathin passivating linker (e.g., halide-compatible ionic dipole) only if needed to prevent metal-induced halide reactions.
2.4 Deposit perovskite on top of the interlayer using a solvent/antisolvent protocol adjusted to avoid interlayer disruption (orthogonal solvent selection) and complete the device stack (HTL + electrode).

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Mechanistic electron/charge transfer validation: 
- TRPL/TCSPC and transient absorption to extract interfacial electron extraction rates and trap-assisted recombination constants.
- Impedance spectroscopy and intensity-dependent J–V to separate transport limitation from recombination (ideality factor changes; recombination resistance).
- Kelvin probe force microscopy under illumination to map photovoltage distribution and confirm reduced interfacial carrier accumulation.
3.2 Nonlinear optical and ‘mode-locking-like’ carrier gating validation (optoelectronic analogue):
- Z-scan or pump–probe on the interlayer (standalone film and within stack) to quantify χ(3), saturable absorption/optical limiting, and recovery time.
- Photocurrent response under modulated/pulsed excitation (GHz–MHz modulation) to test whether the interlayer reduces carrier lag and space-charge formation (frequency-dependent EQE/IMPS).
3.3 Stability and degradation pathway analysis:
- Maximum power point tracking (ISOS-L-2/L-3 style) with temperature/humidity control; compare interlayer vs control.
- ToF-SIMS/XPS depth profiling pre/post aging to detect suppressed ion migration (I−/Br−, MA+/FA+) toward ETL and reduced interfacial Pb0 formation.
- Operando PL mapping and electroluminescence to quantify nonradiative loss evolution; correlate with Voc retention.
3.4 Comparative benchmarking: 
- Compare against single-component interlayers: (i) only Co–N4, (ii) only Co-NP, (iii) only PtNi/NC, and (iv) conventional passivation layers (e.g., fullerene-SAM, alkylammonium 2D capping). Evaluate PCE distribution, hysteresis index, Voc deficit, and stability metrics.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 3 demonstrates that Co–N4 electronically coupled to Co nanoparticles creates a direct electron-transfer bridge by reducing inter-state energy gaps and enabling fast electron flow through a bonded pathway; translating this to PSCs targets the known bottleneck of interfacial recombination and extraction losses at the perovskite/ETL boundary. Asset 2 shows PtNi alloys on N-doped carbon exhibit strong support-to-alloy charge transfer that tunes alloy electronic structure and enhances electron-transfer kinetics; in PSC interfaces this should enable a controllable electron sink/work-function pinning while leveraging N–C as a chemically compatible scaffold. Asset 1 provides precedent that engineered 2D/ultrathin heterostructures with enhanced charge transfer show strong third-order NLO responses and enable mode-locking; here, the same physics is repurposed as ultrafast, intensity-dependent carrier gating that mitigates transient charge accumulation (a driver of hysteresis and ion migration).
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC losses and instability often originate at buried interfaces where defects, band misalignment, and ionic motion couple to local electric fields. A thickness-limited, conformal, MOF-derived N–C interlayer is compatible with solution processing and can be engineered with atomic sites (Co–N4) for defect coordination, metallic bridges (Co-NP) for fast percolation, and alloy sinks (PtNi) for energy-level control—an interface engineering strategy rather than a simple additive swap. The NLO-driven ultrafast response is introduced specifically to address dynamic, illumination-dependent carrier pile-up and field screening that exacerbate hysteresis and accelerate ion migration.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional organic passivators or single-function SAMs, the proposed interlayer is multi-functional but mechanistically integrated: (i) Co–N4 reduces trap density by coordination to under-coordinated Pb/halide-vacancy-associated sites; (ii) Co-NP provides a short, low-resistance electronic bridge without requiring a thick conductive layer; (iii) PtNi/NC charge transfer tunes the interfacial work function and reduces back-transfer, improving Voc and FF; (iv) χ(3)-enabled carrier gating targets fast transient regimes that standard passivation does not address. This combination is expected to reduce Voc deficit, suppress hysteresis, and slow degradation by reducing interfacial charge accumulation and ion migration simultaneously.
final_critique: This is a highly ambitious and largely well-constructed proposal that demonstrates strong command of interfacial physics, catalysis-derived materials chemistry, and perovskite device diagnostics. The engineering plan is unusually detailed for a PSC interface study, with credible synthesis routes (surface-confined MOF growth, staged conversion, photonic annealing) and a rigorous validation framework. The primary score deductions arise from the nonlinear-optical-to-device-performance linkage: while χ(3) enhancement and ultrafast recovery are plausible in PtNi/NC and Co–N–C systems, the causal chain from NLO response to suppression of ion-migration-driven field screening under realistic solar illumination remains only semi-quantitative. The 'self-mode-locking carrier-gating' analogy is intellectually stimulating but risks overextension unless the intensity and timescale regimes relevant to PSC operation are more explicitly bounded. Additionally, the coexistence of metallic Co-NPs and PtNi nanodomains within a 5–15 nm interlayer poses a non-negligible shunt and chemical reactivity risk that is acknowledged but not fully mitigated in the current plan.
hypothesis_summary: A dual-pathway interlayer combining Co–N4 single-atom sites, Co nanoparticles, and PtNi alloy nanodomains accelerates electron extraction while using nonlinear optical gating to suppress recombination and ion migration.

original_chain: Nanocomposites -> Encapsulation -> Polystyrene -> Sorption performance retention (SPR) -> Encapsulation -> Hydrogen-bonded organic frameworks (HOFs) -> ZIF-8 -> Drug loading content
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a dual-porosity reticular nanocomposite (ZIF-8 seeds encapsulated within a hydrogen-bonded organic framework, then embedded in an ultrathin polystyrene (PS) overlayer) on top of a 2D/3D perovskite surface will increase sorption performance retention (SPR) of the device under humidity/thermal cycling while simultaneously improving Voc by suppressing interfacial non-radiative recombination. Methodological adaptation: instead of using porous frameworks as bulk additives (which often introduce leakage pathways and ionic drift), we will form a stratified ‘reticular sponge’ encapsulation where (i) mechanochemical encapsulation preserves high-loading ZIF-8@HOF nanocomposite integrity, (ii) the HOF presents dense H-bond networks that immobilize water at low activity and coordinate undercoordinated Pb2+/I− at the perovskite surface, and (iii) the PS matrix provides a hydrophobic, low-permeability diffusion barrier that prevents continuous moisture flux. Mechanism: water molecules entering from the ambient are preferentially captured and immobilized in ZIF-8 micropores (strong adsorption enthalpy) and then kinetically trapped by the HOF hydrogen-bond network, lowering local water chemical potential at the perovskite interface and suppressing hydrate/solvate formation; concurrently, HOF functional groups (carbonyl/pyridinic/urea-like donors depending on chosen HOF) passivate halide vacancies and undercoordinated Pb, reducing trap-assisted recombination and increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting, thus elevating Voc and FF. The PS encapsulation confines the porous nanocomposite away from direct electrical pathways, minimizing shunts and ion-migration channels, enabling high PCE retention after repeated sorption/desorption cycles (high SPR).
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select baseline high-efficiency, humidity-sensitive stack for clear differentiation: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA0.85MA0.10Cs0.05)Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/2D surface layer (PEAI or BAI, 5–10 mg mL−1)/HTL (PTAA or spiro-OMeTAD)/Au.
1.2 Define SPR protocol in PSC terms: PCE retention after controlled sorption cycling (RH steps + recovery) with concurrent mass uptake. Use: 20↔70% RH cycles at 25 °C (and separately 25↔65 °C at fixed 50% RH) for N=50 cycles; track PCE, Voc, FF, Jsc after each cycle; quantify water uptake by in situ QCM or gravimetric microbalance on witness films.
1.3 Choose a HOF with (a) good film-forming compatibility and (b) Lewis-base/H-bond motifs (e.g., carboxamide/urea/pyridyl). Pre-screen HOF candidates via contact angle, FTIR binding shifts with PbI2, and PLQY changes on perovskite films.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Mechanochemical encapsulation (adapted from reticular-framework APNC stabilization): prepare ZIF-8@HOF composite by ball-milling ZIF-8 nanocrystals (50–150 nm) with HOF precursors (or pre-formed HOF microcrystals) under solvent-minimized conditions (liquid-assisted grinding, ethanol <5 wt%) to avoid framework collapse and to maximize interfacial coupling; target high ‘loading content’ analog: 30–45 wt% ZIF-8 inside/within HOF domains, verified by TGA and ICP (Zn).
2.2 Convert the ZIF-8@HOF powder into a PSC-compatible, electrically benign encapsulation ink: disperse ZIF-8@HOF in PS solution (e.g., PS in anisole or chlorobenzene; adjust MW to tune permeability) with minimal polar cosolvent; optimize solid content to yield 50–200 nm dry film.
2.3 Form a stratified encapsulation that avoids direct incorporation into the perovskite bulk:
  - Deposit perovskite and 2D surface layer as usual.
  - Spin-coat an ultrathin ZIF-8@HOF/PS layer onto the 2D-treated perovskite before HTL (for inverted stacks, place above top electrode as external encapsulation; for n–i–p, evaluate both ‘interlayer’ and ‘topcoat’ placements).
  - Implement a mild thermal anneal (50–70 °C) to consolidate PS without damaging the perovskite.
2.4 Create control architectures to isolate mechanism: (i) neat PS only, (ii) PS+ZIF-8 only, (iii) PS+HOF only, (iv) ZIF-8@HOF without PS (porous-only), (v) baseline encapsulation (e.g., parylene or epoxy/glass) to benchmark.
2.5 Engineer porosity-access vs barrier trade-off: tune PS thickness and ZIF-8@HOF loading to prevent percolation/shunting (below electrical percolation threshold); verify with conductive AFM and leakage current.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Device metrics: stabilized MPP tracking, JV hysteresis index, Voc(T) and ideality factor to diagnose recombination pathways; quantify quasi-Fermi level splitting via absolute PL.
3.2 Moisture/ion interaction mechanistic proof:
  - In situ GIWAXS/XRD under RH ramp to detect hydrate phases (e.g., monohydrate signatures) and suppression thereof.
  - ToF-SIMS depth profiling before/after cycling to track I−/Br− migration and metal diffusion.
  - FTIR and solid-state NMR on ZIF-8@HOF before/after humidity exposure to confirm water binding states; water sorption isotherms to correlate uptake with SPR.
  - Kelvin probe and UPS/XPS to confirm interfacial dipole changes and Pb–Lewis base coordination (Pb 4f shifts), linked to Voc improvements.
3.3 Quantify SPR for PSCs: define SPR_PCE = (PCE_after_cycleN / PCE_initial)×100% while reporting sorbed water mass; aim for ≥90% SPR_PCE after 50 cycles at 70% RH and ≥85% after thermal/RH coupled cycling.
3.4 Statistical rigor: ≥20 devices per condition, two fabrication batches; report Weibull statistics for failure distribution and operational T80 under ISOS-L2 (1 sun, 65 °C, controlled RH).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Polystyrene encapsulation is empirically known to enhance hydrolytic stability and preserve sorption performance of water-labile porous frameworks (high SPR in polymer-encapsulated MOFs). ZIF-8 exhibits water-stable, tunable adsorption behavior and can act as a ‘moisture getter’ without rapid structural collapse. Mechanochemical encapsulation into reticular frameworks (including HOFs) is demonstrated to preserve sensitive nanoscale objects while enabling high loading and microenvironment control, suggesting a route to robust ZIF-8@HOF composites without solvent-induced degradation.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC failure under humidity is governed by water chemical potential at interfaces and defect-mediated degradation pathways. The proposed stratified reticular nanocomposite targets both: (i) moisture chemical potential is reduced by preferential adsorption/kinetic trapping in ZIF-8/HOF pores, (ii) interfacial traps are passivated by HOF functional groups, improving Voc, and (iii) PS provides a low-permeability barrier controlling moisture flux and physically separating porous domains from charge-transport pathways to avoid shunting—critical for optoelectronic compatibility.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional polymer encapsulation alone, the reticular nanocomposite introduces an active, regenerable moisture-buffer that mitigates transient RH spikes (sorption/desorption cycling) rather than merely slowing ingress. Compared to adding MOFs/HOFs directly into perovskite bulk, the stratified PS-confined architecture prevents formation of ionic migration highways and maintains electronic integrity. The mechanochemical route enables high, reproducible ‘loading content’ of ZIF-8 within HOF while avoiding polar solvent exposure that can contaminate perovskite interfaces, improving scalability and reproducibility.
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and largely coherent proposal with strong engineering resolution and a credible mechanistic narrative. The stratified ZIF-8@HOF/PS architecture is well-justified as a means to decouple moisture buffering from electronic pathways, addressing a known failure mode of porous additives in PSCs. The experimental plan is unusually rigorous for an encapsulation concept, with appropriate controls, in situ characterization, and statistically meaningful device testing. Minor deductions arise from (i) partial overextension of the moisture-chemical-potential argument without quantitative modeling or transport simulations, (ii) uncertainty around long-term regeneration kinetics of ZIF-8/HOF under repeated thermal–humidity cycling, and (iii) some ambiguity in interlayer placement relative to charge-selective contacts, which could introduce interfacial resistances or energetic offsets if not carefully engineered. The ‘drug loading content’ analogy is conceptually clear but remains metaphorical rather than quantitatively translated into device-relevant parameters.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a ZIF-8@HOF nanocomposite within an ultrathin polystyrene layer atop perovskite creates a moisture-buffering, defect-passivating barrier that boosts voltage and sustains performance through humidity and thermal cycling.

original_chain: Zn-Car_MOF -> Thymol (Thy) -> Open-circuit voltage (Voc) -> Carbon-based, all-inorganic perovskite solar cell -> Non-radiative recombination -> Organic ligands -> Toxicity -> Vaccine delivery
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Forming a covalently tethered, MOF-derived ligand monolayer at the carbon/perovskite interface—by in situ “carbon-first” growth of a Zn-carboxylate coordination network from oxidized carbon (Zn–COO–C anchors) followed by post-synthetic thymol→thymolate coordination as a surface dipole/defect-capping motif—will suppress interfacial non-radiative recombination and raise Voc in carbon-based all-inorganic CsPbI(1+x)Br(2-x) perovskite solar cells. Mechanistically, (i) the anchored Zn–carboxylate nodes selectively bind and neutralize under-coordinated Pb sites and halide-vacancy-associated Pb-rich terminations at the topmost perovskite surface, reducing interface trap-assisted SRH recombination; (ii) coordinated thymolate introduces an oriented interfacial dipole that increases the perovskite/quasi-metallic carbon contact selectivity (reducing interfacial minority-carrier leakage), thereby increasing quasi-Fermi-level splitting and Voc; and (iii) converting “free” organic additives into an immobilized coordination monolayer eliminates insulating/discontinuous interlayers while minimizing additive migration and associated toxicity concerns.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Baseline absorber: Prepare CsPbIBr2 films and perform controlled slow halide exchange to CsPbI(1+x)Br(2-x) (e.g., 110 °C, 2 h) to establish a low-bulk-defect reference absorber for carbon-based all-inorganic devices.
1.2 Carbon electrode functionalization (new element): Form a thin, conductive carbon contact (printed carbon or carbon cloth/graphite layer) and oxidize only its outermost surface to generate carboxyl/phenolic anchoring sites without degrading conductivity (e.g., mild O2 plasma, UV–ozone, or dilute HNO3; verify via XPS C 1s and four-point probe).
1.3 MOF-precursor chemistry: Prepare a zinc salt solution (Zn(OAc)2 or Zn(NO3)2) and a short, aromatic dicarboxylate linker solution (chosen for rigid, low-thickness coordination networking). Prepare thymol solutions and generate thymolate in situ (weak base, controlled to avoid perovskite attack) for post-coordination.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—“carbon-first anchored coordination monolayer” (CF-ACM): Instead of depositing MOF particles/films on perovskite, grow a sub-nanometric Zn–carboxylate coordination network directly from oxidized carbon so the network is intrinsically tethered to carbon.
  2.1a Anchor growth: Sequentially expose oxidized carbon to Zn2+ then dicarboxylate linker (layer-by-layer, 1–5 cycles) to build an ultrathin Zn-carboxylate coordination network that is electrically benign because it is sparse and carbon-tethered (target thickness <1.5 nm by ellipsometry/AFM step height; confirm Zn signal by XPS/ToF-SIMS).
  2.1b Thymol functionalization as a dipole/defect-cap: Post-treat the anchored network with thymolate so thymolate binds Zn nodes (Zn–OAr) and presents an oriented aromatic/alkyl dipole at the contact. Tune thymolate coverage by concentration/time; verify binding by FTIR (phenolate shift) and XPS O 1s/Zn 2p shifts.
2.2 Device integration: Laminate or print the functionalized carbon electrode onto the perovskite (or deposit perovskite then apply CF-ACM-carbon) to create a chemically passivated, dipole-tuned carbon/perovskite junction without inserting a standalone interlayer. Maintain a fully all-inorganic stack (e.g., FTO/SnO2/CsPbI(1+x)Br(2-x)/CF-ACM–Thy-carbon).
2.3 Process window optimization (DoE): Vary (i) oxidation degree of carbon (surface –COOH density), (ii) number of coordination-growth cycles, (iii) linker identity/length (controls spacing and dipole screening), and (iv) thymolate coverage. Objective functions: maximize Voc and FF while keeping series resistance unchanged.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Quantify recombination suppression and Voc mechanism:
  • Absolute PLQY and quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) on perovskite surfaces contacted with (a) pristine carbon, (b) oxidized carbon, (c) CF-ACM without thymol, (d) CF-ACM+thymol.
  • TRPL at the perovskite surface before/after carbon contact (extract interface recombination velocity via contact-quenching analysis).
  • Light-intensity-dependent Voc (ideality factor changes indicating reduced SRH/interface recombination) and temperature-dependent Voc (activation energy approaching bandgap indicates reduced interface recombination).
3.2 Interfacial energetics/selectivity:
  • UPS/Kelvin probe to map carbon work function shift induced by CF-ACM and thymolate dipole; correlate ΔWF with Voc gains.
  • Impedance spectroscopy under illumination (recombination resistance and chemical capacitance trends).
  • Transient photovoltage/photocurrent (carrier lifetime and extraction kinetics).
3.3 Structural/chemical proof of tethered coordination network:
  • XPS depth profiling/angle-resolved XPS to confirm Zn-carboxylate species reside on carbon side and remain after lamination.
  • ToF-SIMS mapping of Zn and linker fragments at the interface.
  • Cross-sectional TEM/EELS (optional) to visualize an ultrathin interfacial layer without particulate morphology.
3.4 Stability and toxicity-aligned testing:
  • MPP tracking under heat/light (e.g., 65–85 °C, 1 sun) and damp-heat (e.g., 60 °C/85% RH) to test whether immobilized chemistry resists desorption/migration.
  • IEC-like leaching tests: quantify Pb release (ICP-MS) from aged devices with/without CF-ACM; separately quantify Zn/organic leachates to show net toxicity reduction.
3.5 Controls and falsification:
  • Carbon with oxidation only (no Zn/linker), Zn salt treatment only, linker only, thymol/thymolate only.
  • Non-coordinating phenol analog (blocks “dipole” without Zn binding) to decouple dipole vs defect-passivation.
  • Carbon functionalized with a non-metal carboxylate polymer (tests whether coordination chemistry is necessary).
  • Vary linker length: if Voc improvement tracks with interfacial dipole/work-function but not with thickness, supports selectivity mechanism; if thickness correlates with increased Rs, indicates overgrowth failure mode.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Asset 2 establishes Voc in carbon-based all-inorganic CsPbI(1+x)Br(2-x) PSCs is limited by non-radiative recombination and defect/phase issues; therefore, an interface-selective recombination suppression strategy is expected to yield Voc gains. Asset 3 demonstrates that organic-ligand environments govern non-radiative pathways via trap formation/passivation in MOF-like systems, motivating a ligand-controlled interface. Asset 1 evidences Zn-Car_MOF’s compatibility with thymol coordination/hosting in functional devices, supporting thymol-based coordination motifs as chemically viable.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Carbon contacts often suffer from poor energetic selectivity and high interface trap densities in fully printable, all-inorganic PSCs; directly engineering the carbon/perovskite junction—without adding an insulating interlayer—is the most architecture-compatible route to suppress interface SRH recombination and boost Voc. The CF-ACM approach converts MOF chemistry into a tethered, sub-nm coordination network that (i) chemically passivates perovskite surface defects through Zn–O interactions and (ii) tunes carbon work function via thymolate dipoles, directly targeting the Voc-limiting junction physics.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with particulate/discontinuous MOF interlayers (rejected approach), CF-ACM is structurally novel (carbon-anchored, monolayer-scale coordination network rather than deposited MOF material), inherently avoids blocking charge transport (no standalone film), and improves long-term stability by immobilizing organic ligands (reducing additive migration). It additionally addresses toxicity by enabling lower Pb leakage through improved stability and by constraining organic components to a tethered interfacial form; this logic parallels nMOF safety-by-design concepts from Asset 4 (ligand/metal control to mitigate toxicity), while remaining firmly within PSC interface engineering.
final_critique: This is a technically strong and unusually detailed interface-engineering proposal with clear awareness of the known Voc bottleneck in carbon-based all-inorganic PSCs. The CF-ACM concept is logically constructed and experimentally testable, and the validation plan is appropriately rigorous (QFLS, Voc(T), UPS, TRPL, ToF-SIMS). Minor score deductions arise from (i) an overextension of claims regarding selective Pb-defect binding by Zn–carboxylate nodes without atomistic or comparative binding-energy justification versus competing Zn–halide or Zn–O(perovskite) interactions, (ii) limited discussion of chemical robustness of thymolate under operational bias/light (possible oxidation or decoordination), and (iii) a somewhat forced linkage to the far-end concept of 'vaccine delivery', which is not substantively integrated beyond a loose toxicity-by-design analogy. These issues do not undermine feasibility but slightly weaken logical closure and evidence grounding.
hypothesis_summary: A tethered Zn-carboxylate coordination monolayer with thymolate dipoles at the carbon/perovskite interface suppresses non-radiative recombination and boosts voltage in all-inorganic perovskite solar cells.

original_chain: Half-wave potential -> Zinc-air batteries -> Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) -> Hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) -> Near-infrared light (NIR) -> Cell apoptosis -> Fenton reaction -> Glucose oxidase (GOx)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a redox-buffering, NIR-gated oxygen-management interphase (Zn–porphyrin COF + Fe-scavenging PCP) between the perovskite electron-contact and a carbon air electrode will suppress oxygen-driven perovskite degradation by (i) displacing oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) away from the perovskite, (ii) kinetically biasing oxygen reduction at the air-side interphase toward a 2e− outer-sphere route with minimized peroxide activity at the perovskite-side boundary, and (iii) eliminating Fenton-active chemistry via quantitative Fe2+/Fe3+ sequestration.

Mechanistic rationale with operational definitions (addressing reviewer pillars):
1) Quantitative energy-level/kinetic alignment (“outside the quasi-Fermi level” made measurable): Under illumination, the relevant driving force for electron transfer from the perovskite electron-contact stack into O2 at the interphase is ΔG_ET ≈ −e·(E_Fn,contact − E°′(O2/H2O2,local)) after including interfacial band-bending and local electrostatic potential. We define “outside the perovskite electron quasi-Fermi level” as the condition where the *measured* illuminated contact quasi-Fermi level (E_Fn at the C60/BCP/PCP surface, referenced to vacuum via KPFM/UPS) is at least 150 mV less reducing than the *local* apparent ORR onset potential of ZnPor-COF/carbon (E_onset,app at the same interface, referenced to the same scale). Operationally: E_Fn,illum(contact) − E_onset,app(ZnPor-COF) ≤ −0.15 V (insufficient driving force for substantial interfacial ORR at the perovskite-adjacent side), while ORR remains facile at the air-exposed ZnPor-COF/carbon boundary due to O2 activity and photogated kinetics.
2) NIR-gated oxygen pumping without new ROS pathways: NIR (808–850 nm) excites ZnPor triplets that accelerate back-electron transfer / interfacial charge-exchange with O2 at the *air-side* catalyst region, increasing ORR exchange current (j0) at fixed overpotential (η) rather than increasing η. The key falsifiable prediction is: at matched temperature and matched visible photon flux, NIR increases ORR rate (higher j at fixed E) and/or decreases H2O2 surface activity near the perovskite-side boundary, while *not* increasing singlet oxygen (1O2) generation (TEMP/TEMPO EPR and immobilized SOSG/DPBF readouts unchanged within error).
3) Peroxide-handling + Fenton suppression closes the chain: Even if a fraction of 2e− ORR produces H2O2 (Asset 2), the COF nanochannel chemistry (controlled sulfonation/water uptake) reduces H2O2 residence time and activity at the perovskite-side boundary by favoring outward partitioning/diffusion to the air electrode side. Any H2O2 that reaches the perovskite-adjacent region cannot trigger hydroxyl radicals because PCP quantitatively complexes trace Fe2+/Fe3+ (Fenton gate) (Assets 3–4). To preserve the mandated concept chain, glucose oxidase (GOx) is introduced as a calibrated, independent H2O2 generator in a dedicated test fixture to benchmark (a) H2O2 transport through the COF and (b) PCP’s Fe/Fenton suppression, decoupled from perovskite photophysics.

PSC-relevant failure endpoint replacing “apoptosis”: The terminal metric is a ROS-coupled device-physics failure mode quantified as (i) ΔVoc-deficit = (Eg/q − Voc) increase, (ii) trap density rise (tDOS from thermal admittance / SCLC), and (iii) ion-migration markers (hysteresis index, transient ion drift signatures), each fit to a ROS-dependent rate law where the measured H2O2 activity and ·OH/1O2 signals are the causal predictors.
Plan: Step 1 — Device architecture and chemically specified interphase build
1.1 Baseline inverted PSC platform (carbon top electrode compatible): glass/ITO/MeO-2PACz/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/C60/BCP/carbon. Target initial PCE ≥ 18% with carbon electrode; encapsulation kept modular to allow controlled O2/H2O exposure.
1.2 PCP Fe-scavenging sublayer (2–5 nm) directly on BCP or on C60/BCP: poly(catechol-phosphate) deposited by aqueous/alcohol self-assembly (pH 7–8 buffer to avoid perovskite exposure; deposition done on electron-transport layer prior to perovskite integration when required). Acceptance criteria: (i) thickness by ellipsometry/XRR within 2–5 nm, (ii) surface coverage uniformity by AFM/KPFM, (iii) Fe binding capacity quantified by ICP-MS after soaking in Fe2+/Fe3+ (10–500 ppb; and 1–10 ppm stress) in electrolyte-analog solvents; fit Langmuir-type binding isotherm to extract capacity and affinity.
1.3 ZnPor-COF film on carbon (20–50 nm) with controlled sulfonation: interfacial polymerization of Zn-porphyrin dialdehyde + diamine linker. Incorporate 0, 2, 5, 10 mol% sulfonated linker (–SO3−) to tune water uptake/partitioning. Acceptance criteria: (i) thickness 20–50 nm by cross-sectional SEM/TEM, (ii) porosity/channel order by GIWAXS, (iii) water uptake isotherm by QCM-D or ellipsometric porosimetry, (iv) electronic conductivity (in-plane) and series resistance impact in complete stacks.
1.4 Axial-ligand series to tune O2 binding and ORR energetics: Zn axial ligands grafted or coordinated post-synthetically: pyridine, imidazole, 4-fluoropyridine, and 4-(trifluoromethyl)pyridine.
