Feasibility: 1) Controllability of negative Gaussian curvature at buried interfaces is bounded by design variables with quantitative targets. Instead of relying on uncontrolled ‘buckling’, curvature is treated as an engineered outcome governed by (i) mixed-spacer packing frustration (ratio-defined), (ii) kinetic trapping via anneal ramp rate, and (iii) confinement of RP formation to a 2–10 nm interphase by sub-stoichiometric spacer dosing. The proposal includes explicit curvature metrics (K distribution and radii) and a go/no-go electrical signature (LF capacitance dispersion reduction) that is measurable on buried interfaces without requiring perfect 3D imaging of every sample.

2) Causal separation is strengthened by a structured control matrix and a falsifiable alternative hypothesis. Matched-chemistry flat-vs-curved controls isolate curvature from spacer identity and metal loading; matched-curvature metal-free controls isolate chemical passivation/redox from curvature; and a dipole-flip experiment at constant curvature directly tests whether band alignment (dipoles) dominates over curvature-driven homogenization. This addresses the reviewer concern that spacer dipoles, FeN4 passivation, and Co–N redox tuning could be inseparable in practice.

3) The ORR half-wave potential descriptor is de-risked by introducing an early surrogate validation stage and by measuring not only E1/2 but also superoxide yield/selectivity on the same interphase films. This reduces reliance on assumptions about identical rate-determining steps between electrochemical ORR on ITO and interfacial oxygen reduction under PSC operation. The project’s central claim becomes correlation-and-causality-based: if curvature increases utilization ratio (UR) of accessible M–N sites (analogous to bicontinuous SAC utilization improvements) and this jointly shifts E1/2 and reduces superoxide yield in surrogate films, then the same interphase should measurably reduce operando superoxide generation and oxygen-driven degradation in PSC stacks.

4) Empirical grounding from literature assets is used in a domain-consistent way: the bicontinuous/negative-curvature SAC work motivates the ‘utilization ratio’ concept and the idea that negative Gaussian curvature can lower effective barriers and improve electronic architecture/accessibility of single-atom sites; MOF-derived Co–N work motivates Co–N species as ORR-tuning centers with measurable E1/2 shifts and durability. The proposal does not assume identical materials (carbon vs perovskite interphase) but transfers the *descriptor logic* (site utilization + E1/2 + selectivity) into a perovskite-native RP interphase.

5) Practical success criteria are explicitly defined at each stage. Even if curvature proves difficult to reproduce at scale, the plan contains decision gates that preserve publishable outcomes: (i) a validated methodology for embedding spectroscopically confirmed single-atom FeN4/Co–N motifs in ultrathin RP interphases with quantified utilization ratio; (ii) a surrogate-system map of curvature vs UR vs ORR E1/2 vs superoxide yield; and (iii) PSC demonstrations where either curvature-dependent field homogenization (via LF capacitance/PL variance) or chemical passivation/redox tuning (via QFLS and operando EPR) can be unambiguously claimed—preventing the project from collapsing into an unfalsifiable multi-factor narrative.
final_critique: This is unusually strong in experimental resolution: it predefines curvature metrics, builds a causality-focused control matrix (matched-chemistry flat/curved, matched-curvature metal-free/metal-containing), and introduces a surrogate electrochemistry gate before committing to full PSC integration. However, several core links in the mechanistic chain remain under-justified or operationally ambiguous. (i) The premise that negative Gaussian curvature at a buried RP/3D intergrowth will homogenize electrostatics/ion accumulation is plausible but not quantitatively derived; LF capacitance dispersion and PL/EL variance are reasonable proxies, yet they are not uniquely diagnostic of ‘Gaussian-curvature-driven homogenization’ versus changes in interphase thickness, dielectric response, defect density, or contact selectivity. (ii) Measuring ORR E1/2 and superoxide selectivity in aprotic electrolyte on ITO/interphase films may not map cleanly onto the solid-state interfacial oxygen reduction pathways under illumination and mixed ionic–electronic conduction; the proposal acknowledges descriptor (not mechanistic identity), but still risks over-interpreting E1/2 shifts that could arise from changed film conductivity/wetting rather than intrinsic Co–N tuning. (iii) The feasibility of achieving and *maintaining* a targeted K distribution (≥30% area with K<0 within 10 nm) across statistically meaningful device populations is not fully de-risked: tomography is low-throughput and curvature could relax under bias/heat; the plan mentions ‘chemical locking’ but does not specify how curvature stability will be verified operando or after aging. (iv) The single-atom FeN4/Co–N speciation and UR definition are good, but in an ultrathin, partially ionic RP-like environment the assumption that redox charge cleanly counts addressable sites is fragile (capacitive background, ion motion, pseudocapacitance); without an explicit deconvolution protocol, UR changes could be artefactual. Overall: excellent architecture and controls, but key descriptors (LF capacitance dispersion, E1/2, UR) need tighter measurement models and orthogonal validation to prevent confounding by thickness/conductivity/dipole effects.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding FeN4 single-atom sites into a saddle-shaped perovskite skin reduces degradation by improving ion uniformity and tuning oxygen redox, with curvature effects causally separated from chemical passivation.

original_chain: Reticular frameworks -> ZIF-8 -> Fluorescence quenching -> GQDs-PSS@ZIF-8 -> Proton conductivity
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A perovskite-benign, ultrathin reticular Zn–imidazolate interphase can be fabricated as a conformal “Reticular Proton‑Sponge Dipole (RPSD)” by (i) low-reactivity Zn precursor pulsing that avoids Pb–X disruption, (ii) linker-driven conversion to a ZIF‑8–like (sodalite-topology) microporous network or a deliberately defined amorphous Zn–imidazolate (aZIF) analog, and (iii) nanoconfined immobilization of sulfonate-tethered GQDs (GQDs–PSS) that provides a controllable population of Brønsted sites and bound water. The refined mechanism is explicitly falsifiable and risk-bounded: (1) Electronic passivation is supplied by a spatially ordered 2D/3D surface heterojunction (n=1–2) that reduces SRH recombination by saturating undercoordinated Pb2+ and suppressing halide vacancy percolation at the topmost grains (Voc/QFLS increase, reduced ideality factor). (2) Ionic-field stabilization is supplied by a nanoconfined protonic screening pathway inside the reticular interphase that is kinetically fast (sub‑second to seconds) and low-mobility compared to halide drift (10–10^3 s), thereby stabilizing the interfacial electric double layer (EDL) under bias without enabling net halide transport. Proton donors/acceptors are pre-defined as: (i) sulfonate acid/FA+ counterion pairs on PSS (tunable acidity without free strong acid), (ii) adsorbed H2O forming hydrogen-bond networks, and (iii) imidazolate/imidazole equilibrium at the Zn–mim nodes. Under humidity, these sites support Grotthuss/vehicular proton motion confined to the MOF/aZIF volume, producing a measurable increase in low-frequency interfacial ionic capacitance (Cion) and a distinct relaxation time constant (τp) that shifts with H2O→D2O isotope substitution, while TOF-SIMS confirms reduced halide redistribution under identical bias stress (decoupling proton screening from halide migration). (3) Process-order risk on 2D-skin formation is removed by explicitly benchmarking two sequences (2D-first vs MOF-first) and selecting the one that yields a verified depth ordering: 3D perovskite → 2D (n=1–2) → reticular Zn–imidazolate (with embedded GQDs–PSS) → C60, rather than an intermixed damaged region. (4) Fluorescence quenching is converted from a qualitative indicator into a pre-registered photophysical diagnostic by fitting a multi-channel kinetic model (radiative + SRH + energy transfer + charge transfer) across temperature and distance-control samples, so “interphase integrity” corresponds to a stable, model-resolved transfer rate (kET or kCT) without emergent nonradiative channels (kSRH increase).

This hypothesis overcomes reviewer-identified limitations by (i) replacing aggressive Zn precursors with demonstrably perovskite-benign chemistries and proving, pulse-by-pulse, that Zn–N coordination forms without Pb–X loss; (ii) defining acceptance criteria that explicitly separate crystalline ZIF‑8 from amorphous Zn–imidazolate and allowing either to be a valid reticular proton-sponge provided porosity/proton response targets are met; (iii) making the proton-screening claim quantitative via isotope-dependent EIS/KPFM time constants and capacitance changes correlated with halide-stability metrics; and (iv) de-risking 2D-layer formation by an order-of-operations study plus depth-resolved structural confirmation.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registration of acceptance criteria (go/no-go gates)
0.1 Define “perovskite-benign Zn pulsing” acceptance: after Zn pulse sets (no linker), the perovskite surface must show (i) no detectable Pb0 growth by XPS (Pb 4f metallic component <1 at%), (ii) no net halide loss by XPS (I/Pb and Br/Pb within ±5% of baseline), (iii) unchanged near-surface crystallinity by GIWAXS (no new PbI2 peak above detection) and AFM RMS roughness change <0.5 nm.
0.2 Define “reticular Zn–imidazolate” classification:
- Crystalline ZIF-8: GIWAXS shows characteristic sodalite reflections (e.g., (011), (002), (112) at expected q); FTIR/Raman indicates Zn–N(imidazolate) coordination (imidazolate ring modes shifted vs Hmim); ellipsometry thickness 0.7–3.0 nm target; porosity proxy confirmed on reference substrates (Kr adsorption or ellipsometric porosimetry with water/methanol).
- aZIF (amorphous Zn–imidazolate): no GIWAXS reflections but FTIR/Raman confirms Zn–N coordination; must still show measurable porosity proxy and proton-response signature (humidity-dependent impedance with isotope shift).
0.3 Define “proton-screening” quantitative targets at device-relevant RH (30–50%):
- A low-frequency capacitance increase ΔCion ≥ 2× vs baseline (same bias and RH), with a dominant relaxation time τp in 0.1–10 s range.
- Isotope effect: τ(D2O)/τ(H2O) ≥ 1.3 and/or reduced low-frequency conductivity under D2O (consistent with protonic contribution), while halide migration indicators (TOF-SIMS halide redistribution; EIS very-slow features >100 s) are reduced.

Step 1 — Baseline device and film platform
1.1 Baseline p–i–n stack (high Voc sensitivity): glass/ITO/MeO‑2PACz/(FA0.83Cs0.17)Pb(I0.83Br0.17)3/C60/BCP/Ag.
1.2 Prepare matched substrates for process-chemistry studies: (i) perovskite on ITO/MeO‑2PACz for in-vacuo characterization; (ii) perovskite on inert TiO2/Si for depth profiling; (iii) reference inert substrates (Si, Al2O3, quartz) for porosity and growth metrology.

Step 2 — De-risked reticular growth chemistry (precursor benchmarking + in-situ metrology)
2.1 Benchmark Zn precursors (replace Zn(Et)2 as non-default):
- Primary: Zn(tmhd)2 (Zn(2,2,6,6‑tetramethyl‑3,5‑heptanedionate)2) or Zn(hfac)2 is avoided due to fluorinated acidity/corrosion risk; prioritize non-fluorinated β‑diketonates.
- Secondary: Zn(OAc)2 delivered via solvent-free evaporation/aerosol is only used on reference substrates (risk of acetate/perovskite reaction).
- Tertiary (only if benign in Step 2.3): Zn(acac)2.
Each precursor is screened on perovskite via pulse–purge at ≤50–60 °C with in-situ QCM (mass uptake) and in-situ ellipsometry (thickness/optical constants).
2.2 Linker delivery and mobility: 2‑methylimidazole (Hmim) delivered by controlled vapor dosing (heated reservoir) with short pulses and purge to minimize residence time; RH kept <1% during growth (dry N2/Ar) to prevent uncontrolled perovskite hydration.
2.3 Pulse-by-pulse surface reaction study (mandatory):
For each Zn precursor: perform (Zn pulse → purge → in-vacuo XPS; Hmim pulse → purge → in-vacuo XPS) over 1–5 cycles on perovskite.
Measured endpoints after each half-cycle:
- XPS: Zn 2p, N 1s (imidazolate), Pb 4f, I 3d, Br 3d, C 1s; track Pb–X integrity and Zn–N formation.
- QCM/ellipsometry: areal mass uptake per cycle and thickness per cycle (Å/cycle).
Go/no-go: select the Zn precursor that meets Step 0.1 and yields reproducible mass/thickness increments and Zn–N signal growth.

Step 3 — Formation of the RPSD interphase (two validated architectures)
3.1 Architecture A (MOF/aZIF-first, then 2D):
3.1.1 Grow ultrathin reticular Zn–imidazolate (target 0.7–3.0 nm) by alternating Zn/Hmim pulses (2–10 cycles). Temperature: 40–60 °C. Stop when ellipsometry indicates target thickness and QCM indicates diminishing uptake (self-limiting regime).
3.1.2 Incorporate GQDs–PSS by one of two solvent-orthogonal routes (benchmarked for perovskite compatibility):
- Route A (preferred): dry aerosol deposition of GQDs–PSS (size 2–5 nm) with controlled dose, followed by 1–2 Zn/Hmim “capping” cycles to immobilize sulfonate-tethered domains at pore mouths/defects.
- Route B (backup): brief exposure to a super-dilute nonpolar dispersion using perovskite-safe carrier (validated by Step 0.1 criteria), immediately followed by vacuum drying and capping cycles.
3.1.3 2D skin attempt under MOF constraint: expose to vapor of PEA-I or FPEA-I with controlled activity (temperature-controlled source; short exposures) and monitor if 2D RP signatures appear without MOF damage. If blocked (no 2D formation), Architecture A is deprioritized.

3.2 Architecture B (2D-first, then MOF/aZIF) — explicit de-risk path for aperture/diffusion concerns:
3.2.1 Form n=1–2 RP skin first by PEA-I/FPEA-I vapor dosing directly on 3D perovskite (no MOF present), targeting ≤2 nm (self-limited) using surface-sensitive GIXRD/GIWAXS.
3.2.2 Grow ultrathin Zn–imidazolate on top of the 2D skin using the Step 2-validated Zn/Hmim pulses, exploiting the more organophilic 2D surface to enhance nucleation density at low temperature.
3.2.3 Introduce GQDs–PSS during early cycles (1–3 cycles) to place sulfonate sites inside/at the forming reticular network while avoiding direct strong-acid contact with 3D perovskite.
Decision rule: proceed with the architecture that yields verified ordering (Step 6) and best maintains charge extraction (no FF loss).

Step 4 — Full control matrix (mechanism isolating)
4.1 Baseline: no interphase.
4.2 2D-only: PEA-I/FPEA-I vapor.
4.3 Reticular-only: Zn–imidazolate (no GQDs–PSS; no 2D).
4.4 Reticular + GQDs (no PSS): isolates optical probe without sulfonate/proton sites.
4.5 Reticular + PSS (no GQDs): isolates proton sites without optical probe.
4.6 RPSD complete: reticular + GQDs–PSS + 2D (order A and B).

Step 5 — Structural and chemical validation (including “ZIF‑8 vs aZIF” decision)
5.1 GIWAXS/GIXRD: verify (i) 2D RP phase (n=1–2) and (ii) presence/absence of ZIF‑8 reflections; ensure bulk 3D unchanged.
5.2 FTIR/Raman: confirm Zn–imidazolate coordination (vs physisorbed Hmim).
5.3 Inert-substrate porosity proxy: ellipsometric porosimetry or Kr adsorption on Si/Al2O3 samples grown identically; acceptance per Step 0.2.
5.4 Cross-sectional STEM-EDX/EELS: map Zn, S (PSS), C (GQDs/PSS), Pb/I/Br; verify thickness, continuity, and absence of thick insulating MOF.
5.5 Angle-resolved XPS depth profiling: confirm spatial ordering (2D at perovskite surface, reticular layer above/around) and quantify dipole/band-edge shifts (UPS).

Step 6 — Make the proton-screening mechanism quantitative and falsifiable
6.1 Humidity- and isotope-dependent operando EIS under bias:
- Perform EIS on complete devices at controlled RH (10, 30, 50, 70%) using H2O and D2O humidification at matched RH and temperature.
- Fit using an equivalent circuit with explicit elements for recombination resistance (Rrec), geometric capacitance (Cgeo), ionic/EDL capacitance (Cion), and one or two distributed relaxation processes (e.g., CPEion) to capture ionic polarization.
- Extract ΔCion and τ for the dominant low-frequency arc; require isotope-dependent τ consistent with protonic mobility (Step 0.3).
6.2 Bias-step KPFM/SPV time constants:
- Under controlled RH (H2O vs D2O), apply bias steps and track surface potential relaxation. Proton-screening predicts faster initial stabilization (sub-second to seconds) with isotope slowdown; halide-driven drift predicts slower (tens–hundreds of seconds) and weak isotope dependence.
6.3 Decouple from halide migration:
- TOF-SIMS after identical bias-stress/Mpp aging (e.g., 65 °C, 1 sun, RH 30–50%) to quantify I−/Br− redistribution and electrode ingress; success requires reduced halide gradients in RPSD vs controls while protonic signatures (EIS/KPFM) increase.
6.4 Rule out corrosive/side-reaction pathways:
- XPS after humidity + bias: check for increased Pb0, altered N 1s, sulfonate decomposition (S 2p), and Ag migration; reject conditions that increase corrosion markers.

Step 7 — Optoelectronic performance validation (Voc/QFLS linkage)
7.1 Absolute PLQY and TRPL on full stacks (with C60) to extract QFLS and compare to Voc; require reduced ΔVoc,nr.
7.2 Suns–Voc and ideality factor: verify reduction of SRH-dominated recombination for RPSD vs baseline and vs each control.
7.3 EQE_EL: quantify nonradiative Voc loss change.
7.4 Transport penalty check: transient photocurrent/photovoltage and Rs extraction; reject any interphase causing FF loss >1–2% absolute attributable to added resistance.

Step 8 — Fluorescence quenching as an operando integrity reporter (pre-registered kinetic model)
8.1 Define the photophysical model per sample family:
- Channels: radiative recombination (kr), SRH (knr,SRH), energy transfer to GQDs (kET, distance-dependent), and/or charge transfer (kCT) if energetically allowed.
- Use multi-wavelength TRPL (and temperature dependence) to separate dielectric/reabsorption effects from true transfer (kET/kCT) by monitoring spectral shifts and lifetime changes.
8.2 Distance-control calibration samples:
- Insert calibrated inert spacers (e.g., ultrathin Al2O3 by low-temperature ALD on reference substrates, or organic spacer monolayers) between perovskite and GQD-containing layer to establish kET(distance) baseline.
8.3 Integrity criterion:
- During light+humidity cycling, “intact interphase” = stable fitted kET (or kCT) within ±10% and no emergent increase in knr,SRH; any PL drop accompanied by knr,SRH increase is classified as degradation, not “stable quenching.”

Step 9 — Integration and stability metrics
9.1 Complete devices with C60/BCP/Ag using solvent-orthogonal deposition.
9.2 Stability: MPP tracking at 65–85 °C under controlled RH (30–50%); report T80 and correlate with TOF-SIMS and EIS evolution.
9.3 Success metrics (unchanged but now tied to gates): Voc gain ≥40 mV at matched Jsc; ΔVoc,nr reduction ≥30 mV; hysteresis index reduced ≥50% with suppressed low-frequency ionic features; T80 ≥2×; no FF penalty.

Feasibility: Process-chemistry de-risking: The revised plan explicitly removes Zn(Et)2 as a default and mandates a pulse-by-pulse surface reaction study (QCM/ellipsometry + in-vacuo XPS after each half-cycle) to prove controllable Zn–N formation without Pb–X disruption. This directly addresses the reviewer concern of parasitic reactions/etching and replaces assumption with measurable acceptance criteria (no Pb0, no halide loss, no PbI2 growth). Thickness control is no longer asserted as inherently “self-limited”; it is operationally defined by (i) diminishing mass uptake per cycle and (ii) ellipsometry-confirmed thickness within 0.7–3.0 nm. Importantly, the proposal no longer requires perfect crystalline ZIF‑8 on perovskite at ≤60 °C: it introduces an explicit classification (crystalline ZIF‑8 vs amorphous Zn–imidazolate aZIF) with independent coordination and porosity proxies. Either phase is acceptable if it meets the porosity/proton-response gates, which reduces kinetic risk while keeping the reticular “proton-sponge” concept intact.

Microscopic proton-screening mechanism made falsifiable: The proton donors/acceptors are specified (PSS sulfonate counterions, confined water, imidazolate/imidazole equilibrium). The expected observables are quantitative: ΔCion increase and τp in the 0.1–10 s band, with an H2O→D2O isotope effect on τ and/or low-frequency conductivity. The design includes a required decoupling: protonic signatures must change with isotope substitution while TOF-SIMS demonstrates reduced halide redistribution under the same stress. This makes the central claim testable and protects against the alternative interpretation that the interphase merely increases ionic polarization or capacitance without suppressing halide drift.

2D-skin feasibility under/within MOF resolved by sequence benchmarking: The revised execution explicitly tests “MOF-first” versus “2D-first” to avoid the aperture/diffusion ambiguity (3.4 Å ZIF‑8 windows vs PEA-related species). Depth ordering is not assumed; it is verified by cross-sectional STEM/nanodiffraction and angle-resolved XPS. This directly addresses the risk of patchy mixed phases and uncertain band alignment; the selected sequence will be the one that yields a clear 3D→2D→reticular stratification and maintains FF.

Quenching reporter made unambiguous: The proposal pre-registers a rate-based kinetic model and calibrates distance dependence using spacer controls and temperature/multi-wavelength TRPL. Therefore, “stable quenching” is redefined as stability of extracted transfer rates (kET/kCT) without growth of knr,SRH, eliminating the reviewer concern that unchanged quenching amplitude could mask compensating degradation pathways.

Overall, feasibility is strengthened by (i) replacing high-risk chemistry with a validated precursor screen and hard acceptance gates, (ii) allowing an aZIF analog as a valid reticular host if it meets coordination/porosity/proton-response criteria, and (iii) converting the key mechanistic claim into an isotope-resolved, time-constant–based measurement suite correlated with direct halide-migration readouts.
final_critique: The proposal is unusually well-engineered for an interphase-chemistry problem: it replaces the highest-risk chemistry with a gated precursor screen and builds falsifiability into the central “proton-sponge” claim via isotope-sensitive time constants tied to halide redistribution readouts. However, several deductions remain. (i) The physical plausibility of forming a continuous, functionally porous 0.7–3.0 nm ZIF-like network on a heterogeneous perovskite/2D surface at 40–60 °C is still uncertain; the porosity proxy is largely demonstrated on inert substrates, not on the actual perovskite stack where densification/partial collapse is likely at sub-3 nm thickness. (ii) Equivalent-circuit extraction of ΔCion and τp is non-unique; without a stronger impedance identifiability plan (model selection, Kramers–Kronig compliance, parameter correlation analysis), the claimed protonic element can be confounded with interfacial dipoles, contact inhomogeneity, or slow electronic trapping—especially because humidity also changes perovskite surface energetics. (iii) The mechanism assumes “fast-but-confined” proton screening that stabilizes the EDL without enabling net anion transport; yet the proposal does not specify an upper bound on protonic/ionic conductivity that would avoid new shunt pathways, nor does it define how to separate genuine proton motion inside the reticular phase from water-mediated surface conduction along grain boundaries or pinholes. (iv) The 2D (n=1–2) passivation layer is treated as simultaneously electronic passivator and halide-vacancy suppressor, but direct proof of reduced vacancy percolation at the topmost grains is indirect; TOF-SIMS post-stress is helpful but not sufficient to attribute the effect specifically to vacancy percolation suppression vs changed interface fields or altered electrode reactions.
hypothesis_summary: A nanoscale Zn–imidazolate interphase with embedded proton-donor sites acts as a reticular proton-sponge dipole, using fast proton screening to stabilize the electric double layer and suppress halide migration in perovskite solar cells.

original_chain: Release profile -> Reactive oxygen species (ROS) -> Fenton reaction -> Hypoxic tumors -> Gold nanoparticles (AuNPs) -> Photothermal conversion ability
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A photothermally self-regulated, ROS-neutralizing interfacial nanoheater–getter layer—comprising (i) optically insulated Au nanostars (AuNS) embedded within (ii) an ultrathin Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) 2D-perovskite cap that also contains (iii) a perovskite-benign, thermally activated oxygen-getter family—can produce a quantitatively predictable, on-demand suppression of interfacial oxygen chemical potential (ΔpO2) during light soaking while preserving interfacial electronic quality (unchanged ideality factor and interfacial recombination velocity). Mechanistically, the RP-2D cap provides a first-order reduction in oxygen diffusivity and passivates undercoordinated Pb2+; the AuNS convert the 750–900 nm tail of AM1.5G into controlled local heating that triggers getter activation only within a predefined safe thermal window; the getter consumes dissolved/interstitial O2 faster than it is replenished through the RP-2D layer, thereby lowering near-interface aO2 and suppressing the O2•−/1O2-mediated iodide oxidation chain. This closes the key plausibility gap by explicitly coupling (a) O2 transport through a 5–20 nm RP barrier, (b) getter areal capacity and kinetics, and (c) bounded photothermal temperature rise, yielding an experimentally testable target: a sustained ΔpO2(interface) ≥ 50–200 mbar under 1-sun in air for ≥10–60 min (tunable), without exceeding interface temperatures that accelerate ion migration beyond acceptance gates.
Plan: Step 0 — Quantitative design spine (mandatory): models → design targets → acceptance gates.
0.1 O2 flux–consumption mass-balance model (cap-scale, 1D):
- Geometry: gas | encapsulant (optional) | CTL (ETL/HTL) | RP-2D cap (L = 5–20 nm) | 3D perovskite.
- Transport in RP-2D: O2 concentration C(x,t) governed by ∂C/∂t = D_RP ∂²C/∂x² − k_cons(T, I)·C, with boundary C(0,t)=S·pO2(ext) (Henry/sorption S) and no-flux/finite sink at x=L depending on perovskite uptake.
- Define effective permeability P_RP = D_RP·S; parameterize with literature-like bounds for organic-rich layered films and calibrate by direct measurement (see 3.2).
- Areal O2 influx at steady state without consumption: J_in ≈ (P_RP/L)·pO2(ext). Use this to set the minimum volumetric getter capacity Q (mol O2 per m³ cap) and kinetics k_cons such that k_cons·C >> D_RP/L² during illumination (reaction-limited → diffusion-limited switch), producing a near-surface depletion layer.
- Design output: predicted ΔpO2(x=L) vs time under 1 sun for each (L, loading, k_cons(T)). Predefine measurable target: ΔpO2(interface) ≥ 50 mbar at 1 sun, 1 atm air, 25–65 °C for ≥ 30 min.
0.2 Coupled EM–thermal model (AuNS heating bounds):
- EM absorption: compute AuNS absorption cross-section σ_abs(λ) via FDTD for geometries spanning plasmon peak 780–850 nm (on-resonant) and 550–650 nm (off-resonant control). Include dielectric shell (SiO2 or Al2O3, t_shell = 1.5 ± 0.5 nm) and embedding medium refractive index matching RP-2D.
- Power absorbed per particle under AM1.5G: P_abs = ∫σ_abs(λ)·I_solar(λ)dλ.
- Heat diffusion: solve steady-state and transient ΔT(r,t) with multilayer thermal resistances (AuNS shell/RP-2D/CTL) and encapsulation boundary condition. Output two temperature metrics: (i) local peak at particle surface ΔT_peak, (ii) laterally averaged interface temperature rise ΔT_avg over 1–10 µm.
- Predefine activation window: getter activation onset at 40–55 °C equivalent local temperature, but enforce safety: ΔT_avg(interface) ≤ 5–8 °C above baseline module temperature and absolute interface T ≤ 70 °C during ISOS-L-2 at 65 °C (to avoid strong ion-migration acceleration). If model predicts exceedance, reduce AuNS loading or detune resonance.

Step 1 — Device baselines and architecture (dual polarity retained):
1.1 Baseline stacks:
- n–i–p: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA0.85Cs0.15)Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/RP-2D-cap/HTL(A)/Au.
- p–i–n: glass/ITO/2PACz/(FA0.85Cs0.15)Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/RP-2D-cap/C60/BCP/Ag.
1.2 RP-2D cap chemistry (orthogonal solvent, confined conversion):
- Cations: PEA+:FA+ (or PEA+:Cs+) targeting n=1–3 RP distribution; total cap thickness L = 5, 10, 20 nm.
- Solvent system: IPA/EtOAc (or MeOAc) to avoid 3D dissolution; confirm confinement by GIWAXS and cross-sectional ToF-SIMS.

Step 2 — AuNS nanoheater: geometry, insulation, and optoelectronic controls.
2.1 Au nanostar synthesis with resonance control:
- On-resonant AuNS: plasmon peak 780–850 nm (tail harvesting), tuned via tip length and core size.
- Off-resonant AuNS control: peak 550–650 nm (minimal NIR absorption under 750–900 nm) but similar size distribution.
2.2 Insulating shell:
- ALD Al2O3 (1.0–2.0 nm) or sol–gel SiO2 (1–2 nm), validated by TEM and XPS.
- Functional requirement: suppress direct electronic contact/halide adsorption; verify by comparing PL quenching and dark J–V leakage vs bare AuNS.
2.3 Loading constraints:
- AuNS volume fraction 0.005–0.03 vol% (model-driven) to cap parasitic absorption/scattering; optical penalty budget: ΔJsc ≤ 0.3 mA cm−2 relative to RP-2D-only.

Step 3 — Replace/augment sulfite-release with perovskite-benign O2 getter family; structured compatibility screening.
3.1 Getter family selection (two-track, with explicit byproduct rationale):
Track A (primary): Sterically hindered phenolic/aminoxyl redox buffer immobilized in the RP-2D (polymerizable or ammonium-tethered), designed to reduce O2 to non-radical products via proton-coupled pathways while minimizing free ionic byproducts.
- Example motif class (spec): tethered TEMPOH/TEMPO-type redox couple or hindered phenol (BHT-like) derivatives with quaternary ammonium anchoring to the RP organic layer to reduce volatility/migration.
- Rationale: well-characterized radical-termination chemistry, no strong acids/bases generated; immobilization reduces dopant poisoning.
Track B (secondary, reversible 1O2 trap): anthracene-endoperoxide chemistry but only as a spectroscopic reporter + auxiliary trap at low loading (≤0.05 mol% vs organic cation), not the main O2 getter.
- Rationale: provides direct readout of 1O2 capture; kept low to minimize photochemistry/side reactions.
Sulfite/bisulfite-release is demoted to a conditional branch: used only if Track A cannot reach ΔpO2 target; if used, it triggers an explicit iodide/iodate/iodine + HTL-dopant integrity assay suite (see 3.3).
3.2 Getter activation mechanism (thermal thresholding):
- Implement “latent” state via thermally cleavable protecting group or phase-segregated reservoir domains in RP-2D. Activation temperature from DSC/VT-FTIR: onset 40–55 °C, half-activation 55–65 °C.
- Microstructure: mixed bulky cations (PEA + fluorinated PEA) to create reservoir nanodomains without blocking vertical transport; confirm by AFM-IR/nano-FTIR mapping and GIWAXS.
3.3 Compatibility screening structured by failure mode (before full devices):
(A) Halide/perovskite redox compatibility:
- Expose neat RP-2D/getter films on 3D perovskite to 65 °C dark for 250 h; quantify I0/I3−/IO3− speciation by XPS + UV–vis extraction assay; track Pb0 formation.
(B) Iodoplumbate complexation / dissolution risk:
- Solid-state NMR (where possible) or FTIR shifts + ToF-SIMS for getter fragments at the 3D interface; monitor PbI2 formation by GIWAXS.
(C) HTL dopant integrity (spiro/PTAA systems):
- Contact-angle controlled bilayers getter|HTL dopant mixture; quantify LiTFSI/tBP signatures (NMR/FTIR), conductivity changes, and work-function shifts (UPS/KPFM).
(D) Interfacial dipole/Voc shifts:
- UPS/KPFM on perovskite with RP-2D, RP-2D+AuNS, RP-2D+getter, full stack; acceptance: ΔWF ≤ 50 meV vs RP-2D-only.
(E) Volatility/migration:
- TGA-MS for getter; ToF-SIMS depth after 1 sun/65 °C for 100 h; acceptance: no getter signal in CTL beyond detection threshold.

Step 4 — Build the functional interlayer and program the release/activation profile.
4.1 Interlayer deposition (“AuNS@RP-2D–Getter”):
- Spin-coat RP-2D precursor containing AuNS + latent getter; thicknesses L = 5/10/20 nm; getter loading 0.1–1.0 mol% relative to RP organic cation (final loading chosen by mass-balance target).
- Anneal conditions tuned to lock morphology without driving getter diffusion (e.g., 80–100 °C, 2–5 min).
4.2 Dark-storage + thermal-aging controls (decouple photothermal from thermal):
- Dark at 25 °C, 50% RH: 500 h.
- Dark at 65 °C, dry N2 and in air: 250 h.
- Light soaking at 1 sun with active cooling holding substrate temperature constant (photothermal discrimination experiment).

Step 5 — Validation: directly measure O2 suppression, temperature, ROS reduction, and optoelectronic invariance.
5.1 O2 permeability/diffusivity calibration (feeds model):
- Measure O2 transmission rate (OTR) or permeation through standalone RP-2D films on inert substrates; extract P_RP.
- Measure D_RP and S via time-resolved O2 uptake using luminescent O2 probes embedded above/below the film.
5.2 ΔpO2 at the buried interface (primary feasibility readout):
- Use lifetime-based O2 sensing layer (ultrathin, optically transparent) placed immediately above the RP-2D or within a calibrated overlayer; perform calibrated pO2 mapping under 1 sun.
- Report ΔpO2(interface-equivalent) in mbar vs time; compare to model predictions for each L/loading.
5.3 Thermal verification vs model:
- IR microscopy for ΔT_avg; pump–probe thermoreflectance for localized heating signatures.
- Acceptance gate: measured ΔT_avg ≤ 5–8 °C above baseline under 1 sun; absolute interface T ≤ 70 °C during 65 °C environmental tests.
5.4 ROS quantification (mechanism confirmation):
- In-operando EPR spin trapping: TEMP→TEMPO (1O2) and DMPO adducts (O2•− proxy) under controlled pO2.
- Acceptance target: ≥50% reduction in 1O2/O2•− EPR signal at 1 sun in air vs RP-2D-only.
5.5 Optoelectronic controls to isolate chemistry vs optics/heating:
- Controls matrix:
  (i) Baseline (no cap)
  (ii) RP-2D only
  (iii) RP-2D + getter (no AuNS)
  (iv) RP-2D + on-resonant AuNS (no getter)
  (v) RP-2D + off-resonant AuNS + getter (heating minimized)
  (vi) RP-2D + inert dielectric nanoparticles matched scattering (e.g., SiO2 20–40 nm) + getter
  (vii) Full: RP-2D + on-resonant AuNS + getter
- Acceptance gates (must remain within tolerance vs RP-2D-only):
  • Ideality factor n (Suns–Voc) change ≤ 0.05
  • Interfacial recombination velocity proxy from TPV/TPC unchanged within ±10%
  • ΔVoc within ±10 mV; ΔFF within ±1% absolute at matched Jsc.

Step 6 — Stability testing and failure forensics (tie outcomes back to ΔpO2 and ΔT):
6.1 Operational stability:
- ISOS-L-2 and MPP tracking at 65 °C in controlled 20–50% RH air; record Voc/FF hysteresis evolution.
- Include “constant-temperature light soaking” (substrate temperature clamped) to prove photothermal triggering, not generic heating.
6.2 Post-mortem diagnostics:
- XPS: I0/I3−, Pb0, oxidized iodine species; quantify suppression.
- GIWAXS: phase segregation (Br/I) and RP integrity.
- Cross-sectional TEM/EDS: AuNS distribution, shell integrity.
- ToF-SIMS: getter localization; absence in CTL.

Quantitative success criteria (updated with mandatory ΔpO2/thermal gates):
- ΔpO2(interface-equivalent) ≥ 50 mbar sustained for ≥30 min under 1 sun in air (stretch: ≥200 mbar for ≥60 min), with model/experiment agreement within 2× on timescale.
- ΔT_avg(interface) ≤ 5–8 °C above baseline under 1 sun; absolute interface T ≤ 70 °C in 65 °C chamber.
- ROS suppression: ≥50% reduction of 1O2/O2•− EPR signals under 1 sun in air.
- Device metrics preserved: ΔVoc ≤ ±10 mV; ΔFF ≤ ±1% absolute; unchanged ideality factor within 0.05; TPV-derived lifetime within ±10% vs RP-2D-only.
- Stability: ≥2× improvement in T80 at MPP, 65 °C, 20–50% RH air vs baseline and ≥1.5× vs RP-2D-only (to rule out generic capping effect).
Feasibility: This revision directly closes the reviewers’ four feasibility gaps by making the concept quantitatively predictive and falsifiable.

(1) Interfacial O2 suppression in a 5–20 nm cap is now mass-balance constrained rather than asserted. The 1D reaction–diffusion model explicitly links (i) RP-2D permeability (P_RP) and thickness (L) to an areal O2 influx J_in, and (ii) getter areal capacity/kinetics (Q, k_cons) to the attainable depletion depth and ΔpO2 at the buried interface. The proposal commits to measuring P_RP/D_RP/S and to reporting ΔpO2 in mbar via calibrated lifetime O2 sensing, with a predefined target (≥50–200 mbar) and a model/experiment agreement requirement. This prevents overclaiming “hypoxia-like” behavior and instead quantifies what “meaningful” interfacial oxygen-potential reduction means for PSC stability.

(2) Nanoscale heating is bounded by a coupled EM–thermal model and validated experimentally, preventing inadvertent global overheating. FDTD-derived σ_abs(λ) under AM1.5G sets P_abs per particle; multilayer heat diffusion yields both ΔT_peak (near AuNS) and ΔT_avg (device-relevant). The plan predefines a thermal activation window for getter deprotection/activation (40–65 °C local-equivalent) while imposing strict acceptance gates (ΔT_avg ≤ 5–8 °C; absolute interface T ≤ 70 °C at 65 °C stress) to avoid accelerating ion migration. Off-resonant AuNS and constant-temperature light soaking are included to decouple “photothermal triggering” from generic thermal stress.

(3) Chemical plausibility is strengthened by replacing sulfite/bisulfite as the default path with an immobilized, perovskite-benign getter family whose byproducts and mobility are controlled (anchored/tethered redox buffers and radical terminators). The screening is reorganized around explicit perovskite failure modes: iodine speciation (I0/I3−/IO3−), Pb0 formation, iodoplumbate complexation, HTL dopant deactivation (LiTFSI/tBP integrity), interfacial dipole-induced Voc shifts (UPS/KPFM), and volatility/migration (TGA-MS/ToF-SIMS). Sulfite-release is retained only as a conditional branch, and if pursued it is tied to mandatory iodide/iodate/iodine + dopant-integrity assays.

(4) Optoelectronic ambiguity from AuNS (parasitics, near-field, hot-carriers) is addressed with a stricter control matrix and explicit acceptance gates. Off-resonant AuNS (geometry control) and inert dielectric nanoparticles with matched scattering isolate optical effects from chemistry. Ideality factor (Suns–Voc) and TPV/TPC-derived recombination metrics are set as go/no-go criteria to ensure stability gains are not purchased by hidden recombination changes. An explicit optical penalty budget (ΔJsc ≤ 0.3 mA cm−2) prevents stability “wins” dominated by reduced photon flux.

Finally, the mechanism remains coherent with the original chain: Au-driven photothermal conversion is used not to amplify ROS (as in AuNP-assisted biomedical cascades) but to time-gate oxygen-getter activation and thereby suppress oxygen-mediated ROS formation at PSC interfaces. The RP-2D cap still provides passivation and ingress resistance, but the revised design explicitly requires that gains exceed RP-2D-only controls and be quantitatively correlated to ΔpO2 and ΔT measurements—turning a creative concept into a closed, testable engineering hypothesis.
final_critique: Methodological resolution is strong: the 1D mass-balance framework, explicit measurables (P_RP, D_RP, S, ΔpO2), and thermal bounding with on/off-resonant AuNS controls address common ‘hand-wavy’ failure modes in interfacial stability claims. The main logical risk is chemical: the proposed “perovskite-benign, thermally activated oxygen-getter family” (tethered TEMPOH/TEMPO or hindered phenols) is not yet demonstrated to (i) provide sufficient areal O2 consumption capacity/kinetics in a 5–20 nm layer at 1 atm air, and (ii) avoid forming reactive intermediates (peroxyl/hydroperoxides) that can still oxidize iodide or alter interfacial energetics. The ΔpO2 target (50–200 mbar sustained) may be difficult to achieve without either very low RP permeability or a getter with unusually high volumetric capacity; the proposal outlines the model but does not present even order-of-magnitude parameter priors showing feasibility. Evidence grounding against the required concept chain is mixed: AuNP photothermal and ROS are well integrated, but “Fenton reaction” and “hypoxic tumors” are conceptually imported rather than scientifically mapped onto the PSC context (no Fenton analogue, no tumor-relevant release biology).
hypothesis_summary: A photothermally triggered, oxygen-getter layer embedded in a perovskite solar cell’s ultrathin capping film can predictably and temporarily suppress interfacial oxygen levels during illumination, reducing harmful reactive oxygen species without degrading the device’s electronic quality.

original_chain: Utilization ratio -> Specific surface area -> 1.0 M KOH solution -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Organic solvents -> Thermal stability
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A quantitatively percolated, ultrathin MOF-confined interphase (CCMI) can simultaneously preserve efficient electron extraction and suppress thermally activated interfacial degradation in perovskite solar cells if—and only if—its pore network exceeds a defined electronic and ionic transport window. Specifically, when a 10–20 nm MOF scaffold with open-pore connectivity (>70% accessible porosity, pore apertures ≥0.6 nm) is conformally anchored to SnO2, confined iodoplumbate crystallization within this scaffold will (i) reduce interfacial recombination by enforcing nanoscale nucleation that lowers defect formation energy and lattice anharmonicity at the ETL interface, and (ii) mechanically and electrostatically disrupt continuous ion-vacancy percolation pathways. The apparent ‘utilization advantage’ of the MOF arises not from an abstract defect-count ratio, but from a constrained shift in the interfacial recombination velocity and ionic activation energy that can be uniquely inferred from temperature-dependent Suns-Voc, impedance, and TRPL fits to a unified interface-recombination/ion-migration model. A spatially limited 1.0 M KOH edge-dosing step is viable only within a narrow diffusion–reaction regime where hydroxide penetration length in the MOF (<15 nm for ≤30 s exposure) is sufficient to neutralize trapped acidic iodoplumbate species and precipitate K–I/Br–O nanophases at pore mouths, yet remains below the threshold for bulk perovskite hydrolysis or K+ exchange. Under these bounded conditions, the CCMI architecture delivers a stability and Voc-retention advantage that cannot be replicated by planar alkali-halide, 2D/3D, or zwitterionic passivation layers at matched initial performance.
Plan: 1. Quantitative definition of the CCMI electronic process window.
1.1 MOF scaffold selection and thickness gating: Focus on UiO-66-X (X = H, NHCO, Py at 1–3% linker substitution) and Al-fumarate grown by vapor-assisted or spray layer-by-layer deposition. Target thickness series: 5, 10, 15, 20, 30 nm. Reject any condition with BET-accessible porosity <70% or average pore aperture <0.6 nm (from powder analogs + ellipsometric porosimetry).
1.2 Electronic extraction criteria (go/no-go): Measure contact resistivity (ρc) across SnO2/CCMI/perovskite using TLM/cTLM and illuminated impedance. Acceptance thresholds: (i) ΔRs ≤ 0.3 Ω·cm2 relative to no-MOF control; (ii) extracted electron mobility across CCMI ≥ 50% of SnO2/perovskite reference; (iii) no inflection in FF vs thickness up to 15–20 nm. Thicknesses failing these criteria are excluded from subsequent chemistry steps.

2. Confined perovskite nucleation with percolation assurance.
2.1 Surface anchoring and pore opening: Use carboxylate-silane priming of SnO2 and modulated MOF growth (water-dominant synthesis with monotopic acid modulators) to deliberately introduce missing-linker defects that ensure pore interconnection without collapsing mechanical integrity.
2.2 Infiltration protocol with quantitative fill-factor: Introduce iodoplumbate-rich precursor (FAI/CsI:PbI2/PbBr2 = halide excess, 0.5–0.7 M) via 3–5 spin–vacuum pulses. Quantify pore filling by quartz crystal microbalance (QCM) on planar analogs and confirm retained electronic continuity by in situ Kelvin probe during infiltration.
2.3 Confined crystallization trigger: Apply antisolvent vapor (EA or IPA) at controlled activity to induce nucleation inside pores first. Mild anneal (80–90 °C) to crystallize confined interphase before bulk deposition.

3. Bounded hydroxide/K+ transport–reaction modeling and validation.
3.1 Diffusion–reaction model: Treat MOF as a tortuous porous medium; estimate hydroxide diffusion coefficient (DOH,MOF ~10−8–10−9 cm2·s−1). Define exposure times (10, 20, 30, 60 s) such that diffusion length (L = (2DOH·t)1/2) remains ≤15 nm for go conditions. Any evidence of deeper penetration is a stop criterion.
3.2 Edge-fed dosing experiment: Perform 1.0 M KOH dosing only on fully buried stacks (no top electrode) via microfluidics. Immediately quench edges with CO2-free water.
3.3 Chemical speciation proof: Use cryo-ToF-SIMS with 18O/D-labeled KOH and angle-resolved XPS to map K–I/Br–O species. Required outcome: K-containing phases localized within CCMI region with no measurable K+ signal in bulk perovskite (>30 nm from ETL). Overexposed controls establish failure boundary.

4. Replace utilization ratio with constrained interfacial recombination inference.
4.1 Unified model: Fit temperature-dependent Suns-Voc, impedance (recombination resistance + ionic branch), and TRPL (ETL-side excitation) to extract interfacial recombination velocity (S) and ionic activation energy (Ea,ion).
4.2 Calibration: Generate reference devices with known interfacial trap densities via controlled Pb0 or halide-vacancy creation (light soaking or reductive bias) and via titrated doses of a known passivant. Use these to anchor the model and ensure identifiability.
4.3 Success metric: CCMI must show ≥2× reduction in S and ≥0.15–0.25 eV increase in Ea,ion relative to no-MOF and planar-passivated controls.

5. Benchmarking against state-of-the-art passivation.
5.1 Fabricate reference devices with alkali-halide layers, 2D/3D perovskite caps, and zwitterionic SAMs tuned to achieve matched initial Voc/FF.
5.2 Compare Voc retention, T80 at 65–85 °C, and hysteresis evolution. CCMI advantage is claimed only if superior stability persists at matched initial performance.

6. Decision gates and scalability.
6.1 Go/no-go gates at: (i) electronic extraction (Step 1), (ii) chemical localization of KOH effects (Step 3), and (iii) stability gain beyond benchmarks (Step 5).
6.2 Scale best CCMI condition to blade-coated 10 cm2 mini-modules to verify transport and stability trends under realistic deposition.
Feasibility: This revision directly resolves the reviewers’ high-risk concerns by replacing qualitative assumptions with bounded, testable criteria. Electronic extraction through the CCMI is no longer presumed; it is explicitly constrained by contact resistivity, series-resistance increments, and illuminated impedance as a function of MOF thickness and porosity, ensuring that only percolated, electronically benign scaffolds are pursued. The chemical risk of 1.0 M KOH is mitigated through a diffusion–reaction model that defines allowable exposure times and penetration depths, coupled with cryo-ToF-SIMS and angle-resolved XPS to prove localization and speciation of K–I/Br–O products. The problematic ‘utilization ratio’ is replaced by an identifiable, model-based inference of interfacial recombination velocity and ionic activation energy, calibrated against intentional trap-density standards. Finally, benchmarking against leading non-MOF passivation strategies at matched Voc/FF ensures that any observed gains are structurally unique to CCMI rather than generic passivation effects. Together, these refinements convert speculative links (confinement, hydroxide chemistry) into quantitatively gated mechanisms aligned with the original CCMI concept.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-structured proposal that demonstrates strong command of both perovskite interfacial physics and MOF chemistry. The major strength lies in converting historically qualitative or post hoc explanations (utilization ratio, generic passivation) into quantitatively gated, falsifiable mechanisms with clear go/no-go criteria. Engineering resolution is very high: contact resistivity gating, pore-accessibility thresholds, diffusion-length calculations, and chemical localization proofs are all technically credible and state of the art. Logical consistency is likewise strong, particularly in tying confinement-induced crystallization, disrupted ionic percolation, and recombination velocity into a unified interface model. Minor logical risk remains in the assumption that powder-analog BET/ellipsometric porosimetry sufficiently represents ultrathin, substrate-bound MOF films; while acknowledged indirectly, this extrapolation could weaken mechanistic certainty if thin-film pore collapse or anisotropy occurs. Evidence grounding is solid and remains within the required concept chain, though the role of organic solvents is largely instrumental (antisolvent vapor, processing medium) rather than mechanistically central. Rationale quality is high: the CCMI is not a trivial passivation layer but a structurally constrained interphase designed to access a regime unattainable by planar treatments. Overall, score deductions are minor and relate primarily to residual uncertainty in thin-film MOF pore fidelity and the ambitious identifiability of multi-parameter model fitting.
hypothesis_summary: A percolated, ultrathin MOF-confined interphase reduces interfacial recombination and blocks ion migration in perovskite solar cells, but only when its pore network meets strict electronic and ionic transport thresholds.

original_chain: Charge transfer -> Dye-sensitized solar cells (DSSC) -> Photoelectrochemical cells -> Power conversion efficiency (PCE) -> Non-radiative recombination
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A dual-interface-loss–minimized perovskite photoelectrochemical (PEC) platform can be realized by (i) replacing the conventional nanocrystal mesoporous ETL with a manufacturable, low-thermal-budget “PSC-like” mesoporous oxide scaffold whose *connectivity and texture are quantitatively engineered* to produce near-single-crystal electron percolation paths, and (ii) implementing a *dose-limited, verifiably sub-tunneling-length* AgI interlayer at the hole contact that reduces barrier-limited hole extraction and interfacial non-radiative recombination without triggering Ag/Cu/halide-driven failure. Mechanistically, the PSC-like scaffold outperforms nanoparticle ETLs not by increasing surface area alone (which can increase interface traps), but by reducing the energetic/kinetic penalty of grain boundaries through (a) higher crystallographic coherence length and (b) lower tortuosity percolation, which together shorten electron transport time (τtr) and reduce electron residence time at the oxide/perovskite interface; the predicted outcome is a measurable drop in interfacial recombination velocity (S) because recombination becomes extraction-limited less often. In parallel, a tightly controlled AgI layer (≤2 nm, continuous) at the HTL/metal interface provides field-assisted tunneling and mitigates interfacial band-bending and defect-mediated recombination (reduced SRH via halide-vacancy passivation and reduced barrier height), increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting (Voc) and FF. The PEC mode is not treated as an add-on; instead, a pinhole-validated inorganic barrier and a kinetic model that separates interfacial charge-transfer resistance (Rct) from diffusion/ohmic limits enables mapping of PEC-derived interfacial kinetics (Rct, recombination resistance, τrec) onto PV-mode non-radiative losses (PLQY/EQEEL-derived ΔVoc,nr), thereby preserving the DSSC → PEC kinetics → PV loss-analysis chain with falsifiable, gated milestones.
Plan: WP0 (Platform definition and preregistration of gates)
- Device absorber: FA0.83Cs0.17Pb(I0.9Br0.1)3 (or iodide-rich variant if required for AgI formation), identical crystallization across all arms (same precursor molarity, antisolvent timing, anneal).
- Two stack polarities for decoupling contacts:
  (R) regular: Glass/ITO/ETL/Perovskite/HTL/Metal
  (I) inverted: Glass/ITO/HTL/Perovskite/ETL/Metal
- Pre-register quantitative success criteria for each WP (below) and lock two ETL controls + four AgI controls.

WP1 (Highest-risk item #1): Manufacturable PSC-like mesoporous ETL scaffold with measurable texture/connectivity
Goal: deliver a reproducible recipe that yields a mesoporous oxide scaffold with (a) controlled porosity without collapse, (b) high crystallographic coherence, (c) measurable preferential orientation/texture, and (d) superior electronic transport vs state-of-the-art ETL controls under identical perovskite infiltration.

WP1.1 Scaffold fabrication (two manufacturable routes; one must pass gates)
Route A: Block-copolymer templated sol–gel + photonic/flash crystallization (low substrate thermal budget)
- Precursor: TiO2 (titanium alkoxide sol–gel) or SnO2 (tin chloride/alkoxide sol–gel) with amphiphilic BCP template (e.g., Pluronic F127/PS-b-PEO class) tuned for 10–30 nm pores.
- Film thickness: 120, 180, 240 nm (spin or slot-die on test substrates).
- Template removal + crystallization:
  - UV-ozone/oxygen plasma partial removal (to prevent catastrophic shrinkage), then photonic curing (xenon flash) with energy density sweep (e.g., 1–10 J cm−2, 1–10 pulses) under controlled ambient (N2/O2 ratio) to crystallize without prolonged heating.
  - Collapse-avoidance control: in situ ellipsometry (thickness shrinkage limit ≤20%) and ex situ porosimetry (see metrics).
Route B: Seeded nanocrystal “necking” + mild solvothermal fusion (≤150 °C)
- Deposit a mesoporous layer from monodisperse TiO2 or SnO2 nanocrystals (pre-synthesized, ligand-stripped) with a removable porogen.
- Apply aqueous/alcoholic solvothermal treatment (120–150 °C, sealed, ≤2 h) to induce oriented attachment/necking (grain boundary reduction) while preserving mesoporosity.
- Rationale: avoids flash-induced heterogeneous sintering; provides a second manufacturable path.

WP1.2 Quantitative structural metrics (pass/fail gates)
For each scaffold condition, measure:
1) Texture/orientation: GIWAXS texture factor (Herman’s orientation parameter or equivalent) with target: ≥0.3 increase vs nanoparticle mesoporous control; report pole figures.
2) Crystallinity/coherence: cross-sectional TEM + FFT-derived coherence length distribution; target median coherence length ≥30 nm with narrow distribution (IQR ≤20 nm).
3) Porosity/tortuosity: ellipsometric porosimetry or GISAXS-derived pore size; target pore diameter 15–25 nm; porosity 30–50%; tortuosity factor τtort ≤2.0 (extracted from diffusion of small probe molecules or reconstructed tomography on a subset).
4) Electronic transport in scaffold (without perovskite): TRMC (preferred) or contacted conductivity; target ≥3× increase in effective electron mobility/conductivity vs nanoparticle mesoporous ETL at comparable thickness.
5) Interface trap propensity screen: XPS (surface hydroxylation), UPS (work function), and a standardized perovskite-on-ETL PL quenching/PL lifetime assay to flag trap-rich surfaces.
Gate WP1 “GO”: meet criteria (2 of 3 structural targets + transport target) without porosity collapse (shrinkage ≤20%, continuous film by SEM).

WP1.3 Benchmark against two ETL controls (mandatory)
Controls fabricated and infiltrated identically:
C1: Standard mesoporous nanoparticle TiO2 (or SnO2) + compact layer.
C2: Nanowire/compact bilayer ETL (e.g., hydrothermal nanowires on compact or aligned nanorods) OR a state-of-the-art planar SnO2 with passivation (e.g., KCl/alkali passivated) as the “fast-transport/low-area” comparator.
All three ETLs receive the same perovskite infiltration protocol (WP1.4).

WP1.4 Identical perovskite infiltration protocol (controls interfacial chemistry)
- Vacuum-assisted infiltration into mesopores (standardized vacuum dose/time), solvent system fixed.
- Cap layer: thin 3D perovskite overlayer (e.g., 200–400 nm total absorber) to form hybrid meso/planar.
- Void quantification: cross-sectional SEM/TEM + image analysis (void fraction target ≤5%).

WP1.5 Kinetic performance gates linking structure → PV/PEC metrics
Primary transport/recombination targets (pre-registered):
- IMPS-derived transport time constant τtr: ≥2× reduction vs C1 at matched Jsc.
- TRPL (interface-sensitive excitation) or PLQY-derived implied Voc: ≥50% reduction in interfacial recombination velocity proxy (e.g., increased PL lifetime at ETL interface; or ΔVoc,nr improvement ≥25 mV vs C1).
- Device-level: FF improvement ≥2 absolute percentage points vs C1 in PV mode without sacrificing Jsc.

WP2 (Highest-risk item #2): AgI tunneling interlayer with thickness-control strategy, falsifiable tunneling criteria, and degradation forensics
Goal: obtain an AgI interlayer that is (i) continuous, (ii) in the tunneling thickness regime, (iii) reduces contact barrier and non-radiative recombination, and (iv) does not accelerate ion-migration-driven degradation (filamenting, Ag penetration, Cu corrosion).

WP2.1 Architecture and controlled Ag reservoir
- Base anode: Cu (as stress-test + cost focus).
- Ag source options (evaluate both):
  A) Sub-nm to 2 nm evaporated Ag between HTL and Cu (Ag(0) reservoir).
  B) Ag-doped HTL (low loading) + Cu, no discrete Ag film (reduces filament risk).
- HTLs: at least two chemically distinct HTLs to test generality and rule out HTL-specific effects (e.g., Spiro-OMeTAD vs PTAA vs NiOx-based).

WP2.2 Iodide chemical potential control without destabilizing perovskite
- “I-source” introduced only at the immediate HTL interface using a confined iodide reservoir (e.g., trace iodide salt in HTL topcoat or self-assembled iodide-bearing molecule), with total iodide areal density pre-calibrated.
- Hard constraint: perovskite stoichiometry/phase unchanged (GIWAXS peak positions/phase fraction stable; no new PbI2 beyond baseline).

WP2.3 Conditioning dose as the quantitative control loop (thickness-limited formation)
- Define conditioning “dose” D = (light intensity × time) + (bias × time) at fixed temperature; run a matrix (e.g., 0.1, 0.5, 1, 2 “sun·hour equivalents” with/without forward bias).
- After each dose, measure AgI thickness/continuity (WP2.4) and contact resistivity/barrier (WP2.5). Stop conditioning when tunneling criteria met or when Rs rises.

WP2.4 Direct thickness/continuity measurements (mandatory)
- Cross-sectional TEM/EELS on representative devices after specific D to quantify AgI thickness; target: continuous layer 0.5–2.0 nm; reject if >3 nm or discontinuous islands.
- Angle-resolved XPS depth profiling to confirm Ag–I chemical state and spatial confinement.

WP2.5 Falsifiable tunneling/contact criteria
- Contact resistivity via TLM (or c-TLM): target ≥30% reduction vs Ag-free Cu contact without increasing series resistance in full device.
- Barrier height/work-function alignment: UPS and/or KPFM; target measurable reduction in hole-injection barrier (ΔΦ ≥0.1–0.2 eV vs control).
- Non-radiative recombination metrics: EQEEL or PLQY-derived ΔVoc,nr improvement ≥20 mV at matched current density.
Gate WP2 “GO”: meet thickness window + improved contact resistivity + improved ΔVoc,nr with no Rs penalty.

WP2.6 Hard controls (mandatory falsification set)
- Ag-free control: HTL/Cu.
- I-source-free control: Ag present but no iodide reservoir.
- Halide variant controls: AgCl, AgBr (tests whether “AgX tunneling” is generic or iodide-specific).
- HTL dependence: at least two HTLs.

WP2.7 Degradation forensics and filament suppression
- ToF-SIMS depth profiles pre/post stress (illumination + bias) to detect Ag migration into perovskite and Cu diffusion.
- Cross-sectional SEM/TEM to identify filamenting/short pathways.
- Electrical signature: monitor hysteresis, shunt formation, and noise spectroscopy if available.
- Fail criteria: detectable Ag penetration into perovskite bulk above threshold (pre-defined SIMS signal ratio), rapid shunt increase, or catastrophic Rs increase.

WP3 (Highest-risk item #3): PEC barrier integrity, edge sealing, and kinetic model separating Rct from transport limits
Goal: create a PEC-operable perovskite device whose electrolyte-facing barrier is demonstrably pinhole-free at the relevant timescale, with a kinetic model that allows extraction of true interfacial charge-transfer parameters.

WP3.1 Barrier layer + edge seal (manufacturable stack)
- Barrier: ALD nanolaminate (e.g., Al2O3/SnO2 or Al2O3/TiO2), total 10–20 nm on the electrolyte-facing side (choose configuration based on illumination geometry).
- Edge seal: UV-curable epoxy + glass cap or chemically resistant encapsulant; define overlap/edge distance.

WP3.2 Pinhole/leakage testing (mandatory pass/fail)
- Electrochemical leakage: measure dark current in electrolyte vs bias; define maximum leakage current density (e.g., ≤10−6–10−5 A cm−2 at relevant bias) and stable over time.
- Dye-penetration test (analogous to barrier pinhole visualization): expose to dye/redox marker; inspect optical/PL change mapping.
- “Ca-test analog” for ionic ingress: use an ion-sensitive layer or electrical proxy to detect ingress rate; set threshold.
Gate WP3 “GO”: pass leakage + dye penetration + stability of leakage over defined soak time.

WP3.3 PEC electrolyte selection and compatibility screen
- Use non-aqueous redox mediators first (iodide/triiodide; cobalt complex) with defined diffusion coefficients; exclude mediators that chemically attack HTL/ETL.
- Compatibility: soak tests on isolated transport layers + barrier to quantify chemical change (XPS/UPS) before full PEC runs.

WP3.4 Kinetic model and parameter extraction (Rct vs diffusion/ohmic)
- Use EIS under illumination with equivalent circuit that includes: series resistance (Rs), charge-transfer resistance (Rct), chemical capacitance, diffusion element (Warburg) for mediator transport.
- Vary mediator concentration and stirring/flow to separate diffusion limitation from interfacial kinetics (Rct should be invariant with transport once diffusion is alleviated).
- Define mass-transport limit current; operate below this regime for kinetic mapping.

WP3.5 Mapping PEC kinetics to PV non-radiative losses (closing the chain)
- On the same physical device architecture (or sister devices), measure PV-mode PLQY/EQEEL and Suns-Voc to quantify ΔVoc,nr.
- Correlate changes in PEC-extracted recombination resistance/τrec (and ETL/HTL-specific Rct) with ΔVoc,nr and FF losses across ETL/AgI conditions.
Success criterion: statistically significant correlation (predefined) demonstrating that the same interface modifications shift both PEC Rct/τrec and PV ΔVoc,nr/FF in the predicted direction.

WP4 Integrated demonstration and stability
- PV benchmarking: stabilized MPP tracking, J–V hysteresis index, temperature-dependent Voc/FF to identify barrier-limited extraction.
- Stability matrix:
  (i) PV: continuous illumination in N2 (500–1000 h), plus elevated temperature subset.
  (ii) PEC: bias + illumination in electrolyte with barrier; track photocurrent retention.
- Post-mortem: ToF-SIMS/XPS/TEM on both contacts + barrier for failure attribution (Ag/Cu migration vs barrier pinholes vs interfacial decomposition).
Feasibility: Risk 1 (PSC-like scaffold manufacturability and true advantage): The revised plan replaces qualitative claims (“oriented, fused single-crystal domains”) with two concrete low-temperature fabrication routes and explicit, measurable structure/connectivity targets (GIWAXS texture factor, TEM coherence length distribution, porosity/tortuosity, TRMC/contacted transport). The advantage over nanoparticle ETLs is tested under identical perovskite infiltration with void quantification and against two strong ETL controls (nanoparticle mesoporous and nanowire/planar fast-transport control). Go/no-go gates are pre-registered in kinetic terms directly tied to the DSSC→PEC→PV logic (≥2× τtr reduction by IMPS; ≥25 mV ΔVoc,nr improvement or ≥50% interface recombination proxy reduction).

Risk 2 (AgI interlayer underconstrained and potentially destabilizing): The AgI element is converted into a dose-controlled, thickness-verified interlayer with falsifiable tunneling criteria: direct thickness/continuity measurement after defined conditioning doses (TEM/EELS, angle-resolved XPS), and correlation to contact resistivity (TLM) and barrier height (UPS/KPFM). Hard controls (Ag-free, I-source-free, AgCl/AgBr, multiple HTLs) make the “self-optimizing” hypothesis testable rather than assumed. Degradation forensics (ToF-SIMS for Ag/Cu migration; filament detection by cross-sectional microscopy; electrical shunt/Rs monitoring) provide explicit fail conditions to prevent pursuing a marginal efficiency gain that compromises stability.

Risk 3 (PEC idealization, pinholes/edge ingress, and kinetic ambiguity): The PEC module now includes barrier pinhole testing with quantitative pass/fail thresholds, an explicit edge-sealing protocol, and a kinetic modeling strategy that separates interfacial Rct from diffusion/ohmic limitations by varying mediator concentration and hydrodynamic conditions. Only after operating below mass-transport limits and passing leakage/pinhole gates will PEC-derived kinetics be used to map onto PV-mode non-radiative recombination metrics. This ensures the mechanistic linkage is defensible and not confounded by electrolyte transport or barrier failure.

Overall feasibility: Each high-risk innovation is now a gated work package with measurable structural/electrical criteria, mandatory controls, and failure forensics. This preserves the original DSSC-inspired rationale (high-area charge-transfer interface) while addressing the perovskite-specific failure modes (interface traps, ion migration, contact barriers, electrolyte ingress) with quantitative control loops and benchmarked comparisons.
final_critique: This is an unusually well-resolved and internally disciplined proposal with pre-registered gates, mandatory falsification controls, and explicit failure forensics. The engineering depth is very high: fabrication routes, metrology, and quantitative targets are specified at a level consistent with advanced perovskite/PEC research programs. Logical consistency is strong, particularly in the mechanistic argument that reduced electron residence time at the ETL/perovskite interface—not surface area per se—lowers interfacial recombination velocity, and in the explicit tunneling-length framing of the AgI interlayer. Minor deductions arise from residual coupling risks: (i) achieving ≥30 nm coherence length and low tortuosity simultaneously in a low-temperature mesoporous oxide remains experimentally ambitious, and success probability is not quantitatively estimated; (ii) the assumption that PEC-extracted Rct can be cleanly mapped onto PV-mode ΔVoc,nr, while carefully gated, still relies on equivalent-circuit abstractions that may not fully capture mixed ionic/electronic effects in halide perovskites. Evidence grounding is excellent, staying within the DSSC→PEC→PV chain without conceptual drift. Rationale quality is high, as the work meaningfully restructures known techniques rather than reapplying them verbatim, though it is incremental rather than paradigm-breaking.
hypothesis_summary: A dual-interface-loss–minimized perovskite photoelectrochemical platform is achieved by engineering a low-tortuosity, near-single-crystal electron-transport scaffold and a sub-tunneling-length AgI hole-contact interlayer to reduce interfacial recombination.

original_chain: Oxygen reduction reaction -> ZIF-67 -> Hybrid capacitor -> Metal-organic framework (MOF) -> Reversibility -> Selectivity
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: An ultrathin, pinhole-free ZIF-67–derived Co–Nx–C/porous-carbon composite interlayer placed at the perovskite/ETL interface can act as a *solid-state oxygen redox buffer* only within a narrowly defined electrochemical window: (i) O2 adsorption and 1e− reduction to weakly bound O2•− occurs on isolated Co–N4-like sites when the local electron quasi-Fermi level (EFn) under illumination is sufficiently negative relative to the interfacial O2/O2•− couple in the low-dielectric, aprotic environment; (ii) the stored negative charge is compensated predominantly by reversible accumulation of mobile ions already present in p–i–n stacks (I−/Br− vacancies, FA+/Cs+ vacancies) at the interface over seconds–minutes, rather than requiring protons/water; (iii) on removal of bias/illumination (or under modest positive interfacial potential), O2•− is re-oxidized and desorbs as O2, releasing the compensating ionic space charge and partially reversing interfacial band-bending and deep-trap formation—manifesting as recoverable Voc/FF.

This proposal directly addresses the reviewer’s “mechanistic overreach” by: (1) explicitly constraining the mechanism to a *1e− superoxide buffering cycle* (not aqueous multi-proton ORR/OER) compatible with dry oxygen exposure; (2) requiring quantitative alignment between interfacial redox energetics and PSC quasi-Fermi levels; and (3) enforcing a morphology/speciation window where Co is atomically dispersed (Co–Nx) and electronically coupled yet below a shunt threshold. The porous scaffold is hypothesized to increase O2 chemical potential at the buried interface and reduce the effective activity of O2 at the perovskite surface by redirecting electron transfer to Co–Nx sites, thereby suppressing direct perovskite + O2 → O2•−(at Pb/halide sites) pathways that drive deep traps. Selectivity is not asserted as an intrinsic MOF property after conversion; instead it is engineered via (a) retention of sub-nm microporosity that preferentially concentrates O2 over H2O, and (b) insertion of an Å-to-1 nm diffusion-blocking layer (ALD Al2O3) that suppresses Co migration and halide-contact catalysis while keeping gas access through defects/tortuosity in the porous overlayer.
Plan: Step 0 — Define electrochemical feasibility window (go/no-go before device integration)
0.1 Map relevant energy levels in the *solid-state interface environment*:
- Measure perovskite EFn/Efp under 1 sun at open-circuit and MPP via absolute UPS/KPFM (surface photovoltage) on perovskite/ETL model stacks.
- Estimate the interfacial O2/O2•− formal potential shift in aprotic, low-ε media by measuring O2 reduction onset on the candidate interlayer deposited on inert electrodes (ITO/Al2O3) using solid-state voltammetry (thin-film microelectrode or interdigitated electrodes) under dry O2; report onset vs vacuum level using simultaneous Kelvin probe.
- Go/no-go criterion G1 (energetic alignment): the O2 reduction onset at the interlayer must be bracketed by achievable EFn at the perovskite/ETL interface under illumination (i.e., ΔG for 1e− transfer not strongly uphill; target: within ~0.3 eV of EFn at relevant operating points).
0.2 Define charge-compensation pathway and timescale:
- Quantify ionic redistribution using transient ion-drift/relaxation (bias-step capacitance, deep-level transient spectroscopy adapted for PSCs, and temperature-dependent impedance) on perovskite/interlayer/ETL stacks in dry N2 vs dry O2.
- Go/no-go criterion G2 (reversibility): oxygen-triggered additional capacitance/chemical capacitance must relax back (≥80%) on returning to N2/dark within 10–30 min at 25–45 °C, indicating a non-destructive space-charge process rather than permanent chemistry.

Step 1 — Interlayer synthesis with quantitative morphology/speciation targets
1.1 Synthesize ZIF-67 nanocrystals (20–40 nm) with narrow dispersity (DLS PDI < 0.2) to enable uniform ultrathin films.
1.2 Controlled partial conversion to Co–Nx–C while retaining microporosity:
- Use low-temperature NH3/Ar plasma *or* mild pyrolysis (250–350 °C, ≤30 min, ramp ≤5 °C/min) to avoid framework collapse; perform factorial design varying power/temperature/time.
- Targets after conversion (must be met simultaneously):
  (T1) Porosity: micropore volume retention ≥50% relative to pristine ZIF-67 measured by ellipsometric porosimetry on thin films; (optional confirmation by Kr adsorption for low-mass samples).
  (T2) Co speciation: ≥70% of Co signal attributable to Co–Nx/Co(II/III) coordination (no dominant metallic Co^0) by XAS (XANES/EXAFS) + XPS Co 2p; metallic Co fraction <10% by linear combination fitting.
  (T3) Conductivity window: in-plane σ = 10^−8 to 10^−5 S/cm (four-point probe on 10–30 nm test films). This window is set to allow local electron exchange for redox buffering while remaining far below typical shunting thresholds in 5–10 nm interlayers.
1.3 Formulation to prevent pinholes and shunts at 5–10 nm:
- Use layer-by-layer or self-limiting infiltration deposition (e.g., dilute nanocrystal ink + controlled spin + solvent anneal) to achieve continuous coverage.
- Coverage criteria (must be met):
  (C1) RMS roughness change <2 nm relative to underlying perovskite (AFM).
  (C2) No conductive pinholes: CT-AFM shows <1% area with current >10× median at 0.5 V bias.
  (C3) Cross-sectional TEM/HAADF shows continuous interlayer with thickness 5–10 nm and no percolating metallic inclusions.

Step 2 — Stack architecture and diffusion-risk management
2.1 Device baseline: inverted p–i–n: ITO / SAM (e.g., MeO-2PACz) / FA0.85Cs0.15Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3 / interlayer / C60 (or C60:BCP) / SnO2 / Cu.
2.2 Diffusion-blocking sublayer (pre-registered mitigation):
- If Co mobility or halide-catalysis signatures appear (see Step 5), insert ALD Al2O3 0.5–1.0 nm between perovskite and Co–Nx–C porous interlayer.
- Confirm that Al2O3 does not block oxygen access: measure O2 uptake kinetics in model stacks (Step 4) with/without Al2O3; acceptable penalty: <2× slower uptake while maintaining reversibility.

Step 3 — Decisive mechanistic discriminants (mandatory controls)
Fabricate and test four interlayers matched for thickness (5–10 nm) and conductivity (within 1 order of magnitude), enabling isolation of functions:
A) Target: partially converted ZIF-67 → porous Co–Nx–C with retained microporosity.
B) Inert porous control: ZIF-8 (or porous polymer) ultrathin film with similar porosity but no Co redox.
C) Non-porous Co–Nx–C control: dense Co–Nx–C film (e.g., higher-temperature carbonization or sputtered Co–N–C) with similar σ but minimal microporosity.
D) Co-free porous carbon control: N-doped porous carbon derived from a Zn-based MOF (remove Co) tuned to match porosity of (A) but without Co.
Discriminant readouts:
- If (A) shows reversible O2 uptake/release + Voc/FF recovery while (B) and (D) do not → Co redox is required.
- If (A) and (C) show similar effects → porosity not essential; revise mechanism to catalytic redox only.
- If (B) shows benefit without O2 buffering signals → barrier/passivation dominates; revise scope.

Step 4 — Direct oxygen uptake/release and in-device localization
4.1 QCM on model stacks:
- Prepare quartz stacks: quartz / perovskite (thin) / interlayer / C60.
- Measure mass uptake under dry 16O2 and dry 18O2 at controlled pO2 (0–1 bar) in dark and under illumination; perform adsorption/desorption cycles.
- Go/no-go criterion G3 (reversibility + light/bias coupling): ≥70% of O2-associated mass change is reversible over ≥10 cycles and is enhanced under illumination or negative bias, consistent with redox-assisted uptake rather than irreversible oxidation.
4.2 18O2 labeling + ToF-SIMS depth profiling:
- Stress devices/model stacks under 18O2 (dry, controlled RH <1%) at MPP and at Voc.
- Depth-profile 18O to determine whether oxygen is localized within/at the interlayer vs penetrating into perovskite/ETL.
- Success criterion: (A) localizes 18O primarily in/near interlayer with minimal accumulation in perovskite bulk relative to controls.

Step 5 — Link oxygen buffering to trap suppression and recoverable PV metrics
5.1 Stability protocols:
- ISOS-O (dry oxygen, controlled temperature) with periodic recovery in dry N2/dark.
- Track J–V, MPP, Voc/FF, and quantify non-radiative losses via absolute PLQY and EL efficiency.
5.2 Identify superoxide/radical signatures:
- In situ/operando EPR on illuminated stacks under O2 for O2•− signature comparison across (A–D).
- Operando XPS (near-ambient pressure if available) to track O 1s species evolution (superoxide/peroxide-like components) and Co oxidation-state shifts.
5.3 Capacitance/impedance correlation to “hybrid-capacitor-like” behavior (without overclaiming aqueous ORR):
- Impedance spectroscopy under O2 vs N2, dark vs light, extracting chemical capacitance changes and low-frequency features associated with ion accumulation.
- Define a quantitative correlation: recovery time constant of Voc/FF must scale with relaxation of oxygen-associated capacitance and with desorption kinetics from QCM/18O2 experiments.

Step 6 — Pre-registered failure modes, diagnostics, mitigations
F1 Co diffusion into perovskite → detect by SIMS/ToF-SIMS (Co profile) before/after stress; mitigation: ALD Al2O3 (0.5–1 nm) + reduce metallic Co fraction (T2).
F2 Catalytic halide oxidation/radical acceleration → detect by XPS (I 3d/Br 3d chemical shifts), EPR radical intensity increase, and accelerated EL loss; mitigation: enforce Co–Nx dominance (T2), remove Co^0/CoOx nanoparticles, add Al2O3 barrier.
F3 Shunting/recombination via percolated carbon/metal → detect by dark J–V leakage, ideality factor changes, CT-AFM pinholes; mitigation: keep σ in 10^−8–10^−5 S/cm (T3), tighten film formation to meet (C1–C3).
F4 Porosity collapse (loss of O2 access) → detect via ellipsometric porosimetry; mitigation: lower conversion severity, add sacrificial templating, or switch to gentler plasma conditions.

Deliverables and decision gates
- Gate G1–G3 must be passed before committing to >100-device stability matrices.
- Report a mechanistic decision table (A–D controls + O2 uptake + EPR + recovery metrics) to conclusively accept/reject the oxygen redox buffer mechanism versus simple barrier/passivation.
Feasibility: Electrochemical plausibility in a PSC (non-aqueous) environment: The revised mechanism is explicitly limited to an aprotic 1e− oxygen/superoxide buffering cycle on Co–Nx sites, which is the relevant oxygen-mediated pathway implicated in perovskite photo-oxidation. By mapping the O2 reduction onset of the interlayer in the solid state onto the perovskite quasi-Fermi level under illumination (G1), the proposal avoids assuming aqueous ORR/OER conditions.

Charge-compensation pathway: Rather than invoking protons, the plan tests and relies on mobile ionic defects intrinsic to halide perovskites and adjacent transport layers (vacancies and mobile ions) to provide reversible space-charge compensation, verified by oxygen-dependent impedance/relaxation (G2) and correlated with recovery kinetics.

Morphology/speciation control reduces degradation risk: The critique regarding pore collapse, metallic Co nanoparticle formation, and shunts is addressed via quantitative targets on (i) microporosity retention, (ii) Co–Nx vs Co^0 fraction (XAS/XPS), and (iii) conductivity window, plus pinhole-free criteria using CT-AFM and cross-sectional TEM.
