   4.2 TEM/SAED (cross-section + plan-view): confirm nanosheet/lamellar preservation vs amorphous layer; map thickness/continuity.
   4.3 XPS/ToF-SIMS: confirm imidazolate incorporation (N 1s), metal distribution, and absence of excessive metal diffusion into perovskite.
   4.4 XAS (Ni/Fe K-edge on witness films): oxidation state and coordination (M–N vs M–O); screen for redox changes after light/heat bias.

5) Passivation mechanism: quantitative binding prediction + correlation
   5.1 DFT (or high-level cluster calculations if periodic MOF uncertain): compute binding energies of 2-MIM/imidazolate to representative perovskite surface motifs (PbI2-terminated, FA/halide-terminated, iodide-vacancy-adjacent Pb). Predict core-level shifts (qualitative) and interfacial dipole direction.
   5.2 Experimental binding metrics:
       - XPS: Pb 4f shift and emergence of Pb–N component; N 1s coordination shift.
       - UPS/KPFM: work-function and valence-level shifts; define acceptable band shift window: |ΔWF| ≤ 0.2 eV; otherwise flag as transport-risk.
   5.3 Designed correlation series:
       - Vary N uptake systematically (controlled by SVPT dose) at fixed thickness.
       - Plot QFLS and Voc vs Pb–N fraction (XPS) to establish causality; require monotonic correlation to validate passivation claim.

6) Ion migration suppression: replace “size-selective pores” with measurable Deff under bias
   6.1 Primary metric: effective diffusion coefficient Deff for iodide (and optionally A-site) under bias/illumination.
   6.2 Experiments:
       - Bias-stress ToF-SIMS: apply defined bias (e.g., ±1 V, 60 °C, fixed time), then quantify iodide redistribution depth profile; fit to drift–diffusion model to extract Deff.
       - Temperature-dependent transient ion drift (TID) or EIS-based ionic capacitance: extract activation energy (Ea) for ion motion; success criterion: ΔEa ≥ 0.1 eV vs control or Deff reduction ≥10×.
       - Edge/bypass control: fabricate devices with and without intentional edge sealing; compare Deff and hysteresis to verify whether grain-boundary/edge pathways dominate.

7) Piezotronics: treated as a hypothesis test with symmetry and artifact controls
   7.1 Symmetry requirement (go/no-go for piezotronics claim):
       - Second harmonic generation (SHG) microscopy positive from the interlayer region OR polarized-GIWAXS consistent with non-centrosymmetric order.
       - PFM must show switchable phase contrast not attributable to electrostatics (use band-excitation PFM + on/off field protocol).
   7.2 Quantitative estimate and target effect size:
       - Measure effective d33 (PFM calibrated) on witness films; estimate interfacial polarization under ε ≤0.1% strain.
       - Predicted device-relevant signature: strain-modulated Voc and PL intensity changes that track polarization sign and persist when series resistance is held constant.
   7.3 Artifact exclusion controls:
       - Dummy non-piezo interlayer: amorphous Al2O3 (same thickness) and/or centrosymmetric ZIF-8-like Zn–2-MIM layer.
       - Strain-insensitive electrical fixture + in situ 4-probe/contact resistance monitoring to decouple contact changes.
       - If strain effects correlate only with Rs changes, piezotronics claim rejected.

8) Redox/chemical risk controls for Ni/Fe
   8.1 Operando/near-operando screening:
       - Light + bias aging (MPP, 65–85 °C) followed by XPS/ToF-SIMS depth profiles for Ni/Fe migration and iodide oxidation markers.
       - XAS before/after stress to detect Ni/Fe oxidation state shifts.
   8.2 Acceptance criteria:
       - No measurable increase in oxidized iodine species signals relative to control; no Ni/Fe penetration beyond interlayer within SIMS detection limits.
       - Device does not show new deep-trap signature: ideality factor and temperature-dependent Voc should not worsen.

9) Device completion and benchmarking
   9.1 HTL selection based on measured work function: PTAA (anisole) or alternative compatible HTL; only proceed if UPS indicates no extraction barrier.
   9.2 Benchmark controls (thickness-matched): PEAI 2D cap, MeO-2PACz SAM, ~1 nm Al2O3.
   9.3 Performance statistics: ≥30 devices per condition; report Voc distribution, QFLS–Voc offset, hysteresis index, stabilized MPP.

10) Stability qualification (causal readouts linked to mechanisms)
   - ISOS-L2: MPP tracking at 65–85 °C in N2; ISOS-O2 in ambient.
   - Damp heat 85/85 (encapsulated) and humidity cycling (unencapsulated).
   - Post-mortem: XRD (PbI2), SEM/TEM (delamination), XPS/ToF-SIMS (iodide/metal redistribution), and correlate failure mode with Deff and Pb–N metrics.

Go/no-go decision points:
   - D1 (Material): must meet continuity + M–N evidence; otherwise stop.
   - D2 (Passivation): require QFLS increase ≥20 meV and monotonic correlation with Pb–N fraction; otherwise de-emphasize passivation claim.
   - D3 (Ion): require Deff reduction ≥10× or Ea increase ≥0.1 eV; otherwise barrier claim limited.
   - D4 (Piezotronics): require SHG-positive + strain effect independent of Rs; otherwise drop piezotronics from narrative.
Feasibility: This revision directly de-risks the central uncertainties by (i) **pre-registering material identity outcomes** (crystalline MOF vs amorphous hybrid) and tying each to distinct, testable device physics; (ii) making the dominant benefit **passivation-first**, quantified by DFT-predicted Pb–N binding and experimentally by XPS chemical shifts with a required QFLS/Voc correlation; (iii) replacing ambiguous “size selectivity” with an experimentally extracted **effective diffusion coefficient (Deff)** and activation energy for ion motion under bias, including edge/bypass controls to address grain-boundary leakage; (iv) demoting piezotronics to a **symmetry-gated hypothesis test** requiring SHG (non-centrosymmetry) and resistance-artifact exclusion; and (v) explicitly managing Ni/Fe redox risk with operando/near-operando oxidation-state and diffusion checks plus band-alignment acceptance limits (|ΔWF| ≤ 0.2 eV).

The SVPT concept remains feasible because ligand delivery is solvent-free and temperature-bounded, while the NiFe–LDH seed provides a templated, reactive scaffold that can incorporate N-donor ligands at low substrate temperatures. Crucially, the proposal no longer depends on assuming a canonical NiFe–(2-MIM) ZIF analogue exists at 45–70 °C; instead it formalizes a pivot to a metal–imidazolate hybrid if crystallinity is not achieved, preserving the core concept chain (SVPT-derived interlayer → Pb–N passivation + quantified ionic suppression → stability/Voc gains) while preventing over-claiming.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and self-aware proposal that anticipates the most common failure modes in perovskite/MOF-interlayer literature and neutralizes them through pre-registration, pivot logic, and quantitative acceptance criteria. Engineering resolution is very high: the SVPT process window, thickness control, identity verification, and bias-driven ion-transport measurements are all technically credible and appropriately constrained for perovskites. Logical consistency is strong because mutually exclusive material outcomes are defined a priori, each with its own falsifiable mechanism, preventing post hoc narrative drift. The primary deduction arises from the TARGET CONCEPT CHAIN alignment: the proposal explicitly demotes electrocatalysis and piezotronics to conditional or tertiary roles, whereas the chain implies a more direct piezoelectric–electrocatalytic–stability causality. While scientifically correct, this weakens strict adherence to the stated chain. Evidence grounding is otherwise solid, but NiFe electrocatalytic activity is treated mainly as a risk to be suppressed rather than a functional lever, which partially breaks the chain. Rationale quality is high because the work addresses a genuine bottleneck—ambiguous interlayers and overclaimed mechanisms—by structurally redesigning how claims are validated, though it is more corrective and de-risking than radically exploratory.
hypothesis_summary: A low-temperature vapor-phase transformation of an ultrathin NiFe–LDH seed on perovskite yields an interlayer whose passivation and ion-blocking functions depend on whether it forms a crystalline MOF or an amorphous metal–imidazolate hybrid.

original_chain: Tribo-piezoelectric hybrid nanogenerator (TPHG) -> Hydroxyl radical (OH) -> Short-circuit current (Isc) -> Power density -> Cyclic voltammetry (CV) -> Al-MIL-53 -> UiO-66
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A dual-MOF “redox-sink + barrier” interlayer, consisting of an electrophoretically deposited (EPD) UiO-66 film conformally overcoated with an ultrathin Al-MIL-53 layer at the electron-selective contact/perovskite interface, will simultaneously (i) suppress hydroxyl-radical (OH)-initiated interfacial oxidation and (ii) reduce interfacial recombination, thereby increasing short-circuit current (Isc) and stabilizing power density under operational stress. Mechanistically, defect-engineered UiO-66 provides high-density, coordinatively unsaturated Zr-oxo sites and controlled surface oxygen vacancies that act as a redox buffer to preferentially react with/immobilize ROS precursors and trap interfacial electrons that would otherwise drive OH generation, while the “breathing” Al-MIL-53 overlayer undergoes field- and humidity-responsive pore contraction to lower water activity and limit ROS diffusion. The methodological adaptation is to repurpose MOF electrophoretic deposition (normally used for electrochemical thin films) into a PSC-compatible, sub-50-nm, electrically benign interlayer process, and to quantify ROS-suppression efficacy by coupling cyclic voltammetry (CV)-based interfacial redox mapping with in-situ OH-probe assays under illumination and bias.
Plan: Step 1: Interface target selection and baseline mapping.
1.1 Fabricate baseline n–i–p PSCs (e.g., glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/Spiro-OMeTAD/Au) using a stable mixed-cation perovskite (FA/MA/Cs; I/Br) and record Isc, PCE, stabilized power density, EQE, and light-intensity dependent J–V.
1.2 Establish an OH-generation baseline at the SnO2/perovskite interface using an OH-sensitive fluorescence probe (e.g., terephthalic acid to 2-hydroxyterephthalic acid) incorporated in a thin, inert reporting layer adjacent to the interface (kept outside the perovskite bulk), measured under 1-sun illumination and controlled oxygen/humidity.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—EPD-grown dual-MOF interlayer engineered for PSC constraints.
2.1 Synthesize UiO-66 nanoparticles with controlled defect density (modulator-controlled missing-linker defects) and surface functionality (mixed –COOH/–NH2 fraction) to tune zeta potential and enable low-voltage EPD from nonpolar/low-water solvents (toluene/anisole with trace charging agent) to avoid perovskite damage.
2.2 Adapt EPD to deposit UiO-66 directly onto SnO2 (or onto ITO prior to SnO2 if needed) using: (i) pulsed EPD (short pulses with rest intervals) to prevent Joule heating, (ii) <10 V effective bias, (iii) deposition time calibrated to yield 10–30 nm equivalent thickness and continuous coverage while maintaining electron extraction.
2.3 Post-EPD densification/anchoring: apply a vapor-phase linker “stitching” step (mild BDC vapor or benzoic acid vapor) to improve particle necking and reduce pinholes without high-temperature sintering.
2.4 Overcoat with an ultrathin Al-MIL-53 layer (5–15 nm) by a second EPD step using preformed Al-MIL-53 nanocrystals with opposite surface charge to create electrostatic layer-by-layer assembly; optionally introduce a small fraction of phosphonate-terminated linker to improve adhesion and reduce ion permeation.
2.5 Deposit perovskite absorber atop the MOF stack using an antisolvent or vacuum-assisted crystallization route selected to minimize solvent infiltration into MOF pores (e.g., higher viscosity antisolvent, shorter exposure), then complete the device.

Step 3: Mechanistic validation—CV-based interfacial redox mapping linked to OH suppression and Isc.
3.1 Build MOF-modified model electrodes (ITO/SnO2/MOF) and perform CV in an aprotic electrolyte with a redox mediator (e.g., ferrocene derivative) to quantify interfacial charge-transfer resistance changes and to map accessible redox-active/defect sites (via scan-rate dependence and peak separation).
3.2 Perform light-biased CV (photo-CV) and chronoamperometry under controlled O2/H2O partial pressures to correlate interfacial electron availability with ROS signatures; run identical tests with/without MOF layers.
3.3 Quantify OH generation rate under illumination using the OH-probe assay and/or spin trapping EPR (DMPO–OH) in a sealed environmental cell; link OH flux to Isc loss kinetics.
3.4 Device-level diagnostics: (i) transient photovoltage/photocurrent for recombination/collection, (ii) impedance spectroscopy to separate transport vs recombination, (iii) PL/TRPL from the perovskite side to quantify non-radiative recombination suppression.
3.5 Stability testing: maximum power point tracking (MPPT) under 1-sun with controlled humidity/oxygen and thermal bias; track stabilized power density and Isc over 500–1000 h. Post-mortem XPS/ToF-SIMS to detect oxidation products (Pb0/PbOx, iodate species) and interfacial ion migration signatures.
3.6 Compare to single-MOF controls (UiO-66 only, Al-MIL-53 only) and to a standard organic passivation control (e.g., PEAI) to isolate the unique dual-MOF mechanism.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: OH and related ROS are known accelerants of interfacial oxidation and non-radiative recombination in halide perovskites, especially under illumination and oxygen/humidity. MOFs offer tunable pore chemistry and coordinatively unsaturated metal-oxo sites capable of adsorbing/reacting with ROS precursors and constraining diffusion pathways. Electrophoretic deposition has been demonstrated to form electrochemically addressable MOF thin films (including UiO-66 and Al-MIL-53) with controllable density and thickness, and CV can quantify film electroactivity and charge-transfer behavior.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The key PSC limitation is that conventional MOF incorporation often creates electrically resistive, poorly controlled layers. The proposed adaptation explicitly engineers EPD for PSC constraints (low-voltage pulsed EPD, nonaqueous suspensions, vapor stitching) to obtain a continuous ultrathin interlayer that is mechanically stable, solvent-tolerant during perovskite coating, and thin enough to preserve electron extraction while providing chemical functionality.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with single-function passivation (e.g., 2D cations) that mainly targets defect states, the dual-MOF stack introduces a coupled mechanism: (i) UiO-66 defect sites act as a redox buffer reducing electron-driven ROS formation and intercepting reactive species, (ii) Al-MIL-53 dynamically reduces water/oxygen activity via pore breathing, limiting ROS diffusion and sustaining the redox-sink function. This combination is expected to yield higher retained Isc and stabilized power density under humid oxygenated operation than either MOF alone or standard organic passivation, while providing a CV-verifiable, quantitatively linkable interfacial redox signature.
final_critique: This is a technically sophisticated and well-structured proposal that demonstrates strong command of MOF chemistry, interfacial photophysics, and perovskite device diagnostics. The engineering resolution is high: pulsed low-voltage EPD, defect-controlled UiO-66 synthesis, vapor-phase linker stitching, and sequential electrostatic MOF assembly are all actionable and appropriately constrained for PSC compatibility. Logical consistency is also strong, with a credible mechanistic chain linking interfacial electron accumulation, ROS (OH) formation, recombination, and Isc loss, and a plausible dual-function role for the UiO-66/Al-MIL-53 stack. The main deduction arises from evidence grounding: while OH radicals, CV, and the MOFs are rigorously treated, the TPHG element in the target concept chain is effectively absent from the experimental logic, making the chain formally incomplete. Additionally, the redox-buffer role of UiO-66 defect sites, while plausible, relies on inference rather than clearly articulated redox thermodynamics relative to O2/OH formation potentials at the SnO2/perovskite interface. The rationale is creative and goes beyond standard passivation, but it would benefit from tighter quantitative justification of why the MOF layers remain electronically benign at the proposed thicknesses under operating bias.
hypothesis_summary: A dual-layer MOF interlayer combining a redox-buffering UiO-66 film with a humidity-responsive Al-MIL-53 barrier suppresses hydroxyl-radical oxidation and interfacial recombination, boosting current and stabilizing perovskite solar cell performance.

original_chain: Oxygen reduction reaction -> ZIF-67 -> Electrochemical energy storage -> Molybdenum carbide (MoC_x) -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Bioactivity -> Enzyme@peptide-directed metal-organic frameworks (enzyme@MOFs-P) -> Bioactivity
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a ZIF-67-derived, redox-buffering “oxygen-sink” interfacial microreactor at the air-facing side of perovskite solar cells—implemented as a room-temperature grown, ultrathin ZIF-67 skin that is post-loaded with enzyme@MOFs-P nanocapsules and then converted into a hydrated CoOx/Co(OH)2–N–C framework with MoCx nanodots—will suppress oxygen/superoxide-driven perovskite decomposition and concurrently increase Voc by reducing interfacial non-radiative recombination. Methodological adaptation: instead of converting MOFs into a conductive ORR catalyst at the electron-selective contact (rejected approach), we create a spatially decoupled, humidity-tolerant oxygen-reactivity barrier on the illumination/air side (within/atop the top transport layer) where infiltrating O2 and photo-generated ROS first accumulate; enzyme@MOFs-P is used as a transient, peptide-programmed nanoreactor that deposits a controlled Co-oxyhydroxide redox couple and MoCx nanodots at low temperature (≤120 °C), yielding (i) catalytic disproportionation of superoxide/peroxide via Co(II)/Co(III) cycling, (ii) chemical O2/ROS scavenging before reaching the perovskite, and (iii) reduced interfacial electron accumulation by MoCx-assisted lateral charge spreading in the top contact stack. Mechanism: (a) ZIF-67-derived N-coordinated Co sites act as selective binding pockets for O2/ROS, localizing oxidative chemistry away from perovskite; (b) in mildly humid conditions, Co–N–C partially reconstructs into CoOOH/Co(OH)2 domains that mediate fast ROS redox buffering (consuming O2•−/HO2• and decomposing H2O2), preventing iodide oxidation and A-site cation deprotonation; (c) MoCx nanodots provide a percolative, low-barrier electronic pathway inside the top interlayer to prevent local charge build-up that otherwise accelerates O2 reduction at defect-rich interfaces; (d) peptide residues (carboxylate/amine) remaining after enzyme@MOFs-P processing provide Lewis-base coordination to passivate undercoordinated Pb2+ at the perovskite surface without requiring high-temperature carbonization.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Device baseline and stress-relevant architecture: Choose an air- and light-exposed top interface where oxygen ingress dominates. Use n–i–p PSCs with robust bottom contact: glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/perovskite surface treatment/HTL/Au, and in parallel a semi-transparent top-contact stack for direct oxygen exposure studies: glass/ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/ITO (sputter-buffered). Target baseline PCE ≥22% (0.1 cm2) and a module-relevant layout (≥10 cm2 stripes).
1.2 Define the interfacial “oxygen-sink” placement: integrate the MOF-derived layer either (i) within the HTL (top of HTL under Au/ITO) or (ii) as an ultrathin overlayer on the completed stack (encapsulant-facing), ensuring it is electronically benign to perovskite.
1.3 Select enzyme@MOFs-P formulation for low-temperature chemistry: prepare enzyme@MOFs-P nanocapsules using peptide-directed epitaxial growth around enzymes that generate controlled peroxide flux (e.g., glucose oxidase, GOx) and peroxide-decomposing enzymes (catalase, CAT). The enzyme function is used only during synthesis/post-treatment to deposit Co-oxyhydroxide domains and tune porosity, not as a permanent device component.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Room-temperature ZIF-67 skin growth on the top transport layer (structural adaptation): deposit a conformal, 5–15 nm ZIF-67 film onto the HTL surface via a vapor-assisted, solvent-minimized method (to avoid dissolving HTL): pre-adsorb 2-methylimidazole on HTL, then expose to Co2+ in alcohol vapor/mist. Aim for a continuous nanocrystalline skin with sub-10 nm grains to minimize pinholes.
2.2 Peptide-programmed enzyme@MOFs-P nanoreactor loading (functional adaptation): infiltrate enzyme@MOFs-P nanocapsules into/onto the ZIF-67 skin using a brief, low-polarity dispersion (e.g., anisole/toluene compatible with common HTLs). The peptide is designed with (i) imidazole affinity for ZIF-67 docking and (ii) carboxylate/amine motifs for later Pb2+ coordination (if used as a perovskite surface additive in a split experiment).
2.3 Low-temperature “wet reconstruction” to Co-oxyhydroxide/N–C without carbonization: perform a controlled humid-thermal treatment (60–120 °C, 20–60% RH, O2/air) to partially transform the ZIF-67 surface into Co(OH)2/CoOOH-rich domains while preserving an N-containing organic scaffold (no high-T pyrolysis). This creates a redox-buffering, ion-permeable microreactor that can decompose ROS under operational humidity.
2.4 MoCx nanodot incorporation at PSC-compatible temperature (distinct from rejected carburization): introduce a molybdenum precursor that converts to MoCx nanodots via plasma/photochemical conversion at ≤120 °C (e.g., UV-ozone pre-activation followed by low-power CH4/H2 plasma for seconds, or photochemical reduction/carbidization using an organic carbon donor). Confine Mo species within the ZIF-67/oxyhydroxide matrix by chelating peptides to prevent migration.
2.5 Integration with encapsulation: laminate a standard encapsulant (EVA/POE) over the oxygen-sink layer. In a second set, deliberately use a higher-O2-permeability encapsulant to amplify differences and prove function under accelerated oxygen ingress.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Mechanism-specific ROS suppression metrics (must link to oxygen chemistry):
- Operando EPR spin trapping (DMPO/DEPMPO) on complete stacks under 1-sun with controlled O2 and RH to quantify O2•−/HO2• signals with/without oxygen-sink.
- In situ fluorescence ROS probes (e.g., Amplex Red for H2O2 on extracted top layers) to confirm peroxide decomposition by CoOOH/Co(OH)2 domains.
3.2 Perovskite preservation diagnostics after stress:
- XPS/UPS on perovskite surface (through delamination or model stacks) to quantify I0/I3− formation, Pb0 fraction, and shifts indicating suppressed oxidation.
- GIWAXS/XRD for phase stability (δ-phase formation, PbI2 growth) after ISOS-O and ISOS-L tests.
3.3 Photovoltaic and recombination analysis:
- Absolute PLQY and implied Voc on perovskite/HTL stacks before and after oxygen exposure, correlating oxygen-sink presence with reduced non-radiative loss.
- Transient photovoltage/photocurrent and impedance spectroscopy to separate recombination resistance changes from series resistance changes due to the interlayer.
3.4 Transport/energetics compatibility:
- Measure HTL work function and band alignment (UPS, Kelvin probe) before/after oxygen-sink addition to ensure no detrimental barrier.
- Cross-sectional STEM-EDS/TOF-SIMS to confirm Co/Mo confinement to top region and absence of diffusion into perovskite.
3.5 Reliability testing (core success criterion):
- MPP tracking under controlled O2 (1–21%), RH (0–60%), and 1-sun at 45–65 °C. Report T80 and failure modes.
- Thermal cycling and damp-heat with and without the oxygen-sink to decouple moisture-barrier effects from ROS-buffering effects.
- Scale-up: slot-die or spray deposition of ZIF-67 skin and nanocapsule loading on 10–25 cm2 mini-modules; quantify yield and uniformity (mapping Voc, Jsc, FF).

Go/no-go milestones:
M1 (Month 3–4): ≥10× reduction in operando EPR superoxide signal at the top interface vs control.
M2 (Month 6–8): ≥30 mV increase in implied Voc or maintained Voc after oxygen-light stress relative to control.
M3 (Month 9–12): T80 improvement ≥2× under ISOS-O-2-like oxygen exposure at MPP without PCE penalty >3% absolute.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: ZIF-67 is a well-established MOF with tunable Co coordination environments; Co-oxyhydroxide (CoOOH/Co(OH)2) is a known redox-active mediator capable of decomposing peroxide and buffering reactive oxygen species via Co(II)/Co(III) cycling. Enzyme@MOFs-P literature demonstrates peptide-directed hierarchical porosity and stable immobilization microenvironments that can be repurposed as transient synthesis nanoreactors. MoCx nanostructures are conductive and chemically robust, enabling local charge spreading when incorporated as confined nanodots.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Oxygen-triggered PSC degradation is frequently initiated at the device’s air-facing regions and interfaces where O2 ingress and illumination coincide, producing ROS that ultimately oxidize iodide and degrade organic cations. Placing an oxygen/ROS-buffering microreactor at the top interface intercepts oxygen chemistry before it reaches the perovskite, while avoiding direct contact between potentially reactive metal sites and the perovskite bulk. The low-temperature, wet-reconstruction route is compatible with perovskite processing and avoids the high-temperature carburization step that is incompatible with many PSC stacks.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with purely passive barriers (polymeric encapsulants, ALD oxides), the proposed layer is an active, regenerable redox buffer that chemically neutralizes ROS rather than only slowing diffusion. Compared with interface catalysts placed at the electron-selective contact, this top-side placement decouples catalytic oxygen chemistry from electron-rich perovskite/ETL defect sites, reducing the risk of inadvertently accelerating O2 reduction at the perovskite interface. The enzyme@MOFs-P nanoreactor adaptation uniquely enables controlled formation of CoOOH/Co(OH)2 domains and porosity at low temperature while peptides provide optional Pb2+ coordination for additional surface passivation without relying on the rejected in situ carbonization framework.
final_critique:
This is an unusually detailed and conceptually ambitious proposal with strong command of perovskite degradation pathways and interfacial oxygen chemistry. Engineering resolution is high: the ZIF-67 skin growth, enzyme@MOFs-P-assisted wet reconstruction, and confined MoCx nanodot incorporation are articulated with concrete temperatures, thicknesses, and compatible solvents. The validation plan is rigorous and well-matched to the hypothesized mechanisms, particularly the use of operando EPR and controlled-O2 MPP tracking.

The main deductions arise from cumulative complexity and coupled assumptions. Several mechanistic functions (ROS scavenging, charge spreading, Pb2+ passivation) are assigned to distinct subcomponents, but their independence is not fully deconvoluted experimentally; without careful factorial controls, attribution of Voc gains versus stability gains could remain ambiguous. The enzyme@MOFs-P step, while creative, adds synthetic and reproducibility risk, and the reliance on partial ZIF-67 reconstruction under operational humidity presumes stability of CoOOH/Co(OH)2 domains without parasitic ion migration or long-term phase drift. Finally, MoCx formation at ≤120 °C via plasma/photochemical routes is plausible but under-justified in terms of carbide phase control and work-function tuning at ultralow loadings.
hypothesis_summary: A redox-buffering oxygen-sink layer placed at the air-facing side of perovskite solar cells chemically neutralizes reactive oxygen species to suppress perovskite decomposition and boost voltage.

original_chain: Single-atom catalyst -> Adsorption free energy (OH*) -> Oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) -> Power density -> Specific surface area -> Electrochemical detection -> Chemical stability
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a monolayer-level single-atom catalyst (SAC) array (M–N4 centers; M = Fe/Co) within a chemically robust, ultrathin conductive MOF-derived interlayer at the perovskite/ETL interface will simultaneously (i) suppress oxygen-driven degradation by kinetically controlling interfacial oxygen reduction reaction (ORR) via tuning the adsorption free energy of OH* toward the top of the ORR volcano and (ii) reduce non-radiative recombination by passivating halide-vacancy/undercoordinated-Pb surface states. The methodological adaptation is to repurpose rotating-disk ORR descriptor engineering (OH* free-energy targeting used for SAC screening) into a perovskite-specific ‘oxygen sink + defect-passivating’ interfacial architecture: a 2–5 nm SAC@porous-carbon/MOF nanolayer with high specific surface area (SSA) that is electronically coupled to the ETL (SnO2) but ionically and chemically decoupled from the perovskite through a thin 2D-perovskite/ionic-bonding anchoring motif. Mechanistically, optimized OH* binding on isolated M sites promotes a controlled 4e− ORR pathway (or benign peroxide suppression) on the SAC layer rather than on the perovskite/ETL contact, reducing superoxide/peroxide residence time at the perovskite surface, while the interlayer’s Lewis-base nodes coordinate Pb2+ and fill halide-vacancy related trap states, increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting and thereby increasing power density under operation.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Select a benchmark high-efficiency perovskite stack (e.g., glass/ITO/SnO2/(interlayer)/FA-Cs mixed-halide perovskite/spiro-OMeTAD/Au) and a reference without interlayer.
1.2 Build a controlled oxygen/moisture exposure platform: (a) dry O2, (b) O2 + 30–50% RH, (c) N2 control, with continuous MPP tracking and simultaneous in-situ electrochemical detection.
1.3 Pre-screen candidate SAC motifs using DFT: compute ΔG(OH*) on M–N4 sites embedded in (i) phthalocyanine-like coordination, (ii) N-doped graphene fragments, and (iii) MOF-node-like coordination. Use ΔG(OH*) as the primary descriptor to target a narrow window near the volcano apex for low ORR overpotential, while constraining Fermi-level alignment to avoid electron extraction barriers from SnO2.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Synthesize a conductive MOF thin film (2–5 nm) directly on SnO2 by vapor-assisted conversion or layer-by-layer growth (e.g., Zr-based or Fe-based MOF seed modified to be electronically percolating after mild pyrolysis at ≤250–300 °C, compatible with PSC processing). This is the adaptation: MOF chemistry and thickness are tuned for high SSA while staying below the carrier tunneling length to avoid series resistance.
2.2 Introduce isolated M atoms (Fe/Co) as M–N4 SACs within the MOF-derived carbonaceous network using a ‘confined coordination’ route: impregnate with metal precursors + nitrogen ligands, followed by low-temperature fixation to prevent nanoparticle formation (verify single-atom dispersion via HAADF-STEM and XAS).
2.3 Add a perovskite-facing anchoring/passivation skin (≤1 nm) by depositing a sparse 2D Ruddlesden–Popper forming salt (e.g., PEA/BA derivative bearing a coordinating group) that (i) blocks direct contact between SAC and halide lattice to prevent metal diffusion and (ii) provides Lewis-base coordination to undercoordinated Pb while maintaining electronic coupling.
2.4 Integrate the interlayer into full devices and also into ‘half-cells’ for mechanistic studies: SnO2/interlayer/perovskite and perovskite/interlayer/SnO2 test structures.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Electrochemical detection of ORR activity at the interface: use a solid-state three-electrode microcell geometry on SnO2/interlayer films (with oxygen dosing) to measure onset potentials and kinetics proxies; correlate with ΔG(OH*)-ranked SAC candidates.
3.2 Quantify oxygen-induced electronic losses: in-situ PL/TPV/TPC under controlled O2 to track non-radiative recombination changes, and EIS to separate charge-transfer resistance vs recombination resistance.
3.3 Identify degradation pathway suppression: operando XPS/ToF-SIMS to detect iodide oxidation products, Pb0 formation, and metal migration; EPR to quantify superoxide signals with/without interlayer.
3.4 Device metrics: compare Voc, FF, and stabilized power output (power density at MPP) under 1-sun and elevated temperature (65–85 °C) in O2/RH stress. Use statistical batches (n≥20) and accelerated lifetime modeling (e.g., T80 at MPP).
3.5 Mechanism-to-descriptor test: demonstrate that stability gain and power density retention scale with (i) measured ORR suppression at perovskite interface (lower superoxide signature) and (ii) SAC ΔG(OH*) proximity to target window, establishing causality rather than correlation.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: SAC ORR activity follows a volcano trend with adsorption free energy (OH*) as a universal descriptor, enabling rational selection of M–N4 motifs; high-SSA MOF-derived carbons and MN4 site-rich macrocycle/MOF systems are proven to deliver high limiting currents and power density in oxygen electrochemistry, indicating that thin, site-dense layers can strongly modulate oxygen reduction kinetics. In PSCs, oxygen/superoxide is a known driver of surface and interface degradation and can also introduce interfacial recombination; therefore, relocating/controlling ORR away from the perovskite contact while passivating traps is mechanistically aligned with known failure modes.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): The adaptation is not simply adding a catalyst; it re-engineers the perovskite/ETL interface into a dual-function layer: (i) an ‘oxygen-reactivity governor’ designed using ORR descriptor engineering (ΔG(OH*)) and (ii) a perovskite-compatible passivation/anchoring skin to preserve band alignment and prevent metal diffusion. The film is nanometer-thin to maintain electron extraction and can be processed at low temperature to remain compatible with perovskite fabrication.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared to conventional organic passivators or inert 2D layers, this interlayer actively modulates oxygen electrochemistry instead of only blocking oxygen diffusion, providing robustness under realistic oxygen ingress. Compared to nanoparticle catalysts, SACs maximize active-site utilization at minimal loading, reduce optical/electrical parasitics, and allow tunable OH* binding; the high SSA architecture increases the probability of oxygen capture and rapid conversion on the interlayer rather than on the perovskite, improving operational chemical stability and stabilized power density.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and intellectually rigorous proposal with unusually strong cross-domain translation. The engineering plan is detailed, materials-realistic, and largely compatible with perovskite processing constraints. The logical chain linking SAC OH* binding to interfacial ORR relocation and reduced superoxide residence is scientifically defensible and goes beyond simple oxygen blocking. The main deductions arise from two areas: (i) the electrochemical validation of ORR at a buried solid-state interface remains experimentally challenging, and while proxies are proposed, quantitative separation of ORR kinetics from charge extraction effects may be difficult; (ii) the stability of Fe/Co–N4 SACs under perovskite-relevant bias, halide exposure, and illumination is assumed rather than rigorously de-risked, especially regarding metal redox cycling and long-term coordination integrity. These are not fatal flaws, but they introduce execution risk. Overall, the proposal is well above the field’s median in both mechanistic depth and originality.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a monolayer single-atom catalyst array within an ultrathin conductive MOF interlayer at the perovskite/electron-transport-layer interface simultaneously suppresses oxygen-driven degradation and reduces non-radiative recombination, boosting operational stability and power density.

original_chain: bmFeSAC -> Electrocatalytic activity -> Overpotential -> Cobalt (Co) -> Overpotential -> M-N-C active sites
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a bicontinuous mesoporous single-atom M–N–C interlayer (Schwarz P-type architecture) directly at the perovskite/transport-layer interface will simultaneously (i) suppress interfacial non-radiative recombination by coordinative passivation of under-coordinated Pb/I (via FeN4 or CoN4 sites acting as Lewis base/electron-density modulators) and (ii) reduce interfacial electrochemical overpotential for parasitic redox processes (I3−/I−, O2/O2•−) by accelerating charge-transfer kinetics away from the perovskite lattice. A methodological adaptation is proposed: translate bmFeSAC-style negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous mesoporosity—originally optimized for ORR—into a conformal, sub-30-nm-thick ‘electrocatalytic buffer’ that is electrically percolative but ion-blocking, and that can be metal-switched (Fe→Co or Fe/Co dual-SAC) to tune interfacial reaction energetics. Mechanistically, negative-curvature channels increase accessible single-atom site utilization while minimizing local current constriction; this lowers kinetic barriers (effective overpotential) for interfacial redox shuttling and flattens interfacial band bending, thereby increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting (higher Voc) and stabilizing operation under bias/illumination by diverting interfacial radicals from attacking the perovskite.
Plan: Step 1: Device target selection and baseline controls.
- Build baseline n–i–p and p–i–n PSC stacks (e.g., ITO/SnO2/perovskite/HTL/Au and ITO/NiOx/perovskite/ETL/Ag) using a mixed-cation perovskite (FA0.85Cs0.15Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3) to avoid composition-driven artifacts.
- Prepare controls: (a) no interlayer, (b) planar N-doped carbon interlayer without SAC, (c) conventional passivation (e.g., PEAI 2D layer) for benchmarking.

Step 2: Methodological adaptation—bmFeSAC-derived bicontinuous mesoporous SAC thin interlayer integration.
- Synthesize a cubosome-templated bicontinuous mesoporous N-doped carbon scaffold (Schwarz P-type) with thickness control via dilute precursor loading and short deposition times (target: 10–30 nm, RMS roughness < 5 nm).
- Incorporate single-atom sites: generate FeN4, CoN4, and Fe/Co dual-SAC variants by MOF- or chelate-assisted impregnation followed by confined pyrolysis tuned to preserve single-atom dispersion (verify via HAADF-STEM + XAS).
- Convert powder synthesis into a thin-film process: disperse the mesoporous SAC in orthogonal solvents (e.g., alcohols) and deposit by blade-coating or spray-coating onto the transport layer (or onto the perovskite, depending on polarity), followed by low-temperature anneal (<120 °C) to maintain perovskite integrity.
- Add an ion-blocking functional adaptation without sacrificing percolation: infiltrate the bicontinuous channels with an ultrathin perfluorosulfonate (Nafion-like) or zwitterionic polymer at sub-monolayer equivalent coverage to create steric hindrance to mobile iodide while retaining electronic connectivity; systematically vary infiltration fraction to map the trade-off between ion-blocking and series resistance.

Step 3: Mechanism-resolving validation and quantitative analytics.
- Structural/chemical confirmation: GISAXS (bicontinuous periodicity), BET/ellipsometric porosimetry (effective porosity), XPS/UPS (work function shift, Pb–N interaction signatures), HAADF-STEM + XAS (single-atom coordination), ToF-SIMS depth profiling (interlayer continuity and polymer infiltration).
- Photophysical tests: steady-state PL and TRPL on perovskite/interlayer/CTL stacks; absolute PLQY to quantify non-radiative loss; transient photovoltage/photocurrent to extract recombination and transport times.
- Electrochemical overpotential proxy at PSC interfaces: build symmetric cells (CTL/interlayer/CTL and perovskite/interlayer/perovskite) and measure EIS under illumination and bias; use intensity-modulated photovoltage spectroscopy to separate interfacial charge-transfer resistance from ionic contributions; quantify bias-dependent interfacial reaction kinetics by operando UV–vis/photothermal deflection to monitor iodine species formation.
- Device metrics and stability: J–V (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP tracking; Voc(T) to infer dominant recombination pathway; operational stability at 65–85 °C and 1 sun in N2 and dry air; damp-heat (e.g., 85/85 modified) to test moisture barrier effect.
- Comparative mapping: correlate (i) single-atom type (Fe vs Co vs Fe/Co), (ii) curvature/porosity metrics, and (iii) polymer infiltration fraction with Voc, FF, hysteresis index, ion-migration activation energy, and operational lifetime (T80).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: bmFeSAC demonstrates that negative Gaussian curvature bicontinuous mesoporosity maximizes utilization of M–N–C single-atom sites and lowers reaction barriers in electrocatalysis; Co-based catalysts are empirically linked to low overpotential through optimized intermediate adsorption and kinetic acceleration, while M–N–C engineering is a proven lever for tuning charge-transfer resistance and catalytic kinetics. Translating these principles to PSC interfaces targets the known failure mode where interfacial redox (iodine chemistry, oxygen reduction) accelerates degradation and increases interfacial recombination.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC bottlenecks are interfacial recombination and bias/illumination-driven interfacial electrochemistry coupled to ion migration. A conformal bicontinuous SAC interlayer is an interface-engineering solution: (i) coordinative defect passivation improves quasi-Fermi level splitting (Voc), (ii) curvature-enabled high site accessibility provides kinetic ‘sinks’ that redirect deleterious redox away from the perovskite lattice, and (iii) controlled channel infiltration introduces an ion-blocking function analogous to steric hindrance effects (as in Nafion-modified catalysts) but repurposed to suppress iodide flux and reactive species penetration.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional 2D perovskite or small-molecule passivation, the proposed interlayer is multifunctional and tunable: it offers (a) scalable thin-film deposition (spray/blade), (b) programmable interfacial energetics via Fe↔Co single-atom substitution (overpotential tuning), (c) decoupled optimization of electronic percolation and ionic blocking via partial channel infiltration, and (d) mechanistic measurability through electrochemical/operando probes linking ‘overpotential-like’ kinetic barriers to PSC stability. This is not a simple material swap; it is a curvature- and site-utilization-driven architectural adaptation tailored to PSC interfacial electrochemistry and recombination physics.
final_critique: This is a highly sophisticated and technically ambitious proposal with strong command of both electrocatalysis and perovskite interfacial physics. The engineering plan is unusually detailed, spanning synthesis, thin-film translation, and multi-modal characterization. The central logic—that negative-curvature bicontinuous SAC architectures can act as kinetic redox sinks and coordinative passivation layers at PSC interfaces—is internally consistent and intellectually compelling. However, there are two notable weaknesses that limit a perfect score. First, the causal link between 'lowering electrochemical overpotential' (a well-defined electrocatalysis metric) and measurable improvements in Voc and stability in PSCs is conceptually plausible but not yet rigorously formalized; the proposal relies on analogy rather than a quantitative interfacial energy/kinetics model. Second, the ion-blocking strategy via partial Nafion-like infiltration risks undermining the very charge-transfer kinetics the SAC layer is meant to enhance, and the proposal does not yet specify clear percolation or transport criteria (e.g., target conductivity, ionic transference numbers) that would define success versus failure. These gaps slightly weaken the logical closure between mechanism and device-level outcomes, despite the otherwise excellent design.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a bicontinuous mesoporous single-atom M–N–C interlayer at perovskite interfaces simultaneously passivates defects and accelerates redox charge transfer, suppressing recombination and boosting stability.

original_chain: Release profile -> Zn-Car_MOF -> Cu-HHTP -> Response and recovery properties -> Cu-HHTP -> Chemiresistive gas sensors -> Spray layer-by-layer assembly method
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A spray layer-by-layer (sLbL) assembled dual-MOF interlayer composed of (i) an ultrathin conductive Cu-HHTP nanofilm and (ii) a porous Zn-Car_MOF cap can function as a ‘programmable ionic release’ interface in perovskite solar cells (PSCs). Mechanistically, Cu-HHTP provides a high-density, energetically aligned, π–d conduction network that (a) selectively scavenges/immobilizes mobile halide species via Cu–X coordination and (b) passivates under-coordinated Pb2+ surface sites through catecholate-like interactions, suppressing non-radiative recombination (↑Voc, ↑FF). Zn-Car_MOF, deposited atop Cu-HHTP, acts as an ion-buffering reservoir that enforces a controlled release profile of benign counter-ions/ligand fragments and captures moisture/oxygen through reversible adsorption, thereby damping interfacial ion accumulation and hysteresis. The combined structure is predicted to improve operational stability by flattening the temporal ion flux (release profile control) while maintaining fast interfacial equilibration (sensor-like response/recovery analog) under electrical bias and illumination, yielding higher PCE retention under damp heat and maximum power point tracking.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
1.1 Choose a baseline high-efficiency PSC stack where interfacial ion migration is a known limiter: Glass/ITO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/HTL/Au (n–i–p) and a complementary inverted stack Glass/ITO/NiOx/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/ETL/Ag to test universality.
1.2 Prepare perovskite absorbers with controlled surface terminations (slightly PbI2-rich vs stoichiometric) to stress-test passivation and ion trapping.
1.3 Synthesize Cu-HHTP (conductive MOF) and Zn-Car_MOF with particle size control (<50–100 nm) and stable spray inks (alcohol/water mixtures with minimal Lewis base additives to avoid perovskite damage).

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
2.1 Methodological adaptation—sLbL ‘release-profile engineered’ dual-MOF interlayer:
- Implement sequential spray deposition with in-line mild substrate heating (40–60 °C) and brief solvent-free purge steps to prevent perovskite dissolution.
- Deposit Cu-HHTP first (target 10–30 nm): optimize spray pulse number and concentration to form a pinhole-free, percolated film without blocking charge extraction.
- Deposit Zn-Car_MOF second (target 5–20 nm): intentionally keep it slightly porous/discontinuous to enable gas/ion buffering rather than forming an insulating barrier.
- Optional: introduce a controlled defect density in Cu-HHTP via mixed-ligand fraction (HITP/HHTP ratio analog) to tune conductivity and Cu coordination site availability; calibrate to avoid deep trap formation.
2.2 Engineer the ‘release profile’ function for PSCs:
- Pre-load Zn-Car_MOF with a benign ionic species (e.g., small ammonium carboxylate or alkali carboxylate) that can slowly exchange with halides at the interface, buffering ionic chemical potential gradients under bias.
- Quantify and tune release kinetics by varying Zn-Car_MOF thickness/porosity and pre-loading level; establish a target: minimized interfacial halide accumulation during 0.8–1.1 V bias at 60–85 °C.
2.3 Integration points (two architectures):
- Place the dual-MOF interlayer at the perovskite/HTL interface to suppress iodide-driven HTL degradation and improve hole extraction.
- Place the dual-MOF interlayer at the perovskite/ETL interface to test whether halide immobilization reduces SnO2 interfacial reactions and light-soaking drift.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Device metrics: J–V (forward/reverse), stabilized MPP efficiency, Voc deficit analysis, EQE, temperature-dependent JV to identify transport barriers.
3.2 Mechanism proof—ion flux and ‘response/recovery’ analogs:
- Operando impedance spectroscopy (EIS) under illumination and bias to extract ionic vs electronic time constants; define response time as resistance/capacitance settling after bias steps and recovery time after bias removal.
- Transient ion-drift measurements (bias-pulse induced current transients) to quantify ionic mobility reduction.
- Time-of-flight SIMS depth profiling before/after aging to map I−/Br− redistribution and Cu–I signatures near interfaces.
3.3 Passivation and recombination: steady-state PL and TRPL on full stacks; quasi-Fermi level splitting (QFLS) to link Voc gains to non-radiative recombination suppression.
3.4 Interfacial chemistry: XPS/UPS to confirm energy-level alignment shifts and Cu–X coordination; FTIR/Raman for carboxylate coordination changes indicating ion exchange.
3.5 Stability testing: ISOS-L (continuous light), ISOS-D (damp heat 85 °C/85% RH encapsulated), and MPP tracking for >1000 h; compare PCE retention and hysteresis evolution.
3.6 Controls: pristine (no interlayer), Cu-HHTP only, Zn-Car_MOF only, and an inert porous layer (e.g., Al2O3 nanolayer) to isolate ‘release profile’ and Cu-coordination contributions.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Conductive MOF thin films (Cu-HHTP) fabricated by spray layer-by-layer methods can be made smooth, pinhole-free, and defect-tunable, enabling fast, room-temperature chemiresistive response/recovery—evidence that ion/electron interactions in these frameworks occur on practical timescales. Separately, Zn-Car_MOF and Cu-HHTP have demonstrated coupled ‘release profile’ functionality in a hybrid system where electrocatalytic/coordination chemistry drives controlled molecular release, supporting the concept that MOF chemistry can regulate temporal transport phenomena.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): In PSCs, the central degradation pathway involves electric-field-driven migration of I−/Br− and A-site cations, leading to interfacial accumulation, band bending, hysteresis, and interlayer/metal reactions. The proposed dual-MOF sLbL interlayer directly targets this bottleneck by (i) immobilizing halides at coordinatively active Cu sites (flux damping) and (ii) buffering ionic chemical potential via a porous Zn-Car_MOF ‘reservoir’ with tunable exchange/release kinetics—an explicit mapping of ‘release profile’ control into PSC ion-management.
3. Comparative Advantage: Compared with conventional 2D perovskite capping or generic Lewis-base additives, this approach provides (a) an externally tunable kinetic parameter (release profile via Zn-Car_MOF pre-loading and porosity) rather than a static passivation, (b) a conductive interfacial scaffold (Cu-HHTP) that maintains extraction while supplying specific coordination sinks for halides, and (c) scalable, low-temperature spray LbL processing compatible with large-area modules and rough substrates, addressing scale-up without sacrificing interface precision.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and largely well-founded proposal that goes beyond static passivation by introducing kinetic control of interfacial ion flux. The engineering plan is detailed and actionable, with realistic thickness targets, deposition conditions, and a strong suite of operando diagnostics. The logical framework—mapping chemiresistive response/recovery behavior of conductive MOFs onto PSC ion migration phenomena—is creative and mostly convincing. However, there are moderate uncertainties that justify score deductions: (i) the long-term chemical stability of Cu–X coordination under sustained PSC bias and high halide chemical potential is assumed rather than critically bounded (risk of CuI formation or conductivity loss); (ii) the 'programmable release' function of Zn-Car_MOF is conceptually sound but lacks a quantitatively predictive model linking MOF loading/porosity to ionic chemical potential gradients at buried interfaces; and (iii) the dual-MOF stack introduces multiple coupled variables (conductivity, porosity, coordination density) that may complicate mechanistic attribution even with the proposed controls. These issues do not undermine feasibility but slightly weaken causal isolation and predictive rigor.
hypothesis_summary: A spray-coated dual-MOF interlayer combining conductive Cu-HHTP and porous Zn-Car_MOF creates a programmable ion-release interface that traps halides and buffers ions to suppress perovskite solar cell degradation and hysteresis.

original_chain: Hydroxyl radical (OH) -> Reactive oxygen species (ROS) -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Truncated rhombic dodecahedron (TRD) -> Ethylenediamine (EDA) -> Interpenetration twins (IT) -> Solvothermal method
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding an EDA-programmed ZIF-8 morphology gradient (TRD→IT) as a nanoporosity-controlled, ROS-active “oxygen sink” inside the electron-transport layer (ETL)—rather than as a perovskite interlayer—will suppress hydroxyl-radical (OH)-initiated photo-oxidation at the perovskite/ETL vicinity while simultaneously reducing interfacial non-radiative recombination. Methodological adaptation: we will restructure the ETL into a MOF-in-oxide hybrid where TRD-rich ZIF-8 microcrystals provide high-accessibility adsorption/capture of O2/H2O and short-lived ROS, while a controlled fraction of IT domains provides interconnected internal diffusion pathways that spatially displace ROS formation away from the perovskite. Mechanism: (i) the TRD facet distribution tunes pore-aperture accessibility and adsorption enthalpy for O2/H2O, reducing local O2 activity at the perovskite boundary; (ii) IT-induced interpenetrated domains create preferential permeation channels that transport oxidants deeper into the ETL (away from perovskite) where they are quenched at the MOF/oxide surfaces; (iii) residual EDA coordinated within the ZIF-8 (confined inside the ETL composite) provides Lewis-base passivation of oxide surface trap states and reduces interfacial band-tail recombination without risking amine diffusion into the perovskite bulk. The net result is increased quasi-Fermi-level splitting (higher Voc) and improved operational stability under light/oxygen by lowering the interfacial OH generation rate and decoupling ROS chemistry from perovskite surfaces.
Plan: Step 1: System setup and baseline definition.
1.1 Device baseline: fabricate n–i–p PSCs with a robust mixed-cation perovskite (e.g., FA/Cs iodide-rich) on ITO, using a reference compact SnO2 ETL (low-temp processed) and a standard HTL/metal electrode stack.
1.2 Establish oxygen/light degradation baseline: run controlled-stress tests (1 sun, fixed O2 partial pressure, controlled RH, 45–60 °C) while tracking Voc/FF decay, PLQY decay, and interfacial OH formation using operando EPR spin trapping (DMPO–OH) with geometry optimized to probe the ETL/perovskite region.

Step 2: Adapted methodology—MOF-in-oxide hybrid ETL with TRD→IT morphology programming.
2.1 Solvothermal synthesis (off-device): synthesize ZIF-8 powders with systematically tuned morphologies (RD, TRD, TRD+incipient IT, IT-dominant) by varying EDA concentration during solvothermal growth, following time-resolved sampling to lock in TRD→IT boundary conditions. Confirm morphology by SEM/TEM and quantify IT fraction by electron diffraction/statistical image analysis.
2.2 ETL restructuring (on-device, perovskite-safe): create a bilayer hybrid ETL on ITO before perovskite deposition:
  - Bottom: compact SnO2 (electron-selective contact).
  - Top: SnO2:ZIF-8 composite “oxygen-sink layer” (10–40 nm) formed by dispersing TRD/IT ZIF-8 microcrystals into a SnO2 sol, then low-temperature curing (<120 °C). Use a composition gradient by sequentially coating two composite sublayers: (a) TRD-rich near the eventual perovskite interface; (b) IT-enriched nearer the electrode side to maximize oxidant transport away from perovskite.
2.3 EDA confinement strategy: after composite curing, perform a mild, ETL-only vapor treatment (e.g., CO2 or weak electrophile vapor that preferentially associates within MOF pores) to immobilize/free-base EDA inside ZIF-8 and minimize any subsequent release during perovskite deposition.
2.4 Perovskite deposition on hybrid ETL: deposit the perovskite using a solvent system chosen to avoid MOF disruption (validate by GIWAXS/XPS of ETL before/after). Complete devices with the same HTL/electrode used in baseline to isolate ETL effects.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
3.1 Electronic quality and recombination: measure absolute PLQY and time-resolved PL from the perovskite on each ETL variant; extract quasi-Fermi level splitting; determine ideality factor and recombination order from light-intensity dependent JV and Voc.
3.2 ROS/OH suppression mapping: quantify OH (EPR DMPO–OH) and total ROS (fluorogenic probes placed within the ETL region using an inert spacer architecture) under illumination and oxygen. Compare TRD-rich vs IT-rich vs MOF-free controls at matched ETL thickness and conductivity.
3.3 Spatial displacement test (core mechanism): introduce a nanometer-thin “ROS reporter” layer at controlled distances from the perovskite/ETL interface (e.g., an ultrathin inert polymer containing OH-reactive moieties embedded within the ETL stack) to demonstrate that ROS activity peak shifts away from the perovskite when IT-enriched transport sublayers are present.
3.4 Transport/energetics and ETL integrity: measure ETL conductivity and electron mobility (SCLC/impedance), UPS/KPFM for work function and band alignment, and cross-sectional TEM/EDS to verify MOF distribution and the intended TRD→IT gradient.
3.5 Stability protocols: run ISOS-O and ISOS-L stressing (including oxygen-rich illumination) and quantify T80, as well as failure signatures (PbI2 formation via GIWAXS/XRD; interfacial oxidation states via XPS of I/Pb; halide migration via bias-stress hysteresis and transient ion drift).
3.6 Controls to falsify the mechanism:
  - Same MOF loading but randomized morphology (mixture without gradient) vs programmed gradient.
  - SnO2:MOF composite using ZIF-8 synthesized without EDA (to test EDA’s role).
  - TRD/IT MOF replaced with a non-porous inert nanoparticle at similar size/loading (barrier-only control).
  - IT-enriched without TRD-rich interfacial sublayer (tests necessity of TRD at perovskite-adjacent region).
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Literature demonstrates EDA-controlled ZIF-8 morphological evolution from TRD to interpenetration twins (IT) under solvothermal synthesis, and independently establishes that MOFs can strongly interact with oxygen/water and participate in ROS-related chemistry (generation or scavenging depending on local environment). PSC degradation under light/oxygen is mediated by ROS, with hydroxyl radical (OH) being highly destructive; therefore engineering a layer that reduces local oxygen activity and displaces/quench ROS away from the perovskite is a high-leverage stability strategy.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): Instead of exposing perovskite directly to solvothermal processing or adding an interlayer that risks series resistance or chemical incompatibility, the approach relocates the MOF function into a pre-perovskite ETL architecture. The ETL is deliberately restructured into a composite with a programmed TRD→IT morphology gradient, enabling ROS management and trap suppression while preserving standard perovskite deposition routes and scaling-compatible coating of the ETL.
3. Comparative Advantage: Conventional ETLs (compact SnO2/TiO2) mainly provide band alignment and extraction but do not actively manage ROS; conventional barrier layers reduce ingress but cannot modulate where ROS forms. The proposed hybrid ETL adds an “oxygen sink + ROS displacement” function via morphology-programmed porosity (TRD) and diffusion pathways (IT), while confining EDA to the ETL to avoid the instability risks of amine diffusion into perovskites. This is structurally novel relative to interlayers and targets both Voc loss (recombination) and operational oxygen/light degradation (OH-mediated pathways).
final_critique:
This is a technically ambitious and intellectually sophisticated proposal that demonstrates unusually high engineering resolution. The ETL restructuring strategy is concrete, fabrication-aware, and paired with an appropriately rigorous validation framework (operando EPR, spatial ROS reporters, falsification controls). The logical chain connecting TRD facet accessibility, IT-enabled diffusion pathways, and spatial decoupling of ROS chemistry from the perovskite interface is largely consistent and well articulated.

However, two deductions are warranted. First, the proposal implicitly assumes that ZIF-8 within a SnO2 matrix will predominantly act as a ROS sink rather than a ROS generator under illumination; this balance is system-dependent and not fully bounded by preliminary mitigation strategies (e.g., light-driven superoxide formation at MOF/oxide interfaces). Second, while the TRD→IT gradient concept is compelling, the quantitative transport argument (diffusion length scales of O2/ROS relative to ETL thickness and recombination zone width) is not explicitly modeled, leaving some uncertainty about whether the proposed 10–40 nm architecture is sufficient to achieve meaningful spatial displacement of OH formation. These are not fatal flaws, but they slightly weaken the mechanistic closure.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a ZIF-8 morphology gradient (TRD→IT) as a nanoporosity-controlled oxygen sink within the electron-transport layer suppresses hydroxyl-radical-driven perovskite photo-oxidation and reduces interfacial recombination.

original_chain: Negative Gaussian curvature -> Specific surface area -> Electrochemical double-layer capacitors (EDLC) -> Specific surface area -> NaBH4 hydrolysis -> Core-shell structure -> UiO-68
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a UiO-68–derived core–shell interfacial scaffold with quantitatively defined negative Gaussian curvature between the 3D perovskite absorber and charge-transport layers will measurably increase open-circuit voltage (ΔVoc ≥ 30–60 mV) and operational stability by coupling curvature-amplified interfacial capacitance with chemically graded defect passivation. Mechanistically, (i) the UiO-68 core–shell linker distribution provides spatially resolved Lewis-acid/Lewis-base coordination that reduces interfacial trap density (Nt) and suppresses non-radiative recombination, while (ii) a bicontinuous, negatively curved topology increases effective interfacial capacitance (Cint) beyond planar limits, enhancing electrostatic screening of mobile halide vacancies and suppressing bias-induced ion accumulation. Unlike classical EDLCs, this capacitance operates in a low-ion-density, solid-state regime and is governed by curvature-enhanced local density of states and confined ionic polarizability rather than bulk electrolyte adsorption. The combined reduction in interfacial recombination velocity (S) and stabilization of quasi-Fermi level splitting under illumination directly translates into higher Voc and reduced hysteresis.
Plan: Step 1: Curvature-preserving synthesis and verification.
- Synthesize multivariate UiO-68 crystals with a radially resolved core–shell architecture (core: H2TPDC-rich for mechanical rigidity; shell: mixed carboxylate/phosphonate linkers with Pb2+ binding constants >10^4 M−1).
- Impart negative Gaussian curvature using polymer cubosome templates (Schwarz P symmetry, lattice parameter 20–40 nm) infiltrated selectively into the UiO-68 shell.
- Convert only the outer 5–15 nm shell into an amorphous MOF-derived oxide/carbon hybrid via stepwise thermal treatment (150–200 °C in inert atmosphere followed by mild oxidative pulse ≤5 vol% O2), preserving curvature while retaining the crystalline UiO-68 core.
- Structural retention benchmarks: (i) electron tomography and FIB–SEM to confirm bicontinuous curvature continuity; (ii) SAXS to verify preserved Schwarz P periodicity; (iii) BET surface area ≥400 m² g−1 post-conversion with pore size distribution centered at 10–25 nm.

Step 2: Quantitative electrostatic modeling and capacitance extraction.
- Develop a continuum Poisson–Nernst–Planck (PNP) model incorporating curvature-dependent surface charge density (σ ∝ κG, where κG is Gaussian curvature) and realistic interfacial ion densities (10^17–10^18 cm−3).
- Predict curvature-enhanced interfacial capacitance (Cint,target = 0.5–2 μF cm−2) and corresponding Voc shifts using ΔVoc ≈ (ΔQ/Cint)/q, explicitly benchmarking against planar passivation layers (Cint,planar ≈ 0.05–0.1 μF cm−2).
- Experimentally extract Cint via impedance spectroscopy under illumination (10 Hz–1 MHz), separating geometric, chemical, and interfacial capacitance contributions using equivalent circuit fitting.

Step 3: Device integration with explicit benchmarks.
- Deposit a 10–30 nm UiO-68–derived scaffold onto FA/Cs mixed-halide perovskites via low-energy spray or blade coating to avoid surface damage.
- Benchmark against state-of-the-art controls: phenethylammonium iodide (PEAI), alkylphosphonic acid SAMs, and polymeric passivation layers (e.g., PMMA).
- Target metrics: ΔVoc improvement ≥30 mV vs best control, hysteresis index <2%, stabilized power output retention >95% after 1000 h at MPP (65 °C).

Step 4: Mechanistically relevant degradation probes.
- Replace NaBH4 hydrolysis testing with perovskite-relevant stressors: (i) bias-induced iodide migration under 1 sun + forward bias; (ii) controlled Lewis-base exposure (amines, water vapor) to probe interfacial chemical robustness; (iii) thermal/light soaking to monitor curvature–passivation synergy.
- Track degradation pathways using operando PL mapping, TOF-SIMS for ion redistribution, and Kelvin probe force microscopy for interfacial potential stability.
Feasibility: 1. Addressing curvature retention risk: The use of partial shell conversion and low-temperature, stepwise treatment minimizes framework collapse, while polymer cubosome templating has been empirically shown to preserve Schwarz P–type negative Gaussian curvature in MOF-derived materials. Explicit tomography and SAXS benchmarks directly de-risk this step.
2. Adapting EDLC concepts to solid-state PSCs: Rather than invoking classical electrolyte-driven EDLC behavior, the proposal reformulates capacitance in terms of confined ionic polarizability and curvature-enhanced surface charge density under low mobile ion concentrations. Quantitative PNP modeling ties curvature and surface area directly to experimentally measurable Cint and Voc shifts.
3. Chemical relevance of stress testing: By replacing NaBH4 hydrolysis with iodide migration and Lewis-base attack—dominant PSC degradation pathways—the validation strategy aligns with operational chemistry while still probing the scaffold’s chemical and electrostatic robustness.
4. Comparative advantage and benchmarks: Explicit comparison to leading passivation strategies ensures that performance gains are not merely incremental. The rigid, curvature-engineered MOF-derived interlayer uniquely integrates defect passivation, electrostatic field stabilization, and mechanical robustness, targeting both efficiency and long-term stability without modifying the perovskite bulk.
final_critique: This is a highly ambitious and largely well-constructed proposal that demonstrates exceptional engineering resolution and conceptual originality. The synthesis plan is unusually detailed for a grant application, with clear structural benchmarks (tomography, SAXS, BET) that meaningfully de-risk the most speculative steps. The logical chain linking negative Gaussian curvature to enhanced interfacial capacitance and Voc stabilization is internally consistent and thoughtfully distinguishes solid-state behavior from classical EDLCs. However, the central assumption σ ∝ κG is asserted rather than rigorously derived; without a microscopic justification or prior empirical precedent, the curvature–charge coupling risks being viewed as phenomenological. Additionally, the predicted ΔVoc calculation via ΔQ/Cint is somewhat oversimplified for a mixed electronic–ionic interface where quasi-Fermi level splitting, recombination kinetics, and band alignment are all co-determinants. Evidence grounding is strong, though the historical EDLC → NaBH4 hydrolysis link is acknowledged only implicitly and could be more explicitly contextualized to avoid appearing as a conceptual relic rather than a consciously rejected comparator.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a negatively curved UiO-68–derived scaffold between perovskite and charge-transport layers boosts open-circuit voltage and stability by coupling curvature-enhanced capacitance with graded defect passivation.

original_chain: Piezoelectric response -> Carnosine -> Zn-Car_MOF -> Short-circuit current (Isc) -> Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Reflection loss (RL)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that embedding Zn-Car_MOF as a mechanically compliant, piezoelectrically active scaffold inside a quasi-2D/3D perovskite surface reconstruction layer—rather than as a discrete interlayer—will reduce optical reflection loss (RL) and enhance short-circuit current (Isc) via a coupled opto–electro–mechanical mechanism. Methodologically, the adaptation is to induce in-situ growth of a Zn–carnosine MOF within a self-assembled 2D Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) perovskite skin on the 3D absorber, forming a MOF–perovskite interpenetrating heterophase. Mechanistically, (i) the MOF’s nanoporosity and refractive-index averaging suppress Fresnel reflection at the perovskite surface, (ii) carnosine coordinates Pb2+ and halide vacancies, enforcing defect passivation and suppressing non-radiative recombination, and (iii) the intrinsic piezoelectric polarization of Zn-Car_MOF, activated by thermo-elastic strain during illumination and thermal cycling, modulates the local band bending within the 2D/3D perovskite junction (piezo-phototronic effect), thereby enhancing carrier separation and extraction without introducing an additional resistive interface.
Plan: Step 1: Specific system setup or data preparation.
- Baseline device: n–i–p PSC with glass/ITO/SnO2/FA0.8MA0.15Cs0.05Pb(I0.85Br0.15)3/spiro-OMeTAD/Au.
- Prepare a 2D-perovskite precursor solution using bulky ammonium cations (e.g., phenethylammonium, PEA+) mixed with trace carnosine (sub-stoichiometric) to promote surface-confined RP phase formation.
- Independently synthesize Zn-Car_MOF nanoseeds (<10 nm) in aqueous/alcoholic media, ensuring crystallinity and measurable piezoelectric response.

Step 2: Detailed implementation of the adapted methodology.
- Surface reconstruction strategy: After forming the 3D perovskite film, spin-coat the mixed 2D-perovskite/carnosine precursor, followed by mild annealing to create a thin (≈10–20 nm) RP perovskite skin.
- In-situ MOF integration: Expose the reconstructed surface to Zn2+ vapor or dilute Zn2+ alcoholic solution, triggering confined coordination with carnosine already embedded in the 2D lattice, thus nucleating Zn-Car_MOF domains interpenetrated within the 2D perovskite matrix rather than forming a standalone layer.
- Structural tuning: Control MOF loading by Zn2+ exposure time to tune porosity and effective refractive index while maintaining continuous electronic pathways through the perovskite.
- Device completion: Deposit HTL and electrode as usual, ensuring that the MOF remains electronically coupled through the perovskite framework.

Step 3: Rigorous validation and analytical framework.
- Structural/mechanical verification: GIWAXS and cross-sectional TEM to confirm 2D/3D perovskite + MOF heterophase; nanoindentation to probe mechanical compliance.
- Optical analysis: Absolute reflectance and ellipsometry to quantify RL reduction; correlate with EQE enhancement and integrated Jsc.
- Electronic/defect diagnostics: TRPL, PLQY, and SCLC to quantify trap density reduction; UPS/KPFM to map band bending at the reconstructed surface.
- Piezoelectric mechanism validation: PFM and in-operando Jsc measurements under controlled thermal cycling or substrate bending; compare with control devices using a non-piezoelectric Zn-carboxylate MOF or carnosine-free 2D layers.
- Stability testing: ISOS-L and ISOS-T protocols to assess whether the MOF–2D skin suppresses ion migration and preserves Isc over time.
Feasibility: 1. Theoretical/Empirical Basis: Zn-Car_MOF is experimentally proven to possess strong piezoelectric response and chemical functionality via carnosine coordination. Separately, 2D/3D perovskite surface reconstruction is a validated strategy for defect passivation and stability. Integrating MOFs within this reconstruction leverages both effects synergistically rather than additively.
2. Transfer Logic (How the adaptation fits the domain): PSC bottlenecks include surface recombination, optical losses, and instability. The proposed interpenetrating MOF–perovskite heterophase directly addresses these at the absorber surface—the most critical region—without adding a new transport barrier, aligning with state-of-the-art interface engineering paradigms.
3. Comparative Advantage: Unlike conventional antireflection coatings or discrete MOF interlayers, this strategy embeds the MOF inside a semiconducting perovskite phase, preserving charge transport continuity while introducing piezoelectric and optical functionality. Compared to standard 2D passivation layers, the Zn-Car_MOF adds an active, strain-responsive electric field and tunable porosity, offering a fundamentally new control knob over Isc and RL.
final_critique: This is a highly ambitious and intellectually rich proposal that goes beyond incremental interface engineering. The strongest aspect is the interpenetrating heterophase concept, which is well-motivated and experimentally addressable with advanced characterization. The optical argument (refractive-index averaging and porosity-driven Fresnel suppression) is plausible but somewhat under-quantified; effective-medium modeling or optical simulations are not discussed. The piezo-phototronic mechanism, while conceptually attractive, rests on a relatively weak strain source (thermo-elastic cycling under illumination) and lacks an order-of-magnitude estimate to demonstrate that the induced polarization field is sufficient to measurably modulate band bending at the 2D/3D junction. There is also a nontrivial chemical risk: embedding carnosine and Zn2+ within a RP lattice may disrupt crystallographic coherence or introduce ionic pathways unless carefully constrained. Nevertheless, the proposal remains logically coherent and avoids hand-waving by including appropriate control experiments.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding a piezoelectric Zn-Carnosine MOF within a 2D/3D perovskite surface layer reduces reflection loss and boosts current via coupled optical, mechanical, and piezo-phototronic effects.

original_chain: Loading capacity -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Pt1/SnO2/MOF -> Hydrogen evolution rate -> SnO2
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: A SnO2@MOF:Pt1 core–shell electron-transport layer (ETL) can increase Voc/FF and operational stability in perovskite solar cells only if the MOF shell simultaneously (i) passivates interfacial defect chemistry and blocks oxygen/ion access and (ii) remains electronically “transparent” at 1-sun current densities. We hypothesize that this is achievable in a quantitatively defined design window where the MOF shell is ultra-thin and defect-engineered (tMOF ≤ 3–4 nm effective barrier thickness; controlled missing-linker density to provide coordination sites but not deep electronic traps), and where atomically dispersed Pt1 is present at ultralow areal density (sub-percolating, <10^12–10^13 atoms cm−2 equivalent) in Pt–(N/O) coordination that (a) introduces a fast, reversible interfacial redox capacitance (electron micro-reservoir) with redox potential positioned slightly below the SnO2 conduction-band edge / perovskite electron quasi-Fermi level under operation, so that Pt1 accepts/releases electrons without acting as a deep trap, and (b) suppresses harmful oxygen-driven interfacial chemistry by kinetically disfavoring O2→O2•− formation at the perovskite interface (via controlled Pt coordination and electron chemical potential), rather than catalyzing oxygen reduction. In this regime, the MOF provides high-density Lewis-base passivation (reduced surface recombination velocity → higher QFLS and Voc), while Pt1 provides dynamic smoothing of transient electron accumulation (reduced interfacial band-bending spikes → lower hysteresis and higher FF) without increasing ETL series resistance. The central mechanistic claim is therefore conditional and testable: PLQY-implied Voc gains must co-occur with unchanged/improved extraction kinetics and unchanged/improved contact resistivity; otherwise the MOF/Pt1 configuration is rejected.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registered quantitative design window, models, and acceptance criteria (before synthesis).
0.1 Interfacial transport model (series-resistance + barrier model): treat SnO2@MOF contact as SnO2 (degenerately doped semiconductor) in series with a thin barrier (MOF) characterized by effective tunneling/thermionic conductance. Define an operational constraint that added ETL contribution to device series resistance ΔRs,ETL must be ≤ 0.2 Ω·cm2 at 1 sun (to preserve FF gains ≥2% absolute). This translates to a maximum acceptable ETL contact resistivity ρc ≤ 5×10−3 Ω·cm2 (to be measured by TLM on ETL/perovskite test structures and/or c-AFM current mapping with calibrated tip force/area). If ρc exceeds threshold, reduce tMOF and/or increase electronic coupling (linker choice, missing-linker density) and repeat.
0.2 Shell thickness constraint: pre-register tMOF targets: 1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 5.0, 8.0 nm (TEM-verified). Go/no-go: any condition with tMOF ≥5 nm must demonstrate ρc and ΔRs,ETL within thresholds; otherwise excluded from device optimization.
0.3 Pt loading/coordination phase diagram (hard failure modes): matrix over (i) Pt areal density (converted from wt% + surface area + shell thickness): 10^11, 10^12, 10^13, 10^14 atoms cm−2 equivalent; (ii) missing-linker density (low/med/high; quantified by TGA + 1H NMR of digested MOF and/or modulator incorporation); (iii) tMOF (1.5–5 nm for main matrix).
