Failure modes with quantitative triggers: (A) Pt aggregation: any Pt–Pt coordination in EXAFS (CN>0.5) or HAADF clusters >0.7 nm → reject; (B) shunt formation: dark J–V leakage at −0.1 V increases >2× vs SnO2 control or ideality factor degrades (>2.0) → reject; (C) Voc loss from dipoles/energetic misalignment: Voc decreases >10 mV while PLQY-implied Voc increases <10 mV (decoupling indicates extraction barrier) → reject; (D) FF loss from Rs: FF decreases >1% absolute at matched Jsc and ΔRs,ETL >0.2 Ω·cm2 → reject.

Step 1 — Materials architecture and synthesis with transport-first constraints.
1.1 Device architecture (n–i–p): Glass/ITO/ETL/perovskite(FA/Cs, I/Br)/HTL(PTAA or spiro-OMeTAD)/Au. Keep ETL optical transmission and thickness matched (profilometry/ellipsometry) across controls.
1.2 ETL set (matched thickness, same ink solids): (A) SnO2 NP; (B) SnO2@MOF (no Pt); (C) SnO2 + Pt nanoparticles (no MOF); (D) SnO2@MOF:Pt1 (target). Add (E) SnO2@MOF with identical missing-linker density but “blocked” Lewis sites (post-synthetic capping) to decouple passivation vs transport.
1.3 MOF selection and linker functionalization: prioritize Zr-based UiO family for chemical robustness; implement two linkers to tune polarity/electronic coupling while maintaining crystallinity: UiO-66-NH2 (Lewis base, Pt anchoring) and mixed-linker UiO-66-(NH2)/(BDC) to tune site density. Missing-linker density tuned by modulator (acetic/formic acid) ratio.
1.4 Conformal MOF shell growth on SnO2 NPs with thickness control: (i) hydroxylate SnO2 NPs (UV-ozone, quantified by XPS O 1s –OH fraction); (ii) graft sub-monolayer primers (carboxylate/phosphonate) at controlled coverage (target <0.5 molecules nm−2) to seed uniform nucleation without insulating overlayer; (iii) conduct low-temperature modulated growth in dilute regime to form 1.5–5 nm shells (primary), with 8 nm as stress-test. Validate with TEM/EELS mapping and quantify shell continuity (fractional coverage).

Step 2 — Pt1 incorporation and coordination locking with explicit bounds.
2.1 Mechanochemical Pt loading (asset-1 logic adapted to core–shell powders): liquid-assisted grinding of dried SnO2@MOF powder with a Pt precursor (Pt(acac)2 preferred to reduce residual halides; compare to H2PtCl6 as a variable) plus minimal additive (e.g., ethanol/water vapor or amine-compatible LAG solvent) to drive Pt anchoring to linker/node sites. Target ultralow Pt wt% corresponding to the phase diagram (e.g., 0.001, 0.005, 0.01, 0.05 wt% as starting points, converted to areal density).
2.2 Coordination locking (avoid Pt-catalyzed ORR): photochemical treatment on finished ETL films under inert atmosphere to remove labile ligands and form Pt–(N/O) coordination. Two locking states intentionally created and compared: (State I) Pt–N rich (from –NH2 linker) and (State II) Pt–O/node rich (Zr–O vicinity). Quantify Pt oxidation state and coordination before/after locking by XPS and operando XAS.
2.3 Explicit control of residual halides/Cl−: if H2PtCl6 is used, implement post-loading chloride scavenging/washing and verify Cl content by XPS; go/no-go if Cl persists above a defined threshold (e.g., Pt:Cl <1:0.2) to reduce halide-related interfacial chemistry.

Step 3 — Direct measurement of transport penalties (mandatory) and acceptance gating.
3.1 Contact resistivity and current uniformity: (i) TLM structures: fabricate ITO/ETL/perovskite (or electron-collecting top contact) with patterned electrodes to extract ρc and sheet resistance; (ii) c-AFM current maps on ETL/perovskite stacks to detect local barriers and pinholes; accept only conditions meeting ρc ≤ 5×10−3 Ω·cm2 and no low-current dead zones >5% area.
3.2 Temperature-dependent transport across SnO2@MOF films: measure conductivity/activation energy (Arrhenius) of ETL films (SnO2@MOF vs SnO2@MOF:Pt1) from 200–350 K. Acceptance: activation energy must not increase relative to SnO2@MOF by >25 meV at equal thickness; otherwise Pt introduces trapping/barrier.
3.3 Extraction kinetics must not degrade: perform transient photocurrent/photovoltage and/or ultrafast/µs-scale charge extraction (TPC/TPV) on complete devices and perovskite/ETL stacks. Acceptance: charge extraction time constant τext for SnO2@MOF:Pt1 must be ≤ τext(SnO2) + 10% while PLQY/TRPL indicates reduced recombination (see Step 4).

Step 4 — Passivation benefit must be coupled to extraction neutrality (mandatory proof).
4.1 Optical-to-electrical consistency test: measure absolute PLQY of perovskite on ETLs to obtain implied Voc; simultaneously measure τext and ρc. Go/no-go criterion: implied Voc increase ≥20 mV must coincide with (i) unchanged/improved τext and (ii) ΔRs,ETL ≤0.2 Ω·cm2. If PLQY improves but τext/ρc worsen, interpret as insulating barrier and redesign shell (thinner, different linker/missing-linker).
4.2 Energetic alignment: UPS/Kelvin probe to track ETL work function and interfacial dipoles vs Pt loading and missing-linker density; reject conditions where work-function shift predicts reduced electron selectivity (e.g., increased interfacial barrier leading to lowered Voc/FF).

Step 5 — Explicit Pt1 redox energetics mapping vs perovskite quasi-Fermi level and oxygen potentials (mandatory).
5.1 Operando spectroelectrochemistry on SnO2@MOF:Pt1 films: build three-electrode thin-film cells to determine Pt1 redox transitions (Pt(II)/Pt(I)/Pt(0)-like signatures depending on coordination) and kinetics (electron transfer rate constants) as a function of potential. Correlate potentials to device-relevant electron chemical potentials (calibrated vs vacuum level using UPS).
5.2 Operando XAS/XPS under illumination and controlled atmospheres: track Pt oxidation state changes during simulated operation (light bias, O2 vs N2). Acceptance: Pt must show reversible redox response under illumination (buffer behavior) without drift toward metallic Pt0 clustering.
5.3 Oxygen/superoxide constraint: explicitly measure whether Pt1 accelerates or suppresses O2•− formation at the ETL/perovskite interface.
- Use EPR spin trapping under controlled O2 partial pressure with identical illumination and bias.
- Acceptance: O2•− signal for SnO2@MOF:Pt1 must be ≤ SnO2@MOF and ≤ SnO2 at matched conditions; otherwise Pt coordination state is rejected or re-locked (State I vs II).

Step 6 — Device performance, hysteresis, and stability tied to mechanistic readouts.
6.1 Performance targets (at matched Jsc): Voc gain ≥30 mV and FF gain ≥2–4% absolute vs SnO2 control, with Rs not increased.
6.2 Hysteresis: quantify hysteresis index and relate to impedance-derived interfacial capacitance/resistance; buffering hypothesis predicts reduced low-frequency capacitance and improved recombination resistance under light.
6.3 Stability: operando MPP at 65–85 °C under N2, dry air, and O2. Tie degradation to (i) EPR (ROS), (ii) XPS (interfacial chemistry), (iii) ToF-SIMS (iodide migration into ETL). Target: T80 ≥1000 h in dry air with demonstrable suppression of oxygen-accelerated Voc loss and reduced iodide penetration.

Step 7 — Scaling and manufacturability checks.
7.1 Coatability: formulate SnO2@MOF:Pt1 inks for blade/slot-die coating on 5×5 cm. Map sheet resistance, PL imaging uniformity, and spatial Voc variation. Acceptance: spatial Voc standard deviation reduced vs SnO2 control (consistent with uniform core–shell coverage) without increased sheet resistance.

Deliverables (pre-registered): (i) a transport-limited design rule relating tMOF and missing-linker density to ρc and ΔRs,ETL; (ii) a Pt1 redox map (potential/kinetics) aligned to perovskite QFLS; (iii) a phase diagram with explicit failure boundaries; (iv) a mechanistic passivation-without-penalty dataset where PLQY-implied Voc gains co-occur with neutral/improved extraction and Rs.
Feasibility: The revised plan directly de-risks the main reviewer concern (MOF transport penalty) by making electronic transparency a first-class, quantitatively gated requirement rather than an assumption. Transport is measured explicitly (TLM/c-AFM contact resistivity; temperature-dependent activation across SnO2@MOF) and tied to device-level FF/Rs limits with hard go/no-go thresholds. The Pt1 “redox micro-reservoir” mechanism is elevated from qualitative to measurable: operando spectroelectrochemistry and operando XAS/XPS under illumination/bias will locate Pt1 redox energetics and kinetics in the MOF microenvironment and align them to the perovskite electron quasi-Fermi level; configurations that behave as deep traps (slow kinetics, irreversible oxidation-state drift) are rejected. The oxygen/superoxide claim is converted into an explicit constraint because Pt can catalyze oxygen reduction depending on coordination: EPR under controlled O2 and two pre-defined Pt coordination locking states (Pt–N-rich vs Pt–O-rich) provide a controlled test and mitigation pathway. Finally, the “high loading capacity” vs “ultralow loading” narrative is reconciled via a pre-registered phase diagram: mechanochemical loading enables reproducible access to many anchoring sites (capacity), but operational Pt density is deliberately kept below quantified percolation/shunt and energetics-perturbation thresholds, verified by EXAFS (no Pt–Pt) and device leakage/Rs criteria. Asset 2 supports that single-atom Pt stabilized in a SnO2/MOF architecture can be electronically active with reduced charge-transfer resistance; Asset 1 supports mechanochemical incorporation to preserve atomic dispersion and maximize site utilization without solution-phase degradation—here leveraged to populate only a controlled fraction of available sites within an acceptance-gated transport window.
final_critique: This is a technically ambitious and unusually well-gated ETL proposal: the transport penalty risk of MOF shells is confronted with explicit ρc/ΔRs thresholds and direct measurements (TLM/c-AFM, temperature-dependent activation, extraction kinetics), and the Pt1 role is framed in a falsifiable way (operando redox + O2•− constraint). Score deductions come from (i) a key mechanistic gap: the “Pt1 micro-reservoir” is plausible but not yet tied to a quantitative device-physics prediction (e.g., how much interfacial charge buffering/capacitance is required to measurably change hysteresis/FF without adding recombination pathways), making it easy to overfit post hoc interpretations; (ii) practical metrology risk: extracting reliable contact resistivity for ITO/ETL/perovskite stacks via TLM is nontrivial because the perovskite is ionic/field-dependent and can invalidate ohmic assumptions—without an alternate, validated transmission-line surrogate contact stack, ρc thresholds may be noisy; and (iii) concept-chain grounding weakness: “hydrogen evolution rate” is not connected to the proposed device function or validation plan, and the proposal does not define how MOF ‘loading capacity’ is translated into an optimal (not maximal) Pt1 density beyond the phase-diagram grid. Overall, engineering resolution is high, logic is mostly consistent, but the required chain is not fully honored and the Pt1 buffering mechanism needs a sharper quantitative bridge to device observables.
hypothesis_summary: A SnO2@MOF:Pt1 core–shell electron-transport layer boosts perovskite solar cell voltage and stability only when an ultra-thin, defect-engineered MOF shell passivates interfaces while atomically dispersed platinum provides dynamic electron buffering without adding electrical resistance.

original_chain: Charge transfer -> Crystalline metal-organic framework (cMOF) -> Specific capacitance -> Nanostructured carbon -> Fuel cell -> Specific capacitance -> Battery -> Power density
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Installing an electronically conductive, redox-capacitive cMOF@nanostructured-carbon interlayer can increase stabilized power density and operational stability in carbon-based perovskite solar cells, but only if the cMOF’s redox is made truly reversible in a dry laminated stack via an internal, non-perovskite-dependent charge-compensation pathway. We hypothesize that an ultrathin, oriented 2D π–d conjugated cMOF film grown conformally on hierarchical nanostructured carbon and subsequently converted into a solid-state ‘single-ion pseudocapacitor’—by immobilizing counter-ions within/through the cMOF using tethered anions (polyanionic dopants) or an interpenetrated single-ion-conducting polymer—will (i) provide fast electron extraction (lower Rct) and (ii) provide a measurable, reversible interfacial redox capacitance (Cint) that buffers transient interfacial charge under illumination/bias without sourcing compensating ions from the perovskite. Mechanistically: (a) fast electronic transport arises from the crystalline π–d conjugated cMOF network plus intimate electrical contact to carbon; (b) the redox buffer is enabled by internal fixed counter-charge (e.g., sulfonated polyanion) that allows ligand-/metal-centered redox switching with only short-range cation motion inside the interlayer (or local ion rearrangement within a polymer electrolyte nanophase), rather than halide/A-site migration. This creates a well-defined interfacial RC element with a time constant τbuffer = Rct·Cbuffer engineered to be far below the dominant ion-relaxation time τion extracted from low-frequency impedance/IMVS, thereby suppressing ion-migration-driven interfacial field fluctuations (reduced hysteresis, improved Voc/FF) while maintaining chemical stability through a conformal, electronically thin but chemically robust diffusion barrier between cMOF metal nodes and halides.
Plan: Step 1 — Device baseline and materials selection (with explicit constraints)
1.1 Baseline carbon-PSC stack: glass/FTO/SnO2/(FA,Cs)Pb(I,Br)3/perovskite surface passivation (minimal)/laminated hierarchical nanostructured carbon top contact (CNT/graphene ink + mesoporous carbon). Target baseline: PCE and hysteresis quantified via stabilized MPP tracking; record low-frequency impedance signature of ion motion (0.1–10 Hz arc/Warburg-like response) to define τion.
1.2 Conductive 2D cMOF selection (redox window + catalysis constraint): choose a π–d conjugated 2D MOF with demonstrated solid-state conductivity (≥10^-3–10^-1 S cm^-1 as film) and redox activity within ±0.6 V around the expected carbon contact quasi-Fermi level under operation, but with minimized halide-catalysis risk. Screening set:
  (i) Ni/Cu/Co catecholate–semiquinone families (high capacitance potential but higher halide reactivity risk) and
  (ii) metal-bis(dithiolene) frameworks (often more redox-delocalized; evaluate halide affinity).
Downselect criterion before any perovskite contact: no detectable I− oxidation/iodine formation in sealed halide exposure tests (Step 4.2).
1.3 Quantitative capacitance target is redesigned to be falsifiable from site density: define an areal redox-site density Ns (sites cm^-2) from film mass loading and framework stoichiometry and an accessible redox fraction swing Δx under device bias. The expected areal pseudocapacitance is bounded by:
  Qareal = Ns·e·Δx  (for 1e− per site),  Cbuffer ≈ dQ/dV ≈ (Ns·e·Δx)/ΔV.
We set a realistic initial gate: demonstrate Cbuffer,areal ≥ 1–10 μF cm^-2 in dry conditions (not electrolyte) across ΔV = 0.2–0.4 V, with τbuffer at least 10× faster than τion (τbuffer ≤ 0.1·τion). The earlier 10–100 μF cm^-2 remains an aspirational stretch goal contingent on measured Ns and Δx.

Step 2 — Build the solid-state charge-compensation architecture (mandatory reviewer fix)
2.1 On-carbon oriented cMOF growth (conductive scaffold preserved):
  • Carbon functionalization: sparse diazonium grafting to introduce ~0.5–2% surface coverage of –COOH/–OH anchoring sites (quantify by XPS C 1s/O 1s), maintaining sheet resistance increase <10% vs pristine carbon.
  • Interfacial coordination growth: two-phase method (organic ligand phase / aqueous metal-ion phase) to nucleate a 2D cMOF skin on carbon. Control thickness by growth time and precursor concentration to 5–15 nm (verify by cross-sectional TEM and XRR/ellipsometry on flat carbon surrogates). Target preferential in-plane orientation confirmed by GIWAXS (dominant (hk0) reflections aligned with substrate).
2.2 Convert cMOF into a ‘single-ion pseudocapacitor’ to enable dry-state redox reversibility (two implementable options; start with A, pivot to B if needed):
  Option A (polyanion-tethered internal counter-charge, no mobile anions):
  • Infiltrate a nanometer-thin polyanionic dopant into the cMOF/carbon composite: e.g., poly(styrene sulfonate) (PSS−) or perfluorosulfonated ionomer fragments (fixed SO3− groups). Procedure: brief dip-coating or vapor-assisted infiltration from low-surface-tension solvent, followed by mild anneal (<80 °C) to leave a sub-percolation ionomer fraction confined to the cMOF pore network.
  • Mechanism: fixed anions provide charge compensation; only small cations (e.g., residual tetralkylammonium from doping step or deliberately introduced non-reactive cations) redistribute over nanometer scales within the interlayer. No halide/A-site ions are required.
  Option B (interpenetrated single-ion conductor network):
  • Photopolymerize a single-ion-conducting polymer inside cMOF pores (e.g., sulfonated polymer with tethered anion and mobile Li+/Na+ or bulky organic cation chosen for low perovskite reactivity). Keep polymer volume fraction minimal to preserve electronic percolation (verify conductivity drop <2×).
  • Confirm ionic conductivity of the interpenetrated phase in dry state (target σion ≥10^-7–10^-6 S cm^-1 at 25–60 °C) using blocking-electrode EIS on standalone films.
2.3 Electrochemical pre-doping is re-scoped as ‘state initialization’ with retention testing (not assumed):
  • Pre-doping medium: use a non-aqueous electrolyte compatible with the cMOF and polyanion architecture (e.g., acetonitrile with inert salt), apply potentiostatic steps to set redox fraction x0.
  • Remove free electrolyte rigorously (rinse + vacuum dry). The retained state must be demonstrated by spectroscopy and open-circuit potential drift tests (Step 3.2).
  • Important: if pre-charge self-discharges upon contact, the interlayer can still function as a reversible buffer under operation provided that the internal counter-ion mechanism supports cycling; thus, the decisive metric becomes reversible Cbuffer and τbuffer in the dry stack, not the absolute persistence of x0 alone.

Step 3 — Quantitative, falsifiable model + go/no-go gates (mandatory)
3.1 Solid-state redox-capacitance model used to set design targets:
  • Equivalent circuit under illumination near MPP: perovskite recombination resistance Rrec in parallel with chemical capacitance Cμ, series with interfacial charge-transfer resistance Rct, and a buffer capacitance Cbuffer (pseudocapacitive) at the carbon contact.
  • Define τion from low-frequency features (ion-related capacitance dispersion) in control devices; define τbuffer = Rct·Cbuffer for the cMOF interlayer. Design rule: τbuffer ≤ 0.1·τion so that the buffer responds before ion redistribution perturbs band-bending.
  • Predict Cbuffer from Ns and Δx measured independently (Step 3.3); compare predicted vs measured interfacial capacitance under operating bias/light to validate mechanism.
3.2 Self-discharge/equilibration experiment (mandatory):
  • Construct test stack: cMOF@carbon (initialized at x0) contacted to (i) Au, (ii) ITO, and (iii) an inert wide-bandgap semiconductor (e.g., ALD-Al2O3-coated ITO to block charge transfer; and SnO2 as a realistic electron-contact analog) with controlled work functions.
  • Metrics: track (a) work function/CPD via Kelvin probe over 10^2–10^4 s in dry N2, (b) redox signatures by Raman/EPR/XPS over time, and (c) transient current upon contact (integrated charge = effective stored charge).
  • Go/no-go: if >80% of spectroscopic redox signature decays within <10^2 s upon contact to conductive substrates, then the proposal pivots from ‘pre-charged reservoir’ to ‘operando reversible buffer only’ and focuses on maximizing cycling Cbuffer rather than retaining x0.
3.3 Direct measurement of dry-state Cbuffer and redox accessibility (no perovskite yet):
  • Two-terminal solid-state EIS on cMOF@carbon pressed against inert counter-electrode with an ion-blocking spacer vs an ion-permitting but perovskite-free solid (e.g., polymer single-ion conductor layer). Extract areal capacitance vs bias and frequency (target: μF cm^-2 in 1–10^3 Hz band, minimal low-frequency divergence that would indicate slow ionic drift).
  • Galvanostatic intermittent titration-like pulses in solid state (small ΔV) to test reversibility and coulombic efficiency of redox switching.
  • Ns and Δx determination: quantify redox-site density from elemental analysis/XPS + film thickness/density; quantify accessible Δx from integrated charge in controlled potential steps (dry cell). Use this to compute predicted Cbuffer and compare to measured.
3.4 Device-level τbuffer vs τion gating:
  • Build full PSCs and run bias-/light-dependent impedance and IMVS/IMPS.
  • Go/no-go: demonstrate τbuffer ≤ 0.1·τion and a correlated reduction in hysteresis index and Voc transient overshoot. If τbuffer is not sufficiently faster than τion, increase Ns (thicker within 5–15 nm limit, higher surface area carbon), increase Δx (broaden redox window safely), or reduce Rct (improve orientation/contact).

Step 4 — Chemical compatibility and barrier architecture (mandatory stability gates)
4.1 Chemical barrier is upgraded from a <1 nm SAM-only concept to a conformal, electronically permissive diffusion barrier matched to rough topography:
  • Apply an ultrathin (1–3 nm) ALD Al2O3 or alucone (molecular layer deposition) on the cMOF surface facing perovskite OR on perovskite top surface (depending on adhesion), then functionalize with a conductive/semiconductive molecular layer (e.g., ultrathin fullerene derivative or conjugated zwitterion) if needed to maintain tunneling/transport.
  • Design constraint: barrier must block direct coordination of halides to open metal sites while keeping added series resistance ΔRs minimal (verify by TLM/contact resistance mapping).
4.2 Accelerated halide exposure tests prior to device integration (mandatory):
  • Expose cMOF@carbon (with and without barrier) to controlled I2/I−/Br− sources in dry conditions and at 60 °C (e.g., vapor exposure to iodine, and contact with solid halide salts under controlled humidity). Monitor:
    – XPS (metal oxidation state shifts; I 3d uptake),
    – UV–vis-NIR (new charge-transfer bands),
    – Raman/EPR (radical changes),
    – GIWAXS (crystallinity retention).
  • Go/no-go: if halide uptake or metal reduction/oxidation indicates strong irreversible reaction within 24–72 h at 60 °C, switch metal node/ligand family and/or enforce barrier-first architecture.

Step 5 — Full device fabrication and performance validation
5.1 Assemble PSCs by lamination (<80 °C, low pressure) with cMOF@carbon facing perovskite. Ensure conformal contact; quantify real contact area/roughness by cross-sectional SEM/TEM.
5.2 Parametric matrix (kept mechanistically tied):
  • cMOF thickness: 5, 10, 15 nm.
  • Counter-ion architecture: none vs Option A vs Option B.
  • Barrier: none vs 1–3 nm ALD/MLD barrier.
  • Pre-doping level x0: low/medium/high (as defined by integrated charge during initialization).
5.3 Performance metrics:
  • Stabilized MPP power density and J–V hysteresis; Voc/FF changes correlated to Rct, Rrec, and Cbuffer.
  • Operando KP/UPS (work function shifts under light/bias) and operando Raman/EPR (reversible redox signatures) to prove that any observed Cint increase is linked to cMOF redox activity in the dry stack.

Step 6 — Controls and explicit pivot plan
6.1 Controls to isolate mechanism:
  (i) pristine nanostructured carbon;
  (ii) carbon + non-redox crystalline porous layer (thickness-matched);
  (iii) carbon + insulating polymer (thickness-matched);
  (iv) cMOF@carbon without immobilized counter-ion architecture (tests reviewer’s concern directly);
  (v) conventional 2D-perovskite or small-molecule passivation benchmark.
6.2 Pivot if gates fail (mandatory):
  • If dry-state redox reversibility/capacitance is inadequate (Cbuffer < 1 μF cm^-2 or strong irreversibility), pivot to hybrid interlayer: cMOF retained primarily for electronic bridging/passivation, while a separately deposited 5–20 nm solid single-ion conductor (fixed anion polymer) supplies the counter-ion reservoir. The perovskite is protected by a conformal barrier to prevent ion exchange with the absorber; the ion conductor interfaces only with the cMOF/carbon side to enable pseudocapacitance without drawing halides/A-site ions.
Feasibility: 1) Reviewer-critical physics (ion compensation) is explicitly engineered, not assumed. The proposal no longer relies on a ‘dry cMOF redox capacitor’ without ions; instead, it implements internal fixed counter-charge (polyanionic dopant) or an interpenetrated single-ion conductor so that cMOF redox switching can proceed with localized ion rearrangement within the interlayer rather than perovskite ion migration. This directly addresses the contradiction that pseudocapacitance typically requires counter-ion motion.

2) Quantitative, falsifiable capacitance model ties materials to device timescales. We bound Cbuffer by Ns·Δx and require τbuffer = Rct·Cbuffer to be at least 10× faster than τion measured from low-frequency impedance/IMVS. This links the capacitance claim to measurable site density and establishes a concrete success criterion for suppressing ion-driven field fluctuations.

3) Pre-doping persistence is treated as an empirical question with a dedicated self-discharge/equilibration gate. Kelvin probe + Raman/EPR/XPS time-traces on controlled work-function contacts will determine whether an initialized mixed-valence state survives device-relevant times (10^2–10^4 s) or rapidly equilibrates. The project remains viable even if x0 does not persist, because the core mechanism can pivot to operando reversible buffering provided dry-state cycling Cbuffer is demonstrated.

4) Chemical compatibility is moved from ‘minimal SAM if needed’ to a defined, conformal diffusion barrier strategy with accelerated halide exposure go/no-go tests before device integration. This is essential because many conductive 2D cMOFs can coordinate halides or catalyze oxidation; the plan therefore screens chemistry under controlled halide stress and uses ultrathin ALD/MLD barriers that can conform to rough carbon/perovskite interfaces while limiting added series resistance.

5) The approach remains aligned with the original concept chain (cMOF@nanostructured carbon nanoreactor interlayer improving charge transfer + stability), but is now physically self-consistent in a dry PSC stack and includes explicit decision points and a hybrid-interlayer pivot if the solid-state redox-capacitance gates are not met.
final_critique:
This is a substantially improved, physically self-consistent revision versus the usual “dry MOF pseudocapacitance” handwave: you explicitly address the core contradiction (counter-ion requirement) by building a single-ion charge-compensation architecture and you add hard gates (Cbuffer in dry state; τbuffer relative to τion; halide reactivity screens; self-discharge tests). Engineering is strong: oriented thin-film cMOF growth on hierarchical carbon, polymer/polyanion infiltration, and ALD/MLD barriers are all plausible with modern toolsets, and the control matrix is well structured.

Key score deductions come from (i) remaining ambiguity in whether the proposed μF·cm−2-scale Cbuffer at 1–10^3 Hz is realistically achievable in a 5–15 nm interlayer without introducing slow ionic polarization that contaminates the extracted capacitance (CPE/Maxwell–Wagner effects), and (ii) incomplete separation of ‘true redox pseudocapacitance’ from interfacial dipolar/ionic accumulation in the polymer/polyanion phase under device bias. Your EIS plan gestures at this, but the discrimination strategy is not yet sufficiently rigorous (e.g., demonstrating Nernstian/broad redox features, oxidation-state tracking under bias with quantitative charge balance, and frequency/temperature scaling consistent with a bounded finite-site redox process rather than dispersive ion drift).

A second logical vulnerability is the assumption that adding fixed anions + mobile cations inside the interlayer will not introduce new long-time-constant field screening that could worsen hysteresis (even if it avoids perovskite ion migration). You propose σion targets, but you do not bound the ionic relaxation time of the interlayer itself in-device nor show that its polarization will stay in the “fast buffer” regime across temperature and illumination.

Finally, chemical compatibility is treated seriously, but the barrier stack risks undermining the very Rct reductions you seek; the plan lacks a quantitative transport budget (maximum allowable tunneling thickness/energy offset) tied to FF loss, and does not specify how you will ensure uniform 1–3 nm coverage on rough carbon/cMOF without pinholes (a dominant failure mode for halide blocking claims).
hypothesis_summary: Installing a redox-capacitive cMOF interlayer with internal fixed counter-charge creates a fast, reversible interfacial buffer in dry perovskite solar cells, suppressing ion-migration-driven field fluctuations to boost stabilized power and stability.

original_chain: Repetition frequency -> Nonlinear optical (NLO) properties -> Pulse duration -> Saturable absorber (SA) -> Third-order NLO polarizability -> Charge transfer -> Conductivity
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding a perovskite-compatible, electrically percolating “ionic–electronic metainterface” composed of (i) a self-limited ultrathin 2D Ruddlesden–Popper (RP) perovskite skin and (ii) a redox-programmed conjugated MOF (HHTP-like catecholate framework) as a single continuous interphase at the 3D perovskite/charge-transport junction will simultaneously (a) reduce steady-state contact resistivity while preserving carrier selectivity in photovoltaics and (b) provide genuine saturable-absorber (SA) action (intensity-dependent absorption/transfer with a finite recovery time) that can be parameterized and inserted into a standard mode-locking model to predict pulse width and threshold. Mechanistically, the proposal explicitly separates three effects that were previously conflated: 
(1) Coherent third-order nonlinearity χ(3) (Kerr/nonlinear refraction and nonlinear absorption) is treated only as a contributor to intensity-dependent optical response; SA behavior is not assumed from χ(3) alone. Instead, SA arises from population dynamics: under high instantaneous carrier density the interphase exhibits (i) bleaching/state-filling of interfacial delocalized states (MOF band/CT states and/or interfacial charge-transfer states) and (ii) a concurrent increase in interfacial transmission probability (reduced effective injection barrier) due to quasi-Fermi level shifts and occupation of a broad interfacial density-of-states (DOS). These yield a measurable modulation depth ΔT, saturation fluence F_sat (or I_sat), recovery time τ_rec, and nonsaturable loss T_ns.
(2) The “reduced interfacial transfer barrier” is formalized as carrier-density-dependent transport across a thin tunneling/contact region: the RP skin fixes ionic/defect chemistry and provides a controlled dipole and tunneling thickness; the MOF provides a high-DOS, redox-tunable transport manifold. Under a pump pulse, the interfacial quasi-Fermi level splitting (ΔE_F) and DOS filling lower the effective barrier height φ_eff(N) and increase tunneling probability, causing a measurable decrease of specific contact resistivity ρ_c(F) and extraction time constant τ_ext(F) with fluence. This is distinct from photothermal changes (T-dependent mobility) and from field-screening artifacts (transient band flattening without bleaching).
(3) Chemical decoupling is made falsifiable: the RP skin is an ion-blocking and coordination-shielding layer with explicit quantitative acceptance criteria for halide/metal interdiffusion and for MOF node-valence drift under operation. The RP skin prevents direct catecholate–halide coordination and suppresses redox exchange between perovskite surface iodine/defect species and the MOF metal nodes, enabling stable redox programming of the MOF work function/conductivity without triggering perovskite decomposition.
Predicted outcomes: (PV) A reduced ρ_c at the target interface (≥3× improvement) with unchanged or improved surface recombination velocity S and increased implied Voc (iVoc) / PLQY, within a pre-registered go/no-go window. (Ultrafast) Extracted SA parameters (ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, T_ns) inserted into a Haus master equation (or equivalent lumped cavity model) reproduce measured pulse width and mode-locking threshold. The interphase will not change repetition frequency f_rep except via any deliberate cavity-length change; it can change threshold, pulse width, and stability through ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, and insertion loss.
Plan: Step 0 — Device architectures and where the metainterface sits (pre-registered):
0.1 Photovoltaics (n–i–p): Glass/ITO/SnO2/(3D perovskite)/[RP skin + MOF]/HTL (MeO-2PACz or Spiro-OMeTAD) /Au; and a HTL-free carbon-contact variant if MOF is used as an extraction scaffold. The metainterface is implemented only at one junction at a time (perovskite/ETL or perovskite/HTL) to preserve interpretability.
0.2 Ultrafast testbeds (two tiers):
  Tier-1 (stack-level SA metrology without lasing): Substrate/transport/perovskite/[RP+MOF] as an optical stack for pump–probe/Z-scan and ultrafast photocurrent.
  Tier-2 (cavity demonstration): perovskite waveguide or microcavity where the interphase is placed in a region of controlled mode overlap Γ with the optical field (e.g., contact/cladding layer); cavity length L is fixed across interphase variants to isolate effects on pulse width/threshold rather than f_rep.

Step 1 — Self-limited RP skin growth with explicit architectural targets:
1.1 RP thickness and n-value target: n=1–2 RP phase, thickness t_RP = 1.0–2.0 nm (≈ 1–2 inorganic slabs), continuous coverage ≥95% (AFM/ToF-SIMS lateral uniformity).
1.2 Chemistry: vapor-assisted bulky-cation halide treatment using PEA-I, BA-I, or fluorinated-PEA-I to tune dipole; substoichiometric exposure in a sealed chamber at 40–60 °C. Growth is diffusion-limited and stopped in the self-limited regime.
1.3 In-situ growth stop criteria: real-time ellipsometry (ΔΨ/ΔΔ) calibrated to t_RP; stop when Δt <0.1 nm over 10 min. Confirm by angle-resolved XPS (attenuation of Pb 4f / I 3d) and GIWAXS (appearance of RP diffraction at q consistent with n=1–2).
1.4 Dipole/work-function pre-design: target interfacial vacuum level shift ΔWF = 0.15–0.35 eV measured by UPS/Kelvin probe on reference stacks (transport/RP/perovskite). Selection among PEA/BA/F-PEA is made to hit ΔWF without increasing energetic offset that would degrade selectivity.

Step 2 — Surface-confined conjugated MOF growth with thickness/percolation targets and chemical safeguards:
2.1 MOF selection and node strategy: Cu3(HHTP)2 and Ni3(HHTP)2 as endpoints plus mixed-node (Cu/Ni) to tune conductivity and redox stability. Rationale: conjugated π-pathways and redox-tunable carrier density (Asset 2), with proven strong NLO/SA behavior in ultrathin heterostructures (Asset 1) but here implemented without graphene.
2.2 Surface-confined growth (SAG) protocol (explicit):
  (i) Linker-first adsorption: HHTP (or HHTP-derivative) adsorption onto RP surface from anhydrous alcohol at ≤25 °C, 5–10 min, followed by solvent rinse.
  (ii) Metalation cycles: immerse in metal salt solution (Cu(OAc)2 or Ni(OAc)2 in alcohol) at 25–60 °C for 5–10 min, rinse; repeat N cycles to reach t_MOF = 3–7 nm. Thickness is controlled by cycle count; growth is halted before island/grain formation.
  (iii) Anneal: ≤80 °C under inert atmosphere, 10–30 min to improve conjugation without perovskite damage.
2.3 Percolation and optical parasitics targets: sheet resistance R_sh < 10^5 Ω/sq at 5 nm; optical insertion loss at 532–850 nm < 5% for the metainterface stack (integrating sphere measurement). If loss exceeds threshold, reduce t_MOF or adjust redox set point.
2.4 Chemical isolation design rule: MOF is never grown directly on 3D perovskite—only on RP skin. A “no-RP” control is fabricated to prove necessity and to quantify chemical damage risk.

Step 3 — Redox programming with stability windows and monitoring:
3.1 Redox set step: iodine vapor microdose (calibrated partial pressure/time) or mild electrochemical gating on test coupons to achieve partial oxidation that maximizes conductivity while limiting free-carrier absorption. Target: increase conductivity ≥10× from as-grown while keeping insertion loss <5%.
3.2 Redox-state locking: counterion selection via final rinse with bulky, weakly coordinating anions (pre-registered candidates) to stabilize charge density.
3.3 Node valence stability window (acceptance criterion): operando spectroscopies must show node oxidation state drift ≤10% (relative change in characteristic XAS/XPS features) after 100 h 1-sun MPP or after ultrafast pumping dose equivalent.

Step 4 — Quantitative SA model extraction and mode-locking framework (mandatory directive i):
4.1 Measure SA parameters on full stacks (not powders):
  (i) Open-aperture Z-scan to extract nonlinear absorption coefficient and effective saturation: fit transmission T(I) = 1 − (ΔT)/(1 + I/I_sat) − T_ns (or fluence form).
  (ii) Pump–probe transient absorption/reflection to extract τ_rec (fast/slow components) and confirm bleaching dynamics.
  (iii) Separate Kerr vs SA: closed-aperture Z-scan for nonlinear refraction n2; show that mode-locking-relevant behavior is dominated by absorptive saturation (ΔT) and τ_rec rather than purely dispersive n2.
4.2 Insert extracted parameters into a standard cavity model:
  Use Haus master equation (or equivalent lumped model) with saturable absorber term characterized by {ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, T_ns} plus cavity dispersion (GVD), gain bandwidth, and output coupling. Predict pulse width and mode-locking threshold vs interphase variant.
4.3 Repetition frequency statement (pre-registered): f_rep = c/(n_eff·L). Since L and n_eff are fixed across variants, the interphase is not expected to change f_rep measurably; it can change threshold, pulse duration, pulse stability, and achievable fundamental mode-locking regime. Any observed f_rep shift beyond measurement uncertainty triggers an investigation of unintended cavity-length/index changes.

Step 5 — Carrier-density-dependent interfacial transport model + discriminating tests (mandatory directive ii):
5.1 Transport model (measurable predictions):
  Represent the RP as a tunneling/dipole layer with thickness t_RP and barrier φ0. Represent MOF as a redox-tunable conductor with DOS g(E) and quasi-Fermi shift ΔE_F under photoexcitation. Predict:
  φ_eff(F) = φ0 − α·ΔE_F(F) (DOS filling / quasi-Fermi splitting term)
  and contact resistivity ρ_c(F) ∝ exp[β·t_RP·sqrt(φ_eff(F))] / G_MOF(redox)
  giving a monotonic decrease of ρ_c with fluence until saturation when DOS is filled.
  Extraction time τ_ext(F) from TRPL/TA or ultrafast photocurrent should track ρ_c(F) (pre-registered correlation).
5.2 Measurements that directly map ρ_c(F) and τ_ext(F):
  (i) Ultrafast photocurrent sampling (rise-time vs fluence) under fixed average power using pulse-picker (vary peak intensity independent of heating).
  (ii) Fluence-dependent TRPL quenching rate with selective-side excitation (from transport layer side) to isolate interfacial transfer.
  (iii) Intensity-dependent impedance/photovoltage response under constant average power to separate peak-intensity effects from thermal.
5.3 Discriminating against artifacts:
  (i) Temperature-controlled pump–probe/Z-scan (fixed sample temperature using a stage; monitor with IR sensor). A purely thermal mechanism would scale with average power and temperature, not with peak fluence at fixed average.
  (ii) Field-screening control: replicate absorption but alter DOS filling by using an insulating MOF analog (nonconjugated linker) and a conductivity-matched but low-bleaching layer; if band-flattening alone dominated, these would mimic the effect—pre-registered expectation is they will not.
  (iii) Identical linear absorption control: adjust thickness so variants have matched linear absorption; then any change in τ_ext(F) is not due to different absorbed energy.

Step 6 — Operando chemical acceptance criteria + probes (mandatory directive iii):
6.1 Hard quantitative acceptance criteria:
  (A) Halide ingress into MOF: iodine content in MOF region after stress < 1 at.% (ToF-SIMS calibrated, depth-resolved) OR below a pre-set detection-calibrated threshold corresponding to <10^13 cm−2 areal density.
  (B) Metal-node migration into perovskite: Cu/Ni in perovskite bulk < 10^17 cm−3 equivalent (ToF-SIMS quantification on sister devices).
  (C) RP integrity: RP diffraction signature (GIWAXS) retained with <20% reduction in peak intensity after stress.
  (D) MOF redox drift: ≤10% change in node valence indicator (XAS/XPS/Raman band ratios) under illumination/bias.
6.2 In-operando / quasi-operando probes (added beyond post-mortem):
  (i) Bias/light ToF-SIMS on sister devices (time-staggered set) to obtain diffusion kinetics, not only endpoints.
  (ii) In-situ Kelvin probe / UPS shift under illumination to track work-function drift and quasi-Fermi level effects.
  (iii) Operando Raman/IR (MOF vibrational signatures) and operando GIWAXS for structural stability during bias/light.

Step 7 — Photovoltaic selectivity validation + go/no-go (mandatory directive iv):
7.1 Selectivity metrics (explicit):
  (i) Surface recombination velocity S extracted from TRPL (and/or transient photoconductance on suitable films) with selective excitation.
  (ii) Implied Voc and PLQY of full stacks at 1-sun equivalent to detect nonradiative interface losses.
  (iii) UPS/IPES-derived injection barriers and band alignment; confirm that redox tuning does not create minority-carrier leakage pathways.
  (iv) Dark J–V leakage and ideality factor changes; EIS recombination resistance under illumination.
7.2 Go/no-go criterion:
  If redox tuning reduces Rs (or ρ_c) but causes >10 mV drop in implied Voc or a ≥2× increase in interfacial recombination rate (from PLQY/TRPL/EIS), that redox set point is rejected; proceed by (a) adjusting RP dipole (cation choice), (b) lowering MOF DOS via node selection/mixed node, or (c) relocating metainterface to the opposite junction where selectivity constraints differ.

Step 8 — Controls (pre-registered) to isolate each mechanism:
8.1 RP-only (no MOF): isolates ionic blocking/passivation and dipole.
8.2 MOF-only directly on 3D perovskite (intentional stress control): quantifies chemical incompatibility and validates the necessity of RP.
8.3 Insulating MOF analog (nonconjugated linker): similar chemistry/thickness, no delocalized DOS; tests whether conductivity/DOS is essential.
8.4 Conductivity-matched but low-bleaching interlayer: separates electrical improvement from SA behavior.
8.5 Thickness-matched but different redox states: isolates work-function/conductivity effects from geometry.

Milestones and decision gates:
M1 (Materials): Achieve t_RP 1–2 nm and t_MOF 3–7 nm with percolation and insertion loss <5%.
M2 (Chemistry): Meet halide/metal diffusion and redox drift criteria under 100 h 1-sun MPP.
M3 (Transport): Demonstrate ρ_c improvement ≥3× and τ_ext reduction with fluence dependence consistent with DOS-filling model (and not with average-power heating).
M4 (Ultrafast): Extract {ΔT, F_sat, τ_rec, T_ns} and accurately predict pulse width/threshold in cavity using Haus model; confirm f_rep unchanged for fixed L.
M5 (PV): Demonstrate improved stabilized efficiency or stability without selectivity penalty; otherwise pivot to alternative redox/node/cation set points per go/no-go.
Feasibility: 1) Why the SA claim is now mechanistically rigorous: The revised plan no longer equates χ(3) with saturable absorption. χ(3) is measured separately (n2 via closed-aperture Z-scan), while SA action is quantified by ΔT, F_sat (or I_sat), τ_rec, and T_ns extracted from open-aperture Z-scan and pump–probe on complete device-relevant stacks. These parameters are then used in a Haus master-equation framework to predict pulse width and mode-locking threshold, explicitly acknowledging that repetition frequency is set by cavity length and effective index. This directly satisfies the reviewer’s demand for a quantitative dynamical model.

2) Why intensity-dependent “barrier reduction” is now testable and separable from artifacts: The interfacial transport hypothesis is reformulated as DOS filling + quasi-Fermi level shift reducing φ_eff and enhancing tunneling/contact conductance across a thin RP layer, predicting a specific scaling ρ_c(F) and τ_ext(F) with fluence until saturation. The plan pre-registers discriminating experiments that hold average power constant while varying peak intensity, uses temperature-controlled pump–probe to eliminate photothermal explanations, and includes matched-absorption and mechanism-specific controls (insulating MOF analog; conductivity-matched low-bleaching layer). This converts a qualitative claim into falsifiable scaling laws.

3) Why RP genuinely decouples MOF chemistry from perovskite ion chemistry (now with hard acceptance criteria): Catecholate MOFs can coordinate halides and participate in redox exchange; the revised proposal treats this as a primary risk with explicit quantitative diffusion limits (halide ingress, metal-node migration) and redox-drift thresholds. Crucially, operando and time-staggered sister-device ToF-SIMS, in-situ Kelvin probe/UPS under illumination, and operando GIWAXS/Raman/IR are added to establish causality and kinetics rather than relying on post-mortem snapshots. The RP layer is therefore not an assertion but a measured barrier with go/no-go thresholds.

4) Why PSC selectivity is protected despite redox-tuned conductivity: The plan explicitly measures and constrains minority-carrier leakage and recombination via implied Voc/PLQY, TRPL-derived S, UPS/IPES injection barriers, dark leakage, and illuminated EIS. A pre-registered go/no-go rule prevents optimizing Rs at the expense of interfacial recombination. Energetic tuning is split between RP dipole control (coarse alignment) and MOF redox programming (fine conductivity/work-function tuning), reducing the risk that conductivity improvements inadvertently destroy selectivity.

5) Literature and empirical basis supporting feasibility: Conjugated MOFs exhibit semiconducting transport with redox/annealing-dependent conductivity and π-delocalization (Asset 2), enabling a controllable interfacial conductor. Separately, ultrathin MOF-based heterostructures demonstrate strong nonlinear optical response and SA-enabled ultrafast pulse generation (Asset 1); here, that capability is translated into stack-level SA parameters instead of inferred from χ(3) alone. Ultrathin RP surface layers are an established strategy for perovskite defect/ion management when kept in the tunneling-thin regime; the proposal adds in-situ thickness stopping and operando proof of ionic blocking. Together, these elements make the metainterface concept feasible while addressing the reviewers’ mechanistic and validation demands.
final_critique: Methodological execution is unusually well-specified (thickness targets, stop criteria, control matrix, and go/no-go windows) and addresses common reviewer failure modes (χ(3)≠SA; thermal vs peak-fluence artifacts; chemical incompatibility). However, two scientific gaps reduce logical strength. (i) The “carrier-density-dependent barrier reduction” model is presented as an exponential tunneling scaling with an ad hoc φ_eff(F)=φ0−αΔE_F(F), but the proposal does not specify how ΔE_F(F) will be quantitatively obtained/validated at the interface (separate from bulk perovskite photophysics) nor how α relates to a measurable interfacial DOS/charging capacitance; without that, fits risk being phenomenological. (ii) The dual-function interphase (low ρ_c while preserving selectivity, plus SA action) is plausible but not shown to be mutually compatible: the same added DOS/percolation that reduces contact resistance can increase sub-gap absorption, free-carrier absorption, and minority-carrier leakage; the proposal has safeguards (PLQY/iVoc, dark JV), but no explicit design-space mapping (e.g., required ΔT and F_sat vs allowable T_ns and added recombination) that demonstrates simultaneous attainability. Evidence grounding is strong overall, but feasibility hinges on whether 3–7 nm conjugated MOFs can reliably achieve the targeted R_sh and <5% insertion loss on real RP/perovskite stacks (not ideal substrates), and whether operando ToF-SIMS/UPS under illumination can be executed with sufficient depth/energy resolution to cleanly attribute changes to the metainterface rather than ion-migration-induced bulk effects.
hypothesis_summary: A hybrid ionic–electronic interphase combining an ultrathin perovskite skin and a redox-tunable conductive MOF simultaneously lowers contact resistance in solar cells and provides measurable saturable-absorber action for ultrafast pulse generation.

original_chain: Stability enhancement -> Ag44 -> Mechanochemical synthesis -> Thermal stability -> Metal-organic frameworks (MOFs) -> Cascade reaction -> Poly(diallyldimethylammonium chloride)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: Embedding mechanochemically synthesized Ag44@MOF nanocomposites as a crosslinked, ion-selective interpenetrating network (IPN) *within* a PDDA-modified SnO2 ETL (not as a new perovskite-facing interlayer) will improve perovskite solar cell thermal stability (85–105 °C, bias/illumination) by quantitatively reducing the halide chemical-potential gradient and suppressing redox-active interfacial failure pathways—*only if* three falsifiable criteria are met prior to device fabrication: (1) Ag44@MOF exhibits reversible, sub-stoichiometric halide uptake (buffering) without irreversible conversion to AgX (X = I, Br) under relevant halide activities at 85–105 °C; (2) the SnO2 electronic percolation network retains electron selectivity and low resistivity at the MOF/PDDA loadings needed for ion management; and (3) PDDA is immobilized as fixed cationic charge without introducing mobile counterions (e.g., Cl−) that would otherwise add an additional migrating ionic species.

Mechanistic rationale (cascade with de-risked chemistry): (i) PDDA (converted to PDDA-NO3 or PDDA-TFSI and ionically crosslinked) creates *quantified* fixed positive charge domains inside SnO2 that electrostatically retard halide ingress and flatten the interfacial halide concentration gradient; (ii) Ag44, when truly confined intrapore (not surface-deposited) inside a thermally robust MOF, acts as a *kinetically accessible and reversible* halide-acceptor reservoir by forming labile Ag–X interactions that saturate at a defined capacity, thereby buffering transient halide flux without allowing nucleation/growth of bulk AgX or Ag aggregation; (iii) MOF microporosity and particle packing increase ionic tortuosity while the continuous SnO2 matrix preserves an electron-percolation pathway, jointly reducing thermally accelerated ionic conductivity in the ETL without increasing electronic series resistance beyond a defined threshold. If these conditions hold, the ETL/perovskite junction maintains stable stoichiometry under heat and bias, increasing quasi-Fermi level splitting (reduced non-radiative recombination) and preserving Voc/FF during 85–105 °C operation.
Plan: Stage 0 — Quantitative go/no-go design criteria (MANDATORY before any device fabrication)

0.1 Ag44@MOF halide uptake capacity, kinetics, reversibility, and cluster integrity at 85–105 °C
A) Model environment and stimuli (two-tier):
- Tier-1 (powder screening, controlled halide chemical potential): expose Ag44@MOF powders to halide sources that bracket perovskite-relevant chemical potentials:
  (i) solid-state: MAS NMR-grade salts (FAI/FABr/CsI/CsBr) physically mixed at defined mol% and held at 85/105 °C; 
  (ii) vapor/solution: anhydrous acetonitrile or GBL with 10−5 to 10−2 M tetrabutylammonium iodide/bromide (TBAI/TBAB) to avoid water; and 
  (iii) “perovskite-extract” electrolyte: ionic liquid or polar aprotic extract containing MA/FA halides quantified by ion chromatography (IC) as a realistic mixed-ion matrix.
- Tier-2 (bias-relevant redox stress): deposit thin films of SnO2:Ag44@MOF on inert substrates and apply potentiostatic bias (−0.2 to −1.0 V vs Ag/Ag+ in non-aqueous electrolyte containing 10−4–10−2 M halide) at 85 °C to emulate electron-rich ETL conditions.

B) Measurements (quantitative outputs):
- Halide uptake isotherms at 85 and 105 °C: quantify halide removed from solution by IC (or potentiometric titration) and fit to Langmuir/Freundlich to extract capacity (qmax, mmol X− per g composite) and affinity constants.
- Uptake kinetics: time-resolved halide depletion (minutes→hours) to obtain pseudo-first-order rate constants kobs and diffusion-limited regime identification.
- Reversibility/desorption: perform at least 5 adsorption–desorption cycles using halide-free solvent/electrolyte or competing anion (NO3−, TFSI−) at 85 °C; require ≥80% capacity retention after 5 cycles.
- Cluster integrity pass/fail thresholds (must all pass):
  1) Operando/in situ Ag K-edge XANES/EXAFS or in situ XPS during halide exposure at 85–105 °C: 
     - FAIL if spectra show dominant Ag(I) signatures consistent with bulk AgI/AgBr growth or irreversible oxidation beyond a set fraction.
     - PASS criterion: ≤10% shift in edge position/white-line intensity relative to pristine Ag44@MOF and no emergence of AgX long-range order in EXAFS.
  2) PXRD of exposed powders: FAIL if new crystalline AgI/AgBr peaks exceed 2 wt% equivalent (Rietveld/peak area calibration).
  3) TEM/STEM after stress: FAIL if Ag domain growth >2 nm average (cluster aggregation) or loss of cluster-size distribution.

C) Decision metrics linking to device need (design-to-capacity):
- Compute a required halide-buffer capacity target based on an upper-bound halide flux during aging: define a conservative integrated halide dose QX (mol cm−2) from literature ionic current densities (measured later by impedance) and demand qmax·mloading ≥ 5×QX (safety factor 5). If capacity is insufficient, loading must rise or chemistry revised.

0.2 PDDA fixed-charge engineering without mobile Cl− and without insulating SnO2
A) PDDA counterion control (mandatory): obtain/prepare PDDA-NO3 and PDDA-TFSI (anion exchange from PDDA-Cl via dialysis/ion-exchange resin). Verify residual Cl− by IC; PASS: Cl− < 0.5 mol% relative to PDDA monomer.
B) Immobilization/crosslink strategy (quantified):
- Use multivalent anions (SO4^2−, citrate^3−) at controlled equivalents to PDDA charge (0.1–0.5 equiv) to form ionically crosslinked domains.
- Quantify fixed-charge density (Xf) and mobility:
  1) Polyelectrolyte titration (streaming potential or colloid titration) on dissolved PDDA and on extracted ETL films to estimate immobilized charge fraction.
  2) Zeta potential of SnO2 colloids before/after PDDA/crosslinking to confirm adsorption and charge sign/magnitude.
  3) Counterion mobility test: soak ETLs in anhydrous solvent, then analyze leachate by IC (NO3−/TFSI−/SO4^2−/citrate); PASS: <5% of total counterions leached in 24 h at 85 °C.

0.3 ETL electronic transport/percolation constraints vs composition (mandatory)
A) Prepare a composition matrix (no perovskite yet):
- SnO2 baseline; SnO2 + PDDA (0.005, 0.01, 0.02, 0.05 wt% of SnO2 solids); SnO2 + Ag44@MOF (0.05, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0 wt%); full IPN combinations.
B) Transport metrics and pass/fail thresholds:
- Four-point probe conductivity (σ) of ETL films (25–40 nm) on glass at 25 °C and 85 °C.
- Electron mobility via SCLC (electron-only devices) or field-effect measurements.
- Contact resistivity (ρc) to Ag and to perovskite surrogate contact (e.g., PCBM or C60) using TLM.
- Work function/energetics: UPS/Kelvin probe; PASS: SnO2 EF shift < 0.15 eV vs baseline unless it improves alignment.
- Series resistance budget: in full devices later, require ΔRs ≤ +0.5 Ω·cm^2 vs baseline (or ≤15% relative increase) and FF loss <2% absolute attributable to ETL.
C) Electron selectivity safeguard:
- If PDDA/MOF introduces interfacial dipoles or increases surface recombination, implement a *minimal* inorganic capping (1–2 nm ALD Al2O3 or solution SnOx) only after transport pass criteria are met; verify it does not block ion-management function (depth profiling).

0.4 Intrapore vs surface localization validation and leaching resistance (mandatory)
A) Pore-access and localization tests (must triangulate with ≥2 orthogonal methods):
- Gas sorption (N2/CO2) on MOF vs Ag44@MOF: PASS if micropore volume loss is consistent with partial pore occupancy but not complete pore blockage (e.g., retain ≥40–60% of pristine micropore volume).
- Competitive probe uptake: load a size-matched dye/probe molecule known to enter MOF pores (e.g., small aromatic) and quantify reduced uptake upon Ag44 encapsulation; surface-only Ag would not suppress internal uptake comparably.
- Selective etching/leaching: brief exposure to a ligand that can strip surface Ag species without penetrating pores (chosen based on MOF chemistry), then quantify Ag released by ICP-MS; PASS if leachable Ag <5% of total Ag.
- 3D STEM tomography (subset) to spatially localize Ag within MOF particle volume; corroborate with elemental mapping.
B) Cluster-size vs pore-aperture feasibility benchmarking:
- Establish Ag44 size (from literature/measurements) and compare to ZIF-8 aperture (~3.4 Å) vs cage size (~11.6 Å): because aperture is smaller than cluster, specify that ZIF-8 encapsulation is expected to be (i) defect-assisted, (ii) during mechanochemical “pore-breathing/defect generation,” or (iii) predominantly near internal defect/cavity networks. Therefore:
  - Define a ZIF-8 feasibility gate: PASS only if tomography/leaching tests confirm internal localization; otherwise ZIF-8 is relegated to “surface-anchored tortuosity control,” and UiO-66 (or a larger-aperture ZIF derivative) becomes the primary intrapore system.

Stage 1 — Materials synthesis with explicit parameters

1.1 nMOF synthesis (green/low-residue)
- ZIF-8: aqueous synthesis at room temperature using excess 2-methylimidazole (2-MI), target 20–40 nm; wash thoroughly to remove free ligand; activate at 120–150 °C under vacuum.
- UiO-66: room-temperature or water/ethanol route, modulated with monocarboxylate (e.g., acetic acid) to reach 20–40 nm; activate similarly.
- Characterize: PXRD, TGA, DLS/TEM size, BET/CO2 sorption, defect proxies (if available).

1.2 Mechanochemical encapsulation of Ag44 into nMOF (low-damage)
- Use resonant acoustic mixing (RAM) or low-shear tumbling with controlled liquid-assisted grinding (LAG): 0.5–2.0 μL mg−1 of ethanol/water (humidity controlled) to promote diffusion/defect-assisted ingress.
- Avoid high-energy ball milling; temperature rise monitored (<35 °C).
- “Pore-gate/defect-heal” lock-in: brief post-mix with small ligand dose (ZIF-8: 2-MI; UiO-66: monocarboxylate modulator) at defined equivalents to surface sites.
- Confirm Ag44 integrity post-encapsulation: UV–vis fingerprint (if accessible), XPS Ag 3d, XANES/EXAFS (where possible), STEM-EDS.

Stage 2 — ETL ink formulation and IPN construction (only after Stage 0 pass)

2.1 PDDA integration into SnO2 with counterion control
- Use PDDA-NO3 or PDDA-TFSI at 0.005–0.05 wt% relative to SnO2 solids.
- Crosslinking: after coating/anneal, expose film briefly to SO4^2−/citrate in anhydrous/alcoholic medium (avoid water where possible) at controlled ionic strength; rinse/dry. Verify immobilization by leach test and zeta/fixed-charge assays.

2.2 Disperse Ag44@MOF into PDDA-containing SnO2 ink
- Loading range guided by transport pass criteria: start 0.05–0.5 wt% (relative to SnO2 solids).
- Dispersion protocol: mild sonication + filtration (0.45 μm) to prevent aggregates; DLS on ink.

2.3 Film deposition
- Deposit ETL 25–40 nm (spin or blade), anneal ≤150 °C.
- Surface roughness target: RMS < 5 nm by AFM.
- Depth distribution target: PDDA/Ag44@MOF enriched in ETL bulk, not at the perovskite-facing top 3–5 nm; verify by angle-resolved XPS or ToF-SIMS depth profiling.

Stage 3 — Device fabrication (only after Stage 0 + Stage 2 pass)

3.1 Architecture (kept as originally intended to isolate ETL-side stabilization)
- glass/ITO/2PACz (or PTAA)/FA0.8Cs0.2Pb(I0.8Br0.2)3/modified SnO2 (IPN variants)/BCP/Ag.

3.2 Control matrix (unchanged but counterion-corrected)
(i) baseline SnO2; (ii) SnO2+PDDA-NO3 (or TFSI); (iii) SnO2+MOF only; (iv) SnO2+Ag44 only; (v) SnO2+Ag44@MOF; (vi) SnO2+PDDA+Ag44@MOF IPN.
Add a mandatory counterion control: SnO2+PDDA-Cl (if used at all) to explicitly test whether Cl− is detrimental.

Stage 4 — Mechanism validation mapped to reviewer uncertainties

4.1 Ion-transport and ion-profile verification under thermal bias
- Temperature-dependent impedance under illumination/bias to extract ionic time constants and low-frequency capacitance; correlate with halide uptake capacity measured in Stage 0.
- ToF-SIMS depth profiles (I−/Br−, Ag, Zn/Zr, N from PDDA) before/after MPP aging at 85–105 °C to confirm reduced halide penetration and reduced halide pile-up at the perovskite/ETL interface.

4.2 Electronic selectivity preservation
- Conductivity/mobility/contact resistivity on completed ETLs (same stack) and in devices (Rs extraction) to ensure within pass thresholds.
- QFLS/PLQY on glass/ETL/perovskite test stacks; require that IPN ETL does not reduce initial QFLS (or improves it) while improving retention after thermal soaking.
- UPS/Kelvin probe to detect interfacial dipole formation; if dipole causes Voc loss, iterate PDDA loading/capping layer.

4.3 Device stress and post-mortem
- Thermal aging: ISOS-D-2-like (dark, 85–105 °C, N2) + ISOS-L-2-like (1 sun, 65–85 °C, controlled humidity). Track T80, Voc/FF retention, hysteresis.
- Post-mortem: cross-sectional TEM/EDS for Ag/halides; GIWAXS for mixed-halide phase segregation; XPS for Ag oxidation state changes and halide accumulation.

Stage 5 — Mechanism falsification (retained, made more quantitative)
- Replace Ag44 with Au25@MOF: if stability improvement collapses while transport remains similar, supports Ag-specific halide buffering/redox role.
- Replace MOF with non-porous ZrO2 NPs (same size/volume fraction): if stability benefit collapses and ToF-SIMS shows higher halide ingress, supports tortuosity/microporosity role.
- Vary PDDA fixed-charge density systematically (molecular weight and crosslink equivalents); map stability vs fixed-charge density vs ETL conductivity to identify an optimum and prove that “more PDDA” is not trivially better.

Deliverables and down-select logic
- Only MOF/cluster systems passing Stage 0.1/0.4 proceed to devices.
- Only IPN formulations meeting Stage 0.3 transport thresholds proceed.
- If ZIF-8 fails intrapore localization, it becomes a diffusion/tortuosity-only comparator and UiO-66 (or alternative larger-aperture MOF) is used for true confinement claims.
Feasibility: This revision directly de-risks the reviewers’ four uncertainties by converting the cascade from a qualitative narrative into a quantified, falsifiable materials-selection and ETL-engineering workflow.

(1) Ag44@MOF as a reversible halide buffer/redox sink is no longer assumed: it is pre-qualified via halide uptake isotherms/kinetics at 85–105 °C, multi-cycle reversibility, and operando XPS/XANES/EXAFS with explicit pass/fail thresholds against AgX formation and aggregation. This prevents proceeding with a chemistry that would instead seed AgI/AgBr or catalyze degradation.

(2) PDDA risks (insulating domains, work-function shifts, mobile Cl−) are controlled by mandatory counterion exchange (PDDA-NO3/PDDA-TFSI), residual Cl− quantification (IC), fixed-charge density quantification (titration/zeta), and leaching tests at 85 °C. Crosslinking is parameterized by equivalents of multivalent anions, enabling reproducible immobilization rather than qualitative “crosslinking.”

(3) Electronic percolation/selectivity is safeguarded by a required transport characterization matrix (σ, mobility, ρc, UPS/work function) versus composition and temperature, with defined maximum allowable ΔRs and energy-level shift bounds before any perovskite is deposited. This ensures MOF/PDDA loadings that affect ion transport do not inadvertently reduce FF/Voc by increasing series resistance or creating dipoles.

(4) Intrapore vs surface Ag44 localization is treated as a gating item: multiple orthogonal tests (sorption/probe uptake, selective leaching with ICP-MS, tomography) must confirm internal confinement and low leachable Ag during ink processing. The pore-aperture constraint of ZIF-8 is explicitly acknowledged and experimentally adjudicated; if intrapore confinement cannot be proven, ZIF-8 is repositioned as a tortuosity control rather than the centerpiece of the redox-buffer claim.

These additions preserve the original concept chain (mechanochemical Ag44@MOF + PDDA-modified SnO2 IPN + cascade ion-management) while enforcing quantitative causality and minimizing the chance that any observed stability gain is merely morphological or due to unintended counterion/energy-level effects.
final_critique: This is an unusually rigorous and well-de-risked proposal that demonstrates strong command of ion–electron coupling, interfacial thermodynamics, and materials failure modes in perovskite solar cells. The mandatory Stage 0 gating logic is a major strength and directly addresses historical pitfalls of Ag-based additives and polyelectrolyte-modified ETLs. Minor score deductions arise from (i) the practical accessibility of operando XANES/EXAFS at elevated temperature and bias, which may strain feasibility timelines despite being scientifically appropriate, and (ii) residual uncertainty around Ag44 stability under prolonged electron-rich bias, where even sub-10% irreversible Ag(I) formation could have outsized long-term effects not fully bounded by the current thresholds. These are execution-risk concerns rather than conceptual flaws.
hypothesis_summary: Embedding mechanochemically synthesized Ag44@MOF nanocomposites with immobilized PDDA fixed-charge domains inside SnO2 electron transport layers improves perovskite solar cell thermal stability by buffering halide flux and suppressing redox-active interfacial degradation.

original_chain: Oxygen reduction reaction -> Electrical conductivity -> Density functional theory (DFT) -> Photoinduced Stark effect -> Organometallic halide perovskites (OMHPs) -> Photoinduced Stark effect -> Cation-dependent ion movement -> Power conversion efficiency (PCE)
proposal_content:
Hypothesis: In OMHPs, photoexcitation generates a measurable photoinduced Stark response (first- and second-order electroabsorption) that—when the local internal field is not effectively screened—lowers the activation barrier for halide/vacancy motion at/near the surface, producing transient band-bending and interfacial electron accumulation that increases electron leakage into adsorbed O2 and accelerates the first electron-transfer step of the oxygen reduction reaction (O2 + e− → O2−). The resulting superoxide chemistry increases interfacial trap density and decreases electronic conductivity, causing hysteresis growth, Voc loss in O2 under illumination, and stabilized-PCE decay.

The key identifiability risk noted by reviewers (Stark vs photobleach/band-filling vs ion-field feedback) is overcome by enforcing a falsifiable decomposition: (i) phase-sensitive electroabsorption (EA) under known external field modulation isolates field-driven spectral derivatives from population-driven photobleach; (ii) the same EA signatures are required to persist when ionic motion is suppressed (low temperature and/or ion-immobilized surface), proving a genuine Stark contribution; and (iii) operando surface-potential mapping (TR-KPFM/Kelvin probe) under controlled atmosphere directly reports photoinduced band-bending and its oxygen-dependence.

The methodological adaptation is an electrically “Stark-buffered” 2D/3D heterointerface whose function is explicitly split into orthogonal, testable knobs: (A) dielectric/field-screening control via spacer polarizability and controlled dipole orientation to reduce the effective internal field ΔF in the 3D lattice under illumination (reducing Stark amplitude without inadvertently increasing band-bending); (B) ionic-blocking control via increased near-surface migration barriers (raising Ea for iodide-vacancy/iodide motion) that is separable from dipole effects; and (C) ORR-kinetics control via independently quantified O2 uptake/permeability and a measurable increase in interfacial electron-transfer barrier (reduced surface electron density and/or less favorable alignment for O2 reduction). By designing caps and controls that orthogonalize (A) dipole/polarizability and (C) O2 permeability, we can decisively attribute reductions in superoxide generation and conductivity decay to suppressed Stark-driven ion motion and reduced electron leakage into O2, rather than generic passivation/hydrophobicity alone.
Plan: Step 0 — Pre-registered decision metrics (mandatory, falsifiable thresholds)
0.1 Primary ‘successful decoupling’ criteria (all measured at matched absorbed photon flux and matched photocarrier density via calibrated PLQY/TRPL):
- ORR suppression: ≥50% reduction in EPR spin-adduct formation rate (d[O2−]/dt proxy) in dry O2 under illumination for capped vs uncapped, at equal steady-state carrier density.
- Ion suppression: ≥3× increase in extracted near-surface ionic activation energy Ea,ion (from temperature-dependent ionic relaxation/impedance) and ≥2× reduction in effective halide diffusion coefficient D_ion (from drift-relaxation + SIMS depth broadening after standardized bias/light stress).
- Field/band-bending reduction: ≥30% reduction in operando surface photovoltage (SPV) amplitude and/or photoinduced contact potential difference (ΔCPD) under O2 relative to uncapped (TR-KPFM/Kelvin probe), without a compensatory increase in built-in interfacial band-bending in the dark.
- Device stability: ≥50 mV smaller Voc loss in dry O2 vs dry N2 during 1 sun MPP tracking (first 100 h), and ≥2× increase in T80 under dry O2 at MPP.

Step 1 — Materials matrix with orthogonal controls (dipole vs O2 permeability vs ionic blocking)
1.1 Baseline 3D absorbers (A-cation dependence): MAPbI3, FAPbI3, Cs0.1FA0.9PbI3, and MA/FA mixed to span dipole moment and ionic mobility.
1.2 2D RP caps: ultrathin n=1–2 Ruddlesden–Popper top layers deposited by post-treatment (spacer iodide/bromide salt in orthogonal solvent, 0.5–5 mg/mL; spin 3000–5000 rpm; anneal 70–100 °C). Target thickness 2–10 nm verified by spectroscopic ellipsometry and cross-sectional TEM.
1.3 Orthogonalized spacer set (three matched pairs; each pair matched in steric size and packing propensity):
- Low-dipole / high packing (LD-HP): e.g., phenethylammonium (PEA) reference with para-substitution chosen to minimize net dipole.
- High-dipole / matched packing (HD-MP): para-substituted PEA (electron withdrawing/donating) tuned to raise molecular dipole while keeping similar footprint; packing checked by GIWAXS.
- High-dipole / matched O2 permeability control (HD-MPerm): a high-dipole spacer co-formulated with a neutral co-spacer (fixed ratio) to match film density/O2 uptake to LD-HP while preserving dipole (validated by QCM/O2 sorption below).
- Ionic-immobilizing cap control (IonLock): a crosslinkable spacer (e.g., diammonium or polymerizable ammonium) yielding similar O2 uptake to LD-HP but maximally suppressing ion motion (verified by reduced ionic conductivity and SIMS).
1.4 Orientation/disorder controls:
- For each spacer, prepare (i) standard deposition, (ii) alignment-promoting deposition (slow solvent evaporation, mild thermal gradient), and (iii) deliberately disordered deposition (rapid quench), to modulate dipole orientation/disorder at constant chemistry.

Step 2 — Direct observables for dipole orientation, packing density, and O2 uptake/permeability
2.1 GIWAXS: quantify 2D RP formation (n=1–2 signatures), out-of-plane orientation, mosaic spread; ensure comparable crystallinity across LD-HP vs HD-MP.
2.2 NEXAFS (or polarized IR/Raman if NEXAFS unavailable): determine average spacer tilt angle and dipole orientation distribution relative to surface normal; report an “orientation order parameter” per cap.
2.3 Kelvin probe/UPS (dark): measure work function shifts and valence-band positions after capping to quantify interfacial dipole-induced vacuum-level shifts; ensure that “field screening” does not come from unintended stronger band-bending.
2.4 O2 uptake/permeability metrics:
- QCM-based O2 sorption on capped films (controlled O2 partial pressure, 0–1 bar; dry conditions) to extract relative uptake and kinetics.
- Complementary optical O2 permeation proxy using an O2-sensitive dye layer beneath the cap (calibrated response) to compare permeation rates while keeping thickness constant.

Step 3 — Quantitative Stark-separation protocol (falsifiable decomposition)
3.1 Phase-sensitive EA under controlled field modulation (lock-in):
- Device-like stack on transparent electrode (ITO/SnO2/perovskite/cap/HTL/Au grid or semi-transparent top) enabling a known AC field (e.g., 0.1–10 kHz, small-signal 10–200 mV) superimposed on DC bias.
- Measure ΔA(λ) at the modulation frequency and extract first-derivative (Δμ·F) and second-derivative (Δα·F^2) components by fitting to derivatives of the steady absorption spectrum.
- Intensity-scaling: repeat EA under varying optical intensity; Stark terms scale with field modulation, while photobleach/band-filling scales with carrier density and appears largely out-of-phase or in different harmonics. Use harmonic analysis (1f/2f) to separate linear/quadratic field contributions.
3.2 PIA/TA controls to remove population signals:
- Collect PIA/TA in absence of field modulation and subtract matched photobleach components from EA spectra to verify derivative-like Stark residuals.
3.3 Ion-immobilized falsification test:
- Repeat EA at low temperature (e.g., 200–240 K) where ionic drift is strongly suppressed, and on IonLock caps at room temperature. A genuine Stark signature must persist (similar derivative spectral shape), while ion-induced field drift signatures (slow phase lag, low-frequency dispersion) must diminish.

Step 4 — Operando internal-field/band-bending mapping under controlled atmosphere (reviewer-mandated)
4.1 TR-KPFM (or scanning Kelvin probe with chopped illumination) in an environmental cell allowing dry N2 vs dry O2 switching (ppm H2O control):
- Map CPD in dark and under modulated illumination (blue 470 nm vs red 630 nm, matched absorbed photon flux).
- Extract surface photovoltage (SPV = ΔCPD_light−dark) and its rise/decay kinetics. Ion-mediated contributions appear as slow components; purely electronic band-bending changes appear fast.
- Compare SPV(O2) − SPV(N2) to quantify oxygen-specific electron extraction/band-bending.
4.2 Correlate TR-KPFM with EA: samples showing reduced EA Stark amplitude and reduced SPV slow component must also show reduced ionic signatures and ORR.

Step 5 — Ion motion quantification with explicit near-surface sensitivity
5.1 Transient ion-drift/relaxation spectroscopy:
- Apply bias pulses under controlled illumination; record current transient and capacitance relaxation. Fit with distributed RC/Warburg elements to isolate ionic time constants.
5.2 Temperature-dependent impedance (200–330 K):
- Separate ionic and electronic arcs; extract Ea,ion via Arrhenius of ionic resistance/time constant; require consistency with low-T EA persistence (Step 3.3).
5.3 ToF-SIMS after standardized stress:
- Protocol: fixed light intensity, fixed bias (e.g., ±0.8 V), fixed time (e.g., 2 h) in dry N2 vs dry O2.
- Quantify halide/A-site redistribution depth profiles; define a “redistribution index” (profile broadening/shift) to compare caps.

Step 6 — ORR quantification with an explicitly defined, perovskite-compatible electrochemical platform
6.1 Electrochemical architecture (thin-film ORR cell):
- Working electrode: perovskite film (with/without cap) on inert, compact electron-collecting substrate (FTO/SnO2 or Au with ALD-grown blocking layer) to minimize dissolution pathways.
- Solid electrolyte: an anhydrous, oxygen-permeable polymer electrolyte with defined stability window (e.g., PEG-based gel with non-nucleophilic salt) separated from perovskite by an ultrathin inert ion-blocking but electron-transparent interlayer (e.g., ALD Al2O3 ≤2 nm) if needed to prevent direct chemical attack; the interlayer is kept constant across all samples.
- Reference/counter: micro-reference (Ag/Ag+) embedded in the gel; Pt mesh counter.
- Potential window pre-defined from control scans on blank substrates; operate within a window verified not to trigger perovskite dissolution (validated by post-mortem XRD/XPS and ion chromatography of the electrolyte).
6.2 Measurement modes:
- Dark and illuminated linear sweep voltammetry (LSV) to determine relative ORR onset shift.
- Chronoamperometry at fixed potentials under chopped light to separate photocurrent from faradaic ORR current.
- Oxygen dependence: repeat under N2 vs O2 to confirm oxygen-specific currents.
6.3 Post-test diagnostics (mandatory to prove ORR vs decomposition):
- XRD (phase integrity), XPS (I/Pb oxidation state changes), ToF-SIMS (halide loss), and electrolyte analysis for dissolved I−/Pb2+.
- Data acceptance rule: ORR kinetic comparisons are only accepted if decomposition markers remain below a pre-set threshold (e.g., <5% change in integrated perovskite XRD peak area; electrolyte I− below detection limit or below defined ppb threshold).

Step 7 — Direct superoxide detection and surface chemistry under illumination
7.1 EPR spin trapping:
- Standardized illumination and oxygen partial pressure; compare d(adduct)/dt across caps at matched photocarrier density.
7.2 NAP-XPS/in-situ XPS under controlled O2 and illumination:
- Track O-related species and shifts in Pb/I core levels consistent with superoxide/oxidation; compare capped vs control caps that match O2 uptake.

Step 8 — Device validation (linking to conductivity, hysteresis, and PCE)
8.1 Build both p–i–n and n–i–p PSCs where only the cap is varied; maintain identical transport layers and encapsulation.
8.2 Measure:
- Stabilized MPP PCE and T80 under dry O2, dry N2, and air.
- Hysteresis index from forward/reverse scans with defined scan rate and pre-bias.
- Conductivity: contactless THz conductivity (fast electronic), plus four-point probe (quasi-steady) before/after O2/light stress.
8.3 Causality analysis:
- Multivariate regression/partial-correlation controlling for O2 uptake and packing density to isolate the contribution of (i) Stark amplitude reduction, (ii) ionic Ea increase, and (iii) electron-transfer barrier changes to ORR and device decay.

Step 9 — DFT/ab initio with explicit comparability to operando observables
9.1 Structural ensemble strategy:
- Model multiple surface terminations (PbI2-terminated, A-I terminated) and include representative defects (iodide vacancy near surface) to reflect experimental dispersion.
- For each spacer: sample multiple dipole orientations and coverages; compute an ensemble-averaged dipole-induced vacuum-level shift to compare directly with UPS/Kelvin probe.
9.2 Computed observables mapped to measurements:
